3. **Map rights and controls:** encumbrances, planning, heritage, notices, environmental entries, community-title obligations and any use restriction.
4. **Compare documents with the visible property:** extensions, decks, pools, sheds, retaining walls, access, services and signs of recent work or repair.
5. **Write a gap list:** structure, pests, moisture, flood, approval history, services, boundaries, common-property condition and anything concealed or inaccessible.
6. **Assign each gap to the right evidence source:** conveyancer/solicitor, council, surveyor, building inspector, engineer, pest inspector, body corporate, insurer or another specialist.
7. **Resolve mismatches before commitment where possible:** especially before an auction, an unconditional contract or expiry of a contractual due-diligence right.
8. **Keep the evidence together:** the value is not in any single document but in the reconciled picture they create of the property.

## Frequently asked questions
### When did Queensland seller disclosure start?
The mandatory scheme applies to relevant contracts entered into from 1 August 2025 under the Property Law Act 2023.

### Must the Form 2 be given before the buyer signs?
For an ordinary covered private sale, the seller must give the completed disclosure statement and applicable prescribed certificates before the buyer signs. Auctions have separate rules requiring the material to be given or made available before the fall of the hammer.

### What prescribed certificates can be included?
Depending on the property, the prescribed material can include the title search and registered survey plan plus applicable notices or certificates. Queensland Government guidance identifies items such as pool-safety material and community-title documents where relevant.

### Does the Form 2 prove the house is structurally sound?
No. Queensland Government guidance specifically identifies structural soundness as information that is not generally required in the disclosure statement. Physical condition needs separate investigation.

### Does the Form 2 disclose flood history?
Flooding history is specifically identified by Queensland Government guidance as outside the general disclosure requirements. Use property-specific flood and hazard information and ask the insurer about the address.

### Does Form 2 show whether renovations were approved?
Previous building or development approvals are specifically identified as outside the general disclosure requirements. Where visible work raises a question, obtain the approval history and compare the records with what exists.

### Is a body-corporate certificate enough for a unit?
No. Treat it as a starting point. Read it with the community management statement, minutes, budgets and funds, insurance, maintenance records, defect information, disputes, planned works and proposed levies.

### What should I do if the plan or disclosure does not match the property?
Do not assume the reason. Record the mismatch and obtain the evidence capable of resolving it, which may include legal advice, council records, approved plans, a survey or a building inspection.

### Can a buyer terminate for a wrong Form 2?
A statutory right may arise in specified circumstances before settlement. The legal test and interaction with other legislation are fact-specific, so obtain immediate advice from a Queensland solicitor before acting.

### How does the over-$10-million exception work?
Queensland Government guidance describes an exception for a sale price over $10 million where the buyer waives disclosure. Have the waiver and the transaction-specific requirements checked by the acting solicitor.

## Method
Built from the Queensland Government’s own scheme guide and its current cooling-off guidance, written while the scheme is still new enough to surprise people.

## Limitations
This is Queensland legal orientation. Whether a defective Form 2 lets you out depends on the Act, the defect and your circumstances, which is exactly the question for your solicitor.

sections.heading: Opening
sections.markdown:
### Give yourself time to understand the building
- **Scope:** What was assessed and what remains inaccessible
- **Reliance:** The purpose, client and terms governing use of the report
- **Follow-up:** Resolve material questions with the appropriate professional before commitment

_Understand the report before it shapes your bid._

sections.heading: Why auctions change the maths
sections.markdown: At auction, the contract on display is generally the contract you accept by bidding, and cooling-off is usually unavailable. The seller may agree to documented changes before bidding. Complete the physical investigation while there is still time to act on it.

sections.heading: The value case
sections.markdown:
An inspection records accessible conditions, access gaps and issues needing specialist diagnosis. Use those findings to set the bid, discuss the contract or leave the auction.

**How findings should change the next step**

| Finding or limitation | Proportionate next step |
| --- | --- |
| Evidence of active timber pests or damage | Pest scope, extent assessment and repair advice before bidding |
| [Movement with associated distortion](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/cracks-structural-or-cosmetic) | Structural engineer for cause and significance |
| Roof or subfloor inaccessible | Clarify the significance, seek suitable access and further assessment, or reconsider bidding if the uncertainty cannot be carried |
| [Moisture evidence without a clear source](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/damp-and-moisture-in-your-home) | Targeted leak, drainage or moisture investigation |
| Old or suspect electrical installation | Licensed electrician for electrical condition and any quotation required |

Put a number on repairs once the cause and scope are understood. A guessed allowance is how budgets go quietly wrong. See [what drives inspection cost](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/building-and-pest-inspection-cost).

sections.heading: Scope and blind spots
sections.markdown:
### Visual and non-invasive

A standard building inspection is a **visual, non-invasive** assessment to the agreed scope and Australian Standard. It covers accessible areas and leaves walls, fixed floor coverings and heavy stored goods in place.

### What can get missed

Concealed defects and inaccessible areas can escape a visual inspection. The report should record every access limitation. Movement, moisture or a suspected structural issue may justify targeted specialist work.

### Read findings and limitations together

Read the *significant items* and the *limitations* together. The report should show what was seen and identify inaccessible or excluded areas. Both belong in the bidding limit.

### What a standard inspection typically leaves out

**Common exclusions and how to cover them before auction**

| Usually excluded | Who can answer it | Related guide |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Concealed framing, footings below ground and wall cavities | A structural engineer or invasive inspection, if the evidence justifies it | [Cracks](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/cracks-structural-or-cosmetic) |
| Testing of electrical, plumbing and gas services | A licensed electrician, plumber or gasfitter | [Wiring](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/switchboards-wiring-and-safety-switches) and [plumbing](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/plumbing-hot-water-and-leaks) |
| Adequacy of roof drainage and concealed roof areas | A roof plumber, or a roof-space inspection if access allows | [Roofs](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/roofs-tiles-metal-and-leaks) |
| Retaining walls, decks and outbuildings away from the house | A builder or engineer, depending on what they support | [Retaining walls](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/retaining-walls) and [decks](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/decks-balconies-and-balustrades) |
| Permits, approvals and compliance | Council, a building surveyor and your conveyancer | [Section 32](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/reading-a-section-32) |
| Asbestos and lead identification | A licensed asbestos assessor or hygienist, by sampling | [Asbestos](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/asbestos-in-the-home) |
| Shared building elements in strata | Owners corporation records and inspection reports | [Owners corporation records](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/reading-your-owners-corporation-report) |

sections.heading: Timing: book it early enough to act on it
sections.markdown: Arrange access as soon as the property becomes serious. Leave time for clarification, a return visit or specialist advice. Obtain the contract and disclosure material at the same time, using the jurisdiction and contract to set the actual deadline.

sections.heading: How to assess a vendor-supplied report
sections.markdown: Check a seller-commissioned report for its date, property, scope, access restrictions, significant items, timber-pest scope, inspector, professional indemnity insurance and commissioning party. Ask whether the inspector offers assignment or purchaser reliance. Commission your own work where the report is stale, key access was blocked or reliance terms leave you exposed.

sections.heading: How to focus your inspection spend
sections.markdown: An inspection can inform a decision not to buy as well as a successful purchase. Focus spending by checking whether the property, proposed use and likely price are plausible before commissioning detailed work. A [desktop review](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/desktop-vs-physical-report) may help organise the shortlist where the available evidence warrants it; it is an optional service, not a prerequisite or a substitute for necessary investigation.

sections.heading: Work backwards from the decision, not the report delivery
sections.markdown:
The useful deadline is when you must decide whether to commit, not the time a PDF reaches your inbox. Between those events you may need to [read the report](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/how-to-read-a-building-and-pest-report), speak with the inspector, obtain access, arrange a specialist and discuss the result with your legal adviser. A promised report on Friday evening does not leave a usable investigation window for every Saturday auction.

**Build the inspection programme backwards**

| Before the decision | What needs to be ready | What can hold it up |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Assess whether to bid | Findings, unresolved exposure and actual contract position understood | A material question has no answer or agreed way to manage it |
| Interpret follow-up | Specialist findings and any defined repair scope | Access, testing, consultant availability or further opening |
| Clarify the first report | What was found, excluded and recommended | An unavailable inspector or ambiguous recommendation |
| Complete the visit | Agreed inspection and timber-pest work | Locked hatches, unsafe access, stored goods or permission |
| [Book the right service](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/how-to-choose-a-building-and-pest-inspector) | Scope, dates, access arrangements and responsible people | A booking for building-only work when pest work was assumed |

Ask providers for actual availability rather than imposing a standard number of days on every property. If the timeline cannot accommodate a material follow-up, tell your adviser and reconsider the decision path. A rushed inspection is not made more complete by the auction being close. The separate [auction-day guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/auction-day-due-diligence) connects the resulting evidence with contract, finance and bidding decisions.

sections.heading: Clear access with the person who can actually provide it
sections.markdown:
The seller or occupier may need to make a hatch reachable, provide keys or give permission for entry. Ask the inspector what conditions they need, then confirm arrangements through the agent. Do this before the visit. An assurance that 'the house is open' may mean the front door, not the roof space, rear shed or subfloor entrance.

No agreement should require unsafe entry, moving heavy goods without authority or damage to finishes. If the area cannot be assessed, identify exactly what remains unknown and why it matters. Ask whether a return visit, different access or a separately agreed method could answer the question. Photographs supplied later should be assessed for their location and coverage; they do not automatically replace the missing inspection.

sections.heading: Use follow-up to narrow a question
sections.markdown:
Send a specialist the original finding and ask what they can establish within the available access and time. A useful brief might ask whether observed distortion requires further structural investigation, or whether a moisture symptom can be traced to a specific entry path. A generic instruction to 'check everything' can produce another broad report while the decisive uncertainty remains.

Separate identifying the problem from quoting the remedy. A pest-treatment price does not establish timber damage extent. A roof quotation may address the visible junction but exclude concealed support repairs. A moisture reading may justify investigation without proving a membrane failure. Ask the original inspector whether the proposed follow-up addresses the recommendation, then read its assumptions before converting it into a bid allowance.

sections.heading: A supplied report can save duplication when the match is real
sections.markdown:
Assess the supplied report on the work actually done and the terms under which you can use it. Check whether it concerns the whole property you intend to buy, whether important access changed and whether the author will answer your questions. A seller's report is not automatically worthless, and an independently purchased copy is not automatically complete.

[NSW's guidance on pre-purchase report records](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/property-professionals/working-as-an-agent/pre-purchase-inspection-reports) describes information agents must keep about certain reports. Knowing a report exists is a route to finding evidence; it does not itself establish the contents, adequacy or your reliance rights. Obtain those details from the actual report and engagement terms.

For an apartment, check what common-property areas the engagement includes and connect it with [the scheme records](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/reading-your-owners-corporation-report). A clear lot interior and an unresolved building-wide balcony programme can both be true. The common-property investigation may need different access and scope from the unit inspection.

sections.heading: Worked example: Thursday access, Saturday auction
sections.markdown:
**Illustrative reasoning example, not an inspected property.** A Thursday inspection of an older house records uneven flooring and an inaccessible subfloor because the hatch is blocked. The agent offers to have the hatch cleared on Friday. The buyer treats that promise as resolution of the report's limitation.

Clearing access is only the first step. Confirm whether the inspector can return safely, what they can inspect and when their findings can be discussed. If the return visit establishes a specific local issue, the buyer can seek appropriate advice on its scope. If it reveals broader concerns or still cannot reach the area, further investigation may be needed.

There is no requirement for the evidence to become conclusive by Saturday simply because bidding starts then. Ask whether the remaining uncertainty changes the decision and whether any agreed contractual route exists, with legal advice. The useful result is an honest account of readiness, not a green tick for a hatch that someone promised to open.

An inspection has done useful work when it makes a material uncertainty explicit. The next task is deciding whether that uncertainty can be resolved, carried or should stop the purchase.

> Note: Keep the report with later repairs, monitoring and photographs. That record helps the next property decision start from current evidence.

> Important: Complete the full auction plan: contract review, agreed changes, property-specific finance, deposit arrangements and a hard limit. Use [auction-day due diligence](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/auction-day-due-diligence) as the checklist.

faqs.question: What does a pre-purchase building inspection not cover?
faqs.answer: Typically concealed areas such as wall cavities and footings below ground, testing of electrical, plumbing and gas services, the adequacy of roof drainage, permits and compliance, and identification of asbestos or lead. Each needs its own specialist if it matters to your decision.

faqs.question: Is a building inspection worth it before auction?
faqs.answer: Usually, yes, if the condition of the building could change your bid. The report gives you findings to act on, shows which areas could not be reached and leaves time for specialist advice before the contract becomes binding.

faqs.question: Can I get out of an auction purchase if the building has problems?
faqs.answer: Auction sales are generally unconditional and cooling-off is usually unavailable. Complete inspection and contract checks before bidding.

faqs.question: What does a building and pest inspection cover?
faqs.answer: It is a visual, non-invasive assessment of the agreed accessible areas and timber-pest scope. The report should record concealed and inaccessible areas as limitations.

faqs.question: When should I book the inspection before an auction?
faqs.answer: As soon as the property becomes serious, leaving time to read the report, clarify limitations and obtain specialist follow-up before bidding.

faqs.question: Should I trust the building report the agent gives me?
faqs.answer: Check date, scope, access, qualifications, insurance and your contractual right to rely on it. Commission more work where those answers leave material gaps.

faqs.question: How do I reduce inspection spend on properties I may not win?
faqs.answer: Check the property, likely price, intended use and existing evidence before commissioning further work. A desktop review may help organise a shortlist, but it is optional. An inspection that supports a decision not to buy still has value.

faqs.question: Is a report delivered the night before auction early enough?
faqs.answer: Only if you have enough time to understand it and address material findings. Delivery time alone does not allow for clarification, reinspection or specialist work.

faqs.question: Does clearing a blocked hatch resolve an inspection limitation?
faqs.answer: No. It may enable a further inspection, subject to safe access and availability. The condition behind it remains unassessed until appropriate evidence is obtained.

faqs.question: Will a repair quotation answer the inspector’s recommendation?
faqs.answer: Check the question and the quoted scope. A treatment or local repair price may not establish the cause, extent or associated damage that prompted the recommendation.

A useful brief might ask whether observed distortion requires further structural investigation, or whether a moisture symptom can be traced to a specific entry path. A generic instruction to 'check everything' can produce another broad report while the decisive uncertainty remains.

Separate identifying the problem from quoting the remedy. A pest-treatment price does not establish timber damage extent. A roof quotation may address the visible junction but exclude concealed support repairs. A moisture reading may justify investigation without proving a membrane failure. Ask the original inspector whether the proposed follow-up addresses the recommendation, then read its assumptions before converting it into a bid allowance.

## A supplied report can save duplication when the match is real
Assess the supplied report on the work actually done and the terms under which you can use it. Check whether it concerns the whole property you intend to buy, whether important access changed and whether the author will answer your questions. A seller's report is not automatically worthless, and an independently purchased copy is not automatically complete.

[NSW's guidance on pre-purchase report records](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/property-professionals/working-as-an-agent/pre-purchase-inspection-reports) describes information agents must keep about certain reports. Knowing a report exists is a route to finding evidence; it does not itself establish the contents, adequacy or your reliance rights. Obtain those details from the actual report and engagement terms.

For an apartment, check what common-property areas the engagement includes and connect it with [the scheme records](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/reading-your-owners-corporation-report). A clear lot interior and an unresolved building-wide balcony programme can both be true. The common-property investigation may need different access and scope from the unit inspection.

## Worked example: Thursday access, Saturday auction
**Illustrative reasoning example, not an inspected property.** A Thursday inspection of an older house records uneven flooring and an inaccessible subfloor because the hatch is blocked. The agent offers to have the hatch cleared on Friday. The buyer treats that promise as resolution of the report's limitation.

Clearing access is only the first step. Confirm whether the inspector can return safely, what they can inspect and when their findings can be discussed. If the return visit establishes a specific local issue, the buyer can seek appropriate advice on its scope. If it reveals broader concerns or still cannot reach the area, further investigation may be needed.

There is no requirement for the evidence to become conclusive by Saturday simply because bidding starts then. Ask whether the remaining uncertainty changes the decision and whether any agreed contractual route exists, with legal advice. The useful result is an honest account of readiness, not a green tick for a hatch that someone promised to open.

An inspection has done useful work when it makes a material uncertainty explicit. The next task is deciding whether that uncertainty can be resolved, carried or should stop the purchase.

> Note: Keep the report with later repairs, monitoring and photographs. That record helps the next property decision start from current evidence.

> Important: Complete the full auction plan: contract review, agreed changes, property-specific finance, deposit arrangements and a hard limit. Use [auction-day due diligence](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/auction-day-due-diligence) as the checklist.

## Frequently asked questions
### What does a pre-purchase building inspection not cover?
Typically concealed areas such as wall cavities and footings below ground, testing of electrical, plumbing and gas services, the adequacy of roof drainage, permits and compliance, and identification of asbestos or lead. Each needs its own specialist if it matters to your decision.

### Is a building inspection worth it before auction?
Usually, yes, if the condition of the building could change your bid. The report gives you findings to act on, shows which areas could not be reached and leaves time for specialist advice before the contract becomes binding.

### Can I get out of an auction purchase if the building has problems?
Auction sales are generally unconditional and cooling-off is usually unavailable. Complete inspection and contract checks before bidding.

### What does a building and pest inspection cover?
It is a visual, non-invasive assessment of the agreed accessible areas and timber-pest scope. The report should record concealed and inaccessible areas as limitations.

### When should I book the inspection before an auction?
As soon as the property becomes serious, leaving time to read the report, clarify limitations and obtain specialist follow-up before bidding.

### Should I trust the building report the agent gives me?
Check date, scope, access, qualifications, insurance and your contractual right to rely on it. Commission more work where those answers leave material gaps.

### How do I reduce inspection spend on properties I may not win?
Check the property, likely price, intended use and existing evidence before commissioning further work. A desktop review may help organise a shortlist, but it is optional. An inspection that supports a decision not to buy still has value.

### Is a report delivered the night before auction early enough?
Only if you have enough time to understand it and address material findings. Delivery time alone does not allow for clarification, reinspection or specialist work.

### Does clearing a blocked hatch resolve an inspection limitation?
No. It may enable a further inspection, subject to safe access and availability. The condition behind it remains unassessed until appropriate evidence is obtained.

### Will a repair quotation answer the inspector’s recommendation?
Check the question and the quoted scope. A treatment or local repair price may not establish the cause, extent or associated damage that prompted the recommendation.

## Method
An investigation-planning guide worked backwards from the binding decision. Access, specialist follow-up and report reliance are connected to explicit unresolved questions, rather than a universal booking timetable.

## Limitations
General Australian guidance only. Contracts, statutes, policies, site conditions and professional scopes vary; obtain advice for the property and decision in front of you.

sections.heading: What moves the quote
sections.markdown:
- **Property form and size:** apartment lot, freestanding house, multi-level home, acreage, ancillary structures.
- **Access and safety:** low subfloor, roof pitch, locked or stored areas, height, confined spaces and weather.
- **Construction complexity:** mixed eras, additions, retaining structures, balconies, unusual materials or multiple roof voids.
- **Scope:** building only, timber pests, pool, invasive testing, specialist diagnostics or strata records are separate questions.
- **Timing and travel:** urgent auction turnaround, remote call-out, return visit and report deadline.

The quote should reflect the actual accessible scope. For apartments, combine the lot inspection with a [strata or owners-corporation records inspection](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/reading-your-owners-corporation-report).

sections.heading: Understand the inspection limits
sections.markdown:
A conventional pre-purchase inspection is generally visual and non-invasive within the agreed scope and safe access. sections.heading: Vendor reports: test the rights as well as the content

Commission your own inspection or specialist advice when reliance is absent, key areas were inaccessible or your concern sits outside scope.

sections.heading: Allow for specialist follow-up
sections.markdown: A good inspector states the limits of their scope clearly. [Structural movement](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/cracks-structural-or-cosmetic) goes to an engineer, wiring to a licensed electrician, drainage to a plumber, suspect materials to a competent assessor, and air-quality questions to a defined indoor-environment scope (see [building biologist cost](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/building-biologist-cost)). sections.heading: Choose the inspector you can rely on
sections.markdown: A clear scope, good access and a useful conversation after the report can be worth far more than a small saving on the fee. Write down any blind spots before you commit. For an auction, use the [five-gate due-diligence plan](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/auction-day-due-diligence); for early triage, read about [desktop review vs physical inspection](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/desktop-vs-physical-report).

sections.heading: Put every quote on the same payment basis
sections.markdown:
Compare the total payable for the same service before comparing the headline fee. Keep GST treatment, travel, additional structures, urgency and report delivery explicit. A residential-house price may not cover a detached studio, a separate garage or all the roof voids created by additions. Ask whether each item is included, excluded or priced only after the property is reviewed.

A 'from' price is an entry point, not a ceiling. A fixed quote still needs a defined scope and an explanation of what happens if the inspection cannot proceed as planned. Record who can authorise an extra visit or specialist service and the charge, estimate or approval process that applies. Silence about an item should remain a question rather than becoming an assumed inclusion.

**Three different parts of the inspection budget**

| Budget item | What to obtain | What it does not establish |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Agreed base service | Address-specific scope, total payable and delivery arrangements | That every inaccessible or specialist question can be answered |
| Possible additional work | Trigger, rate or quote process, and your authority before commitment | That the extra service will necessarily be required |
| Work to the building | A separate, defined repair scope and appropriate quotation | That the inspection fee includes treatment or repair |

sections.heading: Budget for the unanswered question, not every possible test
sections.markdown:
An inspection can correctly identify a material issue without resolving its cause or repair extent. Reserve room in the programme for relevant follow-up, but do not order every available add-on simply because it appears on a price list. Ask what decision the additional service will change and whether suitable access exists. A drain camera, structural opinion and timber-pest assessment answer different questions.

Likewise, a lower-cost copy of an existing report may be useful where its date, coverage and reliance terms match your need. It may leave the same inaccessible area unexamined. Compare the remaining evidence gap and cost of closing it, not just the cost of obtaining a PDF. [The condition-report guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/what-is-a-property-condition-report) separates report purpose and reliance from appearance and length.

sections.heading: One provider per city is not a city average
sections.markdown:
These observations show prices offered by named providers for specified services. They do not establish the typical fee in each city, relative quality or a reliable national range. Some providers may share pricing structures or related businesses, so matching figures should not be treated as independent market confirmation. Do not infer that Sydney is more expensive than Melbourne from this sample alone.

For an apartment, the lot inspection and the investigation of shared-building issues are different scopes. Scheme records, access to common property and specialist work may involve separate costs. For a large or altered house, multiple construction systems can matter more than bedroom count. Explain the property to each provider using the same brief, then use [the inspector-selection guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/how-to-choose-a-building-and-pest-inspector) to assess competence and the quality of the proposed service.

sections.heading: Worked example: the lower headline fee costs more to finish
sections.markdown:
**Illustrative reasoning example, not an inspected property.** Two fictional quotes cover the same initial building-and-pest visit. Quote A is $500 plus GST, with a $100 plus GST return visit if stored goods block the subfloor. Quote B is $650 including GST and includes one agreed return visit. All other inclusions are assumed equal for this illustration.

The initial totals are $550 and $650. If the stated return visit is needed, A becomes $660 and B remains $650. If access is available at the first visit, A remains cheaper. Confirm the access arrangements and exact return-visit terms rather than assuming either scenario.

Price still does not settle the choice. Verify who attends, what can safely be assessed and when the result will arrive. Neither quote promises a conclusive inspection behind every fixed finish. This comparison identifies a cost dependency; it does not rank the fictional providers' competence.

A useful inspection budget records what you are buying now, what might be commissioned later and the unresolved condition that could change the next decision.

> Important: Licensing and registration differ by state. Confirm qualifications, insurance, engagement terms, access, standard, pest scope and delivery before booking.

faqs.question: How much does a building and pest inspection cost?
faqs.answer: Provider prices checked on 7 September 2026 were $499 plus GST in Perth, $500 plus GST in Melbourne and Brisbane, and $655 including GST in Sydney. These are individual service examples, not city averages. The earlier Adelaide example was not reconfirmed. Obtain an address-specific total and check access, timber-pest scope, written reporting and follow-up.

faqs.question: Why do inspection prices vary?
faqs.answer: Property size, storeys, age, safe roof and subfloor access, outbuildings, timber-pest scope, travel, urgency, report depth and follow-up all affect the fee.

faqs.question: Is the cheapest inspection a bad one?
faqs.answer: A low fee can still buy a useful inspection. Trace the price back to the scope: what was accessed, whether pests are included, what the written report covers, the inspector’s qualifications and insurance, and whether they will take your call afterwards.

faqs.question: Does a building inspection include termites?
faqs.answer: Timber-pest assessment needs an explicit scope. Ask how its findings and limitations will be reported.

faqs.question: Is a vendor-supplied report useful?
faqs.answer: Check date, scope, access, inspector, insurance and your purchaser-reliance or assignment rights. Commission more work where those terms leave material gaps.

faqs.question: Does an apartment inspection cover the whole building?
faqs.answer: A typical inspection focuses on the lot and accessible areas. Use the registered plan and scheme records for common-property condition, funding, insurance, defects and works.

faqs.question: What extra inspections might be needed?
faqs.answer: Only those prompted by material evidence or the property: for example structural engineering, electrical, plumbing/drainage, hazardous material, pool or indoor-environment work.

faqs.question: Are the city examples average market prices?
faqs.answer: No. They are dated observations from named providers with different scopes. They should not be used to rank cities or providers or to infer a national average.

faqs.question: Should I compare prices including GST?
faqs.answer: Compare the total payable on the same basis and ask the provider to confirm any unclear tax treatment. Keep travel, extra structures and follow-up charges visible.

faqs.question: Does the inspection fee include repairing defects or termite treatment?
faqs.answer: Only if expressly included in a separate agreed scope. Inspection, further diagnosis, treatment and building repairs are different services.

Some providers may share pricing structures or related businesses, so matching figures should not be treated as independent market confirmation. Do not infer that Sydney is more expensive than Melbourne from this sample alone.

For an apartment, the lot inspection and the investigation of shared-building issues are different scopes. Scheme records, access to common property and specialist work may involve separate costs. For a large or altered house, multiple construction systems can matter more than bedroom count. Explain the property to each provider using the same brief, then use [the inspector-selection guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/how-to-choose-a-building-and-pest-inspector) to assess competence and the quality of the proposed service.

## Worked example: the lower headline fee costs more to finish
**Illustrative reasoning example, not an inspected property.** Two fictional quotes cover the same initial building-and-pest visit. Quote A is $500 plus GST, with a $100 plus GST return visit if stored goods block the subfloor. Quote B is $650 including GST and includes one agreed return visit. All other inclusions are assumed equal for this illustration.

The initial totals are $550 and $650. If the stated return visit is needed, A becomes $660 and B remains $650. If access is available at the first visit, A remains cheaper. Confirm the access arrangements and exact return-visit terms rather than assuming either scenario.

Price still does not settle the choice. Verify who attends, what can safely be assessed and when the result will arrive. Neither quote promises a conclusive inspection behind every fixed finish. This comparison identifies a cost dependency; it does not rank the fictional providers' competence.

A useful inspection budget records what you are buying now, what might be commissioned later and the unresolved condition that could change the next decision.

> Important: Licensing and registration differ by state. Confirm qualifications, insurance, engagement terms, access, standard, pest scope and delivery before booking.

## Frequently asked questions
### How much does a building and pest inspection cost?
Provider prices checked on 7 September 2026 were $499 plus GST in Perth, $500 plus GST in Melbourne and Brisbane, and $655 including GST in Sydney. These are individual service examples, not city averages. The earlier Adelaide example was not reconfirmed. Obtain an address-specific total and check access, timber-pest scope, written reporting and follow-up.

### Why do inspection prices vary?
Property size, storeys, age, safe roof and subfloor access, outbuildings, timber-pest scope, travel, urgency, report depth and follow-up all affect the fee.

### Is the cheapest inspection a bad one?
A low fee can still buy a useful inspection. Trace the price back to the scope: what was accessed, whether pests are included, what the written report covers, the inspector’s qualifications and insurance, and whether they will take your call afterwards.

### Does a building inspection include termites?
Timber-pest assessment needs an explicit scope. Ask how its findings and limitations will be reported.

### Is a vendor-supplied report useful?
Check date, scope, access, inspector, insurance and your purchaser-reliance or assignment rights. Commission more work where those terms leave material gaps.

### Does an apartment inspection cover the whole building?
A typical inspection focuses on the lot and accessible areas. Use the registered plan and scheme records for common-property condition, funding, insurance, defects and works.

### What extra inspections might be needed?
Only those prompted by material evidence or the property: for example structural engineering, electrical, plumbing/drainage, hazardous material, pool or indoor-environment work.

### Are the city examples average market prices?
No. They are dated observations from named providers with different scopes. They should not be used to rank cities or providers or to infer a national average.

### Should I compare prices including GST?
Compare the total payable on the same basis and ask the provider to confirm any unclear tax treatment. Keep travel, extra structures and follow-up charges visible.

### Does the inspection fee include repairing defects or termite treatment?
Only if expressly included in a separate agreed scope. Inspection, further diagnosis, treatment and building repairs are different services.

## Method
A dated provider-price sample and scope comparison, not a national average or provider endorsement. The guide distinguishes confirmed prices, historic observations, taxes, inclusions and contingent follow-up.

## Limitations
Every quote reflects a particular property, access and scope. Use the examples as bearings, then get the current inclusions, insurance and timing in writing.

cluster.label: How to buy
cluster.blurb: Sequence the checks, understand their limits and be ready before your offer becomes binding.

sections.heading: Opening
sections.markdown:
### Choose the person and the scope together
- **Person:** Relevant experience, standing and independence
- **Scope:** Structures, pests, access, exclusions and standard
- **Report:** Clear findings, visible limits and human follow-up

_The written agreement should match the home and the decision._

sections.heading: Start with the home in front of you
sections.markdown:
Tell each inspector the address, property type, approximate age, storeys, construction, outbuildings, auction or contract deadline and any known access issue. Mention the specific concern that brought you to them, such as cracking, a low subfloor, a flat roof, a balcony leak or termite history.

The aim is a comparable written scope. A person who is excellent with new detached homes may have a different body of experience from someone who regularly reads period houses, apartments, retaining structures or complex additions.

sections.heading: Qualifications and licensing vary by state
sections.markdown:
Ask what qualification and experience support this particular inspection. The [NSW Government recommends a suitably qualified person](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/buying-and-selling-property/buying-property-nsw/inspecting-a-property/inspection-reports), giving a licensed builder, surveyor or architect as examples, and advises checking professional indemnity insurance.

Queensland has a specific [QBCC completed residential building inspection licence class](https://www.qbcc.qld.gov.au/licences/apply-licence/available-licence/inspectors-certifiers/completed-residential-building). Requirements elsewhere differ, so check the relevant state regulator and confirm that the person attending, as well as the contracting business, has the standing needed for the agreed work.

Building and timber-pest work can involve different competencies and authorisations. Ask who performs each part, what licence or qualification applies and whether the findings will appear in one report or separate reports.

**Credentials worth checking before you book**

| Check | What to look for | Why it matters |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Licence or registration | In Queensland, a QBCC completed residential building inspection licence; elsewhere, registration as a builder, building surveyor or architect, checked on the state register | Confirms a regulated professional standing for building work |
| Timber pest authorisation | A current pest management licence for the person doing the timber pest inspection | Timber pest inspection is a separate competency from building inspection |
| Professional indemnity insurance | Current cover, and whether it applies to this inspection type | Gives the report recourse if something material was missed |
| The standards used | Reports to AS 4349.1 for building and AS 4349.3 for timber pests | Sets out a minimum scope and a consistent report structure |
| A sample report | Photographs, clear locations, defined categories and a stated limitations section | Shows how they will communicate a difficult finding |
| Who attends | The name and qualifications of the person on site, not just the business | The person attending determines what is seen |

sections.heading: Ask for the engagement agreement before booking
sections.markdown:
The agreement should identify the client, property, inspection type, included structures, access basis, exclusions, fee, timing, report format and the terms governing reliance. The [AS 4349.1-2007 pre-purchase inspection standard](https://store.standards.org.au/product/as-4349-1-2007) provides a national framework for residential building inspections. Ask which standard and edition the service uses and how the agreed scope relates to it.

**Use the same questions for every quote**

| Question | A useful answer should identify |
| --- | --- |
| Who will attend? | The individual inspector, relevant experience and the business responsible for the report |
| What is included? | Dwelling, site, garage, outbuildings, retaining walls, balconies and agreed timber-pest scope |
| What access is attempted? | Roof exterior, roof space, subfloor, internal rooms and conditions that may prevent safe access |
| What is excluded? | Services, concealed areas, compliance, estimates and specialist matters outside scope |
| What will I receive? | Written report, photographs, significant findings, limitations, recommendations and delivery time |
| Can I ask questions? | A direct conversation with the inspector and a process for written clarification or reinspection |
| What protects the engagement? | Professional indemnity insurance, complaint process and clear reliance terms |

sections.heading: Independence should be easy to explain
sections.markdown:
Ask who recommended the inspector, who pays them and whether they have a financial relationship with the agent, vendor, report marketplace, repairer or pest-treatment provider. A referral can still lead to capable work; a clear answer lets you understand the relationship.

Consumer Affairs Victoria advises buyers to use an inspection service with professional indemnity insurance and to be cautious with a report offered by the seller or agent. Read the [Victorian inspection guidance](https://www.consumer.vic.gov.au/housing/buying-and-selling-property/buying-property/inspect-properties-before-you-buy) before deciding whether a supplied report meets your needs.

sections.heading: Read a sample report
sections.markdown:
A sample reveals how the inspector thinks and communicates. Look for property-specific observations, useful photographs, precise locations, plainly stated access limits and recommendations that identify the next kind of expertise. A template can provide structure; the finished report should still feel like someone paid close attention to this home.

- **Clear significance:** the reader can tell what deserves attention first.
- **Visible limitations:** inaccessible areas are easy to find and understand.
- **Traceable photographs:** images have locations and connect to written findings.
- **Proportionate recommendations:** the next step answers a defined question.
- **Human follow-up:** the inspector is available to explain material findings.

sections.heading: Access often matters more than gadgets
sections.markdown:
Ask what safe-access conditions are needed for the roof exterior, roof space and subfloor, and who will arrange keys, hatches or permission. Tools such as moisture meters and thermal cameras can support defined observations. Their value depends on access, method, conditions and interpretation.

If a critical area is inaccessible on the day, ask about a return visit and its fee. Read the resulting limitation carefully using the [guide to building and pest reports](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/how-to-read-a-building-and-pest-report).

sections.heading: Choose the scope before comparing price
sections.markdown:
Put the quotes beside one another only after the inclusions line up. A lower price may reflect a smaller property, narrower access, building-only work, fewer structures, limited photographs or no follow-up. The [inspection-cost guide and quote decoder](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/building-and-pest-inspection-cost) provides current examples and a comparison framework.

Ask about cancellation, urgent turnaround, travel, reinspection and specialist follow-up fees. For an auction, leave enough time to read the report and act on it with the [pre-auction inspection guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/building-inspection-before-auction).

sections.heading: A short selection checklist
sections.markdown:
1. Write a short property and deadline brief.
2. Confirm the individual inspector and relevant experience.
3. Verify state licensing or registration where it applies.
4. Confirm professional indemnity insurance in writing.
5. Compare building, timber-pest, structures and access scope.
6. Read the engagement agreement and a sample report.
7. Confirm report timing, follow-up and reinspection arrangements.

sections.heading: Test the sample report with one difficult finding
sections.markdown:
Choose one item in the sample and follow it from photograph to conclusion to recommendation. Can you locate it? Does the description distinguish visible damage from its suspected cause? Does the recommendation identify the unanswered question? If the report says 'seek specialist advice', ask what sort of advice and what the reader would need to learn from it. Long reports and many photographs can still leave that chain incomplete.

Try a limitation as well. If the subfloor was inaccessible, does the report explain its significance for that property rather than burying the statement in standard text? A useful conversation is: 'What would you tell me if this happened at my house?' You are assessing how the inspector handles incomplete evidence, not asking them to diagnose a property they have not visited.

**Listen to how the provider answers**

| Question to ask | An answer worth exploring | An answer needing clarification |
| --- | --- | --- |
| What if the roof space cannot be accessed? | Explains safe-access requirements, reporting and possible follow-up | Says the equipment will find everything anyway |
| What does this moisture finding establish? | Separates observation, interpretation and further investigation | Names a hidden failure without explaining the evidence |
| Who deals with a combined building and pest finding? | Identifies responsible practitioners and how their reports connect | Cannot say who performs the pest work |
| How do I clarify a material issue before my deadline? | Identifies a person, response arrangements and limits | Promises a fast PDF without access to the author |

sections.heading: Know who takes responsibility for the work
sections.markdown:
A familiar brand may arrange a local subcontractor. That arrangement can work well, but identify the business you contract with, the person attending and the author responsible for each report. Ask how a substitution would be handled if the named inspector becomes unavailable. The experience you selected should belong to the person doing the relevant work, or be supported by a clear supervision arrangement.

Check insurance evidence against the service and contracting party. Professional indemnity and public liability address different kinds of exposure; a document headed 'insured' may not answer your question about professional advice. Ask the provider or insurer to clarify material uncertainty. Insurance is a protection to investigate, not a guarantee that every missed defect, excluded service or later loss will be covered.

sections.heading: Match the appointment to the building’s difficult parts
sections.markdown:
An older house with several additions may need careful reading of interfaces and changing construction. A relatively new apartment may raise [common-property questions](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/buying-an-apartment-strata) beyond a lot inspection. A sloping site may make retaining structures and drainage central to the brief. Ask about relevant experience and the boundaries of the service. A competent general inspector can identify a need for other expertise; they do not have to claim they can personally resolve every specialist issue.

If a particular symptom already dominates the decision, ask whether a general inspection plus targeted work is appropriate or whether the specialist should be involved first. Specify who will coordinate the findings. A combined booking is convenient only if it includes the actual services and leaves you with clear responsibility for the result.

sections.heading: Avoid turning the selection into a competition for certainty
sections.markdown:
The most reassuring sales answer may be the least useful professional answer. A promise to identify every leak or confirm all structural adequacy goes beyond what a limited visual visit can establish. Conversely, limitations do not excuse vague observations about areas that were examined. Look for precision on both sides: confidence about what was observed and candour about what was not established.

Tools should have a purpose in the agreed service. Ask which question a proposed tool helps answer, under what conditions and how the result will be interpreted. Do not buy the number of devices on the equipment list. Equally, do not demand unsafe access or unapproved opening simply to make the inspection feel thorough. The quality of the method is its fit to the question and the permission available.

sections.heading: Worked example: two quotes for a house with a low subfloor
sections.markdown:
**Illustrative reasoning example, not an inspected property.** Two providers quote for an interwar house. One highlights thermal imaging and same-day delivery. The other asks for the subfloor access dimensions, requests the previous pest report and proposes a call after inspection. Both advertise building and pest services.

The second response identifies useful questions, but does not alone establish competence or make it the automatic choice. Ask both for the attending practitioners, actual building and pest scope, insurance, access method and a sample report. Establish what each would do if the critical area remained inaccessible.

If one service expressly excludes the relevant subfloor and the other proposes an appropriate safe assessment, the quotes are for different evidence. If neither can access it, a lower price or faster turnaround will not close the gap. Choose the appointment that best addresses the property question, and plan separately for what it cannot establish.

Before confirming the booking, write back the agreed scope, access arrangements, report deadline and follow-up contact. That brief is a practical record of what you selected, not just what the advertisement appeared to promise.

> Note: The best appointment is the one that gives a careful inspector enough scope, access and time to answer the questions this particular home raises.

> Important: Verify licence and insurance details with the relevant regulator or insurer where they are material. Business names, licence classes and personnel can change.

faqs.question: What qualifications should a building inspector have?
faqs.answer: Look for qualifications and experience relevant to the property and inspection scope. Government guidance recommends a suitably qualified professional, and state licensing requirements differ. Verify the person attending, their role and their insurance.

faqs.question: Do building inspectors need a licence in Australia?
faqs.answer: Requirements vary by state and by the work performed. Queensland has a completed residential building inspection licence class. Check the regulator for the property location and the separate requirements applying to timber-pest work.

faqs.question: Should a building inspector have professional indemnity insurance?
faqs.answer: Yes. NSW and Victorian buyer guidance both recommend checking professional indemnity insurance. Ask for current evidence and confirm which person and business the policy covers.

faqs.question: Should I use the building inspector recommended by the agent?
faqs.answer: Ask about the relationship, scope, commissioning party and your reliance rights. Review the inspector on their qualifications, insurance, independence, access and report quality.

faqs.question: Does a building inspection include a pest inspection?
faqs.answer: Only when timber-pest work is expressly included. Confirm who performs it, their relevant authorisation, the standard or scope used and how the findings will be delivered.

faqs.question: Is thermal imaging essential in a building inspection?
faqs.answer: It can support a defined investigation under suitable conditions. It does not see through every surface or replace access, experience and careful interpretation.

faqs.question: How many quotes should I compare?
faqs.answer: Enough to understand the available scope and fee for the property. Use the same written questions so you can compare access, inclusions, experience, insurance, report quality and follow-up fairly.

faqs.question: Does a well-known inspection brand guarantee the person attending?
faqs.answer: Confirm the actual inspector, relevant experience, contracting business and arrangements for any substitution or subcontracting. Review the scope and responsibility in writing.

faqs.question: Is public liability insurance the same as professional indemnity?
faqs.answer: No. Ask for the insurance relevant to the inspection and professional advice, and clarify the covered person, business and service. A generic insurance statement is insufficient.

faqs.question: Should I choose the inspector who promises the most certainty?
faqs.answer: Prefer precise explanations of observations, access, scope and limits. A limited visual inspection cannot guarantee that every concealed defect or specialist issue will be found.

## Test the sample report with one difficult finding
Choose one item in the sample and follow it from photograph to conclusion to recommendation. Can you locate it? Does the description distinguish visible damage from its suspected cause? Does the recommendation identify the unanswered question? If the report says 'seek specialist advice', ask what sort of advice and what the reader would need to learn from it. Long reports and many photographs can still leave that chain incomplete.

Try a limitation as well. If the subfloor was inaccessible, does the report explain its significance for that property rather than burying the statement in standard text? A useful conversation is: 'What would you tell me if this happened at my house?' You are assessing how the inspector handles incomplete evidence, not asking them to diagnose a property they have not visited.

**Listen to how the provider answers**

| Question to ask | An answer worth exploring | An answer needing clarification |
| --- | --- | --- |
| What if the roof space cannot be accessed? | Explains safe-access requirements, reporting and possible follow-up | Says the equipment will find everything anyway |
| What does this moisture finding establish? | Separates observation, interpretation and further investigation | Names a hidden failure without explaining the evidence |
| Who deals with a combined building and pest finding? | Identifies responsible practitioners and how their reports connect | Cannot say who performs the pest work |
| How do I clarify a material issue before my deadline? | Identifies a person, response arrangements and limits | Promises a fast PDF without access to the author |

## Know who takes responsibility for the work
A familiar brand may arrange a local subcontractor. That arrangement can work well, but identify the business you contract with, the person attending and the author responsible for each report. Ask how a substitution would be handled if the named inspector becomes unavailable. The experience you selected should belong to the person doing the relevant work, or be supported by a clear supervision arrangement.

Check insurance evidence against the service and contracting party. Professional indemnity and public liability address different kinds of exposure; a document headed 'insured' may not answer your question about professional advice. Ask the provider or insurer to clarify material uncertainty. Insurance is a protection to investigate, not a guarantee that every missed defect, excluded service or later loss will be covered.

## Match the appointment to the building’s difficult parts
An older house with several additions may need careful reading of interfaces and changing construction. A relatively new apartment may raise [common-property questions](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/buying-an-apartment-strata) beyond a lot inspection. A sloping site may make retaining structures and drainage central to the brief. Ask about relevant experience and the boundaries of the service. A competent general inspector can identify a need for other expertise; they do not have to claim they can personally resolve every specialist issue.

If a particular symptom already dominates the decision, ask whether a general inspection plus targeted work is appropriate or whether the specialist should be involved first. Specify who will coordinate the findings. A combined booking is convenient only if it includes the actual services and leaves you with clear responsibility for the result.

## Avoid turning the selection into a competition for certainty
The most reassuring sales answer may be the least useful professional answer. A promise to identify every leak or confirm all structural adequacy goes beyond what a limited visual visit can establish. Conversely, limitations do not excuse vague observations about areas that were examined. Look for precision on both sides: confidence about what was observed and candour about what was not established.

Tools should have a purpose in the agreed service. Ask which question a proposed tool helps answer, under what conditions and how the result will be interpreted. Do not buy the number of devices on the equipment list. Equally, do not demand unsafe access or unapproved opening simply to make the inspection feel thorough. The quality of the method is its fit to the question and the permission available.

## Worked example: two quotes for a house with a low subfloor
**Illustrative reasoning example, not an inspected property.** Two providers quote for an interwar house. One highlights thermal imaging and same-day delivery. The other asks for the subfloor access dimensions, requests the previous pest report and proposes a call after inspection. Both advertise building and pest services.

The second response identifies useful questions, but does not alone establish competence or make it the automatic choice. Ask both for the attending practitioners, actual building and pest scope, insurance, access method and a sample report. Establish what each would do if the critical area remained inaccessible.

If one service expressly excludes the relevant subfloor and the other proposes an appropriate safe assessment, the quotes are for different evidence. If neither can access it, a lower price or faster turnaround will not close the gap. Choose the appointment that best addresses the property question, and plan separately for what it cannot establish.

Before confirming the booking, write back the agreed scope, access arrangements, report deadline and follow-up contact. That brief is a practical record of what you selected, not just what the advertisement appeared to promise.

> Note: The best appointment is the one that gives a careful inspector enough scope, access and time to answer the questions this particular home raises.

> Important: Verify licence and insurance details with the relevant regulator or insurer where they are material. Business names, licence classes and personnel can change.

## Frequently asked questions
### What qualifications should a building inspector have?
Look for qualifications and experience relevant to the property and inspection scope. Government guidance recommends a suitably qualified professional, and state licensing requirements differ. Verify the person attending, their role and their insurance.

### Do building inspectors need a licence in Australia?
Requirements vary by state and by the work performed. Queensland has a completed residential building inspection licence class. Check the regulator for the property location and the separate requirements applying to timber-pest work.

### Should a building inspector have professional indemnity insurance?
Yes. NSW and Victorian buyer guidance both recommend checking professional indemnity insurance. Ask for current evidence and confirm which person and business the policy covers.

### Should I use the building inspector recommended by the agent?
Ask about the relationship, scope, commissioning party and your reliance rights. Review the inspector on their qualifications, insurance, independence, access and report quality.

### Does a building inspection include a pest inspection?
Only when timber-pest work is expressly included. Confirm who performs it, their relevant authorisation, the standard or scope used and how the findings will be delivered.

### Is thermal imaging essential in a building inspection?
It can support a defined investigation under suitable conditions. It does not see through every surface or replace access, experience and careful interpretation.

### How many quotes should I compare?
Enough to understand the available scope and fee for the property. Use the same written questions so you can compare access, inclusions, experience, insurance, report quality and follow-up fairly.

### Does a well-known inspection brand guarantee the person attending?
Confirm the actual inspector, relevant experience, contracting business and arrangements for any substitution or subcontracting. Review the scope and responsibility in writing.

### Is public liability insurance the same as professional indemnity?
No. Ask for the insurance relevant to the inspection and professional advice, and clarify the covered person, business and service. A generic insurance statement is insufficient.

### Should I choose the inspector who promises the most certainty?
Prefer precise explanations of observations, access, scope and limits. A limited visual inspection cannot guarantee that every concealed defect or specialist issue will be found.

## Method
A service-selection guide distinguishing practitioner competence, contracting responsibility, scope, access and useful judgement. Its fictional comparison tests the quality of answers rather than ranking tools or providers.

## Limitations
Licensing, registration and timber-pest requirements vary by jurisdiction and service. Verify the individual, business, licence class and insurance for the property and work commissioned.
