The decision sheet is an original editorial framework. Contract obligations, finance conditions and the legal effect of any change require advice for the actual transaction.

cluster.label: How to buy
cluster.blurb: Sequence the checks, understand their limits and be ready before your offer becomes binding.

sections.heading: Opening
sections.markdown:
### Nothing important waits for the hammer
- **Contract:** Read properly, with any agreed changes in writing
- **Building:** The report understood, and every flag chased down
- **Money:** Finance for this property, the deposit ready, a limit you wrote down

_Bid only when every gate is green._

sections.heading: Why an auction is different
sections.markdown:
When the hammer falls, you are generally bound, and there is usually no cooling-off to save you. So the contract, the finance and the physical checks all get finished first.

In Victoria, the [official cooling-off guidance](https://www.consumer.vic.gov.au/housing/buying-and-selling-property/buying-property/buying-property-by-private-sale) excludes auction purchases and purchases within three clear business days before or after a public auction. Have your adviser confirm the timing and contract in your state. See [cooling-off periods by state](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/cooling-off-period-by-state) for orientation.

sections.heading: The checks to clear before you bid
sections.markdown:
1. **Contract and state disclosure reviewed** by your conveyancer or solicitor, including the [Section 32 vendor statement](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/reading-a-section-32) in Victoria where applicable.
2. **Building report understood**, including the important findings, blind spots and any limits on your right to rely on it.
3. **Property-specific finance readiness**, lender conditions, valuation risk, funds to complete and buffer understood.
4. **Deposit mechanics confirmed**, the amount is set by the contract, with payment timing and method checked with the agent.
5. **Your maximum price set in writing**, with a plan to stop there, whatever the room does.

### Contract and state disclosure

Have a conveyancer or solicitor review the vendor statement and contract early. Ask about title, settlement, deposit, inclusions, adjustments, default terms and special conditions. If the seller agrees to a change, have it recorded in the contract before you bid. Tell your legal adviser about any representation that affects your decision. For the document bundle, use the guide to the [NSW contract for sale](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/reading-a-contract-for-sale-nsw) or [Queensland Form 2 disclosure](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/seller-disclosure-qld) where relevant.

### Building and pest, done in advance

Understand the building before you bid. Check a vendor report's date, scope, access, inspector, insurance and buyer-reliance terms. Commission your own work if those details leave important gaps. The guide to [pre-auction building inspection](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/building-inspection-before-auction) explains timing, access and reliance on a supplied report.

### Property-specific finance readiness

A pre-approval is usually conditional on valuation, final checks and an acceptable property. Give the lender or broker the property type, address, contract and intended price range. Confirm outstanding conditions, valuation-shortfall funding and the cash needed for deposit, duty, costs and settlement. Set a conservative limit and contingency.

### Deposit and your limit

The contract sets the deposit amount and due time. Confirm the agent's payment method and daily transfer limits, then record any negotiated change before bidding. Include acquisition costs, immediate work and a finance buffer in the maximum price.

sections.heading: What happens if you win and can't settle
sections.markdown: If you win and then cannot settle, the deposit is at risk and the seller’s losses, including any shortfall on a resale, can follow you home. That is the whole reason the gates come before the bidding.

sections.heading: A completed checklist needs evidence behind each tick
sections.markdown:
'Contract checked' can mean that a document was emailed, a preliminary review was received or the final version was actually cleared for your proposed terms. These are different states. Record the version, the person who reviewed it, outstanding questions and any agreed change. Apply the same discipline to finance and condition: a booked appointment is not a completed investigation, and an unanswered email is not confirmation.

**What should sit behind the auction-day decision**

| Area | Useful confirmation | Open dependency |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Contract | Your adviser has reviewed the version and terms you would accept | A requested change remains unagreed or the version changed |
| Building | Material findings and access limits have been considered | A significant investigation is still outstanding |
| Finance | Your lender or broker has explained the property-specific position and remaining conditions | Funds depend on an untested assumption |
| Deposit | Amount, due time, method and available funds are established | A transfer limit or unavailable account prevents payment |
| Maximum bid | A written limit reflects the complete purchase and known obligations | The limit assumes a repair or approval outcome not established |

sections.heading: Some uncertainty is an allowance; some changes the decision
sections.markdown:
A quotation for a defined repair is different from an unknown structural scope. You may be able to allow for the first after checking inclusions and contingency. The second might involve a range too wide to price sensibly before bidding. A smaller bid does not make an unsafe condition, unavailable finance or an essential but unapproved alteration acceptable.

Ask whether the unresolved point could change your ability to use, insure, fund or afford the home, and what evidence would settle it. If that evidence cannot arrive before the commitment, decide whether you can knowingly accept the uncertainty or should not bid. Do not manufacture a percentage allowance merely to make the checklist look complete. Technical uncertainty and personal capacity to carry it are separate questions.

sections.heading: Reconcile the money once, without spending the same buffer twice
sections.markdown:
Use one purchase worksheet shared with your broker or lender where appropriate. Keep purchase price, acquisition expenses, deposit timing, settlement funds and post-purchase work separate. The deposit is normally part of the price rather than an additional purchase cost, but it must be available when due. Duty, legal expenses, adjustments and any other applicable costs need their own provision.

A repair reserve and a valuation-shortfall reserve may compete for the same available cash. Ask what happens if both are needed. [Moneysmart's home-buying guidance](https://moneysmart.gov.au/home-loans/buying-a-house) places borrowing and buying costs within the preparation process. Your actual lender's conditions and your funds determine readiness; a general affordability estimate cannot confirm approval for this property at a particular price.

sections.heading: Agree who can bid and what can change on the day
sections.markdown:
Where partners or another bidder are involved, agree the limit and who has authority to act before the auction. Confirm registration, identification and representation requirements with the agent and legal adviser. [NSW's auction guidance](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/buying-and-selling-property/buying-property-nsw/buying-property-at-an-auction) sets out its bidder-registration and authority requirements. Use the process in the property's state, including the arrangements for remote bidding where relevant.

Have a way to contact your adviser if the contract, inclusions, settlement date or an important representation changes. An attractive concession can still require review: extra time to settle might help one arrangement while conflicting with another. Keep any accepted variation in the operative documents. A rushed verbal explanation from someone in the crowd should not replace advice on the terms you will be bound by.

sections.heading: Passed in does not mean the investigation clock resets
sections.markdown:
A post-auction negotiation can feel like a private sale with more breathing room. Confirm the legal position before treating it that way. [Victoria's official guidance](https://www.consumer.vic.gov.au/housing/buying-and-selling-property/buying-property/buying-property-by-private-sale) describes the auction-related cooling-off exclusion, while NSW's auction guidance also addresses a same-day exchange after a property is passed in. The calendar and transaction matter; use your adviser to establish the actual rights and deadline.

A lower negotiated price changes the price. It does not automatically change a defect's cause, complete missing records or add a finance condition. Reuse the same decision sheet and record what has genuinely changed. If further investigation or a condition is needed, have your adviser seek an agreed contractual arrangement before commitment rather than assuming one will be available afterwards.

sections.heading: Worked example: the last concession is not a completed check
sections.markdown:
**Illustrative reasoning example, not an inspected property.** A property is passed in and the seller offers a lower price. The buyer has a pest report recommending further access behind a lined subfloor area. A contractor has quoted for treatment, and the buyer interprets the discount as enough to cover the issue.

The treatment quotation and potential damage extent answer different questions. The price reduction does not establish the condition of hidden timber or the repair scope. Ask whether the inspection gap could materially change the purchase budget or use of the home, and have the adviser confirm the proposed contract's position.

If suitable access and assessment can be obtained under an agreed arrangement, the new evidence can inform the decision. If not, the buyer must assess an unresolved exposure rather than call it a known treatment bill. The ability to walk away is part of preparation; previous inspection spending does not make the next commitment safer.

A useful auction-day record ends with what is ready, what is still conditional and the decision those facts support. The purpose is to keep the final bid connected to the work already done.

> Important: Keep the written limit and the finished checks in front of you on the day. Have every agreed change recorded in the contract before bidding, and tell your legal adviser about any representation you relied on.

> Note: A [desktop read](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/desktop-vs-physical-report) can triage several properties before you commission physical inspections on the strongest candidates. If you buy, keep that evidence as the starting record for ownership.

faqs.question: How recent should a building report be before an auction?
faqs.answer: As recent as practical, because a report records condition on the day of inspection. Weather, storms, new damage or repairs since then can change the picture, so a report from weeks or months earlier, or one commissioned by the seller, deserves a check of its date, scope and limitations.

faqs.question: Can I make an auction purchase subject to finance or inspection?
faqs.answer: A seller may agree to contract changes before the auction. Have each requested change negotiated and documented by the legal representatives before bidding.

faqs.question: Is there a cooling-off period if I buy at auction?
faqs.answer: Cooling-off is generally unavailable for auction purchases. In Victoria, the exclusion also covers purchases within three clear business days before or after the scheduled auction.

faqs.question: Do I need a building inspection before auction?
faqs.answer: If condition could change your decision or maximum bid, obtain an appropriately scoped inspection early enough to assess its findings and blind spots. Test any vendor report's date, access, commissioning party and purchaser-reliance terms. The inspection before auction guide covers timing and what a standard inspection leaves out.

faqs.question: Is pre-approval enough to bid at auction?
faqs.answer: Not by itself. Ask the lender what conditions remain, whether this property is acceptable to them, what happens if the valuation comes in short, and whether you hold the funds and buffer to complete at your intended price.

faqs.question: What happens if I win and then can't settle?
faqs.answer: You risk forfeiting the deposit and may be liable for the seller's losses, including a resale shortfall.

faqs.question: How much deposit do I need at auction?
faqs.answer: The contract sets the amount. Check the due time and payment method, and document any agreed change before bidding.

faqs.question: Does a passed-in property have normal cooling-off rights?
faqs.answer: Do not assume so. Auction-related exclusions differ by state and can extend to negotiations around the auction. Have your adviser confirm the actual transaction and timing before signing.

faqs.question: Can I just lower my bid to allow for an inaccessible area?
faqs.answer: Only if you can meaningfully assess and carry the resulting uncertainty. A discount does not establish the repair scope or resolve a safety, finance or essential-use problem.

faqs.question: What should I do if the contract changes on auction day?
faqs.answer: Have your legal adviser assess the changed terms before you commit. Confirm that any agreed change appears in the version you would accept.

guides.contentMarkdown:
# Auction-day due diligence: the buyer's checklist

Before you bid, have the contract and disclosure reviewed, put any agreed changes in writing and understand the building report, including the areas it could not cover. Ask your lender or broker how valuation, property type and the final price affect approval. Check how the deposit must be paid and write down a hard limit that already includes the immediate work and buying costs.

## Research note
The linked Victorian and NSW authorities support their respective auction examples; Moneysmart supports broader home-buying preparation. The decision sheet is an original editorial framework. Contract obligations, finance conditions and the legal effect of any change require advice for the actual transaction.

## Opening
### Nothing important waits for the hammer
- **Contract:** Read properly, with any agreed changes in writing
- **Building:** The report understood, and every flag chased down
- **Money:** Finance for this property, the deposit ready, a limit you wrote down

_Bid only when every gate is green._

## Why an auction is different
When the hammer falls, you are generally bound, and there is usually no cooling-off to save you. So the contract, the finance and the physical checks all get finished first.

In Victoria, the [official cooling-off guidance](https://www.consumer.vic.gov.au/housing/buying-and-selling-property/buying-property/buying-property-by-private-sale) excludes auction purchases and purchases within three clear business days before or after a public auction. Have your adviser confirm the timing and contract in your state. See [cooling-off periods by state](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/cooling-off-period-by-state) for orientation.

## The checks to clear before you bid
1. **Contract and state disclosure reviewed** by your conveyancer or solicitor, including the [Section 32 vendor statement](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/reading-a-section-32) in Victoria where applicable.
2. **Building report understood**, including the important findings, blind spots and any limits on your right to rely on it.
3. **Property-specific finance readiness**, lender conditions, valuation risk, funds to complete and buffer understood.
4. **Deposit mechanics confirmed**, the amount is set by the contract, with payment timing and method checked with the agent.
5. **Your maximum price set in writing**, with a plan to stop there, whatever the room does.

### Contract and state disclosure

Have a conveyancer or solicitor review the vendor statement and contract early. Ask about title, settlement, deposit, inclusions, adjustments, default terms and special conditions. If the seller agrees to a change, have it recorded in the contract before you bid. Tell your legal adviser about any representation that affects your decision. For the document bundle, use the guide to the [NSW contract for sale](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/reading-a-contract-for-sale-nsw) or [Queensland Form 2 disclosure](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/seller-disclosure-qld) where relevant.

### Building and pest, done in advance

Understand the building before you bid. Check a vendor report's date, scope, access, inspector, insurance and buyer-reliance terms. Commission your own work if those details leave important gaps. The guide to [pre-auction building inspection](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/building-inspection-before-auction) explains timing, access and reliance on a supplied report.

### Property-specific finance readiness

A pre-approval is usually conditional on valuation, final checks and an acceptable property. Give the lender or broker the property type, address, contract and intended price range. Confirm outstanding conditions, valuation-shortfall funding and the cash needed for deposit, duty, costs and settlement. Set a conservative limit and contingency.

### Deposit and your limit

The contract sets the deposit amount and due time. Confirm the agent's payment method and daily transfer limits, then record any negotiated change before bidding. Include acquisition costs, immediate work and a finance buffer in the maximum price.

## What happens if you win and can't settle
If you win and then cannot settle, the deposit is at risk and the seller’s losses, including any shortfall on a resale, can follow you home. That is the whole reason the gates come before the bidding.

## A completed checklist needs evidence behind each tick
'Contract checked' can mean that a document was emailed, a preliminary review was received or the final version was actually cleared for your proposed terms. These are different states. Record the version, the person who reviewed it, outstanding questions and any agreed change. Apply the same discipline to finance and condition: a booked appointment is not a completed investigation, and an unanswered email is not confirmation.

**What should sit behind the auction-day decision**

| Area | Useful confirmation | Open dependency |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Contract | Your adviser has reviewed the version and terms you would accept | A requested change remains unagreed or the version changed |
| Building | Material findings and access limits have been considered | A significant investigation is still outstanding |
| Finance | Your lender or broker has explained the property-specific position and remaining conditions | Funds depend on an untested assumption |
| Deposit | Amount, due time, method and available funds are established | A transfer limit or unavailable account prevents payment |
| Maximum bid | A written limit reflects the complete purchase and known obligations | The limit assumes a repair or approval outcome not established |

## Some uncertainty is an allowance; some changes the decision
A quotation for a defined repair is different from an unknown structural scope. You may be able to allow for the first after checking inclusions and contingency. The second might involve a range too wide to price sensibly before bidding. A smaller bid does not make an unsafe condition, unavailable finance or an essential but unapproved alteration acceptable.

Ask whether the unresolved point could change your ability to use, insure, fund or afford the home, and what evidence would settle it. If that evidence cannot arrive before the commitment, decide whether you can knowingly accept the uncertainty or should not bid. Do not manufacture a percentage allowance merely to make the checklist look complete. Technical uncertainty and personal capacity to carry it are separate questions.

## Reconcile the money once, without spending the same buffer twice
Use one purchase worksheet shared with your broker or lender where appropriate. Keep purchase price, acquisition expenses, deposit timing, settlement funds and post-purchase work separate. The deposit is normally part of the price rather than an additional purchase cost, but it must be available when due. Duty, legal expenses, adjustments and any other applicable costs need their own provision.

A repair reserve and a valuation-shortfall reserve may compete for the same available cash. Ask what happens if both are needed. [Moneysmart's home-buying guidance](https://moneysmart.gov.au/home-loans/buying-a-house) places borrowing and buying costs within the preparation process. Your actual lender's conditions and your funds determine readiness; a general affordability estimate cannot confirm approval for this property at a particular price.

## Agree who can bid and what can change on the day
Where partners or another bidder are involved, agree the limit and who has authority to act before the auction. Confirm registration, identification and representation requirements with the agent and legal adviser. [NSW's auction guidance](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/buying-and-selling-property/buying-property-nsw/buying-property-at-an-auction) sets out its bidder-registration and authority requirements. Use the process in the property's state, including the arrangements for remote bidding where relevant.

Have a way to contact your adviser if the contract, inclusions, settlement date or an important representation changes. An attractive concession can still require review: extra time to settle might help one arrangement while conflicting with another. Keep any accepted variation in the operative documents. A rushed verbal explanation from someone in the crowd should not replace advice on the terms you will be bound by.

## Passed in does not mean the investigation clock resets
A post-auction negotiation can feel like a private sale with more breathing room. Confirm the legal position before treating it that way. [Victoria's official guidance](https://www.consumer.vic.gov.au/housing/buying-and-selling-property/buying-property/buying-property-by-private-sale) describes the auction-related cooling-off exclusion, while NSW's auction guidance also addresses a same-day exchange after a property is passed in. The calendar and transaction matter; use your adviser to establish the actual rights and deadline.

A lower negotiated price changes the price. It does not automatically change a defect's cause, complete missing records or add a finance condition. Reuse the same decision sheet and record what has genuinely changed. If further investigation or a condition is needed, have your adviser seek an agreed contractual arrangement before commitment rather than assuming one will be available afterwards.

## Worked example: the last concession is not a completed check
**Illustrative reasoning example, not an inspected property.** A property is passed in and the seller offers a lower price. The buyer has a pest report recommending further access behind a lined subfloor area. A contractor has quoted for treatment, and the buyer interprets the discount as enough to cover the issue.

The treatment quotation and potential damage extent answer different questions. The price reduction does not establish the condition of hidden timber or the repair scope. Ask whether the inspection gap could materially change the purchase budget or use of the home, and have the adviser confirm the proposed contract's position.

If suitable access and assessment can be obtained under an agreed arrangement, the new evidence can inform the decision. If not, the buyer must assess an unresolved exposure rather than call it a known treatment bill. The ability to walk away is part of preparation; previous inspection spending does not make the next commitment safer.

A useful auction-day record ends with what is ready, what is still conditional and the decision those facts support. The purpose is to keep the final bid connected to the work already done.

> Important: Keep the written limit and the finished checks in front of you on the day. Have every agreed change recorded in the contract before bidding, and tell your legal adviser about any representation you relied on.

> Note: A [desktop read](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/desktop-vs-physical-report) can triage several properties before you commission physical inspections on the strongest candidates. If you buy, keep that evidence as the starting record for ownership.

## Frequently asked questions
### How recent should a building report be before an auction?
As recent as practical, because a report records condition on the day of inspection. Weather, storms, new damage or repairs since then can change the picture, so a report from weeks or months earlier, or one commissioned by the seller, deserves a check of its date, scope and limitations.

### Can I make an auction purchase subject to finance or inspection?
A seller may agree to contract changes before the auction. Have each requested change negotiated and documented by the legal representatives before bidding.

### Is there a cooling-off period if I buy at auction?
Cooling-off is generally unavailable for auction purchases. In Victoria, the exclusion also covers purchases within three clear business days before or after the scheduled auction.

### Do I need a building inspection before auction?
If condition could change your decision or maximum bid, obtain an appropriately scoped inspection early enough to assess its findings and blind spots. Test any vendor report's date, access, commissioning party and purchaser-reliance terms. The inspection before auction guide covers timing and what a standard inspection leaves out.

### Is pre-approval enough to bid at auction?
Not by itself. Ask the lender what conditions remain, whether this property is acceptable to them, what happens if the valuation comes in short, and whether you hold the funds and buffer to complete at your intended price.

### What happens if I win and then can't settle?
You risk forfeiting the deposit and may be liable for the seller's losses, including a resale shortfall.

### How much deposit do I need at auction?
The contract sets the amount. Check the due time and payment method, and document any agreed change before bidding.

### Does a passed-in property have normal cooling-off rights?
Do not assume so. Auction-related exclusions differ by state and can extend to negotiations around the auction. Have your adviser confirm the actual transaction and timing before signing.

### Can I just lower my bid to allow for an inaccessible area?
Only if you can meaningfully assess and carry the resulting uncertainty. A discount does not establish the repair scope or resolve a safety, finance or essential-use problem.

### What should I do if the contract changes on auction day?
Have your legal adviser assess the changed terms before you commit. Confirm that any agreed change appears in the version you would accept.

## Method
A pre-bid decision guide separating completed checks, bounded allowances and unresolved dependencies. State auction examples are explicitly local; legal and lending questions remain with the relevant advisers.

## Limitations
General Australian guidance only. Contracts, statutes, policies, site conditions and professional scopes vary; obtain advice for the property and decision in front of you.

## Sources
- [Buying property by private sale](https://www.consumer.vic.gov.au/housing/buying-and-selling-property/buying-property/buying-property-by-private-sale) — Consumer Affairs Victoria; accessed 2026-07-19
- [Buying a house](https://moneysmart.gov.au/home-loans/buying-a-house) — ASIC Moneysmart; accessed 2026-09-07
- [Buying property at an auction](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/buying-and-selling-property/buying-property-nsw/buying-property-at-an-auction) — NSW Government; accessed 2026-09-07
- [AS 4349.1-2007 Inspection of buildings, Part 1: Pre-purchase inspections, residential buildings](https://store.standards.org.au/product/as-4349-1-2007) — Standards Australia; accessed 2026-07-20

guides.question: How do I find out when my house was built?
guides.title: When was my house built? How to find out, and why it matters
guides.summary: How to work out when an Australian house was built, using council records, historical aerial photographs, the title, old listings and the clues in the building itself, and why the answer shapes what to check.
guides.answer: Most Australian homes do not come with an exact build date, so you usually work it out from three kinds of evidence. Paper records such as council building permits, plans, the title and past listings can give a date or a range. Historical aerial photographs, which state governments publish back to the 1930s and 1940s in many areas, can show when the house first appears. The building itself carries clues in its construction and materials.
guides.methodology: We group dating evidence into records, historical imagery and the building fabric, explain what each can and cannot establish, and weight them so the result is a supported range with its reasons recorded.
guides.limitations: Record holdings, search fees and imagery coverage vary by state, council and location. Construction clues point to an era but cannot date a house on their own, and many homes include later work with different dates.
guides.researchNote: Council record availability varies by council and age of the record. In Victoria, a [regulation 51 building property enquiry](https://www.legislation.vic.gov.au/in-force/statutory-rules/building-regulations-2018) covers permits from the previous ten years, and the [City of Melbourne](https://www.melbourne.vic.gov.au/building-and-development/property-information/Pages/property-enquiries.aspx) holds no building plans from before 1960. Historical aerial photography coverage is described by [NSW Spatial Services](https://data.nsw.gov.au/data/dataset/1-f7c215b873864d44bccddda8075238cb), [QImagery](https://qimagery.information.qld.gov.au/help) and [Landgate](https://www.landgate.wa.gov.au/location-data-and-services/imagery/aerial-imagery/historical-imagery-scans-and-enlargements/).

cluster.label: Read the building
cluster.blurb: Use age and construction as a starting hypothesis, then test it against evidence and physical inspection.

sections.heading: Opening
sections.markdown:
### Three kinds of evidence, one range
- **Paper:** Permits, plans, the title and past listings
- **Pictures:** Aerial photos before and after the house appears
- **Fabric:** Construction and materials that fit an era

_Record a range and your reasons. Additions get their own dates._

Together they usually give a range of a few years, which is enough to know which era questions to ask. Remember that extensions and renovations have their own dates.

sections.heading: Why the build date matters
sections.markdown:
The year a house was built is one of the most useful single facts about it. It points to how the house was likely constructed, which materials were in common use, how the wiring and plumbing were first installed, and which problems tend to show up as homes of that age get older. Insurers ask for it, renovation plans depend on it and it shapes almost every question worth raising at an inspection.

It is a starting point, though, and never a verdict. Two houses from the same year can be in very different condition depending on how they were built, maintained and changed. Use the date to choose your questions, then test them against the evidence for this house. The [red flags by era](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/red-flags-by-era) guide shows how that works across the decades.

**What the build date helps you ask**

| Built around | Questions it raises | Read next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Before the 1920s | Footings and stumps, damp, original wiring and plumbing, lath and plaster, later alterations | [Period homes](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/period-homes-pre-1920s) |
| 1920s to 1940s | Mixed footings, early wiring, steel windows and lintels, fibrous plaster | [Interwar homes](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/interwar-homes-1920s-40s) |
| 1950s to 1970s | Asbestos-containing materials, early brick veneer, original wet areas and services | [Postwar homes](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/postwar-homes-1950s-70s) |
| 1980s and 1990s | Ageing wet areas, roofs and services, materials of the late asbestos period | [1980s and 90s homes](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/homes-1980s-90s) |
| 2000 onwards | Waterproofing, cladding, balconies, slab edges and drainage | [Modern homes](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/modern-homes-2000s-on) |

sections.heading: Start with the paperwork you may already have
sections.markdown:
If you are buying, the contract and the vendor's disclosure documents are the first place to look. In Victoria, the [Section 32 vendor statement](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/reading-a-section-32) lists recent building permits. In New South Wales, the [contract for sale](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/reading-a-contract-for-sale-nsw) includes planning information, and Queensland has its own [seller disclosure statement](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/seller-disclosure-qld). If you already own the home, your settlement papers, any plans or certificates handed over at sale and earlier inspection reports may hold dates too.

**Records that can date a house**

| Record | What it can tell you | Watch out for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Building permit, certificate of occupancy or final inspection | The year work was approved or completed | It may cover an extension or renovation rather than the original house |
| Original or later plans | The date drawn, the builder or designer, and what was built | Plans show what was proposed; the house may differ |
| Title and plan of subdivision | When the land was created, which gives an earliest likely date for most houses | The house can be much later than the subdivision |
| Past real estate listings | A stated year or era, and photographs of earlier layouts | Figures such as 'circa 1950' are often estimates repeated from listing to listing |
| Earlier inspection or valuation reports | An estimated age and notes on alterations | Usually an estimate from appearance, not a record |
| Rates notices and council valuations | Sometimes a recorded year of construction | Recorded years can be rounded or carried forward from old estimates |

sections.heading: Ask the council for its building records
sections.markdown:
Councils hold building records for their area, though how far back they go and what they charge varies a lot. In Victoria, a building property enquiry under [regulation 51 of the Building Regulations 2018](https://www.legislation.vic.gov.au/in-force/statutory-rules/building-regulations-2018) gives details of building permits issued in the previous ten years, plus any current building notices or orders. For older material you usually need a separate search of the council's building archive. As one example, the [City of Melbourne](https://www.melbourne.vic.gov.au/building-and-development/property-information/Pages/property-enquiries.aspx) says it holds no building plans from before 1960 and points people to the [Public Record Office Victoria](https://prov.vic.gov.au/) for older records.

Other states work along similar lines: councils keep development and building approval records, often with an online lookup for recent applications and a paid archive search for older files. Ask what the search covers before paying, and ask for the earliest record they hold for the address. A permit for a carport in 1978 still tells you the house was standing by then.

sections.heading: Look at the house from above: historical aerial photographs
sections.markdown:
Aerial photographs are often the quickest way to date a house to within a few years, and several states publish them free online. The [NSW Historical Imagery Viewer](https://data.nsw.gov.au/data/dataset/1-f7c215b873864d44bccddda8075238cb) covers New South Wales from the 1930s. In Queensland, [QImagery](https://qimagery.information.qld.gov.au/help) holds historical aerial photography captured since the 1930s. In Western Australia, [Landgate](https://www.landgate.wa.gov.au/location-data-and-services/imagery/aerial-imagery/historical-imagery-scans-and-enlargements/) holds aerial photography back to 1948, with scans available to order. Other states and many libraries hold collections too.

The method is simple. Find the latest photograph where the lot is empty and the earliest where the house appears. The house was most likely built between those two flights. Do the same for the outline of the house over later decades and you can often see when a rear extension, a second storey or a carport was added.

> Note: Older photographs can be positioned only approximately. [QImagery notes](https://qimagery.information.qld.gov.au/help) that some images may appear slightly out of place, rotated or at the wrong scale. Check neighbouring houses, street corners and trees to be sure you are looking at the right lot. Flights were also years apart, so the result is a range rather than a single year.

sections.heading: Read the house itself
sections.markdown:
The construction and finishes of a house often point to an era, especially when several clues agree. Treat each one as a hint. Materials were used over long periods, styles were revived later, and many homes have been altered. The [brick veneer vs double brick](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/brick-veneer-vs-double-brick) and [weatherboard](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/weatherboard-homes) guides go deeper on the main wall types.

**Clues in the building and the era they often suggest**

| Clue | Often suggests | Keep in mind |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Solid or cavity brick walls throughout, with no frame behind | Earlier homes, commonly before the 1950s | Some later homes also used cavity brick, notably in Western Australia |
| Brick veneer over a timber frame | Increasingly common from the 1950s onwards | Look at later additions separately; they may be a different system |
| Lath and plaster walls and ceilings | Earlier homes, commonly before the Second World War | Rooms may have been relined with plasterboard since |
| Fibrous plaster ceilings, often with decorative cornices | Interwar and early postwar homes | Common across several decades |
| Timber floors on stumps or piers | Older homes in many areas | Raised timber floors remained common in some regions and on sloping sites |
| Concrete slab-on-ground floor | More common in later decades | Extensions to older homes are often on a slab |
| Fibre cement sheeting (fibro) on walls, eaves or wet areas | Mid-twentieth-century homes and renovations | Before the late 1980s it may contain asbestos |
| Steel-framed windows | Interwar and early postwar homes | Aluminium and timber windows were common replacements |

> Important: For homes built or renovated before 1990, treat suspect materials as possibly containing asbestos until they are identified. Age alone does not prove asbestos is present, but do not cut, drill, sand or sample suspect material yourself. The [asbestos guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/asbestos-in-the-home) explains how to have it identified safely.

sections.heading: Other places a date can turn up
sections.markdown:
Old newspapers can be surprisingly useful. [Trove](https://trove.nla.gov.au/), the National Library's free search, includes digitised newspapers where auction notices and sale advertisements sometimes describe a house as new, or name the street and builder. If the area has heritage controls, a heritage study or database may record the date or era of the house; in Victoria, the [Victorian Heritage Database](https://vhd.heritagecouncil.vic.gov.au/) includes places in local heritage overlays, often with a short history. The [heritage overlay guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/living-in-a-heritage-overlay) explains what that listing means for you.

Local historical societies, old street directories and long-standing neighbours can also fill gaps. Treat these as leads to check against the records and photographs, since memories and old advertisements are not always precise.

sections.heading: A house can have more than one build date
sections.markdown:
Many homes are really several projects joined together: an original house, a rear extension, a converted roof space, a rebuilt bathroom. Each part has its own date, its own construction and its own era questions. A 1920s front with a 1990s rear extension needs both sets of questions, plus a close look at where the two meet, which is a common place for cracks and leaks. The [cracks guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/cracks-structural-or-cosmetic) covers junctions between construction phases.

Aerial photographs, changes in brickwork or roof lines, a step in the floor and council permits for the later work usually reveal the joins. Write down a date or range for each part rather than one figure for the whole house.

sections.heading: Put the evidence together
sections.markdown:
Different evidence carries different weight. A permit with a completion date is strong. A pair of aerial photographs bracketing the build is also strong for the original house. Materials and style support a range. A listing that says "circa" is a weak lead until something else agrees with it.

**How much weight to give each kind of evidence**

| Evidence | Weight | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Permit, certificate or final inspection for the original house | Strong | A dated official record of the work |
| Aerial photographs showing an empty lot, then the house | Strong for a range | Direct evidence, limited by the years between flights |
| Plans, title and subdivision dates | Moderate | Useful bounds, though building may have come later or differed from the plans |
| Construction, materials and style | Supporting | Points to an era, but materials were used for decades and homes are altered |
| Listings, reports and 'circa' figures | Weak on their own | Often estimates repeated without a source |

Working out the era from the evidence is also where a [Homechecker Read](https://homechecker.com.au/) starts. It reads the address's records, imagery and construction to place the home in its era, then turns that into the questions and likely needs that follow. If you have found a permit, plan or old photograph, add it and the Read sharpens around it.

Record what you find in your [home record](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/keeping-a-record-of-your-home): the date or range, the evidence behind it and any parts with different dates. That note will help with insurance, renovation planning and, one day, selling.

sections.heading: Worked example: a brick house listed as circa 1950
sections.markdown:
**Illustrative reasoning example, not an inspected property.** A cream brick house in Melbourne's suburbs is listed as circa 1950. The council's building property enquiry shows a permit for a rear extension in 1994 and nothing older. Historical aerial photographs show an empty lot in an earlier flight and the house in a later one, a few years apart.

The steel-framed windows and fibrous plaster ceilings in the front rooms fit that period, while the rear living area has aluminium windows, plasterboard and a concrete slab. A sensible record would read: original house built between the two flights, extension about 1994. That points to postwar questions for the front, including possible asbestos-containing materials, 1990s questions for the rear, and a careful look at the junction between them.

faqs.question: Can Homechecker work out when my house was built?
faqs.answer: A Homechecker Read estimates the era of a home from its records, imagery and construction, and uses that to set out likely needs and what to confirm in person. Adding a permit, plan or dated photograph sharpens it.

faqs.question: Can I find out when my house was built for free?
faqs.answer: Often, yes, at least to a range. Several states publish historical aerial photographs free online, Trove is free to search, and your own contract, disclosure documents and past listings cost nothing. Council archive searches usually carry a fee.

faqs.question: Does the title show when my house was built?
faqs.answer: Usually not directly. The title and plan of subdivision show when the land was created and who has owned it, which gives an earliest likely date for most houses. The house itself may have been built years later.

faqs.question: Is the year on a real estate listing reliable?
faqs.answer: Treat it as a lead. Listing figures such as 'circa 1950' are often estimates repeated from one campaign to the next. Check them against council records, aerial photographs or the building itself.

faqs.question: What if the council has no record of my house?
faqs.answer: That is common for older homes, since many councils did not keep, or no longer hold, early files. Try historical aerial photographs, state archives such as Public Record Office Victoria, Trove and heritage databases, and read the construction itself.

faqs.question: Why does my insurer ask when the house was built?
faqs.answer: The build date gives the insurer a guide to construction, materials and likely condition. Give the best figure you can support and keep the evidence. The home condition and insurance guide explains why describing the actual home matters.

faqs.question: How accurate are historical aerial photographs?
faqs.answer: They are good for showing whether a house was standing at the time of a flight. Older images can be positioned only approximately and flights were often years apart, so they usually give a range rather than an exact year.

faqs.question: My house has an extension. Which date matters?
faqs.answer: Both. Record a date or range for each part of the house, because each part has its own construction and its own era questions, and the junction between them deserves a closer look.

faqs.question: Does an old house mean asbestos?
faqs.answer: Not necessarily. Age alone does not prove asbestos is present, but for homes built or renovated before 1990, suspect materials should be treated as possibly asbestos-containing until identified by a competent person.

guides.contentMarkdown:
# When was my house built? How to find out, and why it matters

Most Australian homes do not come with an exact build date, so you usually work it out from three kinds of evidence. Paper records such as council building permits, plans, the title and past listings can give a date or a range. Historical aerial photographs, which state governments publish back to the 1930s and 1940s in many areas, can show when the house first appears. The building itself carries clues in its construction and materials.

## Research note
Council record availability varies by council and age of the record. In Victoria, a [regulation 51 building property enquiry](https://www.legislation.vic.gov.au/in-force/statutory-rules/building-regulations-2018) covers permits from the previous ten years, and the [City of Melbourne](https://www.melbourne.vic.gov.au/building-and-development/property-information/Pages/property-enquiries.aspx) holds no building plans from before 1960. Historical aerial photography coverage is described by [NSW Spatial Services](https://data.nsw.gov.au/data/dataset/1-f7c215b873864d44bccddda8075238cb), [QImagery](https://qimagery.information.qld.gov.au/help) and [Landgate](https://www.landgate.wa.gov.au/location-data-and-services/imagery/aerial-imagery/historical-imagery-scans-and-enlargements/).

## Opening
### Three kinds of evidence, one range
- **Paper:** Permits, plans, the title and past listings
- **Pictures:** Aerial photos before and after the house appears
- **Fabric:** Construction and materials that fit an era

_Record a range and your reasons. Additions get their own dates._

Together they usually give a range of a few years, which is enough to know which era questions to ask. Remember that extensions and renovations have their own dates.

## Why the build date matters
The year a house was built is one of the most useful single facts about it. It points to how the house was likely constructed, which materials were in common use, how the wiring and plumbing were first installed, and which problems tend to show up as homes of that age get older. Insurers ask for it, renovation plans depend on it and it shapes almost every question worth raising at an inspection.

It is a starting point, though, and never a verdict. Two houses from the same year can be in very different condition depending on how they were built, maintained and changed. Use the date to choose your questions, then test them against the evidence for this house. The [red flags by era](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/red-flags-by-era) guide shows how that works across the decades.

**What the build date helps you ask**

| Built around | Questions it raises | Read next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Before the 1920s | Footings and stumps, damp, original wiring and plumbing, lath and plaster, later alterations | [Period homes](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/period-homes-pre-1920s) |
| 1920s to 1940s | Mixed footings, early wiring, steel windows and lintels, fibrous plaster | [Interwar homes](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/interwar-homes-1920s-40s) |
| 1950s to 1970s | Asbestos-containing materials, early brick veneer, original wet areas and services | [Postwar homes](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/postwar-homes-1950s-70s) |
| 1980s and 1990s | Ageing wet areas, roofs and services, materials of the late asbestos period | [1980s and 90s homes](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/homes-1980s-90s) |
| 2000 onwards | Waterproofing, cladding, balconies, slab edges and drainage | [Modern homes](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/modern-homes-2000s-on) |

## Start with the paperwork you may already have
If you are buying, the contract and the vendor's disclosure documents are the first place to look. In Victoria, the [Section 32 vendor statement](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/reading-a-section-32) lists recent building permits. In New South Wales, the [contract for sale](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/reading-a-contract-for-sale-nsw) includes planning information, and Queensland has its own [seller disclosure statement](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/seller-disclosure-qld). If you already own the home, your settlement papers, any plans or certificates handed over at sale and earlier inspection reports may hold dates too.

**Records that can date a house**

| Record | What it can tell you | Watch out for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Building permit, certificate of occupancy or final inspection | The year work was approved or completed | It may cover an extension or renovation rather than the original house |
| Original or later plans | The date drawn, the builder or designer, and what was built | Plans show what was proposed; the house may differ |
| Title and plan of subdivision | When the land was created, which gives an earliest likely date for most houses | The house can be much later than the subdivision |
| Past real estate listings | A stated year or era, and photographs of earlier layouts | Figures such as 'circa 1950' are often estimates repeated from listing to listing |
| Earlier inspection or valuation reports | An estimated age and notes on alterations | Usually an estimate from appearance, not a record |
| Rates notices and council valuations | Sometimes a recorded year of construction | Recorded years can be rounded or carried forward from old estimates |

## Ask the council for its building records
Councils hold building records for their area, though how far back they go and what they charge varies a lot. In Victoria, a building property enquiry under [regulation 51 of the Building Regulations 2018](https://www.legislation.vic.gov.au/in-force/statutory-rules/building-regulations-2018) gives details of building permits issued in the previous ten years, plus any current building notices or orders. For older material you usually need a separate search of the council's building archive. As one example, the [City of Melbourne](https://www.melbourne.vic.gov.au/building-and-development/property-information/Pages/property-enquiries.aspx) says it holds no building plans from before 1960 and points people to the [Public Record Office Victoria](https://prov.vic.gov.au/) for older records.

Other states work along similar lines: councils keep development and building approval records, often with an online lookup for recent applications and a paid archive search for older files. Ask what the search covers before paying, and ask for the earliest record they hold for the address. A permit for a carport in 1978 still tells you the house was standing by then.

## Look at the house from above: historical aerial photographs
Aerial photographs are often the quickest way to date a house to within a few years, and several states publish them free online. The [NSW Historical Imagery Viewer](https://data.nsw.gov.au/data/dataset/1-f7c215b873864d44bccddda8075238cb) covers New South Wales from the 1930s. In Queensland, [QImagery](https://qimagery.information.qld.gov.au/help) holds historical aerial photography captured since the 1930s. In Western Australia, [Landgate](https://www.landgate.wa.gov.au/location-data-and-services/imagery/aerial-imagery/historical-imagery-scans-and-enlargements/) holds aerial photography back to 1948, with scans available to order. Other states and many libraries hold collections too.

The method is simple. Find the latest photograph where the lot is empty and the earliest where the house appears. The house was most likely built between those two flights. Do the same for the outline of the house over later decades and you can often see when a rear extension, a second storey or a carport was added.

> Note: Older photographs can be positioned only approximately. [QImagery notes](https://qimagery.information.qld.gov.au/help) that some images may appear slightly out of place, rotated or at the wrong scale. Check neighbouring houses, street corners and trees to be sure you are looking at the right lot. Flights were also years apart, so the result is a range rather than a single year.

## Read the house itself
The construction and finishes of a house often point to an era, especially when several clues agree. Treat each one as a hint. Materials were used over long periods, styles were revived later, and many homes have been altered. The [brick veneer vs double brick](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/brick-veneer-vs-double-brick) and [weatherboard](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/weatherboard-homes) guides go deeper on the main wall types.

**Clues in the building and the era they often suggest**

| Clue | Often suggests | Keep in mind |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Solid or cavity brick walls throughout, with no frame behind | Earlier homes, commonly before the 1950s | Some later homes also used cavity brick, notably in Western Australia |
| Brick veneer over a timber frame | Increasingly common from the 1950s onwards | Look at later additions separately; they may be a different system |
| Lath and plaster walls and ceilings | Earlier homes, commonly before the Second World War | Rooms may have been relined with plasterboard since |
| Fibrous plaster ceilings, often with decorative cornices | Interwar and early postwar homes | Common across several decades |
| Timber floors on stumps or piers | Older homes in many areas | Raised timber floors remained common in some regions and on sloping sites |
| Concrete slab-on-ground floor | More common in later decades | Extensions to older homes are often on a slab |
| Fibre cement sheeting (fibro) on walls, eaves or wet areas | Mid-twentieth-century homes and renovations | Before the late 1980s it may contain asbestos |
| Steel-framed windows | Interwar and early postwar homes | Aluminium and timber windows were common replacements |

> Important: For homes built or renovated before 1990, treat suspect materials as possibly containing asbestos until they are identified. Age alone does not prove asbestos is present, but do not cut, drill, sand or sample suspect material yourself. The [asbestos guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/asbestos-in-the-home) explains how to have it identified safely.

## Other places a date can turn up
Old newspapers can be surprisingly useful. [Trove](https://trove.nla.gov.au/), the National Library's free search, includes digitised newspapers where auction notices and sale advertisements sometimes describe a house as new, or name the street and builder. If the area has heritage controls, a heritage study or database may record the date or era of the house; in Victoria, the [Victorian Heritage Database](https://vhd.heritagecouncil.vic.gov.au/) includes places in local heritage overlays, often with a short history. The [heritage overlay guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/living-in-a-heritage-overlay) explains what that listing means for you.

Local historical societies, old street directories and long-standing neighbours can also fill gaps. Treat these as leads to check against the records and photographs, since memories and old advertisements are not always precise.

## A house can have more than one build date
Many homes are really several projects joined together: an original house, a rear extension, a converted roof space, a rebuilt bathroom. Each part has its own date, its own construction and its own era questions. A 1920s front with a 1990s rear extension needs both sets of questions, plus a close look at where the two meet, which is a common place for cracks and leaks. The [cracks guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/cracks-structural-or-cosmetic) covers junctions between construction phases.

Aerial photographs, changes in brickwork or roof lines, a step in the floor and council permits for the later work usually reveal the joins. Write down a date or range for each part rather than one figure for the whole house.

## Put the evidence together
Different evidence carries different weight. A permit with a completion date is strong. A pair of aerial photographs bracketing the build is also strong for the original house. Materials and style support a range. A listing that says "circa" is a weak lead until something else agrees with it.

**How much weight to give each kind of evidence**

| Evidence | Weight | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Permit, certificate or final inspection for the original house | Strong | A dated official record of the work |
| Aerial photographs showing an empty lot, then the house | Strong for a range | Direct evidence, limited by the years between flights |
| Plans, title and subdivision dates | Moderate | Useful bounds, though building may have come later or differed from the plans |
| Construction, materials and style | Supporting | Points to an era, but materials were used for decades and homes are altered |
| Listings, reports and 'circa' figures | Weak on their own | Often estimates repeated without a source |

Working out the era from the evidence is also where a [Homechecker Read](https://homechecker.com.au/) starts. It reads the address's records, imagery and construction to place the home in its era, then turns that into the questions and likely needs that follow. If you have found a permit, plan or old photograph, add it and the Read sharpens around it.

Record what you find in your [home record](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/keeping-a-record-of-your-home): the date or range, the evidence behind it and any parts with different dates. That note will help with insurance, renovation planning and, one day, selling.

## Worked example: a brick house listed as circa 1950
**Illustrative reasoning example, not an inspected property.** A cream brick house in Melbourne's suburbs is listed as circa 1950. The council's building property enquiry shows a permit for a rear extension in 1994 and nothing older. Historical aerial photographs show an empty lot in an earlier flight and the house in a later one, a few years apart.

The steel-framed windows and fibrous plaster ceilings in the front rooms fit that period, while the rear living area has aluminium windows, plasterboard and a concrete slab. A sensible record would read: original house built between the two flights, extension about 1994. That points to postwar questions for the front, including possible asbestos-containing materials, 1990s questions for the rear, and a careful look at the junction between them.

## Frequently asked questions
### Can Homechecker work out when my house was built?
A Homechecker Read estimates the era of a home from its records, imagery and construction, and uses that to set out likely needs and what to confirm in person. Adding a permit, plan or dated photograph sharpens it.

### Can I find out when my house was built for free?
Often, yes, at least to a range. Several states publish historical aerial photographs free online, Trove is free to search, and your own contract, disclosure documents and past listings cost nothing. Council archive searches usually carry a fee.

### Does the title show when my house was built?
Usually not directly. The title and plan of subdivision show when the land was created and who has owned it, which gives an earliest likely date for most houses. The house itself may have been built years later.

### Is the year on a real estate listing reliable?
Treat it as a lead. Listing figures such as 'circa 1950' are often estimates repeated from one campaign to the next. Check them against council records, aerial photographs or the building itself.

### What if the council has no record of my house?
That is common for older homes, since many councils did not keep, or no longer hold, early files. Try historical aerial photographs, state archives such as Public Record Office Victoria, Trove and heritage databases, and read the construction itself.

### Why does my insurer ask when the house was built?
The build date gives the insurer a guide to construction, materials and likely condition. Give the best figure you can support and keep the evidence. The home condition and insurance guide explains why describing the actual home matters.

### How accurate are historical aerial photographs?
They are good for showing whether a house was standing at the time of a flight. Older images can be positioned only approximately and flights were often years apart, so they usually give a range rather than an exact year.

### My house has an extension. Which date matters?
Both. Record a date or range for each part of the house, because each part has its own construction and its own era questions, and the junction between them deserves a closer look.

### Does an old house mean asbestos?
Not necessarily. Age alone does not prove asbestos is present, but for homes built or renovated before 1990, suspect materials should be treated as possibly asbestos-containing until identified by a competent person.

## Method
We group dating evidence into records, historical imagery and the building fabric, explain what each can and cannot establish, and weight them so the result is a supported range with its reasons recorded.

## Limitations
Record holdings, search fees and imagery coverage vary by state, council and location. Construction clues point to an era but cannot date a house on their own, and many homes include later work with different dates.

## Sources

- [QImagery help: available imagery and locational accuracy](https://qimagery.information.qld.gov.au/help) — Queensland Government; accessed 2026-10-16

guides.question: What are the common property red flags by era and construction type?
guides.title: Property red flags by era: what deserves a closer look
guides.summary: The build date is useful because it changes the questions, not because it predicts the answer. Read the original shell, later alterations, services and present condition together, then use the right evidence to test what is actually there.
guides.answer: Use the era as a first-pass risk map, then verify the actual construction and alteration history. Pre-1920s and interwar homes put footings, moisture, roofs, services and older coatings high on the list. Postwar homes add a high-priority pre-1990 asbestos screen and decades of wet-area and service changes. The 1980s and 1990s are a transition period with mixed materials and renovation histories. Newer homes shift attention toward approvals, waterproofing, drainage, workmanship, condensation and, for apartments, common-property defects, fire systems, cladding, insurance and scheme funding.
guides.methodology: We treat the build date as a first-pass risk map, then test four separate timelines: original construction, later alterations, services/wet areas and defect/repair history.
guides.limitations: Construction practice varies by region, building type, climate and alteration history. An era profile cannot diagnose a defect or establish compliance; confirm materials, condition and service age through property-specific evidence.
guides.researchNote: Age is useful when it changes the inspection brief, not when it becomes a diagnosis. Australian guidance supports a pre-1990 asbestos screen, lead-safe work on older coatings, building-and-pest inspection of existing homes, active moisture/termite management and condensation-aware retrofit decisions. Start with the [YourHome existing-house guide](https://www.yourhome.gov.au/buy-build-renovate/buying-existing-house).

cluster.label: Read the building
cluster.blurb: Use age and construction as a starting hypothesis, then test it against evidence and physical inspection.

sections.heading: Opening
sections.markdown:
### Let the era sharpen your questions
- **Start:** The build date and construction open the questions
- **Look closer:** Plans, invoices, alterations and what you can see
- **Settle it:** An inspection, or a specialist, settles it for this house

_The era points; the evidence decides._

sections.heading: Treat the era as a hypothesis, not a diagnosis
sections.markdown:
A construction date can narrow the list of questions, but it cannot tell you the condition of the home in front of you. A 1930s house may have a new roof, rewired services and a 1990s bathroom. A 1970s house may have a 2018 extension. A 2012 apartment may have years of façade or waterproofing history sitting in the owners-corporation records. The useful question is not simply **how old is the building?** It is **which parts belong to which era, and how are those parts performing now?**

If you are not sure of the date yet, [how to find out when a house was built](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/when-was-my-house-built) walks through council records, historical aerial photographs and the clues in the building itself.

The Australian Government's [YourHome buying guidance](https://www.yourhome.gov.au/buy-build-renovate/buying-existing-house) makes the same distinction in practical terms: building and pest inspections are used to identify structural, damp, drainage, waterproofing and termite issues, while the property records and installed systems add the history that a visual inspection cannot supply.

> Note: A useful era clue should change the evidence you seek, the professional you engage or the decision you make. If it changes none of those things, it is probably just trivia.

sections.heading: The era matrix
sections.markdown:
_[Illustration: Five detailed Australian house models progressing from a pre-1920s home through interwar, postwar, 1980s to 1990s and contemporary construction. Each era leaves its own clues in the roof, walls, footings, services and later alterations. The table below turns those clues into inspection questions.]_

**Where to begin, and which guide to open next**

| Era / form | First useful questions | Follow the evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Pre-1920s | What supports the walls and floors? Where does moisture enter? Which services and finishes are later? | [Period homes](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/period-homes-pre-1920s) → [moisture pathways](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/damp-and-moisture-in-your-home) → footing, roof and repair records. |
| 1920s–40s | Does the original house meet an extension on different supports? Are low walls damp? Which alterations changed drainage? | [Interwar homes](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/interwar-homes-1920s-40s) → [timber fabric](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/weatherboard-homes) or [masonry construction](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/brick-veneer-vs-double-brick). |
| 1950s–70s | What is the wall system? What was replaced? Will proposed work disturb suspect materials? | [Postwar homes](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/postwar-homes-1950s-70s) → [renovation sequence](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/planning-a-renovation) → material and service evidence. |
| 1980s–90s | Which wet areas, roof details and services are original? Is the recent work cosmetic or a documented renewal? | [1980s–90s homes](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/homes-1980s-90s) → [movement](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/cracks-structural-or-cosmetic) or [damp investigation](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/damp-and-moisture-in-your-home). |
| 2000s onward, house | Do approval and completion records match the home? What happens at roof, window, balcony and ground junctions? | [Modern homes](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/modern-homes-2000s-on) → drainage, defect history and repair evidence. |
| Apartment or shared scheme, any era | What is shared, what is already known about the building, and how will work be paid for? | [Apartment due diligence](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/buying-an-apartment-strata) → [scheme records](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/reading-your-owners-corporation-report) → technical reports and funding. |

sections.heading: Read four timelines, not one build year
sections.markdown:
**The four timelines that usually matter**

| Timeline | What to establish | Why it changes the inspection |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Original construction | Footings, wall system, roof form, floor system, openings and original services where known | This establishes the base construction and the era-linked questions that remain relevant. |
| Major alterations | Extensions, enclosed verandas, wall removal, re-roofing, window replacement, façade work and structural changes | Later work may be built under a different code era, may hide original fabric and can create junctions where water or movement concentrates. |
| Wet areas and services | Bathroom, laundry, kitchen, wiring, switchboard, plumbing, hot water, heating/cooling and solar upgrade dates | These systems often age independently of the shell. The house age is a poor proxy for their current age. |
| Repairs and defects | Leaks, cracking, termite treatment, underpinning/restumping, roof repairs, drainage works, cladding or waterproofing rectification | A repair can be reassuring only when the cause, scope, completion and present performance are understood. |

This is why a renovated older home can be harder to read than an untouched one. Renovation can solve genuine defects, but it can also hide interfaces, remove visible clues and mix materials from several periods. Keep asking **what changed, when, why and with what evidence?**

sections.heading: Cross-era red flags that deserve evidence
sections.markdown:
### Water that is not being shed, drained or dried

Across every era, water is one of the highest-value things to follow. Look at the whole path: roof covering, flashings, gutters, downpipes, surface falls, openings, wall cavities, wet areas, subfloor and plumbing. The Australian Government's [repairs and maintenance guidance](https://www.yourhome.gov.au/buy-build-renovate/repairs-and-maintenance) specifically treats leaks, blocked drainage, failed flashings, damp and shower waterproofing as issues that can create larger building damage if the cause is not addressed. Use [the damp guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/damp-and-moisture-in-your-home) to separate source, path and damage.

### Movement without a timeline

Cracks are more useful when read with direction, width, associated distortion, footing type, drainage, trees, soil and change over time. A repaired crack with no explanation is not the same evidence as a diagnosed cause with monitoring and completed structural work. Use [the crack triage](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/cracks-structural-or-cosmetic) and escalate progressive or consequential movement to the appropriate professional.

### Timber-pest risk hidden by finishes or landscaping

Termites are not an 'old house' problem. Risk changes with region, construction, subfloor clearance, moisture, slab edges, service penetrations, landscaping and the condition of any management system. YourHome recommends a building and pest inspection before buying in termite-risk areas, while [QBCC guidance](https://www.qbcc.qld.gov.au/home-owner-hub/maintain-protect/protect-against-termites) shows why later landscaping, paths and renovations can undermine a termite-management system. Ask what system exists, how it has been maintained and what the latest inspection found.

### Services whose age is being guessed from the house

Do not infer wiring, plumbing or hot-water age from the build date. Look for switchboard changes, invoices, certificates and alterations, then use licensed inspection where the system matters to safety, capacity or budget. This becomes especially important where solar, battery, electric-vehicle charging or electrification has increased demand on an older electrical installation.

sections.heading: Hazards with useful date screens
sections.markdown:
### Asbestos-containing materials

The [national householders' guide](https://www.newaste.org.au/asbestos/assets/asbestos-guide-for-householders.pdf) says houses built or renovated before 1990 may contain asbestos products. The [NSW asbestos timeline](https://www.asbestos.nsw.gov.au/safety/safety-in-the-home/when-was-asbestos-banned-in-australia) records the national ban from 31 December 2003. The date is a screening trigger, not a material diagnosis: follow [ASSEA’s asbestos-in-the-home guidance](https://www.asbestossafety.gov.au/about-asbestos/finding-asbestos/home) to identify suspect material before drilling, sanding, cutting or demolition and follow the licensing and disposal rules for the material, amount and jurisdiction.

### Lead in older paint

Older paint, especially paint applied before 1970, may contain much higher lead concentrations than modern coatings. Before sanding, scraping or heat stripping, follow the [Australian Government Lead Alert](https://www.agriculture.gov.au/sites/default/files/documents/lead-paint-fifth-edition.pdf), test where appropriate and use lead-safe controls.

sections.heading: Dated milestones every buyer should know
sections.markdown:
Some of the most useful era evidence is simply a date when a material stopped being used or a safety requirement began. A home built before a milestone is not automatically deficient, because many have been upgraded since, but it tells you what to ask for. Requirements were introduced state by state, so treat the years as national reference points rather than exact dates for every address.

**Milestones that change what an older home is likely to lack**

| When | What changed | What it means for an older home |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Before 1970 | Household paints could contain high levels of lead ([Lead Alert](https://www.agriculture.gov.au/sites/default/files/documents/lead-paint-fifth-edition.pdf)) | Assume older paint layers may contain lead and test before sanding or stripping |
| 1989, revised 1994 | First Australian Standard for waterproofing residential wet areas, [AS 3740](https://store.standards.org.au/product/as-3740-1994) | Original bathrooms from before this rely on older methods; check for leaks and when the bathroom was last renewed ([waterproofing guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/bathroom-waterproofing-and-leaking-showers)) |
| Before 1990 | Asbestos-containing building products in widespread use; a national ban followed from 31 December 2003 ([ASSEA](https://www.asbestossafety.gov.au/about-asbestos/finding-asbestos/home)) | Homes built or renovated before 1990 may contain asbestos; only testing confirms it ([asbestos guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/asbestos-in-the-home)) |
| Around 1991 | Safety switches (RCDs) required on power-point circuits of new homes ([Master Electricians Australia](https://treasury.gov.au/sites/default/files/2020-09/115786_MASTER_ELECTRICIANS_AUSTRALIA.pdf)) | Older homes may have no safety switch unless one has been retrofitted ([wiring guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/switchboards-wiring-and-safety-switches)) |
| Around 1997 | Mains-powered smoke alarms required in new homes under the Building Code of Australia (South Australia from 1995) ([Queensland Parliament](https://documents.parliament.qld.gov.au/explore/ResearchPublications/ResearchBriefs/2006/RBR200619.pdf)) | Older homes may rely on battery alarms; state rules on sale and lease vary |
