# Home condition and insurance: the building behind the policy

Your home's construction, age, alterations, hazards and condition can shape insurance questions and terms, but no single defect determines cover or a claim. Describe the property accurately, read the actual policy, keep the rebuild figure current and preserve dated records. Most importantly, separate existing condition and maintenance from the insured event and any resulting damage.

## Research note
Insurance is policy-specific. Moneysmart recommends checking exclusions, rebuilding cost, excesses and the Product Disclosure Statement; it also warns that inadequate sums insured can leave a gap. See [choosing home insurance](https://moneysmart.gov.au/home-insurance/choosing-home-insurance) and [avoiding underinsurance](https://moneysmart.gov.au/home-insurance/home-underinsurance).

## Opening
### Tell the story of your home clearly
- **Describe:** Describe it straight: construction, occupancy, works, hazards
- **Insure:** Know what it is insured for, and what the fine print excludes
- **Document:** Keep dated evidence before anything goes wrong

_The policy wording has the final word. Make sure you have read it._

## Start with two different questions
Building condition and insurance overlap, but they are not the same subject. A building assessment asks **what is this asset, what condition is it in and what may it need?** Insurance asks **what risks has this insurer agreed to cover, on what terms, for what amount and subject to what exclusions, limits and conditions?** Good decisions require both questions to be answered separately before they are brought together.

[Moneysmart](https://moneysmart.gov.au/home-insurance/choosing-home-insurance) recommends comparing the definition of the building, insured events, exclusions, limits, excesses and optional covers in the actual policy. It also recommends an insurance amount that reflects the cost to rebuild the home rather than its market value.

> Important: A crack, leak, old roof or renovation does not by itself tell you whether an insurer will offer cover, change the premium or pay a future claim. Those are policy- and fact-specific insurance questions. Building evidence helps describe the risk; the insurer and policy determine the insurance response.

## How the physical home enters an insurance decision
When quoting or underwriting, an insurer may ask about the address, construction, roof material, year built, occupancy, use, renovations, security, claims history, local hazards or other property characteristics. Different insurers ask different questions and have different underwriting appetites. The practical rule is simple: **describe the actual property accurately and answer the questions asked**.

For consumer insurance contracts, the [Insurance Contracts Act 1984](https://www.legislation.gov.au/C2004A02944/2024-03-01/text) imposes a duty to take reasonable care not to make a misrepresentation to the insurer. That is more precise than a vague instruction to volunteer everything you can think of: read the insurer's questions carefully, answer them accurately and ask the insurer or broker if you are unsure how a property feature should be described.

## Six insurance questions every building raises
**Where building evidence fits into the insurance decision**

| Question | Useful property evidence | What actually controls the answer |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Will this insurer offer cover? | Address, use, construction, age, alterations, hazard context, condition information and claims history where asked | The insurer’s underwriting criteria and the answers given. |
| What counts as the insured building? | Plans, building description, fixtures, outbuildings, pools, solar and other improvements | The policy definition of home/building and the schedule. |
| Which events are covered? | Property hazard context and the risks you want protected | The insured-event definitions, optional covers, exclusions, limits and endorsements. |
| How much should the building be insured for? | Dimensions, construction, finishes, slope/access, demolition and rebuild complexity | The chosen cover basis, calculator/professional estimate, policy limits and any additional or extended cover. |
| What existing condition or maintenance matters? | Inspection reports, dated photos, maintenance history and known defects | The insurer’s questions, policy wording, exclusions, conditions and the facts of any later claim. |
| What evidence would support a future claim? | Baseline photos, invoices, permits, reports, repair history and event records | Cause of loss, what the policy covers, evidence of pre-loss condition and the insurer’s assessment. |

## Separate four things that are often blurred together
**Condition is not the same thing as an insured event**

| Concept | What it means in building terms | Insurance question to ask |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Existing condition | The state of the building before the event: age, cracking, corrosion, deterioration, prior damage, defects or repairs. | Did the insurer ask about it, and how does the policy treat pre-existing damage or condition? |
| Maintenance / gradual deterioration | Work or degradation that develops through use, weathering, wear, blocked drainage, sealant failure, corrosion or similar processes. | What maintenance, wear, deterioration or gradual-damage exclusions/conditions apply? |
| Insured event | A defined occurrence such as storm, fire, flood or another event listed by the policy. | Does the policy cover this event at this address, and how is the event defined? |
| Resulting damage | Damage that follows an event or condition, sometimes involving several causes at once. | Which part of the damage is attributed to a covered event, which part to excluded condition/deterioration, and what evidence supports that causation? |

The difficult claim is often not about whether damage exists; it is about **why it happened**. A roof may be old and a storm may also occur. A pipe may fail and surrounding materials may already have long-term moisture damage. The policy response turns on the facts, causation and wording, which is why dated condition records can be so useful.

## Read building systems through an insurance lens, carefully
**Physical evidence that may justify an insurance question**

| Building area | Condition evidence to understand | Why it may matter | What not to assume |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Roof and rainwater goods | Age/material, corrosion, broken tiles/sheets, flashings, gutters, downpipes, prior leaks | Weather resistance, maintenance history and the condition present before any future storm or water event | An old roof is not automatically uninsurable and a leak is not automatically an insured loss. |
| Drainage and site water | Surface falls, ponding, blocked drains, low points, retaining walls and discharge paths | Water entry and storm performance can involve both event severity and property condition | Site drainage observations do not determine flood/storm coverage. Read the policy definitions. |
| [Cracking and movement](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/cracks-structural-or-cosmetic) | Location, width, pattern, history, distortion and prior repair | Pre-existing movement can be important context if later damage occurs | A crack does not establish cause, structural significance or insurance response. |
| [Wet areas and moisture](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/damp-and-moisture-in-your-home) | Failed sealants, grout, membranes, plumbing leaks, damp staining and repair history | Long-term leakage and sudden events can look similar after damage has spread | Visible moisture does not establish whether the cause is covered. |
| Electrical systems | Age, alterations, visible defects, switchboard and available certificates | Safety, property description and renovation history may matter to underwriting questions | A building assessment is not an electrical safety certificate. Use a licensed electrician where needed. |
| Plumbing and hot water | Pipe materials, age, leaks, corrosion, heater age/location and repair history | A later escape-of-liquid claim may turn on event and causation evidence | Old plumbing is not itself proof of a future claim outcome. |
| Timber and pests | Termite evidence, decay, subfloor moisture and previous treatment | Existing damage may be relevant to condition and maintenance rather than a later insured event | Do not infer pest absence from a clean-looking room or general inspection. |
| Renovations and additions | What changed, when, by whom, approvals, certificates and before/after records | Alterations can change value, occupancy, construction and the building description | Approval evidence does not prove present condition; missing paperwork does not by itself determine cover. |
| Pools, solar and outbuildings | Presence, type, age, structures, equipment and attachment to the property | They may be treated differently under the policy definition of building or optional cover | Do not assume every improvement is covered in the same way. Check the policy. |

## Before you buy, test insurability as part of due diligence
If insurance availability, exclusions or price would affect your decision to buy, obtain an **address-specific quote before you commit**. This is particularly sensible where the property has unusual construction, extensive renovation, heritage fabric, unresolved defects, significant flood/bushfire/cyclone exposure or another feature you already know may require explanation.

1. **Describe the property accurately:** construction, roof, use, occupancy, renovations, pools, solar, outbuildings and other details the insurer asks about.
2. **Ask about the risks that matter at this address:** especially flood, bushfire, cyclone, storm, actions of the sea or other locally relevant hazards.
3. **Read the PDS and Key Facts Sheet:** do not compare premium alone; compare event definitions, exclusions, limits, excesses and optional covers.
4. **Check the rebuild basis:** make sure the insured amount reflects reconstruction rather than purchase price or land value.
5. **Raise known unusual features or unresolved questions:** ask the insurer or licensed broker how they want the property described and keep important answers in writing.

One distinction matters more than any other: policies and warranties generally respond to sudden events and defective work, not to wear and tear or gradual deterioration. [QBCC's maintenance guide](https://www.qbcc.qld.gov.au/sites/default/files/documents/guide-essential-home-maintenance.pdf) makes the same point about home warranty cover, which does not extend to damage from wear and tear, gradual deterioration or lack of maintenance. A maintenance record is therefore part of your insurance evidence, not just good housekeeping; see [the maintenance guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/the-maintenance-that-prevents-the-big-bills).

## Describe the actual home, not a generic version of it
A surprising amount of insurance quality starts with an accurate property description. Construction type, roof material, year built, occupancy, business use, short-term letting, security, renovations, pools, solar systems, outbuildings and past losses can all be relevant if the insurer asks about them. If you do not know whether the walls are brick veneer, double brick, lightweight cladding or another system, use plans, reports or qualified assessment rather than guessing.

The same applies to alterations. A property advertised as renovated may contain work from several different periods. Keep permits, plans, invoices, certificates and photographs where available so the description of the home can be anchored to evidence rather than memory.

## Read exclusions and conditions against the building you actually own
Policies cover defined risks and also contain exclusions, limits and conditions. [Moneysmart](https://moneysmart.gov.au/home-insurance/choosing-home-insurance) recommends checking what is and is not covered in the PDS. Depending on the policy, wording can address matters such as wear, gradual deterioration, defects, vermin, ground movement, water damage, maintenance, vacancy or unoccupied periods. The wording varies, so a generic list is never a substitute for the actual policy.

The right question is not 'does insurance cover leaks?' or 'does insurance cover cracks?' in the abstract. Ask: **what caused this damage, what event does the policy define, what exclusions or conditions apply, and what evidence establishes the timeline and cause?**

## Set the rebuild basis from the building, not the property price
Home building insurance is about repairing or rebuilding the insured structure, not replacing the land or reproducing the market price. [Moneysmart warns that underinsurance can leave a household unable to meet the full rebuild cost](https://moneysmart.gov.au/home-insurance/home-underinsurance) and recommends reviewing cover as costs and the property change.

**Inputs that can move a rebuild estimate**

| Input | Why it matters to reconstruction |
| --- | --- |
| Floor area and building form | More area, levels, complex geometry and attached structures change quantities and access. |
| Construction and finishes | Masonry, lightweight systems, heritage fabric, custom joinery and higher-grade finishes can carry different replacement costs. |
| Site access and slope | Restricted access, steep sites, retaining and difficult demolition can materially change rebuild logistics. |
| Demolition and debris removal | A total-loss rebuild often includes work before new construction can begin. |
| Professional and statutory costs | Design, engineering, approvals and other professional/statutory inputs may be relevant depending on the loss and policy. |
| Code and standard changes | Reconstruction may need to satisfy requirements different from those applying when the original building was built. |
| Pools, garages, decks, solar and other structures | Whether and how these are included depends on the policy definition and selected cover. |
| Cost escalation after a disaster | Demand, labour and material constraints can change actual reconstruction cost; check whether the policy provides any additional/extended cover. |

Use a detailed insurer or industry calculator and keep the inputs. Consider a professional rebuild estimate for heritage, high-value, unusual, extensively altered or otherwise complex buildings.

## Hazard risk and building condition are different layers
Flood, storm, bushfire, cyclone and other natural hazards are address-specific exposures. Building condition influences how a home may perform, but hazard exposure is not established by a building inspection alone. [Moneysmart's storm, flood and fire guidance](https://moneysmart.gov.au/home-insurance/storm-flood-and-fire-insurance) recommends checking local hazard information and the policy definition of the event. For household and property preparation, use the [extreme-weather guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/preparing-your-home-for-extreme-weather) alongside current local emergency advice.

**Keep hazard, resilience and insurance separate but connected**

| Layer | Question |
| --- | --- |
| Hazard | Can flood, bushfire, cyclone, storm surge or another event affect this address, and at what severity/frequency? |
| Building vulnerability | How might the actual roof, openings, drainage, floor level, materials or surrounding site respond? |
| Resilience | What practical work could reduce damage or improve recovery? |
| Insurance | Does this policy cover the relevant event, at what excess/limit and subject to what definition or exclusion? |

## Renovations change both the asset and the insurance story
Renovations can change occupancy, security, construction, services, value and the period during which parts of a home are open or incomplete. Before significant work begins, tell the insurer or broker what is planned and ask whether the policy continues unchanged, requires an endorsement or excludes/limits part of the construction period. Do the same for extended vacancy, short-term letting, business use or another change where the policy asks you to notify the insurer.

After work is complete, update the rebuild amount and property description where necessary. Keep contracts, approved plans, permits, certificates, warranties, invoices and before/during/after photographs. Those records can explain both **what changed** and **what existed before a later loss**.

## Build an evidence stack before you ever need to claim
- **Identity and construction:** plans, specifications, property description, dimensions and major construction details.
- **Baseline condition:** dated exterior, roof-from-ground, room, wet-area, service and improvement photographs; inspection reports where available.
- **Maintenance:** invoices, service records, cleaning/clearing records where material, repair recommendations and evidence that identified work was completed.
- **Renovations:** contracts, permits, plans, certificates, warranties, product details and before/during/after photographs.
- **Monitoring:** crack measurements, moisture investigations, leak history, pest treatment and other time-series evidence where a condition is being watched.
- **Insurance:** proposal answers, schedules, PDS versions, Key Facts Sheets, endorsements, renewal notices and important written answers from the insurer or broker.
- **Loss:** photographs before clean-up where safe, emergency-work invoices, damaged-item evidence, weather/event information and a contemporaneous timeline of what occurred.

These records do not guarantee a claim. They improve the evidence available to establish what the building was, what work had been done, what condition existed beforehand and how the loss unfolded. Continue with [keeping a record of your home](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/keeping-a-record-of-your-home).

## When a claim happens, preserve cause and timeline
If damage occurs, protect people and prevent further loss where it is safe to do so, then follow the insurer's claim instructions. [Moneysmart's claims guidance](https://moneysmart.gov.au/home-insurance/how-to-make-a-home-insurance-claim) recommends reviewing the policy and keeping records through the claims process. Photographs before clean-up, emergency invoices, dates, communications and any expert reports can help distinguish the event itself from pre-existing or progressive condition.

> Important: The policy schedule, PDS, Key Facts Sheet, endorsements, insurer questions, applicable insurance law and the facts of the loss determine cover. For property-specific insurance advice, confirm the position with the insurer or a licensed insurance broker; for a disputed claim, obtain appropriate specialist or legal advice.

## Frequently asked questions
### Does home insurance cover gradual damage or wear and tear?
Generally not. Policies typically respond to sudden events, while wear and tear, gradual deterioration and lack of maintenance are common exclusions. Check your policy wording, and keep maintenance records that show the home has been looked after.

### Does my home's condition affect my insurance premium?
It can be relevant to underwriting where the insurer asks about condition or related property characteristics, but there is no universal formula. Location, hazard, construction, use, claims history, rebuild cost and insurer appetite can all affect the quote.

### Do I have to tell my insurer about every defect?
For consumer insurance, the legal duty is to take reasonable care not to make a misrepresentation. Answer the insurer’s questions accurately and ask the insurer or broker if you are unsure how a known property feature should be described. Policy notification obligations can also apply after cover starts.

### Does an old roof mean storm damage will not be covered?
Not automatically. The outcome depends on the policy wording and the facts, including the cause of damage and any relevant exclusions or conditions. Evidence of the roof’s pre-loss condition can be important.

### Does insurance cover gradual leaks or failed waterproofing?
Policies differ and causation matters. Check the actual event definitions, water-damage cover, exclusions for wear/gradual deterioration/defects and any maintenance conditions. Do not rely on a generic answer.

### Will maintenance lower my premium?
It may or may not affect price depending on the insurer and measure. The more reliable benefit is reducing avoidable damage and maintaining evidence that the property has been looked after. Ask the insurer before spending money for an assumed premium benefit.

### Does a condition report guarantee a claim will be paid?
No. A report can establish useful evidence about pre-loss condition and timing. The cause, policy wording, exclusions, limits and insurer assessment determine the claim.

### Should I get an insurance quote before buying?
Yes where insurance availability, price or exclusions could affect the purchase decision, particularly for hazard-exposed, heritage, unusual, extensively renovated or defect-affected properties.

### Is the rebuild cost the same as the purchase price?
No. The purchase price includes land and market factors. Building insurance should be based on the cost to repair or rebuild the insured structure and applicable associated costs under the policy.

### How do I avoid underinsurance?
Use a detailed rebuild calculator or professional estimate where appropriate, keep the property inputs accurate, update the amount after renovations and review it regularly as construction costs change.

### Should I tell the insurer before renovating?
For significant work, ask the insurer or broker before work starts whether the proposed renovation changes cover, requires an endorsement or creates a construction-period limitation. Keep the answer and the project records.

### What records are most useful after a claim?
Dated pre-loss photos, maintenance and repair records, renovation documents, policy records, photographs of the damage before clean-up where safe, emergency invoices, communications and a clear event timeline can all help establish what happened.

## Method
We followed the policy the way an insurer reads it: how the property is described, what it is insured for, what is excluded, what upkeep it expects, and what evidence a claim will need.

## Limitations
No record guarantees cover, a cheaper premium or a paid claim. The policy wording and the insurer’s assessment decide; good records just make sure your side of the story is on the table.

## Sources

- [Underinsurance: what it is and how to avoid it](https://moneysmart.gov.au/home-insurance/home-underinsurance) — Moneysmart, Australian Securities and Investments Commission; accessed 2026-07-19
- [Storm, flood and fire insurance](https://moneysmart.gov.au/home-insurance/storm-flood-and-fire-insurance) — Moneysmart, Australian Securities and Investments Commission; accessed 2026-07-19
- [Your essential home maintenance guide](https://www.qbcc.qld.gov.au/sites/default/files/documents/guide-essential-home-maintenance.pdf) — Queensland Building and Construction Commission; accessed 2026-10-14
- [Repairs and maintenance](https://www.yourhome.gov.au/buy-build-renovate/repairs-and-maintenance) — YourHome, Australian Government; accessed 2026-07-19

guides.question: What records should I keep for my home?
guides.title: Home records: what documents to keep for your house
guides.summary: Your future self will thank you for a home record that is easy to search. Keep the plans, permits, invoices, warranties, photographs and reports that explain what changed and who did it.
guides.answer: Keep enough information for someone to answer five questions: what is here, where is it, when did it change, who did the work and what proves it? Save the title and plans, permits, certificates, contracts, invoices, warranties, dated photographs, product details, inspection reports, repair records, insurance documents and useful contacts. A Homechecker Read can hold that record in one place: it keeps the documents and photos you add for the home, and its reading updates as new evidence arrives.
guides.methodology: An evidence-management guide distinguishing original records, scope, chronology and verification. The worked example demonstrates a partial replacement being mistaken for a whole-building history.
guides.limitations: Records can be incomplete, and occasionally wrong. For permits, title, boundaries and present condition, the authority or the professional is the source of truth; the record is your map to them.
guides.researchNote: The document distinctions and index examples are original editorial applications. [Victoria's conveyancing guidance](https://www.consumer.vic.gov.au/housing/buying-and-selling-property/selling-property/conveyancing-and-contracts-for-sellers) anchors the distinction between a private property record and formal sale documentation; it does not prescribe this filing system.

cluster.label: Own, maintain and change
cluster.blurb: Keep useful records, maintain the fabric safely and plan works without over-promising what condition can prove.

sections.heading: Opening
sections.markdown:
### Make the useful things easy to find
- **What:** Plans, permits, invoices, warranties, photos, reports
- **Where:** Tied to a room, an element, a product, a name
- **When:** Dated: done, checked, fixed, and due again

_Keep the originals. And when you are not sure, write down that you are not sure._

Keep the originals, use filenames you can understand at a glance and add a one-page index.

sections.heading: Build a record you will use
sections.markdown:
A useful record is retrievable by any future reader. Every item should answer four fields: **date**, **element or location**, **event or work**, and **source**. Keep the original file with a descriptive filename.

**The minimum home record**

| Folder | Keep | Why it matters |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 01 Property and title | Title, deposited/registered plan, survey, easements, covenants, planning and hazard reports | Defines the land, restrictions and property context |
| 02 Approvals | Planning and building permits, endorsed plans, inspections, occupancy and trade certificates | Records the approval pathway and approved scope |
| 03 Works and products | Contracts, quotes, variations, invoices, warranties, manuals, model numbers, colours and materials | Explains what was installed, by whom and on what terms |
| 04 Condition and reports | Building, pest, engineering, plumbing, electrical, roof, moisture, strata and other reports | Creates dated professional observations and limitations |
| 05 Photographs | Wide and close views before, during and after work; concealed services before closing | Locates evidence and preserves what later becomes hidden |
| 06 Maintenance and monitoring | Service dates, filters, treatments, cleaning, crack or moisture logs and next review | Shows change and keeps recurring tasks visible |
| 07 Insurance and incidents | Schedules, PDS versions, valuations, claims, loss photos and insurer correspondence | Preserves the wording and evidence relevant to a loss |
| 08 Shared building | Plan, by-laws/rules, minutes, budgets, funds, insurance, levies and scheme correspondence | Connects the lot to common-property decisions and costs |
| 09 Contacts | Designer, builder, certifier/surveyor, engineer, trades, insurer, strata manager and warranties | Makes follow-up and responsibility traceable |

### The records that change an assessment most

Some documents carry far more weight than others when a buyer, insurer, inspector or Homechecker Read assesses the home. Chase these first.

**High-value records and what each settles**

| Record | What it can settle | Related guide |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Electrical certificate for work done (names vary by state) | That licensed work was done and when, such as a rewire or switchboard upgrade | [1980s–90s homes](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/homes-1980s-90s) |
| Waterproofing certificate for a bathroom renovation | That a membrane was installed, by whom and when | [Damp and moisture](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/damp-and-moisture-in-your-home) |
| Roof replacement or restoration invoice with scope | Which roof sections were renewed, in what material | [What your home needs by decade](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/what-your-home-needs-by-decade) |
| Termite system installation notice and service records | What protection exists and whether servicing has been kept up | [Maintenance guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/the-maintenance-that-prevents-the-big-bills) |
| Restumping, underpinning or footing repair design and invoice | Where the footings were repaired and to what design | [Cracks guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/cracks-structural-or-cosmetic) |
| As-installed services plan | Where sewer, stormwater, water and gas lines run before anyone digs | Below |
| Asbestos test results | Which materials were tested and the result | [Dated milestones](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/red-flags-by-era#milestones) |

For a newer home, [QBCC's essential home maintenance guide](https://www.qbcc.qld.gov.au/sites/default/files/documents/guide-essential-home-maintenance.pdf) notes that builders should give owners a plan showing the as-installed location of sewer pipes, stormwater drains, water and gas lines. If you have one, it belongs in the record; if you are buying a newer home, ask for it.

sections.heading: Use filenames that sort themselves
sections.markdown: Use ISO dates and plain language: 2026-07-19_roof_north-valley_leak-photo_01.jpg or 2026-08-04_bathroom-waterproofing_certificate.pdf. Add a one-page index with the element, current known status, latest evidence and next action. Keep a cloud copy and a separate backup, with sensitive identity and financial material protected.

sections.heading: Take photographs that will still help later
sections.markdown:
1. **Orient:** one wide photograph showing the room, elevation or element.
2. **Locate:** a mid-range view connecting the issue to a window, corner, joint or service.
3. **Detail:** a clear close view with a scale where dimension matters.
4. **Date and describe:** weather/event, direction, dimensions and whether the condition changed.
5. **During work:** capture framing, membranes, flashings, pipes and cables before they are concealed.
6. **Close out:** finished work, invoice, specification, certificate and warranty in the same indexed folder.

sections.heading: Record uncertainty explicitly
sections.markdown: Write 'installation date unknown' or 'reported by previous owner, unverified' where appropriate. A receipt records a purchase; a permit records an approval; a photograph records what the frame caught that day. Let each document say only what it truly knows.

sections.heading: Update at decision moments
sections.markdown:
- **On purchase:** save the contract/disclosure, reports and a dated baseline.
- **Before work:** save approvals, condition photos, service locations and insurer advice.
- **During work:** variations, concealed work and inspection evidence.
- **At completion:** certificates, final plans, warranties, manuals and a next-maintenance date.
- **After an event:** safe pre-clean-up evidence, emergency work and the claim timeline.
- **At sale:** copy the releasable, accurate set for legal review; retain sensitive or irrelevant material separately.

sections.heading: Keep the record and the reading together
sections.markdown:
A folder of documents tells you what you have. It does not tell you what they mean for the house together. This is what a [Homechecker Read](https://homechecker.com.au/) is built for. A Read is a desktop reading of one home: its era, construction, likely needs and what is worth confirming in person, drawn from public records, imagery and anything you upload. Reads never expire, and you can add documents or photos at any time, such as a roof invoice, a new inspection report, a waterproofing certificate or photos from your own walk-around. The Read updates wherever the new evidence reaches.

Used this way, a Read becomes a living home record. The documents sit with the home they belong to, and each one is read against everything else you know about the house. That is useful at the decision moments above: after purchase, before and after works, after a storm and when you come to sell. It stays a desktop reading. It records and interprets evidence, and it does not replace a physical inspection, a certificate or a specialist's assessment where one is needed.

**Adding to a Read at each decision moment**

| Moment | What to add | What it helps the Read answer |
| --- | --- | --- |
| After purchase | The contract, disclosure documents and any inspection reports | Which findings to act on first and what to budget for |
| After works | Invoices, certificates, warranties and completion photos | What changed, what is now newer and what is still original |
| After an event | Dated photos and repair invoices | What was affected and whether the repair reached the cause |
| Before selling | The record built up over the years | A clear, dated account of the home and its work |

sections.heading: The limits of a home record
sections.markdown: A good record shortens every future search and supports the insurance, maintenance, renovation and [sale decisions](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/selling-your-home) to come. Verify current condition and legal effect for the decision in front of you. For insurance-specific use, read [home condition and insurance](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/home-condition-and-insurance); for works, read [planning a renovation](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/planning-a-renovation).

sections.heading: Give each record a job
sections.markdown:
The index should help someone make a decision without opening every attachment. Give each item an identifier and record the question it answers. A roof invoice might establish a contractor and billed scope; it may not identify the actual sheet product, show concealed flashings or establish that a later leak has the same cause. Connect the invoice to the accepted quotation, variations and completion evidence instead of calling the whole folder 'roof fixed'.

**What a record establishes, and what still needs checking**

| Record | Useful evidence | Unresolved question |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Approval or endorsed plan | The authorised proposal and conditions recorded by that document | Was that version built, and what completion evidence applies? |
| Invoice and payment | Billed work and payment history | Which locations and components were actually included? |
| Photograph during work | Visible details at a particular stage | What sits outside the frame or was altered afterwards? |
| Trade or specialist report | Findings within its date, scope and access | Were exclusions investigated and recommendations completed? |
| Warranty | Stated provider, product or work and contractual terms | Does it apply to this defect, owner and maintenance history? |

For example, [Victoria's seller guidance](https://www.consumer.vic.gov.au/housing/buying-and-selling-property/selling-property/conveyancing-and-contracts-for-sellers) describes a legal disclosure document with prescribed information. A private home index is useful preparation for that process; it does not replace the required documents or professional review.

sections.heading: Separate the three dates
sections.markdown:
The event date, document date and date you received the file may differ. An invoice issued in March can describe February work; a photograph uploaded in June may have been taken years earlier. Record the distinction when it matters. If the only known date is the email date, say so. Do not rename an uncertain photograph in a way that invents an inspection date.

Keep the original email and attachments when they establish who supplied information or qualify a claim. Store a corrected version beside the superseded one with a short explanation, rather than silently replacing it. A summary can change as evidence improves while the original remains an accurate record of what was said then. This is especially useful where a contractor first suspects one cause and later identifies another.

sections.heading: Close the loop without overstating success
sections.markdown:
A useful repair history has five links: symptom, investigation, agreed scope, completion evidence and subsequent performance. Mark each separately. 'Invoice received' is not the same status as 'recommended work completed'; 'completed' is not the same as 'no recurrence after comparable weather'. If follow-up has not happened, leave it open with the next useful observation or professional review.

Tie location names to a simple plan. 'Bathroom' becomes ambiguous after an extension adds another one. Identify the room, wall or roof section consistently across quotes and photographs. For concealed work, ask the responsible contractor to supply the relevant evidence while access exists. Never enter an unsafe work area just to improve the record. See [renovation planning](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/planning-a-renovation) for agreeing handover information before construction.

sections.heading: Reconstruct gaps and prepare a useful handover
sections.markdown:
When records are missing, begin with the actual question: installation age, approval status, recurring damage or maintenance requirement. Ask the previous owner, contractor, authority or scheme for the relevant material, noting where it came from. A new inspection can establish present observations but cannot recreate unseen historic work. Mark estimates and conflicting accounts instead of choosing the most reassuring version.

Prepare a portable index and readable copies, so the record remains useful if a particular account or app closes. Check that a backup can actually be opened. Keep personal identity papers, banking details and unrelated correspondence out of a general property handover. Where a report has distribution or reliance terms, retain them with the report and obtain advice before circulating it. For a strata lot, reference the scheme's current record and custodian; a downloaded copy may become stale.

sections.heading: Worked example: the roof was replaced, but which roof?
sections.markdown:
**Illustrative reasoning example, not an inspected property.** An owner has a 2022 invoice headed 'roof replacement', two finished photographs and a new stain at the rear addition. The family history has become 'all the roof is four years old'.

The invoice's detailed scope covers the front pitched roof. The photographs show that section only. A later email excludes the rear low-pitch addition. The supported record is a documented front-roof replacement; the rear roof's installation date remains unknown. Neither the invoice nor the stain diagnoses the present water-entry path.

Update the index with separate roof locations, retain the excluded-scope email and arrange a current assessment of the rear symptom. If a quotation follows, attach it to that investigation. The record now helps the professional avoid assuming a single-age roof, without pretending to establish a cause remotely.

Keep conclusions at the level the evidence supports: observed, reported, inferred or confirmed. An unavailable document is a gap in the record; it does not prove the work was never done.

> Note: The best record is modest and precise: original evidence, clear dates, known limits and an explicit next action. That is more credible than a polished history that hides uncertainty.

guides.contentMarkdown:
# Home records: what documents to keep for your house

Keep enough information for someone to answer five questions: what is here, where is it, when did it change, who did the work and what proves it? Save the title and plans, permits, certificates, contracts, invoices, warranties, dated photographs, product details, inspection reports, repair records, insurance documents and useful contacts. A Homechecker Read can hold that record in one place: it keeps the documents and photos you add for the home, and its reading updates as new evidence arrives.

## Research note
The document distinctions and index examples are original editorial applications. [Victoria's conveyancing guidance](https://www.consumer.vic.gov.au/housing/buying-and-selling-property/selling-property/conveyancing-and-contracts-for-sellers) anchors the distinction between a private property record and formal sale documentation; it does not prescribe this filing system.

## Opening
### Make the useful things easy to find
- **What:** Plans, permits, invoices, warranties, photos, reports
- **Where:** Tied to a room, an element, a product, a name
- **When:** Dated: done, checked, fixed, and due again

_Keep the originals. And when you are not sure, write down that you are not sure._

Keep the originals, use filenames you can understand at a glance and add a one-page index.

## Build a record you will use
A useful record is retrievable by any future reader. Every item should answer four fields: **date**, **element or location**, **event or work**, and **source**. Keep the original file with a descriptive filename.

**The minimum home record**

| Folder | Keep | Why it matters |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 01 Property and title | Title, deposited/registered plan, survey, easements, covenants, planning and hazard reports | Defines the land, restrictions and property context |
| 02 Approvals | Planning and building permits, endorsed plans, inspections, occupancy and trade certificates | Records the approval pathway and approved scope |
| 03 Works and products | Contracts, quotes, variations, invoices, warranties, manuals, model numbers, colours and materials | Explains what was installed, by whom and on what terms |
| 04 Condition and reports | Building, pest, engineering, plumbing, electrical, roof, moisture, strata and other reports | Creates dated professional observations and limitations |
| 05 Photographs | Wide and close views before, during and after work; concealed services before closing | Locates evidence and preserves what later becomes hidden |
| 06 Maintenance and monitoring | Service dates, filters, treatments, cleaning, crack or moisture logs and next review | Shows change and keeps recurring tasks visible |
| 07 Insurance and incidents | Schedules, PDS versions, valuations, claims, loss photos and insurer correspondence | Preserves the wording and evidence relevant to a loss |
| 08 Shared building | Plan, by-laws/rules, minutes, budgets, funds, insurance, levies and scheme correspondence | Connects the lot to common-property decisions and costs |
| 09 Contacts | Designer, builder, certifier/surveyor, engineer, trades, insurer, strata manager and warranties | Makes follow-up and responsibility traceable |

### The records that change an assessment most

Some documents carry far more weight than others when a buyer, insurer, inspector or Homechecker Read assesses the home. Chase these first.

**High-value records and what each settles**

| Record | What it can settle | Related guide |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Electrical certificate for work done (names vary by state) | That licensed work was done and when, such as a rewire or switchboard upgrade | [1980s–90s homes](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/homes-1980s-90s) |
| Waterproofing certificate for a bathroom renovation | That a membrane was installed, by whom and when | [Damp and moisture](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/damp-and-moisture-in-your-home) |
| Roof replacement or restoration invoice with scope | Which roof sections were renewed, in what material | [What your home needs by decade](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/what-your-home-needs-by-decade) |
| Termite system installation notice and service records | What protection exists and whether servicing has been kept up | [Maintenance guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/the-maintenance-that-prevents-the-big-bills) |
| Restumping, underpinning or footing repair design and invoice | Where the footings were repaired and to what design | [Cracks guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/cracks-structural-or-cosmetic) |
| As-installed services plan | Where sewer, stormwater, water and gas lines run before anyone digs | Below |
| Asbestos test results | Which materials were tested and the result | [Dated milestones](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/red-flags-by-era#milestones) |

For a newer home, [QBCC's essential home maintenance guide](https://www.qbcc.qld.gov.au/sites/default/files/documents/guide-essential-home-maintenance.pdf) notes that builders should give owners a plan showing the as-installed location of sewer pipes, stormwater drains, water and gas lines. If you have one, it belongs in the record; if you are buying a newer home, ask for it.

## Use filenames that sort themselves
Use ISO dates and plain language: 2026-07-19_roof_north-valley_leak-photo_01.jpg or 2026-08-04_bathroom-waterproofing_certificate.pdf. Add a one-page index with the element, current known status, latest evidence and next action. Keep a cloud copy and a separate backup, with sensitive identity and financial material protected.

## Take photographs that will still help later
1. **Orient:** one wide photograph showing the room, elevation or element.
2. **Locate:** a mid-range view connecting the issue to a window, corner, joint or service.
3. **Detail:** a clear close view with a scale where dimension matters.
4. **Date and describe:** weather/event, direction, dimensions and whether the condition changed.
5. **During work:** capture framing, membranes, flashings, pipes and cables before they are concealed.
6. **Close out:** finished work, invoice, specification, certificate and warranty in the same indexed folder.

## Record uncertainty explicitly
Write 'installation date unknown' or 'reported by previous owner, unverified' where appropriate. A receipt records a purchase; a permit records an approval; a photograph records what the frame caught that day. Let each document say only what it truly knows.

## Update at decision moments
- **On purchase:** save the contract/disclosure, reports and a dated baseline.
- **Before work:** save approvals, condition photos, service locations and insurer advice.
- **During work:** variations, concealed work and inspection evidence.
- **At completion:** certificates, final plans, warranties, manuals and a next-maintenance date.
- **After an event:** safe pre-clean-up evidence, emergency work and the claim timeline.
- **At sale:** copy the releasable, accurate set for legal review; retain sensitive or irrelevant material separately.

## Keep the record and the reading together
A folder of documents tells you what you have. It does not tell you what they mean for the house together. This is what a [Homechecker Read](https://homechecker.com.au/) is built for. A Read is a desktop reading of one home: its era, construction, likely needs and what is worth confirming in person, drawn from public records, imagery and anything you upload. Reads never expire, and you can add documents or photos at any time, such as a roof invoice, a new inspection report, a waterproofing certificate or photos from your own walk-around. The Read updates wherever the new evidence reaches.

Used this way, a Read becomes a living home record. The documents sit with the home they belong to, and each one is read against everything else you know about the house. That is useful at the decision moments above: after purchase, before and after works, after a storm and when you come to sell. It stays a desktop reading. It records and interprets evidence, and it does not replace a physical inspection, a certificate or a specialist's assessment where one is needed.

**Adding to a Read at each decision moment**

| Moment | What to add | What it helps the Read answer |
| --- | --- | --- |
| After purchase | The contract, disclosure documents and any inspection reports | Which findings to act on first and what to budget for |
| After works | Invoices, certificates, warranties and completion photos | What changed, what is now newer and what is still original |
| After an event | Dated photos and repair invoices | What was affected and whether the repair reached the cause |
| Before selling | The record built up over the years | A clear, dated account of the home and its work |

## The limits of a home record
A good record shortens every future search and supports the insurance, maintenance, renovation and [sale decisions](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/selling-your-home) to come. Verify current condition and legal effect for the decision in front of you. For insurance-specific use, read [home condition and insurance](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/home-condition-and-insurance); for works, read [planning a renovation](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/planning-a-renovation).

## Give each record a job
The index should help someone make a decision without opening every attachment. Give each item an identifier and record the question it answers. A roof invoice might establish a contractor and billed scope; it may not identify the actual sheet product, show concealed flashings or establish that a later leak has the same cause. Connect the invoice to the accepted quotation, variations and completion evidence instead of calling the whole folder 'roof fixed'.

**What a record establishes, and what still needs checking**

| Record | Useful evidence | Unresolved question |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Approval or endorsed plan | The authorised proposal and conditions recorded by that document | Was that version built, and what completion evidence applies? |
| Invoice and payment | Billed work and payment history | Which locations and components were actually included? |
| Photograph during work | Visible details at a particular stage | What sits outside the frame or was altered afterwards? |
| Trade or specialist report | Findings within its date, scope and access | Were exclusions investigated and recommendations completed? |
| Warranty | Stated provider, product or work and contractual terms | Does it apply to this defect, owner and maintenance history? |

For example, [Victoria's seller guidance](https://www.consumer.vic.gov.au/housing/buying-and-selling-property/selling-property/conveyancing-and-contracts-for-sellers) describes a legal disclosure document with prescribed information. A private home index is useful preparation for that process; it does not replace the required documents or professional review.

## Separate the three dates

## Reconstruct gaps and prepare a useful handover
When records are missing, begin with the actual question: installation age, approval status, recurring damage or maintenance requirement. A new inspection can establish present observations but cannot recreate unseen historic work. Mark estimates and conflicting accounts instead of choosing the most reassuring version.

guides.question: What does a home need as it ages, decade by decade?
guides.title: What your home needs by decade, and how to plan ahead
guides.summary: A home's age gives you a useful starting point, not a replacement schedule. Separate the original shell from later work, track each major system by its own date and condition, and turn uncertainty into a practical evidence and renewal plan.
guides.answer: Use the build date to choose the first questions, then build a timeline for the actual house. Separate the original structure from later roofs, wet areas, services, windows, insulation and extensions. For each major element, record what is installed, when it was installed or repaired, what evidence exists, how it is performing now and what consequence failure would have. That produces a much better plan than generic lifespan tables.
guides.methodology: We use age to choose the first questions, then separate five timelines: original shell, renewals, alterations, defects/repairs and shared-building history. Each major element is then judged by installed system, date, exposure, maintenance, current evidence, uncertainty and decision consequence.
guides.limitations: Era profiles are national screening tools. Regional construction, climate, soil, exposure and alteration history can outweigh the decade. Generic lifespan or cost bands do not establish the remaining life or repair scope of a specific element.
guides.researchNote: The build date is a routing clue, not a replacement schedule. Australian Government guidance supports building-and-pest inspection of structural, damp, drainage, waterproofing and termite risk, while its maintenance, insulation and renovation guidance shows why later work must be read with the system already in the house. Use the [YourHome existing-house guide](https://www.yourhome.gov.au/buy-build-renovate/buying-existing-house) as the national starting point.

sections.heading: Opening
sections.markdown:
### Give every system its own clock
- **Original shell:** What the first build still contributes to structure, water and access
- **Later layers:** Renewals, alterations and repairs, each with their own date
- **Decision:** Current evidence, uncertainty and consequence deciding what comes next

_The address has one build date. The building can have a dozen useful ages._

sections.heading: Age is a prior, not a programme
sections.markdown:
The year on the listing is useful because it narrows the likely construction systems and the questions worth asking first. It does not tell you which parts are original, which parts have already been renewed, or what condition they are in today. A 1910 frontage can sit over a restumped subfloor, a 2004 roof and a 2019 bathroom. A 1970s house can have a newer extension and old stormwater. A 2012 apartment can already have a decade of defect, waterproofing or cladding history in the scheme records.

Listing years are often estimates. [Working out when a house was built](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/when-was-my-house-built) shows how to check the date against council records, aerial photographs and the building itself, and how to date later additions separately.

The Australian Government's [YourHome guidance for existing houses](https://www.yourhome.gov.au/buy-build-renovate/buying-existing-house) recommends looking at structural, damp, drainage, waterproofing and termite risk and using qualified building and pest inspection where needed. Era helps you aim that work. The property-specific records and physical evidence decide what is actually there.

> Note: A useful age clue should change the evidence you seek, the inspection brief or the decision you make. If it changes none of those, it is probably just a label.

sections.heading: Build five timelines before you forecast anything
sections.markdown:
**One address can contain several different ages**

| Timeline | What belongs on it | Why it matters |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Original shell | Footings, floor, frame or masonry walls, roof structure and original drainage layout | These elements often set the basic movement, moisture and access behaviour of the home. |

sections.markdown:
A buyer needs to know which findings are routine, which need investigation and which could change the capital story. Generic national dollar bands can be misleading because access, extent, finish, location and concealed damage change scope quickly. A more robust first pass is to classify the decision consequence.

**A practical significance scale before you have a defined scope and quote**

| Significance | What it means | Next move |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Routine upkeep | Known maintenance with limited uncertainty and no evidence of wider damage | Schedule it and keep the record. |
| Investigate before relying | The symptom could have more than one cause or the concealed extent matters | Obtain targeted inspection, testing or opening-up before pricing the solution. |

sections.heading: Turn the evidence into a renewal register

**A simple evidence-led capital register**

| Field | Example entry |
| --- | --- |
| Element | North roof slope and box gutter |
| System / material | Metal sheet roof; concealed box gutter |
| Known date / source | Roof invoice dated 2004; gutter date unknown |
| Current evidence | No internal stain; corrosion at two gutter joints |
| Uncertainty / access | Valley concealed from ground; no recent roof inspection |

faqs.question: What changed in Australian homes by decade?
faqs.answer: Key dated changes include lead paint before 1970, the first wet-area waterproofing standard in 1989, asbestos products before about 1990 (banned from 2003), safety switches on power circuits from around 1991, mains-powered smoke alarms from around 1997, and a 7-star energy minimum from October 2023.

faqs.question: How long do houses last?
faqs.answer: Australian Government guidance says many homes can remain in use for 50 or 100 years. Continued use depends on maintenance, adaptation and renewal of individual systems rather than one expiry date for the whole house.

faqs.question: Can a build date tell me what needs replacing?
faqs.answer: It can suggest the first questions. Replacement planning should use the actual installed system, its installation or alteration date, exposure, maintenance, current condition and failure consequence.

faqs.question: Why is renovation history as important as the build date?
faqs.answer: Because roofs, bathrooms, wiring, plumbing, windows, extensions and insulation can each belong to a different decade. Later work creates its own material, approval and condition history.

faqs.question: Should I use generic component lifespan tables?
faqs.answer: Use them as prompts, not conclusions. Property-specific inspection evidence, installation records and manufacturer or specialist guidance are stronger evidence for planning work.

faqs.question: How should I budget by era?
faqs.answer: Create an element register with known dates, current evidence, uncertainty, decision significance, next action and quotations where the scope is defined. Separate routine maintenance from major capital renewal.

faqs.question: What is the asbestos date for an Australian home?
faqs.answer: Homes built or renovated before 1990 may contain asbestos-containing materials, while all uses were prohibited nationally from 31 December 2003. Identify suspect material before disturbance rather than relying on age alone.

faqs.question: Does an older home always cost more?
faqs.answer: No. A well-renewed older home can have modest near-term needs, while a newer building can carry expensive defects or shared-building liabilities. Cost follows scope, condition, responsibility and uncertainty, not age alone.

faqs.question: How do regional differences affect era patterns?
faqs.answer: Climate, soil, hazards, exposure, local construction practice and alterations can materially change the profile. Combine era with the actual property and location.

Key dated changes include lead paint before 1970, the first wet-area waterproofing standard in 1989, asbestos products before about 1990 (banned from 2003), safety switches on power circuits from around 1991, mains-powered smoke alarms from around 1997, and a 7-star energy minimum from October 2023.

### How long do houses last?
Australian Government guidance says many homes can remain in use for 50 or 100 years. Continued use depends on maintenance, adaptation and renewal of individual systems rather than one expiry date for the whole house.

### Can a build date tell me what needs replacing?
It can suggest the first questions. Replacement planning should use the actual installed system, its installation or alteration date, exposure, maintenance, current condition and failure consequence.

### Why is renovation history as important as the build date?
Because roofs, bathrooms, wiring, plumbing, windows, extensions and insulation can each belong to a different decade. Later work creates its own material, approval and condition history.

### Should I use generic component lifespan tables?
Use them as prompts, not conclusions. Property-specific inspection evidence, installation records and manufacturer or specialist guidance are stronger evidence for planning work.

### How should I budget by era?
Create an element register with known dates, current evidence, uncertainty, decision significance, next action and quotations where the scope is defined. Separate routine maintenance from major capital renewal.

### What is the asbestos date for an Australian home?
Homes built or renovated before 1990 may contain asbestos-containing materials, while all uses were prohibited nationally from 31 December 2003. Identify suspect material before disturbance rather than relying on age alone.

### Does an older home always cost more?
No. A well-renewed older home can have modest near-term needs, while a newer building can carry expensive defects or shared-building liabilities. Cost follows scope, condition, responsibility and uncertainty, not age alone.

### How do regional differences affect era patterns?
Climate, soil, hazards, exposure, local construction practice and alterations can materially change the profile. Combine era with the actual property and location.

## Method
We use age to choose the first questions, then separate five timelines: original shell, renewals, alterations, defects/repairs and shared-building history. Each major element is then judged by installed system, date, exposure, maintenance, current evidence, uncertainty and decision consequence.

## Limitations
Era profiles are national screening tools. Regional construction, climate, soil, exposure and alteration history can outweigh the decade. Generic lifespan or cost bands do not establish the remaining life or repair scope of a specific element.
