cluster.label: Own, maintain and change
cluster.blurb: Keep useful records, maintain the fabric safely and plan works without over-promising what condition can prove.

sections.heading: Opening
sections.markdown:
### Help the house shed, drain and dry
- **Shed:** Roof, flashings and cladding turning rain away
- **Drain:** Gutters, downpipes and falls carrying water to the proper discharge
- **Dry:** Drying paths, safe clearances and prompt attention to leaks

_Maintenance can extend service life and reduce avoidable damage. Keep renewal in the plan._

Walk around the home regularly enough to notice change, and keep separate future allowances for the roof, wiring, plumbing, waterproofing and footings.

sections.heading: Observation, maintenance, inspection and renewal are different
sections.markdown:
**Name the job correctly before budgeting it**

| Job | Purpose | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Observe | Notice change without unsafe access or diagnosis | Photograph a stain, crack or overflowing downpipe with a date |
| Maintain | Keep a serviceable element operating as intended | Clean an accessible drain or renew a failed seal with the correct system |
| Inspect / service | Use a competent person to test or access a risk area | Roof inspection, termite inspection or licensed electrical check |
| Renew | Replace an element that has failed, is obsolete or has reached condition-based end of service | Re-roofing, switchboard upgrade, membrane replacement or footing repair |

Routine maintenance slows avoidable deterioration. Capital renewal covers major work driven by age, condition and evidence: re-roofing, wiring upgrades, renewed membranes or footing repairs where they are needed. Budget it separately because its timing and cost behave differently.

sections.heading: Follow the water path
sections.markdown: Trace rain from the roof surface through valleys, flashings, gutters, downpipes, stormwater connection, surface falls and lawful discharge. Then check walls, openings, balconies, wet areas, plumbing and subfloor. Investigate staining, salt, soft timber, corrosion, musty odour, lifted finishes or ponding using [the damp and moisture guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/damp-and-moisture-in-your-home).

sections.heading: A safe rhythm that works
sections.markdown:
**Adapt intervals to exposure, material and manufacturer guidance**

| Element | Owner observation | Professional or trade trigger |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Roof and rainwater goods | From ground after heavy rain: overflow, sagging, displaced material, staining | Unsafe access, leaks, storm damage, deteriorated flashings or unclear roof condition |
| Ground and drainage | Ponding, erosion, blocked grates, discharge toward the building | Persistent water, subsidence, failed drains or a change needing hydraulic/civil advice |
| Wet areas and plumbing | Loose finishes, failed sealant, swelling, stains, odour or unexplained meter use | Recurring moisture, suspected concealed leak or waterproofing failure |
| Timber and subfloor | Vent openings clear; no obvious soil contact or new damage from safe areas | Restricted/unsafe access, pest evidence, damp timber or structural change |
| Electrical and fire safety | Use test buttons and replace alarms as required by local rules/manufacturer | Any electrical defect, shock, heat, burning smell, old installation concern or required licensed work |
| [Cracks and movement](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/cracks-structural-or-cosmetic) | Dated photos with a stable reference point; note doors, floors and weather | Progression, displacement, repeated repair failure or associated distortion |

### A year at a glance

Most of the routine fits into a simple calendar. Adjust it for your exposure: more often under trees, near the coast or in bushfire-prone areas, and always after major storms. The rules of thumb below draw on [QBCC's essential home maintenance guide](https://www.qbcc.qld.gov.au/sites/default/files/documents/guide-essential-home-maintenance.pdf), which is written for Queensland but applies widely.

**Routine maintenance calendar**

| How often | Task | Why it matters |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Monthly | Press the test button on each smoke alarm, and test the safety switches at the switchboard regularly | Fire services advise monthly smoke alarm tests; a safety switch that does not trip needs an electrician ([wiring guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/switchboards-wiring-and-safety-switches), [smoke alarms guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/smoke-alarms-and-fire-safety-at-home)) |
| After heavy rain | From the ground, watch gutters and downpipes for overflow, and check water runs away from the house | Overflow near walls is one of the most common causes of damp, footing movement and termite risk ([drainage guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/site-drainage-and-stormwater)) |
| Before the wet season, and more under trees | Clear gutters, valley gutters, downpipes, rainwater heads and drainage pits | Blocked gutters cause many roof leaks that look like building defects ([roofs guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/roofs-tiles-metal-and-leaks)) |
| Every few months | Check under sinks, vanities and around dishwashers for drips; look at flexible tap hoses; compare water bills | An unexplained jump in water use can be the first sign of a hidden leak ([plumbing guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/plumbing-hot-water-and-leaks)) |
| Every few months | Check shower and bath silicone, grout and the base of screens | Failed seals let water into walls and floors before anything shows |
| At least every 12 months | Licensed timber pest inspection, and servicing of any termite system to its manufacturer schedule | Most termite systems require professional servicing at least annually ([termites guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/termites-in-australian-homes)) |
| Annually | Service heating, cooling and ventilation; clean exhaust fans | Keeps moisture moving out of the house and equipment efficient; gas heaters at least every two years ([heating guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/heating-cooling-and-gas-safety)) |
| Every year or two, or after storms | Have a licensed roofer check tiles or sheets, flashings and valleys | Small roof defects become ceiling and framing damage |
| Every 10 years | Replace smoke alarms | Smoke alarms have a limited life, generally up to 10 years |

### Rules of thumb around the house

**Simple measures that protect footings, walls and termite barriers**

| Rule | Detail |
| --- | --- |
| Paths and paving fall away from the house | At least 50 mm over the first metre, so water drains away rather than towards the footings |
| Keep weep holes clear | Never let soil, mulch or paving cover the weep holes along the base of brick walls |
| Keep the termite inspection zone visible | Paths next to a slab should sit at least 75 mm below the termite barrier, about one brick course |
| Plant trees well away | Plant trees and hedges at least 1 to 1½ times their mature height from the house |
| Discharge water away from footings | Air-conditioner condensate, hot water relief valves and tank overflows should not drain onto the ground next to the house |
| No sprinklers against the walls | Automated watering near footings keeps the soil wet and can move reactive clay |

sections.heading: Keep maintenance work safe
sections.markdown: Use licensed or appropriately competent people for roof access, ladders, electrical systems, confined or contaminated subfloors, termite treatment and asbestos-containing materials. Before drilling, sanding or demolition in a home built or renovated before 1990, screen for possible asbestos.

sections.heading: Budget from the asset register
sections.markdown:
Build a short asset register covering roof, drainage, exterior, openings, wet areas, services, structure and shared property. Record known age, observed condition, last work, next review and quotation ranges for defined scopes.

Keep a routine annual allowance and a capital-renewal reserve. Update both when evidence changes. The [home record guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/keeping-a-record-of-your-home) provides the structure; [the era planning guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/what-your-home-needs-by-decade) helps set inspection priorities.

If you would rather not build the register from scratch, a [Homechecker Read](https://homechecker.com.au/) gives you a starting point for your address: the parts of the home most likely to need attention given its era and construction, what that work could cost and what to check first. Each time you add an invoice or a report, the Read updates, so the budget reflects the house as it is now.

sections.heading: An escalation rule that stays useful
sections.markdown:
1. **Record:** date, location, weather or event, dimensions and photographs.
2. **Make safe:** isolate water or power only if safe and within your competence; use emergency help where needed.
3. **Find the cause:** engage the discipline that owns the pathway behind the damaged finish.
4. **Define the work:** diagnosis and scope before comparing repair prices.
5. **Close the record:** invoice, permits or certificates, photos, warranty and next review date.

sections.heading: Give priority to consequence and active change
sections.markdown:
A faded surface and an active leak may both need attention, but they have different consequences if delayed. Start with safety, ongoing water entry and deterioration that can spread into concealed material. Then consider the access and timing of planned work. Renewing a finish while its source of damage remains active can create a second repair bill.

[YourHome's maintenance guidance](https://www.yourhome.gov.au/buy-build-renovate/repairs-and-maintenance) connects roof, wall, shower and pipe leaks with their repair pathways. Use that relationship to decide what to ask a contractor. 'Clear the gutter' and 'investigate recurring overflow' may need different scopes if the problem continues after cleaning.

sections.heading: Set a rhythm for the property you actually have
sections.markdown:
Start with manufacturer and installer requirements for the installed products, any inspection plan and relevant local obligations. Then adjust observations for exposure and experience: overhanging trees, coastal corrosion, wind-driven rain, long vacancies and recent construction changes can alter what deserves attention. A universal annual checklist cannot establish that every system is safe for the next twelve months.

Use events as prompts as well as dates. After significant weather, observe from safe ground for new overflow, displaced materials or internal marks. After a bathroom or window repair, follow performance under the conditions that previously caused trouble. After landscaping, check whether drainage, clearances or access zones have changed. Record the event so a later problem has a useful timeline. Before severe conditions arrive, use [preparing your home for extreme weather](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/preparing-your-home-for-extreme-weather) to plan for the household and the property.

sections.heading: Protect inspection access as part of maintenance
sections.markdown:
[QBCC's termite guidance](https://www.qbcc.qld.gov.au/home-owner-hub/maintain-protect/protect-against-termites) highlights ongoing inspection and the effect of later changes on protection. A treatment notice is a record of a system, not a substitute for its continuing inspection and care. Ask the pest professional for the schedule and conditions relevant to the property, and keep access available where it is needed.

Garden beds, storage, decks and new paving can make formerly visible areas harder to inspect. A sensible maintenance action may be arranging access or moving stored goods safely, rather than undertaking a repair yourself. Keep suspected pest activity undisturbed until the appropriate professional advises you; record what you saw and where.

sections.heading: Group work only when the sequence makes sense
sections.markdown:
Shared access can make coordinated work worthwhile: inspect vulnerable roof junctions before repainting eaves, or check wall details before repainting an elevation. Ask whether the proposed combination genuinely avoids repeat access and whether it risks hiding a problem that needs testing first. Convenience alone should not determine the repair sequence.

**Keep four kinds of cost visible**

| Budget line | What belongs there | What changes it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Routine care | Defined cleaning, servicing and minor upkeep | Product requirements, exposure and the observed maintenance burden. |
| Investigation | Access, testing or specialist advice for an unresolved issue | What must be established before a repair can be scoped. |
| Repair | A defined defect and remedy | Cause, affected extent, access and reinstatement. |
| Renewal | Replacement of an assessed component or system | Condition, performance, parts availability and an agreed replacement scope. |

A component's age can prompt an inspection or future reserve. It is not a compulsory replacement date. Conversely, a new component can need attention if its installation or performance is poor. Keep the basis of each allowance in the [home record](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/keeping-a-record-of-your-home) so a new quote or inspection can update the plan without rewriting its whole logic.

sections.heading: Check the result, including what was not done
sections.markdown:
Ask an invoice to identify the location, task, product or parts and any exclusions. If an inaccessible section was left untouched, retain that as an open item. A paid maintenance invoice establishes expenditure; the scope and follow-up observations establish what was done and whether the symptom improved.

In a shared building, distinguish reporting an issue from permission to work on it. Notify the manager or owners corporation using the property's process, attach the evidence and ask for the responsible party and next action. Do not treat common-property gutters, membranes or fire systems as an individual owner's discretionary project. Use the [records guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/reading-your-owners-corporation-report) to follow the response.

sections.heading: Worked example: the gutter cleaned twice
sections.markdown:
**Illustrative reasoning example, not an inspected property.** An owner has paid for two gutter cleans, but an eave stain grows after heavy rain. The invoices record leaf removal without describing the outlet, junction or overflow behaviour. Cleaning has been performed; the recurring water-entry question remains.

Ask a suitable trade to investigate the relevant rainwater path and define the cause and repair, rather than ordering another identical clean by default. If the problem is a local obstruction, targeted maintenance may resolve it. If it involves a failed junction or drainage design, a different scope is needed. Check performance after relevant rainfall before reinstating the stained finish.

> Note: Maintenance reduces avoidable deterioration and helps catch change early. Keep capital renewal visible in the same plan.

faqs.question: How do I know what maintenance my house will need?
faqs.answer: Start from the home's era, construction and the age of its roof, services and wet areas, then check current condition. A Homechecker Read sets out likely needs and indicative costs for one address, and updates when you add invoices or reports.

faqs.question: How far should trees be from my house?
faqs.answer: As a rule of thumb, plant trees and hedges at least 1 to 1½ times their mature height from the house, so their roots do not dry out or disturb the soil under the footings. Seek engineering advice before removing a large established tree near a house.

faqs.question: How often do I need a termite inspection?
faqs.answer: At least every 12 months is the usual minimum, and most termite management systems require a licensed pest controller to service them at least annually. Inspect more often in high-risk areas or where the inspection zone has been covered.

faqs.question: Which way should paths slope next to a house?
faqs.answer: Away from the house, by at least 50 mm over the first metre, so rainwater drains away from the footings. Paths next to a slab should also sit at least 75 mm below the termite barrier.

faqs.question: What maintenance prevents expensive repairs?
faqs.answer: Manage water pathways, repair leaks promptly, maintain safe clearances and drainage, and observe change early. Fund age- and condition-driven renewal separately.

faqs.question: How much should I budget each year?
faqs.answer: Build an element register, keep a routine-maintenance allowance and separately fund capital renewal from evidence and quotations.

faqs.question: Can I inspect the roof and subfloor myself?
faqs.answer: Observe from safe, accessible locations. Roofs, ladders and confined or contaminated subfloors can be hazardous; use appropriately competent professionals when access or work is unsafe.

faqs.question: What does clearing gutters help prevent?
faqs.answer: Overflow and the damage it can feed, including damp walls, rotting eaves and water pooling near footings. Roof renewal still follows the roof’s material, exposure and condition.

faqs.question: What should I record after maintenance?
faqs.answer: The date, element, observed issue, diagnosis, work scope, contractor, invoice, photos, product, permits or certificates, warranty and next review date.

faqs.question: Should I replace a roof simply because it reaches a certain age?
faqs.answer: Use age to prompt planning, then assess material, condition, repairs, exposure and performance. A defined roof assessment should inform retention, repair or replacement.

faqs.question: Why does a problem recur despite regular maintenance?
faqs.answer: The task may not address the cause, may omit an inaccessible area or may have become insufficient for the current condition. Revisit the scope and evidence rather than automatically repeating it.

faqs.question: Can I maintain common property in my apartment building myself?
faqs.answer: Use the scheme’s reporting and approval process. Establish responsibility and authorisation before arranging work on shared fabric or systems.

| Monthly | Press the test button on each smoke alarm, and test the safety switches at the switchboard regularly | Fire services advise monthly smoke alarm tests; a safety switch that does not trip needs an electrician ([wiring guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/switchboards-wiring-and-safety-switches), [smoke alarms guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/smoke-alarms-and-fire-safety-at-home)) |
| After heavy rain | From the ground, watch gutters and downpipes for overflow, and check water runs away from the house | Overflow near walls is one of the most common causes of damp, footing movement and termite risk ([drainage guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/site-drainage-and-stormwater)) |
| Before the wet season, and more under trees | Clear gutters, valley gutters, downpipes, rainwater heads and drainage pits | Blocked gutters cause many roof leaks that look like building defects ([roofs guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/roofs-tiles-metal-and-leaks)) |
| Every few months | Check under sinks, vanities and around dishwashers for drips; look at flexible tap hoses; compare water bills | An unexplained jump in water use can be the first sign of a hidden leak ([plumbing guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/plumbing-hot-water-and-leaks)) |
| Every few months | Check shower and bath silicone, grout and the base of screens | Failed seals let water into walls and floors before anything shows |
| At least every 12 months | Licensed timber pest inspection, and servicing of any termite system to its manufacturer schedule | Most termite systems require professional servicing at least annually ([termites guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/termites-in-australian-homes)) |
| Annually | Service heating, cooling and ventilation; clean exhaust fans | Keeps moisture moving out of the house and equipment efficient; gas heaters at least every two years ([heating guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/heating-cooling-and-gas-safety)) |
| Every year or two, or after storms | Have a licensed roofer check tiles or sheets, flashings and valleys | Small roof defects become ceiling and framing damage |
| Every 10 years | Replace smoke alarms | Smoke alarms have a limited life, generally up to 10 years |

### Rules of thumb around the house

**Simple measures that protect footings, walls and termite barriers**

| Rule | Detail |
| --- | --- |
| Paths and paving fall away from the house | At least 50 mm over the first metre, so water drains away rather than towards the footings |
| Keep weep holes clear | Never let soil, mulch or paving cover the weep holes along the base of brick walls |
| Keep the termite inspection zone visible | Paths next to a slab should sit at least 75 mm below the termite barrier, about one brick course |
| Plant trees well away | Plant trees and hedges at least 1 to 1½ times their mature height from the house |
| Discharge water away from footings | Air-conditioner condensate, hot water relief valves and tank overflows should not drain onto the ground next to the house |
| No sprinklers against the walls | Automated watering near footings keeps the soil wet and can move reactive clay |

## Keep maintenance work safe
Use licensed or appropriately competent people for roof access, ladders, electrical systems, confined or contaminated subfloors, termite treatment and asbestos-containing materials. Before drilling, sanding or demolition in a home built or renovated before 1990, screen for possible asbestos.

## Budget from the asset register
Build a short asset register covering roof, drainage, exterior, openings, wet areas, services, structure and shared property. Record known age, observed condition, last work, next review and quotation ranges for defined scopes.

Keep a routine annual allowance and a capital-renewal reserve. Update both when evidence changes. The [home record guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/keeping-a-record-of-your-home) provides the structure; [the era planning guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/what-your-home-needs-by-decade) helps set inspection priorities.

If you would rather not build the register from scratch, a [Homechecker Read](https://homechecker.com.au/) gives you a starting point for your address: the parts of the home most likely to need attention given its era and construction, what that work could cost and what to check first. Each time you add an invoice or a report, the Read updates, so the budget reflects the house as it is now.

## An escalation rule that stays useful
1. **Record:** date, location, weather or event, dimensions and photographs.
2. **Make safe:** isolate water or power only if safe and within your competence; use emergency help where needed.
3. **Find the cause:** engage the discipline that owns the pathway behind the damaged finish.
4. **Define the work:** diagnosis and scope before comparing repair prices.
5. **Close the record:** invoice, permits or certificates, photos, warranty and next review date.

## Give priority to consequence and active change
A faded surface and an active leak may both need attention, but they have different consequences if delayed. Start with safety, ongoing water entry and deterioration that can spread into concealed material. Then consider the access and timing of planned work. Renewing a finish while its source of damage remains active can create a second repair bill.

[YourHome's maintenance guidance](https://www.yourhome.gov.au/buy-build-renovate/repairs-and-maintenance) connects roof, wall, shower and pipe leaks with their repair pathways. Use that relationship to decide what to ask a contractor. 'Clear the gutter' and 'investigate recurring overflow' may need different scopes if the problem continues after cleaning.

## Set a rhythm for the property you actually have
Start with manufacturer and installer requirements for the installed products, any inspection plan and relevant local obligations. Then adjust observations for exposure and experience: overhanging trees, coastal corrosion, wind-driven rain, long vacancies and recent construction changes can alter what deserves attention. A universal annual checklist cannot establish that every system is safe for the next twelve months.

Use events as prompts as well as dates. After significant weather, observe from safe ground for new overflow, displaced materials or internal marks. After a bathroom or window repair, follow performance under the conditions that previously caused trouble. After landscaping, check whether drainage, clearances or access zones have changed. Record the event so a later problem has a useful timeline. Before severe conditions arrive, use [preparing your home for extreme weather](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/preparing-your-home-for-extreme-weather) to plan for the household and the property.

## Protect inspection access as part of maintenance
[QBCC's termite guidance](https://www.qbcc.qld.gov.au/home-owner-hub/maintain-protect/protect-against-termites) highlights ongoing inspection and the effect of later changes on protection. A treatment notice is a record of a system, not a substitute for its continuing inspection and care. Ask the pest professional for the schedule and conditions relevant to the property, and keep access available where it is needed.

Garden beds, storage, decks and new paving can make formerly visible areas harder to inspect. A sensible maintenance action may be arranging access or moving stored goods safely, rather than undertaking a repair yourself. Keep suspected pest activity undisturbed until the appropriate professional advises you; record what you saw and where.

## Group work only when the sequence makes sense
Shared access can make coordinated work worthwhile: inspect vulnerable roof junctions before repainting eaves, or check wall details before repainting an elevation. Ask whether the proposed combination genuinely avoids repeat access and whether it risks hiding a problem that needs testing first. Convenience alone should not determine the repair sequence.

**Keep four kinds of cost visible**

| Budget line | What belongs there | What changes it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Routine care | Defined cleaning, servicing and minor upkeep | Product requirements, exposure and the observed maintenance burden. |
| Investigation | Access, testing or specialist advice for an unresolved issue | What must be established before a repair can be scoped. |
| Repair | A defined defect and remedy | Cause, affected extent, access and reinstatement. |
| Renewal | Replacement of an assessed component or system | Condition, performance, parts availability and an agreed replacement scope. |

A component's age can prompt an inspection or future reserve. It is not a compulsory replacement date. Conversely, a new component can need attention if its installation or performance is poor. Keep the basis of each allowance in the [home record](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/keeping-a-record-of-your-home) so a new quote or inspection can update the plan without rewriting its whole logic.

## Check the result, including what was not done
Ask an invoice to identify the location, task, product or parts and any exclusions. If an inaccessible section was left untouched, retain that as an open item. A paid maintenance invoice establishes expenditure; the scope and follow-up observations establish what was done and whether the symptom improved.

In a shared building, distinguish reporting an issue from permission to work on it. Notify the manager or owners corporation using the property's process, attach the evidence and ask for the responsible party and next action. Do not treat common-property gutters, membranes or fire systems as an individual owner's discretionary project. Use the [records guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/reading-your-owners-corporation-report) to follow the response.

## Worked example: the gutter cleaned twice
**Illustrative reasoning example, not an inspected property.** An owner has paid for two gutter cleans, but an eave stain grows after heavy rain. The invoices record leaf removal without describing the outlet, junction or overflow behaviour. Cleaning has been performed; the recurring water-entry question remains.

Ask a suitable trade to investigate the relevant rainwater path and define the cause and repair, rather than ordering another identical clean by default. If the problem is a local obstruction, targeted maintenance may resolve it. If it involves a failed junction or drainage design, a different scope is needed. Check performance after relevant rainfall before reinstating the stained finish.

> Note: Maintenance reduces avoidable deterioration and helps catch change early. Keep capital renewal visible in the same plan.

## Frequently asked questions
### How do I know what maintenance my house will need?
Start from the home's era, construction and the age of its roof, services and wet areas, then check current condition. A Homechecker Read sets out likely needs and indicative costs for one address, and updates when you add invoices or reports.

### How far should trees be from my house?
As a rule of thumb, plant trees and hedges at least 1 to 1½ times their mature height from the house, so their roots do not dry out or disturb the soil under the footings. Seek engineering advice before removing a large established tree near a house.

### How often do I need a termite inspection?
At least every 12 months is the usual minimum, and most termite management systems require a licensed pest controller to service them at least annually. Inspect more often in high-risk areas or where the inspection zone has been covered.

### Which way should paths slope next to a house?
Away from the house, by at least 50 mm over the first metre, so rainwater drains away from the footings. Paths next to a slab should also sit at least 75 mm below the termite barrier.

### What maintenance prevents expensive repairs?
Manage water pathways, repair leaks promptly, maintain safe clearances and drainage, and observe change early. Fund age- and condition-driven renewal separately.

### How much should I budget each year?
Build an element register, keep a routine-maintenance allowance and separately fund capital renewal from evidence and quotations.

### Can I inspect the roof and subfloor myself?
Observe from safe, accessible locations. Roofs, ladders and confined or contaminated subfloors can be hazardous; use appropriately competent professionals when access or work is unsafe.

### What does clearing gutters help prevent?
Overflow and the damage it can feed, including damp walls, rotting eaves and water pooling near footings. Roof renewal still follows the roof’s material, exposure and condition.

### What should I record after maintenance?
The date, element, observed issue, diagnosis, work scope, contractor, invoice, photos, product, permits or certificates, warranty and next review date.

### Should I replace a roof simply because it reaches a certain age?
Use age to prompt planning, then assess material, condition, repairs, exposure and performance. A defined roof assessment should inform retention, repair or replacement.

### Why does a problem recur despite regular maintenance?
The task may not address the cause, may omit an inaccessible area or may have become insufficient for the current condition. Revisit the scope and evidence rather than automatically repeating it.

### Can I maintain common property in my apartment building myself?
Use the scheme’s reporting and approval process. Establish responsibility and authorisation before arranging work on shared fabric or systems.

## Method
We prioritize active consequences, adapt observation to exposure and events, and separate routine care, investigation, repair and renewal so recurring symptoms trigger a better scope.

## Limitations
Timing depends on exposure, material and manufacturer guidance. Leave roof access, electrical work and confined subfloors to properly equipped professionals.

## Sources

- [Protect against termites](https://www.qbcc.qld.gov.au/home-owner-hub/maintain-protect/protect-against-termites) — Queensland Building and Construction Commission; accessed 2026-09-07
- [Your essential home maintenance guide](https://www.qbcc.qld.gov.au/sites/default/files/documents/guide-essential-home-maintenance.pdf) — Queensland Building and Construction Commission; accessed 2026-10-14
- [Smoke alarms](https://www.cfa.vic.gov.au/plan-prepare/fires-in-the-home/home-fire-safety-communications-kit/smoke-alarms) — Country Fire Authority (Victoria); accessed 2026-10-16

sections.heading: Opening
sections.markdown:
### The funding gap is the tell
- **Plan:** Current scopes, timing and the evidence behind allowances
- **Money:** Cash, receivables and commitments reconciled separately
- **Gap:** What remains unfunded, and when it is needed

_The funding gap shapes the next decision: levy, loan, staged work, recovery or changed scope._

sections.heading: Begin with the registered plan
sections.markdown:
The registered plan and state legislation define lot and common-property boundaries. Read the plan and any by-law or rule granting exclusive use or responsibility before assigning a balcony leak, window, service pipe, slab, roof or courtyard. Compare [NSW strata roles](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/strata/roles) with the equivalent guidance in the property's state.

In Victoria, [Consumer Affairs Victoria describes the owners corporation's responsibilities](https://www.consumer.vic.gov.au/housing/owners-corporations/buying-into-an-owners-corporation/what-is-an-owners-corporation) for common property, financial records, its register and certificates, with special rules for some schemes. Read the plan of subdivision and identify the relevant owners corporation before interpreting those records. NSW examples in this guide illustrate a separate state process; they are not national rules.

sections.heading: The records stack
sections.markdown:
**Read each record for its specific evidence value**

| Record | Useful question | Watch for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Registered plan and scheme documents | What is lot, common property or exclusive use? | Use the plan to establish each boundary |
| Minutes over multiple years | Which issues recur, escalate, disappear or are deferred? | Vague references, missing attachments and open decisions |
| Maintenance / capital-works plan | What work, timing and forecast cost are recognised? | A stale plan, omitted major systems or unsupported costs |
| Budgets and financial statements | What income, operating cost, liabilities and fund movements exist? | One-off underspends, unpaid bills, loans or transfers masking the trend |
| Levy and arrears schedule | Who is paying, what has been struck and what remains unpaid? | High arrears, repeated special levies or collection disputes |
| Insurance | What building and liability cover exists, with what excesses and exclusions? | Obtain the schedule, valuation basis and known coverage issues |
| Defect, fire, cladding and legal material | What investigation, order, claim or limitation period is active? | Open reports, expired rights or unfunded rectification |

sections.heading: The funding gap is the tell
sections.markdown:
Put the maintenance or capital-works plan beside the current balance, forecast contributions, existing liabilities, cash restrictions and near-term projects. Check whether the plan is current and its cost assumptions reflect actual scopes and quotes. Calculate the timing and size of any unfunded gap.

Funding responses can include revised ordinary contributions, a special levy, borrowing, staging or changing the work, or a recovery where available. Ask what has actually been approved, what remains contingent and how delay affects the building. The guide to [strata risks for apartment owners and buyers](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/strata-risks-for-owners) sets out the wider exposures.

Check the long-term plan against your state's rules: a 10-year capital works fund plan in NSW, a maintenance plan for tier 1 and tier 2 owners corporations in Victoria, or a sinking fund budget covering the current year and the next 9 years in Queensland. The [state planning table](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/buying-an-apartment-strata#state-plans) sets out the details and sources.

sections.heading: Trace recurring issues through the minutes
sections.markdown: Trace a recurring leak, façade investigation or lift breakdown from first report through investigation, decision, funding, completion and warranty. Ask for missing reports or explanations where the chain breaks. Recent and unresolved issues may sit outside the formal minutes.

sections.heading: Insurance boundaries vary
sections.markdown: The scheme generally insures building or common-property interests required by state law. Lot owners may need contents, improvements, landlord, liability or other cover. Check the plan, legislation, policy schedule, insured value, excesses, exclusions, claims history and responsibility for lot improvements. The [home condition and insurance](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/home-condition-and-insurance) guide explains how building condition fits into that review.

sections.heading: Special levies and settlement need legal review
sections.markdown: Special-levy liability can turn on the resolution date, instalment due dates, sale contract, disclosure and settlement adjustments. Ask the legal representative to identify existing resolutions, proposed motions and post-contract decisions, then allocate each amount under the contract.

sections.heading: A ten-question close-out
sections.markdown:
1. What does the registered plan define as lot and common property for the elements I care about?
2. Which physical issues recur across at least three years of minutes?
3. What reports, orders or quotations sit behind those references?
4. Is the maintenance or capital-works plan current and complete for this building?
5. What near-term work is planned, and what evidence supports the cost?
6. How much unrestricted money is available after liabilities and committed work?
7. What levies, loans, arrears or special contributions exist or are being discussed?
8. What does the full insurance schedule cover and exclude, with what excess?
9. What defects, disputes, cladding, fire-safety or legal limitation issues remain open?
10. How does the sale contract allocate current and proposed levy liability?

sections.heading: Check what the records search actually covered
sections.markdown:
Start with the search date, scheme identifiers, years covered and documents requested. Ask which records were unavailable, which attachments were referenced but missing, and whether later correspondence or meetings could change the result. The report is a view of the material supplied, not a guarantee that every issue has been recorded or disclosed.

[NSW's buyer guidance distinguishes a records search from the section 184 certificate](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/strata/buying-a-strata-property). Use the appropriate process in the property's state. A certificate with current contributions cannot by itself explain a decade of leaks, repair proposals or changed scopes. If more than one scheme or management arrangement serves the building, establish which one the report covers.

sections.heading: Reconcile cash, commitments and receivables
sections.markdown:
The financial statements may show cash in the bank, money owed to the scheme and unpaid obligations in different places. Ask the records reviewer to explain the accounting basis and reconcile those figures to the funds available for a proposed project. Arrears are amounts still to be collected; they should not be treated as cash already available, or automatically deducted a second time from a bank balance.

**A practical reading of the numbers**

| Figure or record | Question to resolve |
| --- | --- |
| Bank or investment balance | Which fund owns it, what is committed and are there restrictions on its use? |
| Levy receivables / arrears | What is unpaid, how old is it and what collection assumptions are in the forecast? |
| Invoices, liabilities and contracts | Which costs are already incurred or committed but not yet reflected in payments? |
| Budget surplus | Does it reflect efficient spending, deferred work or a timing difference? |
| Forecast capital expenditure | Does the estimate include the current scope, access, fees, tax and contingency on a consistent basis? |

[NSW's finance guidance](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/strata/living/levies-finances-insurance) explains the separate purposes of administrative and capital-works funds. Do not assume money shown in one fund is freely available for any project. Have the manager or records reviewer explain any proposed transfer, borrowing or special contribution and the applicable approval process.

sections.heading: Translate short minutes into the underlying decision
sections.markdown:
Minutes are a decision record and can be terse. 'Obtain quotes' leaves the scope open. 'Approved' may describe expenditure authority. 'Completed' should lead to the completion evidence. 'Monitor' should lead to the observation method, interval and escalation trigger. Ask for the technical report behind the words before inferring the cause or extent of a defect.

Follow the same issue under different names: roof leak, top-floor water ingress and ceiling damage might refer to one event, while 'balcony leaks' could refer to several unrelated areas. Map dates and locations before combining costs or assuming repeated references prove one repair repeatedly failed. Recent correspondence and invoices can help bridge the gaps between meetings.

sections.heading: Test whether the works plan still describes this building
sections.markdown:
Read the date and scope of the condition input behind the plan. Was it prepared from an inspection, a [desktop review](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/desktop-vs-physical-report) or earlier records? Check whether major systems actually present are included and whether completed work has been removed or redated. An allowance based on age can flag future budgeting; it does not confirm that the component currently needs replacement.

A new defect can sit outside an otherwise reasonable long-term plan. Ask how the scheme has incorporated the new scope, what cost evidence supports it and whether funding decisions have caught up. A large balance alongside a stale plan is not automatically reassuring, and a low balance immediately after documented renewal is not automatically a failure.

sections.heading: Worked example: the roof was approved, but which roof?
sections.markdown:
**Illustrative reasoning example, not an inspected property.** A report says roof works were approved last year. The bank balance is now lower, but this year's minutes still discuss water entry. The accepted quote turns out to cover the front roof only; the later complaint concerns a rear roof over different lots. The records describe two scopes, not necessarily a failed single project.

Request the completion evidence for the front work and the investigation and funding proposal for the rear. Reconcile the remaining cash with unpaid front-work invoices before estimating the gap. Then ask the legal reviewer how any resolved contributions affect the sale. This produces a traceable set of physical, financial and contractual questions instead of one vague conclusion that 'the roof is sorted'.

> Important: Terminology and legal responsibilities differ across Australian states and schemes. Use state-specific strata and legal advice, then inspect the lot and accessible building separately.

faqs.question: What should a strata sinking fund or capital works plan cover?
faqs.answer: Major common property items likely to need repair or replacement over the next decade, with estimated timing and cost, such as roofs, lifts, facades, painting, waterproofing and fire systems, and the levies needed to fund them. Check that its date and items reflect the building as it is now.

faqs.question: What should I look for in strata minutes?
faqs.answer: Trace recurring issues from first report through investigation, decision, funding, completion and warranty. Ask for missing reports or attachments where the chain breaks.

faqs.question: How much should a capital-works or maintenance fund hold?
faqs.answer: Compare the balance and future contributions with the current plan, liabilities, committed work and evidence-based project costs.

faqs.question: Who pays a special levy when an apartment is sold?
faqs.answer: It depends on state law, the resolution and due dates, the contract, disclosure and settlement adjustments. Have the legal representative allocate each current or proposed amount.

faqs.question: Does strata insurance cover the inside of my apartment?
faqs.answer: The boundary depends on the plan, legislation and policy. Contents, improvements and owner-installed items may require separate cover.

faqs.question: What can clean records tell me about defects?
faqs.answer: Records can be incomplete, delayed or silent. Read them with a physical inspection and ask about recent events still outside the formal minutes.

faqs.question: Are levy arrears the same as available money?
faqs.answer: No. Arrears are amounts not yet collected. Ask how cash, receivables, liabilities and commitments reconcile; do not double-count unpaid amounts in a funding calculation.

faqs.question: Does an approved motion prove the work is finished?
faqs.answer: No. Obtain the accepted scope, delivery records and completion evidence. Approval, funding and physical completion are separate stages.

faqs.question: What if the strata report refers to a missing engineer’s report?
faqs.answer: Ask for the underlying report and any later updates, including its access limitations and recommended scope. Treat the material conclusion as unresolved until that evidence is available.

| Budgets and financial statements | What income, operating cost, liabilities and fund movements exist? | One-off underspends, unpaid bills, loans or transfers masking the trend |
| Levy and arrears schedule | Who is paying, what has been struck and what remains unpaid? | High arrears, repeated special levies or collection disputes |
| Insurance | What building and liability cover exists, with what excesses and exclusions? | Obtain the schedule, valuation basis and known coverage issues |
| Defect, fire, cladding and legal material | What investigation, order, claim or limitation period is active? | Open reports, expired rights or unfunded rectification |

## The funding gap is the tell
Put the maintenance or capital-works plan beside the current balance, forecast contributions, existing liabilities, cash restrictions and near-term projects. Check whether the plan is current and its cost assumptions reflect actual scopes and quotes. Calculate the timing and size of any unfunded gap.

Funding responses can include revised ordinary contributions, a special levy, borrowing, staging or changing the work, or a recovery where available. Ask what has actually been approved, what remains contingent and how delay affects the building. The guide to [strata risks for apartment owners and buyers](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/strata-risks-for-owners) sets out the wider exposures.

Check the long-term plan against your state's rules: a 10-year capital works fund plan in NSW, a maintenance plan for tier 1 and tier 2 owners corporations in Victoria, or a sinking fund budget covering the current year and the next 9 years in Queensland. The [state planning table](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/buying-an-apartment-strata#state-plans) sets out the details and sources.

## Trace recurring issues through the minutes
Trace a recurring leak, façade investigation or lift breakdown from first report through investigation, decision, funding, completion and warranty. Ask for missing reports or explanations where the chain breaks. Recent and unresolved issues may sit outside the formal minutes.

## Insurance boundaries vary
The scheme generally insures building or common-property interests required by state law. Lot owners may need contents, improvements, landlord, liability or other cover. Check the plan, legislation, policy schedule, insured value, excesses, exclusions, claims history and responsibility for lot improvements. The [home condition and insurance](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/home-condition-and-insurance) guide explains how building condition fits into that review.

## Special levies and settlement need legal review
Special-levy liability can turn on the resolution date, instalment due dates, sale contract, disclosure and settlement adjustments. Ask the legal representative to identify existing resolutions, proposed motions and post-contract decisions, then allocate each amount under the contract.

## A ten-question close-out
1. What does the registered plan define as lot and common property for the elements I care about?
2. Which physical issues recur across at least three years of minutes?
3. What reports, orders or quotations sit behind those references?
4. Is the maintenance or capital-works plan current and complete for this building?
5. What near-term work is planned, and what evidence supports the cost?
6. How much unrestricted money is available after liabilities and committed work?
7. What levies, loans, arrears or special contributions exist or are being discussed?
8. What does the full insurance schedule cover and exclude, with what excess?
9. What defects, disputes, cladding, fire-safety or legal limitation issues remain open?
10. How does the sale contract allocate current and proposed levy liability?

## Check what the records search actually covered
Start with the search date, scheme identifiers, years covered and documents requested. Ask which records were unavailable, which attachments were referenced but missing, and whether later correspondence or meetings could change the result. The report is a view of the material supplied, not a guarantee that every issue has been recorded or disclosed.

[NSW's buyer guidance distinguishes a records search from the section 184 certificate](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/strata/buying-a-strata-property). Use the appropriate process in the property's state. A certificate with current contributions cannot by itself explain a decade of leaks, repair proposals or changed scopes. If more than one scheme or management arrangement serves the building, establish which one the report covers.

## Reconcile cash, commitments and receivables
The financial statements may show cash in the bank, money owed to the scheme and unpaid obligations in different places. Ask the records reviewer to explain the accounting basis and reconcile those figures to the funds available for a proposed project. Arrears are amounts still to be collected; they should not be treated as cash already available, or automatically deducted a second time from a bank balance.

**A practical reading of the numbers**

| Figure or record | Question to resolve |
| --- | --- |
| Bank or investment balance | Which fund owns it, what is committed and are there restrictions on its use? |
| Levy receivables / arrears | What is unpaid, how old is it and what collection assumptions are in the forecast? |
| Invoices, liabilities and contracts | Which costs are already incurred or committed but not yet reflected in payments? |
| Budget surplus | Does it reflect efficient spending, deferred work or a timing difference? |
| Forecast capital expenditure | Does the estimate include the current scope, access, fees, tax and contingency on a consistent basis? |

[NSW's finance guidance](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/strata/living/levies-finances-insurance) explains the separate purposes of administrative and capital-works funds. Do not assume money shown in one fund is freely available for any project. Have the manager or records reviewer explain any proposed transfer, borrowing or special contribution and the applicable approval process.

## Translate short minutes into the underlying decision
Minutes are a decision record and can be terse. 'Obtain quotes' leaves the scope open. 'Approved' may describe expenditure authority. 'Completed' should lead to the completion evidence. 'Monitor' should lead to the observation method, interval and escalation trigger. Ask for the technical report behind the words before inferring the cause or extent of a defect.

Follow the same issue under different names: roof leak, top-floor water ingress and ceiling damage might refer to one event, while 'balcony leaks' could refer to several unrelated areas. Map dates and locations before combining costs or assuming repeated references prove one repair repeatedly failed. Recent correspondence and invoices can help bridge the gaps between meetings.

## Test whether the works plan still describes this building
Read the date and scope of the condition input behind the plan. Was it prepared from an inspection, a [desktop review](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/desktop-vs-physical-report) or earlier records? Check whether major systems actually present are included and whether completed work has been removed or redated. An allowance based on age can flag future budgeting; it does not confirm that the component currently needs replacement.

A new defect can sit outside an otherwise reasonable long-term plan. Ask how the scheme has incorporated the new scope, what cost evidence supports it and whether funding decisions have caught up. A large balance alongside a stale plan is not automatically reassuring, and a low balance immediately after documented renewal is not automatically a failure.

## Worked example: the roof was approved, but which roof?
**Illustrative reasoning example, not an inspected property.** A report says roof works were approved last year. The bank balance is now lower, but this year's minutes still discuss water entry. The accepted quote turns out to cover the front roof only; the later complaint concerns a rear roof over different lots. The records describe two scopes, not necessarily a failed single project.

Request the completion evidence for the front work and the investigation and funding proposal for the rear. Reconcile the remaining cash with unpaid front-work invoices before estimating the gap. Then ask the legal reviewer how any resolved contributions affect the sale. This produces a traceable set of physical, financial and contractual questions instead of one vague conclusion that 'the roof is sorted'.

> Important: Terminology and legal responsibilities differ across Australian states and schemes. Use state-specific strata and legal advice, then inspect the lot and accessible building separately.

## Frequently asked questions
### What should a strata sinking fund or capital works plan cover?
Major common property items likely to need repair or replacement over the next decade, with estimated timing and cost, such as roofs, lifts, facades, painting, waterproofing and fire systems, and the levies needed to fund them. Check that its date and items reflect the building as it is now.

### What should I look for in strata minutes?
Trace recurring issues from first report through investigation, decision, funding, completion and warranty. Ask for missing reports or attachments where the chain breaks.

### How much should a capital-works or maintenance fund hold?
Compare the balance and future contributions with the current plan, liabilities, committed work and evidence-based project costs.

### Who pays a special levy when an apartment is sold?
It depends on state law, the resolution and due dates, the contract, disclosure and settlement adjustments. Have the legal representative allocate each current or proposed amount.

### Does strata insurance cover the inside of my apartment?
The boundary depends on the plan, legislation and policy. Contents, improvements and owner-installed items may require separate cover.

### What can clean records tell me about defects?
Records can be incomplete, delayed or silent. Read them with a physical inspection and ask about recent events still outside the formal minutes.

### Are levy arrears the same as available money?
No. Arrears are amounts not yet collected. Ask how cash, receivables, liabilities and commitments reconcile; do not double-count unpaid amounts in a funding calculation.

### Does an approved motion prove the work is finished?
No. Obtain the accepted scope, delivery records and completion evidence. Approval, funding and physical completion are separate stages.

### What if the strata report refers to a missing engineer’s report?
Ask for the underlying report and any later updates, including its access limitations and recommended scope. Treat the material conclusion as unresolved until that evidence is available.

## Method
We reconcile the records by date, location, scope and accounting meaning, then trace each material issue to a decision and the evidence of completion.

## Limitations
The records only hold what someone wrote down, so recent or unresolved issues can be missing. A state-specific records inspection and legal advice on adjustments and levies close that gap.

guides.question: What causes damp in a house and how do I deal with it?
guides.title: Damp and moisture in your home: finding the cause
guides.summary: Damp marks can look alike even when the water is coming from somewhere completely different. Follow when and where the moisture appears before paying for a treatment.
guides.answer: Visible moisture may come from the ground, rain, condensation, plumbing, the roof or poor drainage, and more than one source can be active at once. Timing is the best first clue: damp that follows rain points to water getting in, damp that is worst on cold winter mornings points to condensation, damp that persists regardless of weather points to plumbing or the ground, and a low band with white salts on older masonry points to salt damp.
guides.methodology: We compare plausible moisture sources, identify the evidence that distinguishes them and separate diagnosis, source repair, drying and reinstatement. The worked example is fictional.
guides.limitations: Reading patterns from a distance cannot find a concealed leak or judge a health effect. Anything significant, recurring or post-flood needs eyes, instruments and advice on site.
guides.researchNote: Use [NSW Health](https://www.health.nsw.gov.au/environment/factsheets/Pages/mould.aspx) for health precautions and [YourHome](https://www.yourhome.gov.au/passive-design/condensation) for climate-dependent moisture behaviour. Instrument interpretation also draws on clearly identified UK technical guidance; it is not presented as Australian law.

cluster.label: Read the building
cluster.blurb: Use age and construction as a starting hypothesis, then test it against evidence and physical inspection.

sections.heading: Opening
sections.markdown:
### Follow the water
- **Source:** Where it comes from: rain, pipes, ground or the air indoors
- **Path:** How it gets in: roof, wall, opening, service or soil
- **Damage:** What it leaves behind: stains, salts, rot, mould

_Fix the source first. A repaint over live moisture is a countdown._

Fix the confirmed source before the finish, and avoid hard cement render or impermeable paint on old masonry, which can push damp higher.

sections.heading: Why damp is the problem behind the problems
sections.markdown: Moisture can contribute to rot, mould, coating failure, salt-damaged masonry and ground movement. A visible symptom can have several possible sources. Before selecting a treatment, record timing and location, check urgent electrical or health risk, and investigate rain, plumbing, drainage, indoor humidity and ground moisture.

sections.heading: What you'll notice
sections.markdown:
Damp is usually noticed before it is seen properly. Note what you sense, and when, then use the table below it to narrow the source.

**Signs of moisture, by sense**

| Sense | Sign | Often points to |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Smell | Musty or earthy smell, worse when the house is closed up or after rain | Hidden damp in walls, floors or the subfloor |
| See | Tide mark or stain along the lower wall, with white powder (salts) | Rising or salt damp; see [salt damp](#salt-damp) |
| See | Black spots of mould in corners, behind furniture or on window reveals | Condensation; see [condensation](#condensation-detail) |
| See | Stains or bubbling paint near windows, chimneys or below the roof line | Water getting in from outside |
| See | Swollen skirting, cupped floorboards or stains beside a bathroom | A leak; see [leaking showers](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/bathroom-waterproofing-and-leaking-showers) |
| Feel | Walls that feel cold and damp, or plaster that is soft or crumbly | Persistent moisture in the wall |
| Feel | Damp, humid air under the floor or a musty draught from floor vents | Subfloor moisture; see [subfloors](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/subfloors-stumps-and-restumping) |

sections.heading: Four possible moisture pathways
sections.markdown:
_[Illustration: Architectural house cutaway showing ground moisture and salt bloom, rain penetration, condensation and a localised roof or plumbing leak. The mark is a clue. Its location, timing and relationship to rain, plumbing, ventilation and ground conditions help trace the source.]_

**Clues to investigate, not standalone diagnoses**

| Type | Where it comes from | Typical signs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Rising damp | Groundwater drawn up through porous masonry | Low-wall staining or salts; other moisture sources can create similar marks |
| Penetrating / lateral damp | Water entering sideways through walls | Damp patches that worsen after rain, often near a leaking gutter, cracked render or a wall below ground level |
| Condensation | Moist indoor air meeting cold surfaces | Mould in corners, behind furniture and on window reveals; worse in winter, bathrooms and kitchens |
| Leaks | Plumbing, roof or shower failures | Localised or travelling moisture; roof leaks may respond to rain and plumbing leaks to use |

### Rising damp

Capillary moisture can move from the ground through porous masonry. Low-wall staining, salts or a tide-like mark also occur with bridged damp-proofing, rain, plumbing, condensation and historic salts. Work out the pathway before anyone sells you an injection, a drain, a fan or a repaint. The treatments only work on the problem they were built for.

### Penetrating and lateral damp

Rain can enter through cracked render, failed pointing, leaking gutters or downpipes, and walls below external ground level. A pattern that appears or worsens after rain can help locate the external pathway.

### Condensation

Condensation forms when warm, moist indoor air meets a cold surface. It commonly appears in corners, behind furniture against external walls and on window reveals, especially in winter or poorly ventilated rooms. [YourHome explains how ventilation, insulation, thermal bridges and indoor moisture loads interact](https://www.yourhome.gov.au/passive-design/condensation). The response should suit the climate, construction and confirmed source.

### Leaks

A plumbing, roof or wet-area leak can produce a localised mark, while water may travel before becoming visible. Investigation may need moisture mapping, safe access, service testing or owner-approved opening-up.

sections.heading: Telling the sources apart
sections.markdown:
Before anyone quotes for a treatment, the pattern of the damp usually narrows the source. Note when it appears, where, and what it looks like.

**Timing, location and look**

| Source | When it shows | Where and how it looks | Common misread |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Rising or salt damp | Slowly, and worse after prolonged wet periods | A band along the lower wall, often up to about a metre, with white salt deposits, crumbling mortar or blistering paint | Blamed on a missing damp-proof course when garden beds, paving or render are bridging a sound one |
| Penetrating or falling damp | During or soon after rain, especially wind-driven rain | Patches near windows, chimneys, parapets, gutters or below roof junctions | Treated as rising damp because it reaches low on a wall |
| Condensation | Cold mornings, winter, after showers and cooking | Black mould spots in corners, behind furniture, on window reveals and cold ceilings; no salts | Treated with damp-proofing when ventilation and heating are the issue |
| Plumbing leak | Any time, regardless of weather, often worse with use | Localised staining near wet areas, pipes or appliances, sometimes some distance from the leak | Painted over, then returns |
| Subfloor moisture | Persistent, often worse in winter | Musty smell, cupping floorboards, decay or fungus under the floor | Missed entirely because the subfloor was not accessed |

### Salt damp in older masonry

In older brick and stone homes, moisture rising from the ground carries salts that crystallise as the wall dries, slowly breaking down bricks, mortar and render. [The technical guide to salt attack and rising damp](https://www.environment.nsw.gov.au/sites/default/files/salt-attack-and-rising-damp-guide.pdf) produced for the Heritage Councils of NSW and Victoria, South Australia and the City of Adelaide calls this combination **salt damp**. It notes the problem affects older buildings across much of Australia, and is especially common in Adelaide.

Three common responses often make it worse. Hard cement render over the base of a wall traps moisture and pushes damp and salts higher. Impermeable paints and sealers do the same. Raising ground levels, paving against walls or banking garden beds above the damp-proof course bridges it. A new damp-proof course stops further rising damp, but the salts already in the wall remain and may need separate treatment before replastering.

### Condensation is a building and a lifestyle question

Condensation forms when moist indoor air meets a surface cold enough to drop below the air's dew point. [CSIRO's building technology resource on condensation](https://research.csiro.au/infratech/btr/) explains the balance of moisture produced, ventilation and surface temperature. Showers, cooking, drying clothes indoors, unflued gas heaters and sealed-up homes all add moisture. Exhaust fans that vent outside rather than into the roof space, regular airing and keeping surfaces warmer usually do more than any damp treatment.

sections.heading: Why the diagnosis is the whole job
sections.markdown: Match the repair to the confirmed moisture pathway. Fix the source first, allow the materials to dry properly, then restore the finishes. If movement or deterioration is also present, use the [cracks guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/cracks-structural-or-cosmetic) to frame the next professional question.

sections.heading: Keeping water where it belongs
sections.markdown: Keep gutters and downpipes clear, direct drainage away from the house, maintain wet-area seals and provide suitable ventilation. The [maintenance guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/the-maintenance-that-prevents-the-big-bills) sets out the wider water-management routine.

sections.heading: Build a moisture history before choosing a treatment
sections.markdown:
Record the location on a room sketch, the date, recent weather, plumbing use, heating and ventilation, and whether the mark is changing. Ask when it was first seen and what happened just before it: a new bathroom, window replacement, paving, blocked gutter or extended vacancy. Keep separate records for separate patches until evidence connects them. One house can have a leaking gutter and condensation in a different room. Keep these notes in your [home record](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/keeping-a-record-of-your-home).

**Evidence that can change the working explanation**

| Question | Useful observation or record | Limit |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Does rainfall matter? | Dated photographs after relevant wind-driven rain, roof/gutter inspection | A dry-day visit cannot test rain entry; correlation does not locate the defect. |
| Does use of a fixture matter? | Timing after showering or appliance use, licensed plumbing tests | Water can travel; the nearest fixture is not automatically the source. |
| Do indoor conditions matter? | Temperature/humidity history, ventilation operation, surface patterns | One reading does not represent the season or explain concealed layers. |
| Is this active or historic? | Repair records, drying evidence and repeat observations | A clean or repainted surface can conceal the history. |

sections.heading: What instruments can and cannot establish
sections.markdown:
A moisture meter is useful for comparing areas when its mode, substrate and limitations are understood. A high reading should prompt interpretation, not automatically become a diagnosis of rising damp or a percentage moisture content for every material. Ask the practitioner what the instrument measures and how the reading was corroborated. Salts, conductive materials and the assembly can affect interpretation; an isolated number without its location and method is weak evidence. See [Historic England's instrument guidance](https://historicengland.org.uk/images-books/publications/assessing-damp-historic-buildings/heag311-assessing-damp-historic-buildings/), used here for measurement principles in traditional buildings, rather than Australian regulatory requirements.

Thermal imaging can help locate temperature differences worth investigating. It does not see through a wall or prove the location of a leak. An apparent anomaly might relate to moisture, insulation, air leakage or thermal bridging. A useful report connects the image to visual observations and appropriate testing, and states what could not be checked.

sections.heading: The same mark means different things in different construction
sections.markdown:
In an older solid-masonry home, investigate ground levels, rainwater disposal, salts and repair compatibility together. In veneer, ask about the cavity, window flashings and drainage exits. In a weatherboard house, follow wetting at openings and bottom boards and consider the frame behind them. In an apartment, the source may lie in common property or another lot, so access and responsibility become part of the investigation. The guides to [masonry systems](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/brick-veneer-vs-double-brick), [weatherboards](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/weatherboard-homes) and [strata purchases](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/buying-an-apartment-strata) help narrow those questions.

Condensation is also climate-dependent. In a cool winter climate, cold internal surfaces may be important; in a hot humid climate, air conditioning can create cold surfaces within an assembly. The direction of moisture movement can change. This is why [YourHome recommends climate-appropriate moisture control](https://www.yourhome.gov.au/passive-design/condensation). Ask what changed after insulation, draught sealing or ventilation work rather than assuming the upgrade must have improved every aspect of performance.

sections.heading: Separate immediate safety from building diagnosis
sections.markdown:
Water near electrical equipment, a sagging saturated ceiling or unstable material needs prompt professional attention. Keep away from the affected area and arrange the appropriate emergency or licensed service; do not open wet electrical fittings or enter a compromised roof space to investigate. Photographs can wait until access is safe.

[NSW Health explains that mould can affect susceptible people and recommends medical advice for symptoms](https://www.health.nsw.gov.au/environment/factsheets/Pages/mould.aspx). Visible growth deserves moisture investigation, but its colour or a listing photograph cannot establish a person's exposure or medical risk. Extensive, recurrent or concealed contamination may need specialist assessment. A cleaning or sampling result alone does not demonstrate that the moisture source has been repaired. If specialist indoor-environment work is proposed, the [building-biologist cost and scope guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/building-biologist-cost) explains how to compare the investigation, sampling, laboratory work and report.

sections.heading: A repair needs a way to demonstrate that it worked
sections.markdown:
Ask the investigation to identify the suspected or confirmed source, its supporting evidence, the proposed repair and the uncertainty left behind. Separate source repair, drying, removal of damaged material and reinstatement in the scope. That makes it possible to compare quotations that otherwise all say 'fix damp'. Avoid agreeing an extensive treatment solely from a sales visit that has not tested plausible alternatives.

After work, retain photographs of concealed details and the repair description. Agree how drying and performance will be checked before closing up or decorating. The relevant test might involve subsequent rainfall, normal fixture use or measurements interpreted over time. No recurrence during a short dry spell is less informative about a rain leak than performance through the weather that previously triggered it.

sections.heading: Worked example: a low stain beside a renewed bathroom
sections.markdown:
**Illustrative reasoning example, not an inspected property.** A 1970s home has a low bedroom stain next to a renovated bathroom and a raised garden bed outside. Three plausible lines of enquiry remain: wet-area or plumbing leakage, external moisture and indoor condensation. The low position alone does not establish rising damp.

Ask for the bathroom repair history, compare the timing with shower use and rain, and have external levels and plumbing assessed. If testing identifies a service leak, define that repair and check residual damage. If the result is inconclusive, retain the competing explanations and agree the next discriminator. An injection treatment priced before that work is a proposed intervention, not evidence of the cause.

> Note: Record the moisture location, timing, weather, source investigation, repair and drying evidence. Recurrence then becomes easier to trace.

> Important: Persistent damp and extensive mould warrant property-specific investigation. Seek health advice for symptoms and qualified building advice for the moisture source.

faqs.question: How do I find the source of moisture in a wall?
faqs.answer: Note when it appears (after rain, on cold mornings, after showers, or constantly), where it sits (low, high, near openings or wet areas) and what it looks like (salts, mould, staining). Rule out plumbing with a water meter test. The pattern usually narrows the source before any instrument is used.

faqs.question: What is the white powder on my bricks?
faqs.answer: Usually efflorescence: salts carried to the surface by water moving through the masonry, left behind as it dries. It is not harmful in itself, but it shows moisture is passing through the wall, so find where the water comes from.

faqs.question: Does a damp-smelling bathroom mean there is a leak?
faqs.answer: Not necessarily. Bathrooms often smell damp from condensation and poor ventilation. Swollen skirting, staining beyond the bathroom or loose tiles point more to a leak.

faqs.question: How do I know what kind of damp I have?
faqs.answer: Use location, timing, weather and plumbing-use history to compare possible sources. Similar marks can arise from different pathways and several sources may coexist. Physical investigation and appropriate testing establish the cause.

faqs.question: What is rising damp?
faqs.answer: It is capillary moisture moving from the ground through porous masonry. Low-wall staining and salts are possible clues. Rain, plumbing, condensation, bridged damp-proofing and historic salts can produce a similar pattern, so confirm the pathway.

faqs.question: Is mould always a sign of a building leak?
faqs.answer: Mould needs moisture. Sources include indoor humidity and condensation, rain entry, plumbing, drainage and combinations of these pathways. Building repair, ventilation, heating, source control and health precautions depend on the cause.

faqs.question: Why does my damp keep coming back after repairs?
faqs.answer: The source, moisture path, drying time or replacement finish may remain unresolved, or several sources may exist. Reassess the evidence before further work.

faqs.question: Can I fix damp myself?
faqs.answer: Safe maintenance may include clearing accessible drainage, improving ventilation and renewing suitable seals. Persistent damp and extensive or health-affecting mould warrant professional assessment.

faqs.question: Does damp affect my home insurance?
faqs.answer: Cover depends on the policy, cause and circumstances. Ask the insurer or broker about the specific damage and relevant exclusions; keep repair and maintenance evidence. A damp mark alone does not establish a claim outcome.

faqs.question: What is salt damp?
faqs.answer: Salt damp is rising damp combined with salt attack: groundwater carries salts into older masonry, and as the wall dries the salts crystallise and break down bricks, mortar and render. It is common in older buildings across much of Australia, especially Adelaide.

faqs.question: Will cement render stop rising damp?
faqs.answer: No. Hard cement render over the base of an old masonry wall traps moisture and tends to push damp and salts higher up the wall. Compatible, breathable repairs and removing the source of moisture work better.

faqs.question: How can I tell condensation from rising damp?
faqs.answer: Condensation is worst on cold mornings, appears as black mould spots in corners, behind furniture and on window reveals, and leaves no salts. Rising damp shows as a band along the lower wall, often with white salt deposits, and changes slowly with wet seasons.

faqs.question: Does a high moisture-meter reading prove rising damp?
faqs.answer: No. The instrument, material, measurement mode and surrounding evidence matter. Ask what the reading establishes and how the proposed moisture pathway was confirmed.

faqs.question: Can thermal imaging find every leak?
faqs.answer: No. It records temperature patterns under the conditions of the survey. Those patterns need interpretation and corroborating evidence; it cannot see through walls or certify the absence of leaks.

faqs.question: What proves that a damp repair worked?
faqs.answer: A documented source repair, suitable drying evidence and follow-up under the conditions that previously caused the problem provide a stronger basis than fresh paint or one dry-day visit.
