guides.contentMarkdown:
# Damp and moisture in your home: finding the cause

Visible moisture may come from the ground, rain, condensation, plumbing, the roof or poor drainage, and more than one source can be active at once. Timing is the best first clue: damp that follows rain points to water getting in, damp that is worst on cold winter mornings points to condensation, damp that persists regardless of weather points to plumbing or the ground, and a low band with white salts on older masonry points to salt damp.

## Research note
Use [NSW Health](https://www.health.nsw.gov.au/environment/factsheets/Pages/mould.aspx) for health precautions and [YourHome](https://www.yourhome.gov.au/passive-design/condensation) for climate-dependent moisture behaviour. Instrument interpretation also draws on clearly identified UK technical guidance; it is not presented as Australian law.

## Opening
### Follow the water
- **Source:** Where it comes from: rain, pipes, ground or the air indoors
- **Path:** How it gets in: roof, wall, opening, service or soil
- **Damage:** What it leaves behind: stains, salts, rot, mould

_Fix the source first. A repaint over live moisture is a countdown._

Fix the confirmed source before the finish, and avoid hard cement render or impermeable paint on old masonry, which can push damp higher.

## Why damp is the problem behind the problems
Moisture can contribute to rot, mould, coating failure, salt-damaged masonry and ground movement. A visible symptom can have several possible sources. Before selecting a treatment, record timing and location, check urgent electrical or health risk, and investigate rain, plumbing, drainage, indoor humidity and ground moisture.

## What you'll notice
Damp is usually noticed before it is seen properly. Note what you sense, and when, then use the table below it to narrow the source.

**Signs of moisture, by sense**

| Sense | Sign | Often points to |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Smell | Musty or earthy smell, worse when the house is closed up or after rain | Hidden damp in walls, floors or the subfloor |
| See | Tide mark or stain along the lower wall, with white powder (salts) | Rising or salt damp; see [salt damp](#salt-damp) |
| See | Black spots of mould in corners, behind furniture or on window reveals | Condensation; see [condensation](#condensation-detail) |
| See | Stains or bubbling paint near windows, chimneys or below the roof line | Water getting in from outside |
| See | Swollen skirting, cupped floorboards or stains beside a bathroom | A leak; see [leaking showers](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/bathroom-waterproofing-and-leaking-showers) |
| Feel | Walls that feel cold and damp, or plaster that is soft or crumbly | Persistent moisture in the wall |
| Feel | Damp, humid air under the floor or a musty draught from floor vents | Subfloor moisture; see [subfloors](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/subfloors-stumps-and-restumping) |

## Four possible moisture pathways
_[Illustration: Architectural house cutaway showing ground moisture and salt bloom, rain penetration, condensation and a localised roof or plumbing leak. The mark is a clue. Its location, timing and relationship to rain, plumbing, ventilation and ground conditions help trace the source.]_

**Clues to investigate, not standalone diagnoses**

| Type | Where it comes from | Typical signs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Rising damp | Groundwater drawn up through porous masonry | Low-wall staining or salts; other moisture sources can create similar marks |
| Penetrating / lateral damp | Water entering sideways through walls | Damp patches that worsen after rain, often near a leaking gutter, cracked render or a wall below ground level |
| Condensation | Moist indoor air meeting cold surfaces | Mould in corners, behind furniture and on window reveals; worse in winter, bathrooms and kitchens |
| Leaks | Plumbing, roof or shower failures | Localised or travelling moisture; roof leaks may respond to rain and plumbing leaks to use |

### Rising damp

Capillary moisture can move from the ground through porous masonry. Low-wall staining, salts or a tide-like mark also occur with bridged damp-proofing, rain, plumbing, condensation and historic salts. Work out the pathway before anyone sells you an injection, a drain, a fan or a repaint. The treatments only work on the problem they were built for.

### Penetrating and lateral damp

Rain can enter through cracked render, failed pointing, leaking gutters or downpipes, and walls below external ground level. A pattern that appears or worsens after rain can help locate the external pathway.

### Condensation

Condensation forms when warm, moist indoor air meets a cold surface. It commonly appears in corners, behind furniture against external walls and on window reveals, especially in winter or poorly ventilated rooms. [YourHome explains how ventilation, insulation, thermal bridges and indoor moisture loads interact](https://www.yourhome.gov.au/passive-design/condensation). The response should suit the climate, construction and confirmed source.

### Leaks

A plumbing, roof or wet-area leak can produce a localised mark, while water may travel before becoming visible. Investigation may need moisture mapping, safe access, service testing or owner-approved opening-up.

## Telling the sources apart
Before anyone quotes for a treatment, the pattern of the damp usually narrows the source. Note when it appears, where, and what it looks like.

**Timing, location and look**

| Source | When it shows | Where and how it looks | Common misread |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Rising or salt damp | Slowly, and worse after prolonged wet periods | A band along the lower wall, often up to about a metre, with white salt deposits, crumbling mortar or blistering paint | Blamed on a missing damp-proof course when garden beds, paving or render are bridging a sound one |
| Penetrating or falling damp | During or soon after rain, especially wind-driven rain | Patches near windows, chimneys, parapets, gutters or below roof junctions | Treated as rising damp because it reaches low on a wall |
| Condensation | Cold mornings, winter, after showers and cooking | Black mould spots in corners, behind furniture, on window reveals and cold ceilings; no salts | Treated with damp-proofing when ventilation and heating are the issue |
| Plumbing leak | Any time, regardless of weather, often worse with use | Localised staining near wet areas, pipes or appliances, sometimes some distance from the leak | Painted over, then returns |
| Subfloor moisture | Persistent, often worse in winter | Musty smell, cupping floorboards, decay or fungus under the floor | Missed entirely because the subfloor was not accessed |

### Salt damp in older masonry

In older brick and stone homes, moisture rising from the ground carries salts that crystallise as the wall dries, slowly breaking down bricks, mortar and render. [The technical guide to salt attack and rising damp](https://www.environment.nsw.gov.au/sites/default/files/salt-attack-and-rising-damp-guide.pdf) produced for the Heritage Councils of NSW and Victoria, South Australia and the City of Adelaide calls this combination **salt damp**. It notes the problem affects older buildings across much of Australia, and is especially common in Adelaide.

Three common responses often make it worse. Hard cement render over the base of a wall traps moisture and pushes damp and salts higher. Impermeable paints and sealers do the same. Raising ground levels, paving against walls or banking garden beds above the damp-proof course bridges it. A new damp-proof course stops further rising damp, but the salts already in the wall remain and may need separate treatment before replastering.

### Condensation is a building and a lifestyle question

Condensation forms when moist indoor air meets a surface cold enough to drop below the air's dew point. [CSIRO's building technology resource on condensation](https://research.csiro.au/infratech/btr/) explains the balance of moisture produced, ventilation and surface temperature. Showers, cooking, drying clothes indoors, unflued gas heaters and sealed-up homes all add moisture. Exhaust fans that vent outside rather than into the roof space, regular airing and keeping surfaces warmer usually do more than any damp treatment.

## Why the diagnosis is the whole job
Match the repair to the confirmed moisture pathway. Fix the source first, allow the materials to dry properly, then restore the finishes. If movement or deterioration is also present, use the [cracks guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/cracks-structural-or-cosmetic) to frame the next professional question.

## Keeping water where it belongs
Keep gutters and downpipes clear, direct drainage away from the house, maintain wet-area seals and provide suitable ventilation. The [maintenance guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/the-maintenance-that-prevents-the-big-bills) sets out the wider water-management routine.

## Build a moisture history before choosing a treatment
Record the location on a room sketch, the date, recent weather, plumbing use, heating and ventilation, and whether the mark is changing. Ask when it was first seen and what happened just before it: a new bathroom, window replacement, paving, blocked gutter or extended vacancy. Keep separate records for separate patches until evidence connects them. One house can have a leaking gutter and condensation in a different room. Keep these notes in your [home record](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/keeping-a-record-of-your-home).

**Evidence that can change the working explanation**

| Question | Useful observation or record | Limit |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Does rainfall matter? | Dated photographs after relevant wind-driven rain, roof/gutter inspection | A dry-day visit cannot test rain entry; correlation does not locate the defect. |
| Does use of a fixture matter? | Timing after showering or appliance use, licensed plumbing tests | Water can travel; the nearest fixture is not automatically the source. |
| Do indoor conditions matter? | Temperature/humidity history, ventilation operation, surface patterns | One reading does not represent the season or explain concealed layers. |
| Is this active or historic? | Repair records, drying evidence and repeat observations | A clean or repainted surface can conceal the history. |

## What instruments can and cannot establish
A moisture meter is useful for comparing areas when its mode, substrate and limitations are understood. A high reading should prompt interpretation, not automatically become a diagnosis of rising damp or a percentage moisture content for every material. Ask the practitioner what the instrument measures and how the reading was corroborated. Salts, conductive materials and the assembly can affect interpretation; an isolated number without its location and method is weak evidence. See [Historic England's instrument guidance](https://historicengland.org.uk/images-books/publications/assessing-damp-historic-buildings/heag311-assessing-damp-historic-buildings/), used here for measurement principles in traditional buildings, rather than Australian regulatory requirements.

Thermal imaging can help locate temperature differences worth investigating. It does not see through a wall or prove the location of a leak. An apparent anomaly might relate to moisture, insulation, air leakage or thermal bridging. A useful report connects the image to visual observations and appropriate testing, and states what could not be checked.

## The same mark means different things in different construction
In an older solid-masonry home, investigate ground levels, rainwater disposal, salts and repair compatibility together. In veneer, ask about the cavity, window flashings and drainage exits. In a weatherboard house, follow wetting at openings and bottom boards and consider the frame behind them. In an apartment, the source may lie in common property or another lot, so access and responsibility become part of the investigation. The guides to [masonry systems](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/brick-veneer-vs-double-brick), [weatherboards](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/weatherboard-homes) and [strata purchases](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/buying-an-apartment-strata) help narrow those questions.

Condensation is also climate-dependent. In a cool winter climate, cold internal surfaces may be important; in a hot humid climate, air conditioning can create cold surfaces within an assembly. The direction of moisture movement can change. This is why [YourHome recommends climate-appropriate moisture control](https://www.yourhome.gov.au/passive-design/condensation). Ask what changed after insulation, draught sealing or ventilation work rather than assuming the upgrade must have improved every aspect of performance.

## Separate immediate safety from building diagnosis
Water near electrical equipment, a sagging saturated ceiling or unstable material needs prompt professional attention. Keep away from the affected area and arrange the appropriate emergency or licensed service; do not open wet electrical fittings or enter a compromised roof space to investigate. Photographs can wait until access is safe.

[NSW Health explains that mould can affect susceptible people and recommends medical advice for symptoms](https://www.health.nsw.gov.au/environment/factsheets/Pages/mould.aspx). Visible growth deserves moisture investigation, but its colour or a listing photograph cannot establish a person's exposure or medical risk. Extensive, recurrent or concealed contamination may need specialist assessment. A cleaning or sampling result alone does not demonstrate that the moisture source has been repaired. If specialist indoor-environment work is proposed, the [building-biologist cost and scope guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/building-biologist-cost) explains how to compare the investigation, sampling, laboratory work and report.

## A repair needs a way to demonstrate that it worked
Ask the investigation to identify the suspected or confirmed source, its supporting evidence, the proposed repair and the uncertainty left behind. Separate source repair, drying, removal of damaged material and reinstatement in the scope. That makes it possible to compare quotations that otherwise all say 'fix damp'. Avoid agreeing an extensive treatment solely from a sales visit that has not tested plausible alternatives.

After work, retain photographs of concealed details and the repair description. Agree how drying and performance will be checked before closing up or decorating. The relevant test might involve subsequent rainfall, normal fixture use or measurements interpreted over time. No recurrence during a short dry spell is less informative about a rain leak than performance through the weather that previously triggered it.

## Worked example: a low stain beside a renewed bathroom
**Illustrative reasoning example, not an inspected property.** A 1970s home has a low bedroom stain next to a renovated bathroom and a raised garden bed outside. Three plausible lines of enquiry remain: wet-area or plumbing leakage, external moisture and indoor condensation. The low position alone does not establish rising damp.

Ask for the bathroom repair history, compare the timing with shower use and rain, and have external levels and plumbing assessed. If testing identifies a service leak, define that repair and check residual damage. If the result is inconclusive, retain the competing explanations and agree the next discriminator. An injection treatment priced before that work is a proposed intervention, not evidence of the cause.

> Note: Record the moisture location, timing, weather, source investigation, repair and drying evidence. Recurrence then becomes easier to trace.

> Important: Persistent damp and extensive mould warrant property-specific investigation. Seek health advice for symptoms and qualified building advice for the moisture source.

## Frequently asked questions
### How do I find the source of moisture in a wall?
Note when it appears (after rain, on cold mornings, after showers, or constantly), where it sits (low, high, near openings or wet areas) and what it looks like (salts, mould, staining). Rule out plumbing with a water meter test. The pattern usually narrows the source before any instrument is used.

### What is the white powder on my bricks?
Usually efflorescence: salts carried to the surface by water moving through the masonry, left behind as it dries. It is not harmful in itself, but it shows moisture is passing through the wall, so find where the water comes from.

### Does a damp-smelling bathroom mean there is a leak?
Not necessarily. Bathrooms often smell damp from condensation and poor ventilation. Swollen skirting, staining beyond the bathroom or loose tiles point more to a leak.

### How do I know what kind of damp I have?
Use location, timing, weather and plumbing-use history to compare possible sources. Similar marks can arise from different pathways and several sources may coexist. Physical investigation and appropriate testing establish the cause.

### What is rising damp?
It is capillary moisture moving from the ground through porous masonry. Low-wall staining and salts are possible clues. Rain, plumbing, condensation, bridged damp-proofing and historic salts can produce a similar pattern, so confirm the pathway.

### Is mould always a sign of a building leak?
Mould needs moisture. Sources include indoor humidity and condensation, rain entry, plumbing, drainage and combinations of these pathways. Building repair, ventilation, heating, source control and health precautions depend on the cause.

### Why does my damp keep coming back after repairs?
The source, moisture path, drying time or replacement finish may remain unresolved, or several sources may exist. Reassess the evidence before further work.

### Can I fix damp myself?
Safe maintenance may include clearing accessible drainage, improving ventilation and renewing suitable seals. Persistent damp and extensive or health-affecting mould warrant professional assessment.

### Does damp affect my home insurance?
Cover depends on the policy, cause and circumstances. Ask the insurer or broker about the specific damage and relevant exclusions; keep repair and maintenance evidence. A damp mark alone does not establish a claim outcome.

### What is salt damp?
Salt damp is rising damp combined with salt attack: groundwater carries salts into older masonry, and as the wall dries the salts crystallise and break down bricks, mortar and render. It is common in older buildings across much of Australia, especially Adelaide.

### Will cement render stop rising damp?
No. Hard cement render over the base of an old masonry wall traps moisture and tends to push damp and salts higher up the wall. Compatible, breathable repairs and removing the source of moisture work better.

### How can I tell condensation from rising damp?
Condensation is worst on cold mornings, appears as black mould spots in corners, behind furniture and on window reveals, and leaves no salts. Rising damp shows as a band along the lower wall, often with white salt deposits, and changes slowly with wet seasons.

### Does a high moisture-meter reading prove rising damp?
No. The instrument, material, measurement mode and surrounding evidence matter. Ask what the reading establishes and how the proposed moisture pathway was confirmed.

### Can thermal imaging find every leak?
No. It records temperature patterns under the conditions of the survey. Those patterns need interpretation and corroborating evidence; it cannot see through walls or certify the absence of leaks.

### What proves that a damp repair worked?
A documented source repair, suitable drying evidence and follow-up under the conditions that previously caused the problem provide a stronger basis than fresh paint or one dry-day visit.

## Method
We compare plausible moisture sources, identify the evidence that distinguishes them and separate diagnosis, source repair, drying and reinstatement. The worked example is fictional.

## Limitations
Reading patterns from a distance cannot find a concealed leak or judge a health effect. Anything significant, recurring or post-flood needs eyes, instruments and advice on site.

guides.question: What should I check before renovating my home?
guides.title: Planning a renovation: the checks before you start
guides.summary: The cheapest time to find a renovation constraint is before the drawings harden. Clear the title, planning, hazards, structure, services and insurance questions while you still have room to change course.
guides.answer: Before design gets too far, check the title and planning controls, likely approvals, licensed-trade requirements, possible pre-1990 hazardous materials, and the capacity of the existing structure and services. Tell the home insurer about relevant work and get the cover position in writing. Keep a contingency for the things no one can see until the building is opened up.
guides.methodology: We organise renovation decisions around retained fabric, investigations that can change design, clear scope assumptions and evidence at concealed-work and completion stages.
guides.limitations: Approval, licensing, insurance and disclosure obligations vary. Confirm them before design or demolition with the relevant authority and insurer.
guides.researchNote: The [Victorian planning](https://www.planning.vic.gov.au/guides-and-resources/guides/guide-to-victorias-planning-system/planning-permits) and [building-permit](https://www.bpc.vic.gov.au/resource-hub/practice-notes/bp-01-when-is-a-building-permit-required) examples are jurisdiction-specific. The broader decision sequence uses existing-condition evidence and clear scope assumptions before commitment.

cluster.label: Own, maintain and change
cluster.blurb: Keep useful records, maintain the fabric safely and plan works without over-promising what condition can prove.

sections.heading: Opening
sections.markdown:
### Clear the path while change is still cheap
- **Site:** What the title, easements and overlays already decided
- **Approval:** Planning approval and a building permit: separate questions
- **Delivery:** Licensed hands, insured work, inspections passed, records kept

_Settle the pathway while the design is still a pencil sketch._

sections.heading: Reduce uncertainty before design hardens
sections.markdown:
Run the early checks on title, planning, hazards, structure and services while the design can still bend around what they find. Then write down the assumptions you are still carrying, decide whether it is worth opening anything up to test them, and make the contract say who owns the risk of what nobody could see.

A [Homechecker Read](https://homechecker.com.au/) is a quick way to start that list for an existing home. It reads the era, construction and records of the house and flags the questions a renovation is likely to meet, such as materials that may contain asbestos, original services and what the structure may be carrying. Add your plans, quotes or earlier reports and it updates, which gives your designer and builder a clearer brief before anything is opened up.

sections.heading: Approvals for the proposed work
sections.markdown: Planning permits, building permits, trade licences and compliance certificates serve different purposes. Requirements vary by state, council, site and scope. In Victoria, use the official guides to [planning permits](https://www.planning.vic.gov.au/guides-and-resources/guides/guide-to-victorias-planning-system/planning-permits) and [building permits](https://www.bpc.vic.gov.au/resource-hub/practice-notes/bp-01-when-is-a-building-permit-required). Ask the relevant authority and building surveyor to confirm the pathway before design is locked.

sections.heading: Hazardous materials: know before you disturb
sections.markdown:
Renovation can disturb hazardous materials. Screen the property before drilling, sanding or demolition.

### Asbestos

For a home built or renovated before 1990, [ASSEA advises that asbestos-containing materials may be present](https://www.asbestossafety.gov.au/about-asbestos/finding-asbestos/home). Identify suspect material before disturbance and confirm the relevant state licensing and disposal requirements. A photograph or build date cannot confirm the material.

### Lead paint

Older paint layers may contain lead even when newer coatings look sound. Before sanding, scraping or stripping, follow the [Australian Government Lead Alert](https://www.agriculture.gov.au/sites/default/files/documents/lead-paint-fifth-edition.pdf), identify the material and use the appropriate precautions. The paint's age is a screening clue; it does not establish its lead concentration.

sections.heading: Structure and services: what the building can take
sections.markdown:
### Load-bearing walls and structure

Establish the load-bearing structure before removing or opening a wall; whether the house is [brick veneer or double brick](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/brick-veneer-vs-double-brick) changes that question. Structural changes need engineering and an appropriately sized support. Where the home already shows movement, read [the guide to wall cracks](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/cracks-structural-or-cosmetic) and obtain professional assessment before adding load.

### Wiring, plumbing and the switchboard

A new kitchen, bathroom or extension may require switchboard, wiring, plumbing or drainage upgrades. Assess the installed services while planning and budget coordinated work while walls are open. The [era planning guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/what-your-home-needs-by-decade) helps identify the first questions.

**Checks to complete before anyone opens a wall**

| Check | When it applies | Who does it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Asbestos sampling of materials to be disturbed | Homes built or renovated before 1990 ([ASSEA](https://www.asbestossafety.gov.au/about-asbestos/finding-asbestos/home)) | A licensed asbestos assessor or competent person, with laboratory testing |
| Lead paint testing before sanding or stripping | Paint applied before 1970 ([Lead Alert](https://www.agriculture.gov.au/sites/default/files/documents/lead-paint-fifth-edition.pdf)) | A test kit or a qualified assessor |
| Electrical safety check | Before adding insulation, opening walls with wiring, or where the house predates safety switches | A licensed electrician |
| Structural assessment of walls to be removed or opened | Any loadbearing wall, in brick veneer as well as double brick ([guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/brick-veneer-vs-double-brick)) | A structural engineer |
| Wet-area waterproofing design and certificate | Every bathroom, laundry and shower | A licensed waterproofer, to AS 3740 or the NCC Housing Provisions |
| Termite and moisture check of concealed framing | Older homes and any area with past leaks | A timber pest inspector and the builder |

sections.heading: Title and planning: what you are allowed to build
sections.markdown: Check the title and planning information before commissioning a detailed design. An **easement** may require authority consent for building work. A **restrictive covenant** can control height, materials or dwelling numbers. **Overlays** add controls to the zone. These are the same layers covered in a Victorian [Section 32](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/reading-a-section-32). For a home in a Victorian Heritage Overlay, the [heritage-overlay guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/living-in-a-heritage-overlay) explains how to read the schedule and related controls.

sections.heading: Build the homework into the budget
sections.markdown: Link the contingency to recorded assumptions and the decision points that could change scope. Before work begins, notify the home insurer or broker and confirm how renovation, vacancy, security and contract works affect cover.

sections.heading: Separate what is staying from what is changing
sections.markdown:
Make a simple existing-condition record before choosing the finished layout: construction system, known alterations, roof and wall condition, wet-area history and the services you intend to retain. Ask which parts have been inspected and which assumptions come only from old drawings. A new kitchen can depend on an old floor, concealed plumbing and a switchboard that have never been assessed for the proposal.

[YourHome's renovation guidance](https://www.yourhome.gov.au/buy-build-renovate/renovations-and-additions) encourages considering the existing building and coordinating performance upgrades. For the decision in front of you, compare retaining the layout with moving services or opening a wall. The valuable comparison includes enabling work and uncertainty as well as the visible finishes.

sections.heading: Spend investigation effort where it can change the design
sections.markdown:
**Resolve an assumption before it becomes expensive**

| Proposed change | Question before commitment | Useful input |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Remove a wall or enlarge an opening | What supports the loads now, and where will they go? | Plans, structural assessment and a design including temporary support. |
| Move a bathroom or kitchen | Can the proposed service routes and floor build-up work? | Licensed service advice, levels and appropriate access to the existing assembly. |
| Replace cladding or add insulation | How will the existing and new layers drain and dry? | Product details and climate-appropriate assembly design. |
| Extend beside a boundary or service asset | Which rights, approvals, access and protection measures apply? | Title and authority review, surveyed information where needed. |
| Retain an old roof over new interiors | What evidence supports retaining the covering and drainage? | A defined roof assessment before finishes conceal the consequences of a leak. |

Opening-up can be useful when a concealed fact would materially change the scope. Agree its location, purpose, authority, safety precautions and reinstatement first. A destructive inspection is not a casual extension of a visual report, especially before purchase or where hazardous material may be present. If investigation is deferred, carry the assumption explicitly into the design and budget.

sections.heading: Compare quotes using the same assumptions
sections.markdown:
Give tenderers the same drawings, specification, investigation information and list of exclusions. Ask them to identify what is fixed, what is an allowance, what has been excluded and what triggers a variation. A lower headline figure can simply leave more services, access or making-good outside the price. Keep tax treatment and the intended quality of reinstatement consistent when comparing totals.

Use a short uncertainty schedule instead of relying only on an unexplained percentage contingency. For each unknown, record the possible consequence, when it becomes knowable and who approves a scope or price change. A concealed pipe route might affect a local allowance; uncertain support under an addition might change the design itself. They deserve different investigation decisions.

sections.heading: Assign responsibility at the junctions between trades
sections.markdown:
Window replacement, roof-to-wall junctions, wet-area penetrations and deck connections often cross trade boundaries. Ask who details the junction, who installs each layer and who checks the work before it is covered. A collection of individual product warranties does not establish that the assembled junction will perform.

For an apartment, establish the common-property boundary, required scheme approvals and any continuing responsibility for the alteration. For a house, plan how retained rooms will remain safe, secure and weatherproof while work proceeds. Confirm with the insurer or broker how the proposed works and occupancy arrangement affect your actual cover; use [the insurance guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/home-condition-and-insurance) to organise that discussion.

sections.heading: Define the evidence you want at completion
sections.markdown: Agree which plans, inspection records, certificates, product details, concealed-work photographs and operating instructions you will receive for your [home record](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/keeping-a-record-of-your-home). Ask how defects will be listed and followed up, and what maintenance keeps the new systems serviceable. The completion process should address both the relevant approvals and delivery of the contracted scope; neither a photograph of the finished room nor one invoice records all of that.

sections.heading: Worked example: the open-plan kitchen with a provisional beam allowance
sections.markdown:
**Illustrative reasoning example, not an inspected property.** A 1970s brick-veneer house is quoted for wall removal and a new kitchen, with a provisional allowance for a beam. No one has established the support below its proposed end. The visible design can be attractive while that structural assumption remains unresolved.

Have the load path and support arrangement assessed before relying on the allowance. If an appropriate existing support is confirmed, the scope may remain close to the proposal. If new foundations, service diversion or access work are needed, the budget and sequence change. Resolve that dependency while the layout can still move, then compare quotes against the same documented design.

> Note: A current home record gives the design team the best available picture of the structure, services, prior work and unresolved questions.

> Important: Confirm permit requirements with your local council or a building surveyor. Use licensed asbestos professionals and a qualified engineer for structural change.

faqs.question: What should I find out about my house before renovating?
faqs.answer: Its era and construction, the condition of the parts you will change, hazardous materials, services capacity and what the title and planning controls allow. A Homechecker Read can surface the era and condition questions for the address from records, imagery and your documents before design starts.

faqs.question: What should I test for before renovating an older home?
faqs.answer: Test materials you plan to disturb for asbestos if the home was built or renovated before 1990, and paint for lead if it was applied before 1970. Have an electrician check older wiring, and an engineer assess any wall you plan to remove or open.

faqs.question: What should I check before renovating my home?
faqs.answer: Check approvals, hazardous materials, structure, services, title constraints, planning controls and insurance before the design is locked. Decide which plans, photographs, certificates and invoices you will keep as the work unfolds.

faqs.question: Do I need a permit to renovate?

guides.contentMarkdown:
# Planning a renovation: the checks before you start

Before design gets too far, check the title and planning controls, likely approvals, licensed-trade requirements, possible pre-1990 hazardous materials, and the capacity of the existing structure and services. Tell the home insurer about relevant work and get the cover position in writing. Keep a contingency for the things no one can see until the building is opened up.

## Research note
The [Victorian planning](https://www.planning.vic.gov.au/guides-and-resources/guides/guide-to-victorias-planning-system/planning-permits) and [building-permit](https://www.bpc.vic.gov.au/resource-hub/practice-notes/bp-01-when-is-a-building-permit-required) examples are jurisdiction-specific. The broader decision sequence uses existing-condition evidence and clear scope assumptions before commitment.

## Opening
### Clear the path while change is still cheap
- **Site:** What the title, easements and overlays already decided
- **Approval:** Planning approval and a building permit: separate questions
- **Delivery:** Licensed hands, insured work, inspections passed, records kept

_Settle the pathway while the design is still a pencil sketch._

## Reduce uncertainty before design hardens
Run the early checks on title, planning, hazards, structure and services while the design can still bend around what they find. Then write down the assumptions you are still carrying, decide whether it is worth opening anything up to test them, and make the contract say who owns the risk of what nobody could see.

A [Homechecker Read](https://homechecker.com.au/) is a quick way to start that list for an existing home. It reads the era, construction and records of the house and flags the questions a renovation is likely to meet, such as materials that may contain asbestos, original services and what the structure may be carrying. Add your plans, quotes or earlier reports and it updates, which gives your designer and builder a clearer brief before anything is opened up.

## Approvals for the proposed work
Planning permits, building permits, trade licences and compliance certificates serve different purposes. Requirements vary by state, council, site and scope. In Victoria, use the official guides to [planning permits](https://www.planning.vic.gov.au/guides-and-resources/guides/guide-to-victorias-planning-system/planning-permits) and [building permits](https://www.bpc.vic.gov.au/resource-hub/practice-notes/bp-01-when-is-a-building-permit-required). Ask the relevant authority and building surveyor to confirm the pathway before design is locked.

## Hazardous materials: know before you disturb
Renovation can disturb hazardous materials. Screen the property before drilling, sanding or demolition.

### Asbestos

For a home built or renovated before 1990, [ASSEA advises that asbestos-containing materials may be present](https://www.asbestossafety.gov.au/about-asbestos/finding-asbestos/home). Identify suspect material before disturbance and confirm the relevant state licensing and disposal requirements. A photograph or build date cannot confirm the material.

### Lead paint

Older paint layers may contain lead even when newer coatings look sound. Before sanding, scraping or stripping, follow the [Australian Government Lead Alert](https://www.agriculture.gov.au/sites/default/files/documents/lead-paint-fifth-edition.pdf), identify the material and use the appropriate precautions. The paint's age is a screening clue; it does not establish its lead concentration.

## Structure and services: what the building can take
### Load-bearing walls and structure

Establish the load-bearing structure before removing or opening a wall; whether the house is [brick veneer or double brick](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/brick-veneer-vs-double-brick) changes that question. Structural changes need engineering and an appropriately sized support. Where the home already shows movement, read [the guide to wall cracks](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/cracks-structural-or-cosmetic) and obtain professional assessment before adding load.

### Wiring, plumbing and the switchboard

A new kitchen, bathroom or extension may require switchboard, wiring, plumbing or drainage upgrades. Assess the installed services while planning and budget coordinated work while walls are open. The [era planning guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/what-your-home-needs-by-decade) helps identify the first questions.

**Checks to complete before anyone opens a wall**

| Check | When it applies | Who does it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Asbestos sampling of materials to be disturbed | Homes built or renovated before 1990 ([ASSEA](https://www.asbestossafety.gov.au/about-asbestos/finding-asbestos/home)) | A licensed asbestos assessor or competent person, with laboratory testing |
| Lead paint testing before sanding or stripping | Paint applied before 1970 ([Lead Alert](https://www.agriculture.gov.au/sites/default/files/documents/lead-paint-fifth-edition.pdf)) | A test kit or a qualified assessor |
| Electrical safety check | Before adding insulation, opening walls with wiring, or where the house predates safety switches | A licensed electrician |
| Structural assessment of walls to be removed or opened | Any loadbearing wall, in brick veneer as well as double brick ([guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/brick-veneer-vs-double-brick)) | A structural engineer |
| Wet-area waterproofing design and certificate | Every bathroom, laundry and shower | A licensed waterproofer, to AS 3740 or the NCC Housing Provisions |
| Termite and moisture check of concealed framing | Older homes and any area with past leaks | A timber pest inspector and the builder |

## Title and planning: what you are allowed to build
Check the title and planning information before commissioning a detailed design. An **easement** may require authority consent for building work. A **restrictive covenant** can control height, materials or dwelling numbers. **Overlays** add controls to the zone. These are the same layers covered in a Victorian [Section 32](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/reading-a-section-32). For a home in a Victorian Heritage Overlay, the [heritage-overlay guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/living-in-a-heritage-overlay) explains how to read the schedule and related controls.

## Build the homework into the budget
Link the contingency to recorded assumptions and the decision points that could change scope. Before work begins, notify the home insurer or broker and confirm how renovation, vacancy, security and contract works affect cover.

## Separate what is staying from what is changing
Make a simple existing-condition record before choosing the finished layout: construction system, known alterations, roof and wall condition, wet-area history and the services you intend to retain. Ask which parts have been inspected and which assumptions come only from old drawings. A new kitchen can depend on an old floor, concealed plumbing and a switchboard that have never been assessed for the proposal.

[YourHome's renovation guidance](https://www.yourhome.gov.au/buy-build-renovate/renovations-and-additions) encourages considering the existing building and coordinating performance upgrades. For the decision in front of you, compare retaining the layout with moving services or opening a wall. The valuable comparison includes enabling work and uncertainty as well as the visible finishes.

## Spend investigation effort where it can change the design
**Resolve an assumption before it becomes expensive**

| Proposed change | Question before commitment | Useful input |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Remove a wall or enlarge an opening | What supports the loads now, and where will they go? | Plans, structural assessment and a design including temporary support. |
| Move a bathroom or kitchen | Can the proposed service routes and floor build-up work? | Licensed service advice, levels and appropriate access to the existing assembly. |
| Replace cladding or add insulation | How will the existing and new layers drain and dry? | Product details and climate-appropriate assembly design. |
| Extend beside a boundary or service asset | Which rights, approvals, access and protection measures apply? | Title and authority review, surveyed information where needed. |
| Retain an old roof over new interiors | What evidence supports retaining the covering and drainage? | A defined roof assessment before finishes conceal the consequences of a leak. |

Opening-up can be useful when a concealed fact would materially change the scope. Agree its location, purpose, authority, safety precautions and reinstatement first. A destructive inspection is not a casual extension of a visual report, especially before purchase or where hazardous material may be present. If investigation is deferred, carry the assumption explicitly into the design and budget.

## Compare quotes using the same assumptions
Give tenderers the same drawings, specification, investigation information and list of exclusions. Ask them to identify what is fixed, what is an allowance, what has been excluded and what triggers a variation. A lower headline figure can simply leave more services, access or making-good outside the price. Keep tax treatment and the intended quality of reinstatement consistent when comparing totals.

Use a short uncertainty schedule instead of relying only on an unexplained percentage contingency. For each unknown, record the possible consequence, when it becomes knowable and who approves a scope or price change. A concealed pipe route might affect a local allowance; uncertain support under an addition might change the design itself. They deserve different investigation decisions.

## Assign responsibility at the junctions between trades
Window replacement, roof-to-wall junctions, wet-area penetrations and deck connections often cross trade boundaries. Ask who details the junction, who installs each layer and who checks the work before it is covered. A collection of individual product warranties does not establish that the assembled junction will perform.

For an apartment, establish the common-property boundary, required scheme approvals and any continuing responsibility for the alteration. For a house, plan how retained rooms will remain safe, secure and weatherproof while work proceeds. Confirm with the insurer or broker how the proposed works and occupancy arrangement affect your actual cover; use [the insurance guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/home-condition-and-insurance) to organise that discussion.

## Define the evidence you want at completion
Agree which plans, inspection records, certificates, product details, concealed-work photographs and operating instructions you will receive for your [home record](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/keeping-a-record-of-your-home). Ask how defects will be listed and followed up, and what maintenance keeps the new systems serviceable. The completion process should address both the relevant approvals and delivery of the contracted scope; neither a photograph of the finished room nor one invoice records all of that.

## Worked example: the open-plan kitchen with a provisional beam allowance
**Illustrative reasoning example, not an inspected property.** A 1970s brick-veneer house is quoted for wall removal and a new kitchen, with a provisional allowance for a beam. No one has established the support below its proposed end. The visible design can be attractive while that structural assumption remains unresolved.

Have the load path and support arrangement assessed before relying on the allowance. If an appropriate existing support is confirmed, the scope may remain close to the proposal. If new foundations, service diversion or access work are needed, the budget and sequence change. Resolve that dependency while the layout can still move, then compare quotes against the same documented design.

> Note: A current home record gives the design team the best available picture of the structure, services, prior work and unresolved questions.

> Important: Confirm permit requirements with your local council or a building surveyor. Use licensed asbestos professionals and a qualified engineer for structural change.

## Frequently asked questions
### What should I find out about my house before renovating?
Its era and construction, the condition of the parts you will change, hazardous materials, services capacity and what the title and planning controls allow. A Homechecker Read can surface the era and condition questions for the address from records, imagery and your documents before design starts.

### What should I test for before renovating an older home?
Test materials you plan to disturb for asbestos if the home was built or renovated before 1990, and paint for lead if it was applied before 1970. Have an electrician check older wiring, and an engineer assess any wall you plan to remove or open.

### What should I check before renovating my home?
Check approvals, hazardous materials, structure, services, title constraints, planning controls and insurance before the design is locked. Decide which plans, photographs, certificates and invoices you will keep as the work unfolds.

### Do I need a permit to renovate?
It depends on the proposal, site and jurisdiction. Planning and building permits are separate, and licensed plumbing or electrical work is a separate compliance question again. Confirm the pathway before design is locked.

### How do I know if my home has asbestos before renovating?
For a home built or renovated before 1990, treat suspect material as potentially asbestos-containing until appropriately identified. Follow your state’s licensing and disposal requirements before disturbance.

### How do I know if a wall is load-bearing?
Establish the structural system from plans and professional assessment before removal. Load-bearing changes need engineering and an appropriately sized support.

### Will my switchboard and wiring handle a renovation?
Have a licensed electrician assess the proposed load, switchboard, safety switches and installed wiring during planning.

### Can I build an extension anywhere on my land?
Easements, restrictive covenants, overlays, setbacks and approval rules can limit the location and form. Check title and planning information before design.

### How should I set a renovation contingency?
Link it to specific unresolved assumptions and their possible consequences. Decide which can be investigated before contract and how later scope changes will be approved.

### Is the cheapest quote necessarily better value?
Compare the same scope, exclusions, allowances, access, service upgrades and reinstatement. A lower total may leave important work outside the price.

### What records should I receive at handover?
Agree the applicable approvals and inspection records, final plans, product and service details, concealed-work photographs, warranties and operating/maintenance instructions before work begins.

## Method
We organise renovation decisions around retained fabric, investigations that can change design, clear scope assumptions and evidence at concealed-work and completion stages.

## Limitations
Approval, licensing, insurance and disclosure obligations vary. Confirm them before design or demolition with the relevant authority and insurer.

## Sources
- [Planning permits](https://www.planning.vic.gov.au/guides-and-resources/guides/guide-to-victorias-planning-system/planning-permits) — Victorian Government; accessed 2026-07-19
- [When is a building permit required?](https://www.bpc.vic.gov.au/resource-hub/practice-notes/bp-01-when-is-a-building-permit-required) — Building and Plumbing Commission Victoria; accessed 2026-07-19
- [Asbestos in the home](https://www.asbestossafety.gov.au/about-asbestos/finding-asbestos/home) — Asbestos and Silica Safety and Eradication Agency; accessed 2026-09-07
- [Lead Alert: the six step guide to painting your home](https://www.agriculture.gov.au/sites/default/files/documents/lead-paint-fifth-edition.pdf) — Australian Government; accessed 2026-07-19
- [Renovations and additions](https://www.yourhome.gov.au/buy-build-renovate/renovations-and-additions) — YourHome, Australian Government; accessed 2026-09-07
- [AS 3740-1994 Waterproofing of wet areas within residential buildings](https://store.standards.org.au/product/as-3740-1994) — Standards Australia; accessed 2026-10-14

guides.question: What does a period home (pre-1920s) need?
guides.title: Period homes (pre-1920s): what to expect and what they need
guides.summary: What to check in a period home built before 1920: footings, damp, roofs, chimneys, services and alterations, and what should change your decision.
guides.answer: With a pre-1920s home, start below the floor and at the base of the walls. Identify the actual footing, floor and wall systems, check subfloor clearance and ventilation, drainage, low-wall moisture and salt, then follow water up through roofs, chimneys and openings. After that, map the service upgrades, wet areas, extensions and repairs that may be decades younger than the original shell. Treat older coatings and pre-1990 alterations as material-identification questions before disturbance, and check any heritage controls separately from physical condition.
guides.methodology: We read the building from ground to roof: identify the structural and material system, follow moisture paths through subfloor and masonry, inspect roof/timber/pest interfaces, then separate every later service, wet-area and alteration timeline from the original shell.
guides.limitations: Pre-1920s construction varies substantially across Australia. Heritage guidance can inform repair principles but planning controls and conservation requirements are property- and jurisdiction-specific. Diagnose moisture, structure, services and hazardous materials from property-specific records and physical evidence.
guides.researchNote: Pre-1920s homes need a fabric-first reading: actual footings and floor, subfloor clearance, older masonry and moisture, roof/chimney junctions, timber and pest access, then the services and renovations layered in later. National YourHome guidance supports the moisture, termite, maintenance and existing-home checks; the multi-agency [salt attack and rising damp guide](https://cdn.environment.sa.gov.au/environment/docs/saltdamp_techguide.pdf) adds specialist context for historic masonry and compatible repair.

cluster.label: Read the building
cluster.blurb: Use age and construction as a starting hypothesis, then test it against evidence and physical inspection.

sections.heading: Opening
sections.markdown:
### Read it from the ground up
- **Stand:** Footings, floor and subfloor showing how the house is supported today
- **Dry:** Drainage, older masonry, roof and chimneys showing how water moves
- **Layers:** Services, wet areas and additions proving which parts are actually younger

_Old fabric is not a defect. Unexplained movement, moisture or incompatible repair is the question._

sections.heading: Style is the label; construction is the evidence
sections.markdown:
Pre-1920s housing includes terraces, cottages and villas, freestanding masonry houses, timber-framed homes and many regional forms. Victorian, Edwardian and Federation are useful style labels, but they do not tell you whether the building sits on timber stumps, masonry piers, strip footings or a later mixed foundation, nor whether the walls are solid masonry, framed and clad, rendered, altered or partly rebuilt.

Many older homes carry only a rough date such as 'circa 1910'. [Working out when a house was built](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/when-was-my-house-built) explains how to narrow it down and date later additions separately.

That distinction matters because the same visible symptom can mean different things in different assemblies. Floor slope in a raised timber house sends you toward stumps, bearers, joists, moisture and termite evidence. Low-wall deterioration in older masonry sends you toward ground levels, drainage, damp-proofing, salts and repair compatibility. A rear extension may sit on a completely different footing system from the original front rooms. If you are not sure whether the walls are solid brick, cavity brick or a later veneer, [how to tell which wall system you have](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/brick-veneer-vs-double-brick#tell) sets out the clues.

> Note: Do not inspect a 'Victorian house'. Inspect this footing system, this wall system, this roof, this subfloor and every later layer attached to them.

### Signs worth following in an older house
- **Floors:** Slopes, bounce, or doors that bind and free up with the seasons
- **Walls:** Salt bloom, crumbling mortar or blistering paint low on masonry walls
- **Ceilings:** Stains near chimneys or valleys, and any sag in an old plaster ceiling

_Each sign has more than one possible cause. Follow it to the source before choosing a repair._

sections.heading: A century-old house is usually several houses layered together
sections.markdown:
**Separate the original shell from the work that followed**

| Layer | What to establish | Common evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Original shell | Footings, floor, walls, roof structure, chimneys and original openings | Subfloor/roof access, visible materials, plans where available and building inspection |
| Early alterations | Enclosed verandas, lean-tos, fireplaces removed, reroofing, early plumbing or electrical work | Changes in materials, floor levels, roof lines, old permits or plans and service evidence |
| Mid-century work | Bathrooms, kitchens, sheet materials, services and additions installed decades after the original build | Material identification, invoices/records where they survive, physical junctions and pre-1990 hazard screening |
| Recent renovation | Restumping, rewiring, replumbing, roofing, insulation, wet areas, extensions and cosmetic work | Invoices, permits/certificates where applicable, photographs, warranties and present condition |
| Repair history | Damp treatment, termite work, cracking, drainage changes and recurring leaks | Reports, scopes, before/after photos, monitoring and evidence that the cause was resolved |

A renovated period home should therefore make you ask a more precise question, not fewer questions: **which systems were actually renewed, and what remained behind the new finishes?** A new kitchen does not date the subfloor. New paint does not date the roof plumbing. A restumping invoice does not tell you the condition of every bearer, joist or masonry wall.

sections.heading: Start at ground level: footings, floor and subfloor
sections.markdown:
Raised timber floors are common in many period homes, but not universal. Identify whether the property uses timber or concrete stumps, masonry piers, strip footings, suspended floors or later concrete additions. Then look for differential floor levels, sticking doors, distorted openings, [wall cracks](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/cracks-structural-or-cosmetic), decayed timber, improvised packing, evidence of earlier restumping or underpinning and changes where old and new construction meet.

Subfloor moisture deserves particular attention. [YourHome's maintenance guidance](https://www.yourhome.gov.au/buy-build-renovate/repairs-and-maintenance) identifies poor subfloor ventilation or clearance, leaking pipes, obstructed vents and excess ground moisture as sources of underfloor and wall-cavity moisture. Garden beds, mulch, additions and later paving can quietly reduce the clearance or ventilation an older house once relied on.

**Ground-level clues and the questions they should trigger**

| Clue | Possible pathways | Evidence to seek |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sloping or springy floor | Footing movement, stump/pier deterioration, bearer/joist issue, local decay or historic settlement | Subfloor inspection, floor-level pattern, timber condition and movement history |
| Blocked or buried vents | Reduced subfloor drying, later landscaping or paving, addition built over original ventilation | Clearance around vents, subfloor humidity/moisture evidence and drainage route |
| Garden beds or paving against walls | Bridged damp-proofing, splashback, reduced inspection access and higher local moisture | Damp-proof course where visible, ground levels, moisture/salt pattern and stormwater behaviour |
| Cracks at old/new junction | Different footing systems, differential movement, poor connection or simple finish cracking | Plan/alteration date, crack pattern, distortion, monitoring and structural advice where indicated |
| Timber close to soil | Decay and termite access risk | Clearance, pest evidence, moisture source and professional pest inspection |

sections.heading: Older masonry needs a moisture diagnosis before a cosmetic repair
sections.markdown:
Low-wall staining, fretting, blistered paint or salt deposits are not one diagnosis. Moisture can arrive from capillary rise, a bridged or deteriorated damp-proof course, roof or plumbing leaks, hard paving and poor drainage, garden irrigation, condensation or an old event that left salts behind. The first task is to identify the source and pathway, not to choose a coating.

The multi-agency [Salt attack and rising damp technical guide](https://cdn.environment.sa.gov.au/environment/docs/saltdamp_techguide.pdf) for historic and older buildings warns that hard cement repairs can be incompatible with older lime-based masonry and can shift moisture and salt damage into the surrounding brick or stone. Heritage Victoria likewise publishes specific guidance on lime mortars, repointing and rising damp. That does not mean every pre-1920 wall needs lime work. It means the existing masonry and mortar should be identified before repointing, rendering or sealing it.

If the damp pattern is significant, recurring or structurally consequential, use [the damp and moisture guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/damp-and-moisture-in-your-home) to separate rain, ground, plumbing and condensation pathways and bring in the appropriate specialist before destructive treatment.

sections.heading: Roof, chimneys and rainwater are a connected system
sections.markdown:
Period roofs may include slate, terracotta, corrugated metal or later replacement coverings. What matters is not only the field of the roof but the junctions: valleys, flashings, parapets, chimney abutments, penetrations, gutters, downpipes and where the water goes after it leaves the roof. A sound-looking roof can still leak at one poorly maintained junction.

Chimneys deserve their own line in the inspection. Check masonry condition, mortar, flashings, caps and whether redundant fireplaces or flues have been altered. Water entry at a chimney can present as ceiling or wall staining well away from the obvious external defect. Heritage Victoria's maintenance material puts structural soundness and watertightness ahead of cosmetic conservation, which is the right sequence for a buyer too.

sections.heading: Timber, openings and termites: keep access visible
sections.markdown:
Older timber floors, bearers, joists, [weatherboards](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/weatherboard-homes), joinery and roof framing can remain serviceable for very long periods when they stay dry and ventilated. The inspection question is therefore less about age than **moisture, pest access, section loss, movement and previous repair**. Look closely where timber meets masonry, soil, leaking wet areas or poorly ventilated subfloors.

YourHome recommends termite inspection before purchase in most Australian regions and identifies inadequate subfloor clearance and ventilation, moisture, buried timber and compromised barriers as risk factors. Later decks, paths, extensions and garden work can create new access routes around an old house. A past termite treatment is useful history; it is not a substitute for current inspection access and current evidence. [Where termites get in](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/termites-in-australian-homes#entry-points) shows the routes to keep visible around an older house.

sections.heading: Services often tell a different age story from the building
sections.markdown:
A pre-1920s address can contain several generations of wiring, switchboards, water pipes, sewer connections, gas work, hot-water systems and heating/cooling. Establish what is installed now and what the claimed upgrade actually covered. 'Rewired' might mean a full replacement or a much narrower job. 'Replumbed' might refer only to water supply and say nothing about drains.

Before adding insulation to an existing home, [YourHome recommends a licensed electrician assess the wiring and electrical fittings](https://www.yourhome.gov.au/passive-design/insulation), specifically noting that older homes can contain damaged or outdated wiring and other hazards. That is a good model for all service upgrades: understand the existing system before covering, extending or loading it. For older pipes and drains, see [what the pipes tell you](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/plumbing-hot-water-and-leaks#pipes); for wiring, see [signs of old or failing wiring](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/switchboards-wiring-and-safety-switches#wiring).

sections.heading: Wet areas and additions belong to their own era
sections.markdown:
Most period homes have bathrooms, kitchens and laundries that are much younger than the original shell. Read each wet area by its renovation date and current moisture evidence. Look for loose finishes, swelling, failed sealants, staining, leaks below and junctions where newer waterproofing meets older floors or walls. Current NCC guidance can explain modern waterproofing principles, but it should not be used as a retrospective declaration about whether historic work complied when carried out.

Extensions need the same separation. Compare footing and floor systems, roof lines, drainage, wall materials and movement at the junction. A masonry front and lightweight rear addition can behave differently under the same seasonal conditions. Plans, permits and invoices can help date the work, while inspection tells you how the junction performs now. [How the age of the bathroom changes the question](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/bathroom-waterproofing-and-leaking-showers#by-era) covers reading the wet areas themselves.

sections.heading: Hazardous materials follow the alteration timeline
sections.markdown:
Older coatings can contain lead. Pre-1990 additions and renovations may also introduce asbestos-containing products even though the original house predates those materials. Use [Lead Alert](https://www.agriculture.gov.au/sites/default/files/documents/lead-paint-fifth-edition.pdf) and the [national asbestos householders' guide](https://www.newaste.org.au/asbestos/assets/asbestos-guide-for-householders.pdf) before sanding, drilling, cutting or demolition. The age of the original façade is not enough to date every material behind it.

sections.heading: Heritage status and physical condition are separate questions
sections.markdown:
A period appearance does not automatically mean a property is heritage-listed, and a heritage control does not tell you whether the building is in good condition. Check the planning and heritage controls that apply to the address, then assess the building fabric separately. In Victoria, the [Section 32 guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/reading-a-section-32) and [heritage-overlay guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/living-in-a-heritage-overlay) show how to read those planning layers.

**Turn period-home findings into next actions**

| Finding | Why it matters | Useful next action |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Unknown footing/restumping history with material floor distortion | The structural support and remaining scope are uncertain | Subfloor inspection and structural assessment where movement evidence warrants it |
