sections.heading: Opening
sections.markdown:
### Character on top, clues underneath
- **Ground:** What the ground has done to it: footings, drainage, movement
- **Envelope:** How the roof, walls and windows are keeping water out
- **Layers:** The decades of work layered on since

_The style is the easy part. Confirm the construction behind it._

sections.heading: Interwar style is not the same thing as interwar construction
sections.markdown:
Interwar housing includes Californian bungalows, Spanish Mission, Art Deco and early functionalist forms, but style tells you less than people often think about the structure underneath. Across Australia, these houses can use [weatherboard](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/weatherboard-homes), brick, rendered masonry and mixed construction; raised timber floors, piers, stumps or strip footings; tiled or metal roofs; and decades of later additions.

If you are not sure whether a home is genuinely interwar or a later house in a revival style, [working out when a house was built](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/when-was-my-house-built) shows how to check.

That means the first inspection task is classification: **what is original, what is later and how are the two joined?** The rear extension, bathroom, wiring and roof may each belong to a different era. A good record separates those layers rather than calling the entire property '1930s'.

### Signs worth following in an interwar home
- **Floors:** Uneven or springy floors, and gaps opening above skirtings
- **Walls:** Cracks above doors and windows, and marks near the base of brick walls
- **Openings:** Sticking windows, tired putty, and stains around chimneys

_Each sign has more than one possible cause. Follow it to the source before choosing a repair._

sections.heading: Start underneath: footings, subfloor and ground moisture
sections.markdown:
### Identify the footing system before talking about repairs

Interwar homes can stand on timber or concrete stumps, masonry piers, strip footings or combinations created by later additions. Find out what the house actually stands on before assuming it needs restumping, underpinning or another structural intervention. Record floor levels, bounce or distortion, cracks, pier/stump condition, subfloor access and any evidence of previous footing work.

Movement needs context. Drainage, soil, trees, leaking services, altered ground levels and extensions can all affect the way an older house moves. Where cracks are progressive or accompanied by sticking doors, sloping floors or other distortion, use [the crack guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/cracks-structural-or-cosmetic) and obtain appropriate engineering assessment. [Restumping and reblocking](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/subfloors-stumps-and-restumping#restumping) explains what that work involves and what a quote should name.

### Subfloor ventilation, clearance and termite access

Raised floors can make structure inspectable, but only when the subfloor remains accessible, ventilated and reasonably dry. Look for low clearances, stored timber, garden beds or paving against walls, leaking services and areas where later additions have enclosed the original subfloor. [YourHome maintenance guidance](https://www.yourhome.gov.au/buy-build-renovate/repairs-and-maintenance) identifies inadequate subfloor clearance and ventilation, damp areas and concealed access paths as termite-risk factors.

Previous termite treatment is not the same thing as current protection. Ask where activity occurred, what damage was repaired, what treatment or barrier exists and what the latest licensed pest inspection found. The numbers are in [clearance and ventilation](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/subfloors-stumps-and-restumping#clearance), and [where termites get in](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/termites-in-australian-homes#entry-points) covers the routes to keep visible.

sections.heading: Follow water through an older envelope
sections.markdown:
### Do not label every low-wall mark as rising damp

A damp-proof course may be present, altered, bridged or ineffective, but low-wall moisture can also come from rain penetration, plumbing, condensation, high external ground levels, blocked cavities or salts left from an older event. Diagnose the pathway using [damp and moisture in your home](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/damp-and-moisture-in-your-home). The visible stain is evidence of moisture history; it is not a diagnosis by itself.

Check roof coverings, chimneys, valleys, flashings, gutters, downpipes, window and door junctions and the way stormwater leaves the site. Older homes often have had multiple generations of repairs, and water commonly exploits the join between original and later work.

### Roofs, chimneys and openings

Assess the roof by its actual material and repair history. Look for cracked or displaced elements, corrosion, flashings, valleys, penetrations, chimney junctions and evidence of previous leaks. Timber windows and joinery should be read for decay, failed coatings, operation and water entry; replacement windows should be checked for how they were flashed and sealed into the older wall.

sections.heading: Hazardous materials often belong to several eras at once
sections.markdown:
### Lead paint

Older paint layers may contain lead. Before sanding, scraping or heat stripping, follow the [Australian Government Lead Alert](https://www.agriculture.gov.au/sites/default/files/documents/lead-paint-fifth-edition.pdf), test where appropriate and use lead-safe controls. New paint over old coatings does not remove the underlying hazard.

### Asbestos may be original or a later renovation layer

An interwar house can contain asbestos-containing materials from original or later work. The [national householders' guide](https://www.newaste.org.au/asbestos/assets/asbestos-guide-for-householders.pdf) uses a practical screen: homes built or renovated before 1990 may contain asbestos products. Identify suspect materials before disturbance and follow the relevant licensing and disposal requirements. [Where asbestos is most often found](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/asbestos-in-the-home#where) lists the places to identify first.

sections.heading: Services rarely belong to one date
sections.markdown:
**Service questions for an interwar home**

| System | What to establish | Useful evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Electrical | Original remnants, partial rewiring, switchboard changes and current capacity | Licensed inspection, invoices/certificates where applicable and visible alteration history |
| Water supply | Pipe materials, leaks, pressure and replacement history | Plumbing invoices, visible pipework, licensed assessment where needed |
| Sewer/drainage | Original versus repaired sections, blockage history, tree-root or ground-movement issues | Drain records, CCTV where justified, repair invoices and site drainage observations |
| Hot water/heating/cooling | Installed system age, location, safety and service history | Service records, model information and current condition |
| Solar/electrification | Later generation or high-load additions to an older electrical system | System specifications and electrical assessment of the whole installation |

Do not infer service condition from the age of the house or the age of the kitchen. A renovated room can sit over much older wiring, drainage or structure.

An interwar house predates every modern electrical safety requirement. Safety switches were only required on the power-point circuits of new homes from around 1991, and on lighting circuits from around 2000–01. Original wiring is now well over 80 years old, so ask an electrician whether and when the house was rewired, whether the switchboard has been upgraded, and which circuits have safety switches. The [dated milestones table](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/red-flags-by-era#milestones) sets out the other dates worth checking. [Reading the switchboard](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/switchboards-wiring-and-safety-switches#switchboard) is the quickest first look at the wiring’s story.

sections.heading: Later wet areas and extensions deserve their own due diligence
sections.markdown:
Bathrooms, laundries and rear additions are often the youngest parts of an interwar home, and they can dominate the repair budget. Establish when they were constructed, whether approvals or records exist, and whether there is evidence of leakage, movement or poorly resolved roof and wall junctions.

Current [NCC waterproofing guidance](https://ncc.abcb.gov.au/ncc-navigator/waterproofing-houses) explains the modern building principles behind wet areas: coordinated waterproofing, water-resistant materials, junctions, penetrations and drainage. It is useful context, but it should not be applied retrospectively as a simple pass/fail test to older work. Existing-work compliance depends on the relevant date, approvals and jurisdiction. [How the age of the bathroom changes the question](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/bathroom-waterproofing-and-leaking-showers#by-era) covers dating a wet area separately from the house.

sections.heading: Energy retrofits need moisture awareness
sections.markdown: Interwar homes are frequently upgraded with ceiling insulation, draught sealing, new glazing, heating/cooling and sometimes wall insulation. These changes can improve comfort, but older walls and roofs still need to manage moisture. [YourHome](https://www.yourhome.gov.au/passive-design/condensation) explains that condensation depends on humidity, temperature, ventilation and the ability of the building fabric to drain and dry. If an older house has been made much tighter, look for recurrent window condensation, mould, roof-space moisture and the way bathrooms and cooking moisture are exhausted.

sections.heading: Heritage and character controls can shape what you can change
sections.markdown: Interwar homes in established suburbs may sit under heritage or character controls, particularly where the street-facing form contributes to a precinct. Confirm the actual planning controls before designing an extension, façade change, demolition or replacement. For Victorian purchases, review the planning information in the [Section 32](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/reading-a-section-32) and use [the heritage-overlay guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/living-in-a-heritage-overlay) where relevant.

sections.heading: Common interwar misreads
sections.markdown:
**What a clue does and does not tell you**

| Clue | Reasonable inference | What still needs evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fresh paint to lower walls | There may have been cosmetic repair or previous moisture work | Whether moisture is active, what caused it and whether salts/material damage remain. |
| Floors feel uneven | The house may have settlement, stump/pier variation or normal old-floor irregularity | Whether movement is active, structurally important or related to a later addition. |
| “Restumped” | Some footing work may have occurred | Which parts, what material/system, why it was done and whether levels/movement are now stable. |
| New bathroom | The wet area is younger than the shell | Membrane/detailing, plumbing changes, approvals and current moisture performance. |
| New switchboard | Electrical work has occurred | Whether the whole installation or only part of it was upgraded. |
| No visible termite damage | No obvious damage was seen in the visible area | Whether inaccessible or concealed areas are affected and whether the property has a current management/inspection history. |

sections.heading: A buyer evidence stack for an interwar home
sections.markdown:
1. **Construction:** identify floor, footing, wall and roof systems and where later additions begin.
2. **Water:** trace roof-water disposal, drainage, external ground levels, subfloor moisture, plumbing and wet areas.
3. **Movement:** record cracks, distortion, footing condition, drainage and prior repairs rather than relying on a “restumped” claim.
4. **Timber and pests:** obtain appropriate pest evidence and keep subfloor/inspection zones visible.
5. **Hazards:** consider lead in older coatings and pre-1990 asbestos-containing materials before planned disturbance.
6. **Services:** establish the age and scope of electrical, plumbing, drainage and hot-water upgrades.
7. **Alterations:** find plans, permits, invoices and repair history for wet areas, extensions, roof work and wall removal.
8. **Planning:** check heritage or character controls before assuming the house can be altered as freely as a newer one.

sections.heading: Worked example: restumped, but still uneven
sections.markdown:
**Illustrative reasoning example, not an inspected property.** A 1935 bungalow is advertised as restumped. A bedroom floor slopes and a crack appears at the later kitchen connection. The invoice turns out to cover the front rooms only. That narrows the evidence: work to those rooms is documented, while the rear supports and the junction remain separate questions.

An accessible subfloor inspection and review of the alteration history could show retained geometry, a local support issue or a wider movement concern. Until then, neither “restumping failed” nor “the house needs complete restumping” is justified. Any repair allowance should name the uncertain area and the investigation needed to define its scope.

sections.heading: Confirm the property’s current condition
sections.markdown:
A good interwar purchase is not one where every original component has disappeared. It is one where the construction, moisture pathways, movement, timber condition, services, hazardous materials and later work are understood well enough to make the next decision. Compare adjacent eras in [period homes](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/period-homes-pre-1920s), [postwar homes](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/postwar-homes-1950s-70s) and the broader [era planning guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/what-your-home-needs-by-decade).

> Note: For an interwar home, keep three records distinct: how the original house stands, what later work changed, and what the current condition shows today.

faqs.question: Were 1920s houses built on stumps or a slab?
faqs.answer: Most were built with suspended timber floors on stumps or brick piers. Concrete slab floors became common much later, so a 1920s house on a slab usually reflects later work or a different construction history worth confirming.

faqs.question: Are original interwar terracotta roof tiles still sound?
faqs.answer: Often, if they have been maintained. Terracotta tiles can last many decades; the weak points are usually the ridge bedding and pointing, valleys, cracked or slipped tiles, battens and fixings. A roof plumber can tell you whether repair or partial relaying is needed.

faqs.question: Does an interwar house need rewiring?
faqs.answer: Not automatically, but its original wiring is now well over 80 years old, and the house predates safety switch requirements (power circuits from around 1991). Ask for the rewiring history and have a licensed electrician check the switchboard and circuits.

faqs.question: What should I investigate in a 1920s–40s home?
faqs.answer: Identify the footing, floor, wall, roof, drainage and damp-management systems; establish service upgrade history; assess termite and timber evidence; review later wet areas and extensions; and screen relevant hazardous materials before disturbance.

faqs.question: Do interwar homes have a damp-proof course?
faqs.answer: Some do, but presence does not prove performance. Confirm whether one exists, whether it has been bridged or altered, and diagnose low-wall moisture against rain, plumbing, ground levels, condensation and salts.

faqs.question: Does a Californian bungalow have asbestos?
faqs.answer: It may, either in original fabric or later alterations. Australian household guidance uses a pre-1990 screening threshold; identify suspect material before disturbance.

faqs.question: How do I know if an interwar home needs restumping?
faqs.answer: Identify the actual footing system and assess decay, movement, floor levels, soil, drainage and prior work before defining a repair. “Restumped” should be supported by scope and evidence. The subfloors and restumping guide sets out the signs, clearances and permits.

faqs.question: Are uneven floors always structural?
faqs.answer: No. Older floors can have longstanding irregularity, local timber issues or movement. The important questions are whether distortion is progressive, what the footing/subfloor condition shows and whether doors, cracks or additions tell the same story.

faqs.question: Why are damp problems common in older houses?
faqs.answer: Older homes can have several moisture pathways: rain penetration, plumbing, high ground levels, bridged damp-proofing, subfloor moisture, condensation and historical salts. The cause has to be diagnosed rather than assumed from the stain location.

faqs.question: Can I renovate an interwar home in a heritage area?
faqs.answer: Often yes, but controls can shape demolition, frontage, additions and materials. Confirm the actual overlay or character provisions, title constraints and permit pathway before designing around an assumption.

faqs.question: Does insulation make an old house more likely to get condensation?
faqs.answer: Not by itself. Condensation depends on moisture generation, ventilation, surface temperatures and the way the roof/wall assembly manages vapour and drying. Poorly considered retrofit work can change that balance, so inspect the installed system rather than treating insulation as automatically good or bad.

These changes can improve comfort, but older walls and roofs still need to manage moisture. [YourHome](https://www.yourhome.gov.au/passive-design/condensation) explains that condensation depends on humidity, temperature, ventilation and the ability of the building fabric to drain and dry. If an older house has been made much tighter, look for recurrent window condensation, mould, roof-space moisture and the way bathrooms and cooking moisture are exhausted.

## Heritage and character controls can shape what you can change
Interwar homes in established suburbs may sit under heritage or character controls, particularly where the street-facing form contributes to a precinct. Confirm the actual planning controls before designing an extension, façade change, demolition or replacement. For Victorian purchases, review the planning information in the [Section 32](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/reading-a-section-32) and use [the heritage-overlay guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/living-in-a-heritage-overlay) where relevant.

## Common interwar misreads
**What a clue does and does not tell you**

| Clue | Reasonable inference | What still needs evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fresh paint to lower walls | There may have been cosmetic repair or previous moisture work | Whether moisture is active, what caused it and whether salts/material damage remain. |
| Floors feel uneven | The house may have settlement, stump/pier variation or normal old-floor irregularity | Whether movement is active, structurally important or related to a later addition. |
| “Restumped” | Some footing work may have occurred | Which parts, what material/system, why it was done and whether levels/movement are now stable. |
| New bathroom | The wet area is younger than the shell | Membrane/detailing, plumbing changes, approvals and current moisture performance. |
| New switchboard | Electrical work has occurred | Whether the whole installation or only part of it was upgraded. |
| No visible termite damage | No obvious damage was seen in the visible area | Whether inaccessible or concealed areas are affected and whether the property has a current management/inspection history. |

## A buyer evidence stack for an interwar home
1. **Construction:** identify floor, footing, wall and roof systems and where later additions begin.
2. **Water:** trace roof-water disposal, drainage, external ground levels, subfloor moisture, plumbing and wet areas.
3. **Movement:** record cracks, distortion, footing condition, drainage and prior repairs rather than relying on a “restumped” claim.
4. **Timber and pests:** obtain appropriate pest evidence and keep subfloor/inspection zones visible.
5. **Hazards:** consider lead in older coatings and pre-1990 asbestos-containing materials before planned disturbance.
6. **Services:** establish the age and scope of electrical, plumbing, drainage and hot-water upgrades.
7. **Alterations:** find plans, permits, invoices and repair history for wet areas, extensions, roof work and wall removal.
8. **Planning:** check heritage or character controls before assuming the house can be altered as freely as a newer one.

## Worked example: restumped, but still uneven
**Illustrative reasoning example, not an inspected property.** A 1935 bungalow is advertised as restumped. A bedroom floor slopes and a crack appears at the later kitchen connection. The invoice turns out to cover the front rooms only. That narrows the evidence: work to those rooms is documented, while the rear supports and the junction remain separate questions.

An accessible subfloor inspection and review of the alteration history could show retained geometry, a local support issue or a wider movement concern. Until then, neither “restumping failed” nor “the house needs complete restumping” is justified. Any repair allowance should name the uncertain area and the investigation needed to define its scope.

## Confirm the property’s current condition
A good interwar purchase is not one where every original component has disappeared. It is one where the construction, moisture pathways, movement, timber condition, services, hazardous materials and later work are understood well enough to make the next decision. Compare adjacent eras in [period homes](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/period-homes-pre-1920s), [postwar homes](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/postwar-homes-1950s-70s) and the broader [era planning guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/what-your-home-needs-by-decade).

> Note: For an interwar home, keep three records distinct: how the original house stands, what later work changed, and what the current condition shows today.

## Frequently asked questions
### Were 1920s houses built on stumps or a slab?
Most were built with suspended timber floors on stumps or brick piers. Concrete slab floors became common much later, so a 1920s house on a slab usually reflects later work or a different construction history worth confirming.

### Are original interwar terracotta roof tiles still sound?
Often, if they have been maintained. Terracotta tiles can last many decades; the weak points are usually the ridge bedding and pointing, valleys, cracked or slipped tiles, battens and fixings. A roof plumber can tell you whether repair or partial relaying is needed.

### Does an interwar house need rewiring?
Not automatically, but its original wiring is now well over 80 years old, and the house predates safety switch requirements (power circuits from around 1991). Ask for the rewiring history and have a licensed electrician check the switchboard and circuits.

### What should I investigate in a 1920s–40s home?
Identify the footing, floor, wall, roof, drainage and damp-management systems; establish service upgrade history; assess termite and timber evidence; review later wet areas and extensions; and screen relevant hazardous materials before disturbance.

### Do interwar homes have a damp-proof course?
Some do, but presence does not prove performance. Confirm whether one exists, whether it has been bridged or altered, and diagnose low-wall moisture against rain, plumbing, ground levels, condensation and salts.

### Does a Californian bungalow have asbestos?
It may, either in original fabric or later alterations. Australian household guidance uses a pre-1990 screening threshold; identify suspect material before disturbance.

### How do I know if an interwar home needs restumping?
Identify the actual footing system and assess decay, movement, floor levels, soil, drainage and prior work before defining a repair. “Restumped” should be supported by scope and evidence. The subfloors and restumping guide sets out the signs, clearances and permits.

### Are uneven floors always structural?
No. Older floors can have longstanding irregularity, local timber issues or movement. The important questions are whether distortion is progressive, what the footing/subfloor condition shows and whether doors, cracks or additions tell the same story.

### Why are damp problems common in older houses?
Older homes can have several moisture pathways: rain penetration, plumbing, high ground levels, bridged damp-proofing, subfloor moisture, condensation and historical salts. The cause has to be diagnosed rather than assumed from the stain location.

### Can I renovate an interwar home in a heritage area?
Often yes, but controls can shape demolition, frontage, additions and materials. Confirm the actual overlay or character provisions, title constraints and permit pathway before designing around an assumption.

### Does insulation make an old house more likely to get condensation?
Not by itself. Condensation depends on moisture generation, ventilation, surface temperatures and the way the roof/wall assembly manages vapour and drying. Poorly considered retrofit work can change that balance, so inspect the installed system rather than treating insulation as automatically good or bad.

## Method
We read an interwar home from the ground up: footing and subfloor first, then water and envelope, services and hazardous materials, and finally the later work layered onto the original shell.

## Limitations
Confirm footing, wall, timber-pest, service, damp-proofing and alteration condition through records and physical evidence. Heritage controls and existing-work compliance are property- and jurisdiction-specific.

guides.title: Modern homes (2000s onward): what to expect and what they need

sections.heading: Opening
sections.markdown:
### Newer homes have histories too
- **House:** For a house: approvals, drainage, waterproofing, workmanship
- **Apartment:** For an apartment: the building’s defects, cladding and funds
- **Both:** For both: warranty clocks, alterations, condition today

_Check the paperwork and present condition, even in a young home._

sections.heading: A newer home has less history, so the history it has matters more
sections.markdown:
Modern homes are often easier to document than older ones because plans, approvals, contracts, warranties and product information may still exist. That makes missing evidence more noticeable, not less important. A young building can still contain original defects, poorly resolved repairs, unauthorised alterations, waterproofing failures, drainage problems or common-property liabilities.

For a newer home the build date is usually on record. [Working out when a house was built](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/when-was-my-house-built) shows where to find the permit and completion documents.

The inspection approach should therefore combine **present condition** with **the paper trail**. A defect report that has been diagnosed, scoped, funded and closed out is different from a recurring leak described vaguely in minutes. A completion certificate or permit helps establish an approval pathway; it does not prove that every concealed detail still performs today.

### Signs worth following in a newer home
- **Wet areas:** Staining beside a shower or below a balcony, and grout that keeps cracking
- **Envelope:** Cracked render at window corners, or damp around window junctions
- **Drainage:** Water pooling against the slab edge, or soil and paving covering it

_In a newer home, check whether statutory warranty periods may still apply before arranging a repair._

sections.heading: First split: detached house or shared building
sections.markdown:
**Two modern-home evidence systems**

| Question | Detached house | Apartment / shared building |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Who controls the fabric? | Usually the owner, subject to title, easements, covenants and planning/building controls | Depends on the registered plan and state law: lot, common property and exclusive-use areas must be separated |
| Where does defect history live? | Owner records, builder correspondence, inspections, warranties, insurers and authorities | Minutes, defect registers, engineering/fire/cladding reports, strata/OC managers, committees, developers and insurers |
| Who pays? | Usually the owner unless a warranty/insurance/other recovery path applies | Depends on lot/common-property responsibility, scheme decisions, funds, levies and recovery rights |
| What can be hidden? | Concealed waterproofing, drainage, framing, insulation and undocumented alterations | The same, plus defects elsewhere in the building and liabilities not visible from the lot |

sections.heading: For a newer house, read the build as a system
sections.markdown:
### Approvals and completion records

Collect the available planning/building approvals, approved plans, certificates, builder information and records of later additions. The exact documents vary by state and project. Treat approvals as one evidence layer: they help explain what was authorised, while a physical inspection tests what is present and how it is performing now.

### Site drainage and water disposal

Newer houses still depend on simple water management. Check surface falls, ponding, downpipe connections, retaining walls, garden beds, paving levels, slab-edge visibility and whether water is being directed away from the building. Later landscaping can materially change a site that was compliant and well drained at completion.

### Wet areas and waterproofing

Bathrooms, laundries and similar wet areas rely on coordinated materials and detailing that disappear behind finishes. The [NCC guide to waterproofing in houses](https://ncc.abcb.gov.au/ncc-navigator/waterproofing-houses) explains the current framework: required areas are waterproof or water resistant, with particular attention to junctions, penetrations, shower zones and drainage, and AS 3740 can form part of a Deemed-to-Satisfy pathway. For an existing home, use the code edition and approvals relevant to the date of the work, then investigate present signs such as staining, swelling, loose finishes, failed sealants and moisture to adjacent areas.

A modern bathroom can look perfect while the membrane remains completely concealed. That is why renovation date, leak history, inspection evidence and [current moisture behaviour](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/damp-and-moisture-in-your-home) matter more than visual styling. [Signs of a leaking shower](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/bathroom-waterproofing-and-leaking-showers#signs) apply just as much to a young bathroom.

### Cladding, wraps, flashings and window junctions

Modern wall systems rely on several layers working together. [YourHome's cladding guidance](https://www.yourhome.gov.au/materials/cladding-systems) describes the outer cladding, framing, pliable membrane and insulation as an interacting system: the cladding sheds most water and the drainage/water-control layers manage what gets behind it. Inspect junctions around windows, doors, balconies, parapets, roofs and dissimilar materials because local detailing often matters more than the broad cladding label.

### Condensation, ventilation and insulation

A more insulated or airtight home can still have moisture problems if ventilation, vapour control and drying paths are poorly resolved. [YourHome](https://www.yourhome.gov.au/passive-design/condensation) explains that condensation is driven by temperature, humidity and air/vapour movement and can occur within roofs, walls and around windows. Recurrent window condensation, mould at cold bridges or moisture in roof spaces deserves a building-physics explanation rather than a generic instruction to open a window.

### Termite management does not become maintenance-free because the house is newer

Where termite risk applies, identify the management system and its inspection/maintenance requirements. [QBCC guidance](https://www.qbcc.qld.gov.au/home-owner-hub/maintain-protect/protect-against-termites) is a useful example of the principle: slab edges, penetrations and barriers need to remain inspectable, and later landscaping, patios or renovations can compromise the original system. Look for the termite-management notice where one exists, treatment records and recent licensed inspection evidence. [Finding the durable notice](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/termites-in-australian-homes#durable-notice) shows where the system is usually recorded.

sections.heading: For a newer apartment, you are buying into the building’s history
sections.markdown:
### Read the registered plan before assigning responsibility

The visible defect does not tell you who owns or repairs the affected element. Use the registered plan and the applicable state law to distinguish the lot from common property, then read the scheme records for how similar issues have been handled. Continue with [buying an apartment with strata](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/buying-an-apartment-strata) and [reading the owners-corporation report](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/reading-your-owners-corporation-report).

### Defects need a lifecycle, not just a label

**Read every significant building defect through the same lifecycle**

| Stage | Question |
| --- | --- |
| Observed | What is actually happening, where and how often? |
| Diagnosed | Has the cause been established by the appropriate professional, or is it still suspected? |
| Scoped | Is there a defined rectification scope, including interfaces and consequential work? |
| Costed | Is there a credible cost, contingency and allowance for professional/authority inputs? |
| Funded | Which fund, levy, loan, developer recovery, insurer or warranty path is expected to pay? |
| Approved | Has the scheme resolved to proceed and are approvals/procurement in place? |
| Completed | What work was actually done and is there close-out evidence? |
| Monitored | Has the issue recurred, and what remains under observation? |

A minute saying 'waterproofing issue noted' is weak evidence. A consultant report, adopted scope, levy resolution, contract, completion report and subsequent dry performance tell a very different story.

### External walls and combustible cladding

Some multi-storey buildings have been assessed or rectified for combustible external-wall products. Obtain the external-wall or cladding assessment, authority correspondence, fire-engineering advice, rectification scope/status, funding, warranty position and insurance response. Programs and legal pathways are state- and date-specific, so use current jurisdictional advice rather than assuming an assessment in one state applies nationally.

### Fire systems and life-safety records

For apartment buildings, ask for current fire-safety records, defect notices and reports where relevant. The Homechecker guide is not a fire-safety audit; the aim is to identify whether significant unresolved issues, planned upgrades or funding obligations exist in the records before you buy into them.

### Scheme finances must be read against the building

A healthy-looking fund balance is meaningless without the maintenance/capital-works plan and known projects. Compare current funds, liabilities, arrears, insurance, planned works, active defects, special levies, loans and recovery from builders/developers. A building with $500,000 in the bank and a $2 million façade project is not 'well funded' merely because the bank balance sounds large.

sections.heading: Which standards a newer home was built to
sections.markdown:
Requirements kept tightening through this period, so a 2005 home and a 2024 home are built to different rules. Use the approval date. Energy requirements are tracked through [NatHERS](https://www.nathers.gov.au/governance); the 7-star minimum arrived with [NCC 2022](https://cpd.nccb.gov.au/news/2022/overview-changes-energy-efficiency-and-condensation).

**Requirements that changed after 2000**

| When | What changed | What to check |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Around 2000–01 | Safety switches required on lighting as well as power circuits in most states | Which circuits are protected at the switchboard |
| Around 2010–11 | Minimum 6-star energy rating for new homes in most states | The energy rating certificate or stamped plans |
| May 2014 | Interconnected smoke alarms in new homes and major renovations | That alarms sound together and are within their 10-year life |
| 2018 wiring rules | Safety switches on all final circuits in new installations | Whether later electrical work was certified |
| From October 2023 (state variations) | 7-star minimum, a whole-of-home energy budget and condensation provisions under NCC 2022 | Ventilation, exhaust fans and any condensation in roof spaces or walls |

sections.heading: Warranty and defect rights run on dates
sections.markdown: Modern buildings can have statutory warranties, domestic-building insurance or other defect/recovery mechanisms depending on the state, building type, contract and dates. These systems are not uniform nationally, and the available pathway can change while a defect remains physically the same. Record practical completion/occupation dates, contracts, notices and prior claims, then obtain current jurisdiction-specific advice before relying on a warranty or limitation period.

sections.heading: Later alterations can make a young home harder to read
sections.markdown: A 2010 house with a 2024 bathroom or a 2015 apartment with an altered balcony door already contains multiple construction dates. Ask what changed, whether approvals or scheme consent were required, who performed the work and whether the alteration affects waterproofing, structure, fire separation, façade systems, services or common property.

sections.heading: Modern-home evidence worth keeping
sections.markdown:
- **Build identity:** approved plans, specifications, builder/developer details, completion/occupation documents and major product information.
- **Defects:** reports, notices, correspondence, scopes, quotes, contracts, completion records and monitoring evidence.
- **Wet areas and envelope:** renovation dates, waterproofing/inspection records where available, façade/cladding assessments and leak history.
- **Termites:** management notice/system details, inspection history and treatment records where applicable.
- **Energy systems:** solar, battery, EV charger, heating/cooling, insulation and glazing specifications and relevant electrical work records.
- **Alterations:** permits, plans, owners-corporation approvals, certificates, invoices and warranties.
- **Apartments:** registered plan, minutes, budgets, capital-works plan, insurance, defect/cladding/fire reports, litigation and levy/loan history.

sections.heading: What a physical inspection still adds
sections.markdown: Documents can tell you what should have been built, what somebody reported and what somebody says was repaired. A physical inspection tests accessible present condition: moisture, cracking, drainage, roof and façade junctions, service clues, timber-pest evidence and workmanship. The two evidence systems are complementary. A young building with excellent paperwork can still have a present defect; a defect report can also be stale after successful repair.

sections.heading: Worked example: a balcony repaired twice
sections.markdown:
**Illustrative reasoning example, not an inspected property.** A 2016 apartment has two recorded balcony repairs and a clean ceiling below. The minutes mention a wider waterproofing proposal. The clean ceiling is useful current visual evidence, but it does not explain the proposal. Obtain the technical report and later decisions to establish whether the earlier work was local, whether broader work remains and how it would be funded.

If a defined repair was completed and the follow-up evidence supports its effectiveness, uncertainty reduces. If the earlier works were temporary and a larger project remains unpriced, the buyer has a different financial and disruption question. Neither “new building, no concern” nor “two leaks, reject it” captures that distinction.

sections.heading: What a modern home needs from you after purchase
sections.markdown:
Start routine maintenance early (see [maintenance that reduces avoidable repair bills](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/the-maintenance-that-prevents-the-big-bills)). Keep gutters and drainage working, maintain seals, coatings and joints, respond quickly to leaks, follow termite-system requirements where applicable and keep the building record current. [YourHome](https://www.yourhome.gov.au/buy-build-renovate/repairs-and-maintenance) recommends an annual maintenance schedule because early attention to leaks, cracks, settlement, damp and termites can prevent larger problems.

For an apartment, maintenance also means governance: read notices, attend to major defect decisions, understand the capital plan and make sure completed work is documented. The owner's view is in [strata risks for owners](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/strata-risks-for-owners).

> Note: Newer buildings reward documentary discipline. Keep approvals, defect reports, warranty material, repairs and scheme records together, and update the file as the building changes.

> Important: Do not assume current building-code provisions, warranty periods or cladding programs apply to a property without checking the building type, jurisdiction and relevant dates.

faqs.question: Is a house built in 2015 a 7-star home?
faqs.answer: Not necessarily. Most states required 6 stars for new homes from around 2010–11; the 7-star minimum came with NCC 2022, with energy provisions taking effect from October 2023 and state variations. Check the energy rating certificate or stamped plans.

faqs.question: Do new homes have problems too?
faqs.answer: Yes. Newer homes can have workmanship, waterproofing, drainage, façade, condensation, termite-management, service or approval issues. Apartments add shared-building defects, fire systems, cladding, governance and funding.

faqs.question: What are builder defects?
faqs.answer: Issues attributed to original design, materials or construction. Diagnosis, responsibility and available warranty or statutory paths are jurisdiction- and time-specific, so trace reports, notices, completed work and remaining rights.

faqs.question: Why do modern bathrooms and balconies leak?
faqs.answer: Wet areas and balconies depend on coordinated falls, drainage, membranes, flashings, joints and penetrations. A visible leak may result from several interfaces, so diagnosis should identify the complete water path before repair scope is set.

faqs.question: Can I tell whether waterproofing is compliant by looking at the bathroom?
faqs.answer: Usually not. Much of the system is concealed. Present-condition evidence, renovation date, approvals/inspection records where available and the requirements that applied when the work was done are all relevant.

faqs.question: Is cladding a risk on a newer apartment?
faqs.answer: It can be. Obtain the external-wall assessment, authority records, rectification and funding status, fire advice and insurance information, then use the current state program or legal pathway for that building.

faqs.question: Why does condensation matter in a modern home?
faqs.answer: Condensation can occur when warm moist air meets cold surfaces or within building assemblies. Repeated moisture can support mould or damage materials, so ventilation, humidity, insulation, thermal bridges and drying paths need to be considered together.

faqs.question: Do newer homes need termite inspections?
faqs.answer: Where termite risk applies, yes. A management system reduces risk only when it remains intact, inspectable and maintained. Later landscaping, paving and alterations can compromise inspection zones or barriers.

faqs.question: Does an occupation or completion certificate prove there are no defects?
faqs.answer: No. It is evidence in the approval/completion pathway, not a guarantee of present condition or freedom from concealed defects.

faqs.question: Is a newer apartment safer because the sinking/capital fund has money in it?
faqs.answer: Not necessarily. Read the fund balance against planned work, known defects, liabilities, special levies and recovery prospects. The funding gap matters more than the headline balance.

faqs.question: Is a newer home lower-maintenance?
faqs.answer: It may have fewer age-related renewals at first, but waterproofing, seals, roofing, services, drainage, termite systems and finishes begin ageing from handover. A maintenance plan belongs in the first year of ownership.

The inspection approach should therefore combine **present condition** with **the paper trail**. A defect report that has been diagnosed, scoped, funded and closed out is different from a recurring leak described vaguely in minutes. A completion certificate or permit helps establish an approval pathway; it does not prove that every concealed detail still performs today.

### Signs worth following in a newer home
- **Wet areas:** Staining beside a shower or below a balcony, and grout that keeps cracking
- **Envelope:** Cracked render at window corners, or damp around window junctions
- **Drainage:** Water pooling against the slab edge, or soil and paving covering it

_In a newer home, check whether statutory warranty periods may still apply before arranging a repair._

## First split: detached house or shared building
**Two modern-home evidence systems**

| Question | Detached house | Apartment / shared building |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Who controls the fabric? | Usually the owner, subject to title, easements, covenants and planning/building controls | Depends on the registered plan and state law: lot, common property and exclusive-use areas must be separated |
| Where does defect history live? | Owner records, builder correspondence, inspections, warranties, insurers and authorities | Minutes, defect registers, engineering/fire/cladding reports, strata/OC managers, committees, developers and insurers |
| Who pays? | Usually the owner unless a warranty/insurance/other recovery path applies | Depends on lot/common-property responsibility, scheme decisions, funds, levies and recovery rights |
| What can be hidden? | Concealed waterproofing, drainage, framing, insulation and undocumented alterations | The same, plus defects elsewhere in the building and liabilities not visible from the lot |

## For a newer house, read the build as a system
### Approvals and completion records

Collect the available planning/building approvals, approved plans, certificates, builder information and records of later additions. The exact documents vary by state and project. Treat approvals as one evidence layer: they help explain what was authorised, while a physical inspection tests what is present and how it is performing now.

### Site drainage and water disposal

Newer houses still depend on simple water management. Check surface falls, ponding, downpipe connections, retaining walls, garden beds, paving levels, slab-edge visibility and whether water is being directed away from the building. Later landscaping can materially change a site that was compliant and well drained at completion.

### Wet areas and waterproofing

Bathrooms, laundries and similar wet areas rely on coordinated materials and detailing that disappear behind finishes. The [NCC guide to waterproofing in houses](https://ncc.abcb.gov.au/ncc-navigator/waterproofing-houses) explains the current framework: required areas are waterproof or water resistant, with particular attention to junctions, penetrations, shower zones and drainage, and AS 3740 can form part of a Deemed-to-Satisfy pathway. For an existing home, use the code edition and approvals relevant to the date of the work, then investigate present signs such as staining, swelling, loose finishes, failed sealants and moisture to adjacent areas.

A modern bathroom can look perfect while the membrane remains completely concealed. That is why renovation date, leak history, inspection evidence and [current moisture behaviour](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/damp-and-moisture-in-your-home) matter more than visual styling. [Signs of a leaking shower](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/bathroom-waterproofing-and-leaking-showers#signs) apply just as much to a young bathroom.

### Cladding, wraps, flashings and window junctions

Modern wall systems rely on several layers working together. [YourHome's cladding guidance](https://www.yourhome.gov.au/materials/cladding-systems) describes the outer cladding, framing, pliable membrane and insulation as an interacting system: the cladding sheds most water and the drainage/water-control layers manage what gets behind it. Inspect junctions around windows, doors, balconies, parapets, roofs and dissimilar materials because local detailing often matters more than the broad cladding label.

### Condensation, ventilation and insulation

A more insulated or airtight home can still have moisture problems if ventilation, vapour control and drying paths are poorly resolved. [YourHome](https://www.yourhome.gov.au/passive-design/condensation) explains that condensation is driven by temperature, humidity and air/vapour movement and can occur within roofs, walls and around windows. Recurrent window condensation, mould at cold bridges or moisture in roof spaces deserves a building-physics explanation rather than a generic instruction to open a window.

### Termite management does not become maintenance-free because the house is newer

Where termite risk applies, identify the management system and its inspection/maintenance requirements. [QBCC guidance](https://www.qbcc.qld.gov.au/home-owner-hub/maintain-protect/protect-against-termites) is a useful example of the principle: slab edges, penetrations and barriers need to remain inspectable, and later landscaping, patios or renovations can compromise the original system. Look for the termite-management notice where one exists, treatment records and recent licensed inspection evidence. [Finding the durable notice](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/termites-in-australian-homes#durable-notice) shows where the system is usually recorded.

## For a newer apartment, you are buying into the building’s history
### Read the registered plan before assigning responsibility

The visible defect does not tell you who owns or repairs the affected element. Use the registered plan and the applicable state law to distinguish the lot from common property, then read the scheme records for how similar issues have been handled. Continue with [buying an apartment with strata](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/buying-an-apartment-strata) and [reading the owners-corporation report](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/reading-your-owners-corporation-report).

### Defects need a lifecycle, not just a label

**Read every significant building defect through the same lifecycle**

| Stage | Question |
| --- | --- |
| Observed | What is actually happening, where and how often? |
| Diagnosed | Has the cause been established by the appropriate professional, or is it still suspected? |
| Scoped | Is there a defined rectification scope, including interfaces and consequential work? |
| Costed | Is there a credible cost, contingency and allowance for professional/authority inputs? |
| Funded | Which fund, levy, loan, developer recovery, insurer or warranty path is expected to pay? |
| Approved | Has the scheme resolved to proceed and are approvals/procurement in place? |
| Completed | What work was actually done and is there close-out evidence? |
| Monitored | Has the issue recurred, and what remains under observation? |

A minute saying 'waterproofing issue noted' is weak evidence. A consultant report, adopted scope, levy resolution, contract, completion report and subsequent dry performance tell a very different story.

### External walls and combustible cladding

Some multi-storey buildings have been assessed or rectified for combustible external-wall products. Obtain the external-wall or cladding assessment, authority correspondence, fire-engineering advice, rectification scope/status, funding, warranty position and insurance response. Programs and legal pathways are state- and date-specific, so use current jurisdictional advice rather than assuming an assessment in one state applies nationally.

### Fire systems and life-safety records

For apartment buildings, ask for current fire-safety records, defect notices and reports where relevant. The Homechecker guide is not a fire-safety audit; the aim is to identify whether significant unresolved issues, planned upgrades or funding obligations exist in the records before you buy into them.

### Scheme finances must be read against the building

A healthy-looking fund balance is meaningless without the maintenance/capital-works plan and known projects. Compare current funds, liabilities, arrears, insurance, planned works, active defects, special levies, loans and recovery from builders/developers. A building with $500,000 in the bank and a $2 million façade project is not 'well funded' merely because the bank balance sounds large.

## Which standards a newer home was built to
Requirements kept tightening through this period, so a 2005 home and a 2024 home are built to different rules. Use the approval date. Energy requirements are tracked through [NatHERS](https://www.nathers.gov.au/governance); the 7-star minimum arrived with [NCC 2022](https://cpd.nccb.gov.au/news/2022/overview-changes-energy-efficiency-and-condensation).

**Requirements that changed after 2000**

| When | What changed | What to check |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Around 2000–01 | Safety switches required on lighting as well as power circuits in most states | Which circuits are protected at the switchboard |
| Around 2010–11 | Minimum 6-star energy rating for new homes in most states | The energy rating certificate or stamped plans |
| May 2014 | Interconnected smoke alarms in new homes and major renovations | That alarms sound together and are within their 10-year life |
| 2018 wiring rules | Safety switches on all final circuits in new installations | Whether later electrical work was certified |
| From October 2023 (state variations) | 7-star minimum, a whole-of-home energy budget and condensation provisions under NCC 2022 | Ventilation, exhaust fans and any condensation in roof spaces or walls |

## Warranty and defect rights run on dates
Modern buildings can have statutory warranties, domestic-building insurance or other defect/recovery mechanisms depending on the state, building type, contract and dates. These systems are not uniform nationally, and the available pathway can change while a defect remains physically the same. Record practical completion/occupation dates, contracts, notices and prior claims, then obtain current jurisdiction-specific advice before relying on a warranty or limitation period.

## Later alterations can make a young home harder to read
A 2010 house with a 2024 bathroom or a 2015 apartment with an altered balcony door already contains multiple construction dates. Ask what changed, whether approvals or scheme consent were required, who performed the work and whether the alteration affects waterproofing, structure, fire separation, façade systems, services or common property.

## Modern-home evidence worth keeping
- **Build identity:** approved plans, specifications, builder/developer details, completion/occupation documents and major product information.
- **Defects:** reports, notices, correspondence, scopes, quotes, contracts, completion records and monitoring evidence.
- **Wet areas and envelope:** renovation dates, waterproofing/inspection records where available, façade/cladding assessments and leak history.
- **Termites:** management notice/system details, inspection history and treatment records where applicable.
- **Energy systems:** solar, battery, EV charger, heating/cooling, insulation and glazing specifications and relevant electrical work records.
- **Alterations:** permits, plans, owners-corporation approvals, certificates, invoices and warranties.
- **Apartments:** registered plan, minutes, budgets, capital-works plan, insurance, defect/cladding/fire reports, litigation and levy/loan history.

## What a physical inspection still adds
Documents can tell you what should have been built, what somebody reported and what somebody says was repaired. A physical inspection tests accessible present condition: moisture, cracking, drainage, roof and façade junctions, service clues, timber-pest evidence and workmanship. The two evidence systems are complementary. A young building with excellent paperwork can still have a present defect; a defect report can also be stale after successful repair.

## Worked example: a balcony repaired twice
**Illustrative reasoning example, not an inspected property.** A 2016 apartment has two recorded balcony repairs and a clean ceiling below. The minutes mention a wider waterproofing proposal. The clean ceiling is useful current visual evidence, but it does not explain the proposal. Obtain the technical report and later decisions to establish whether the earlier work was local, whether broader work remains and how it would be funded.

If a defined repair was completed and the follow-up evidence supports its effectiveness, uncertainty reduces. If the earlier works were temporary and a larger project remains unpriced, the buyer has a different financial and disruption question. Neither “new building, no concern” nor “two leaks, reject it” captures that distinction.

## What a modern home needs from you after purchase
Start routine maintenance early (see [maintenance that reduces avoidable repair bills](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/the-maintenance-that-prevents-the-big-bills)). Keep gutters and drainage working, maintain seals, coatings and joints, respond quickly to leaks, follow termite-system requirements where applicable and keep the building record current. [YourHome](https://www.yourhome.gov.au/buy-build-renovate/repairs-and-maintenance) recommends an annual maintenance schedule because early attention to leaks, cracks, settlement, damp and termites can prevent larger problems.

For an apartment, maintenance also means governance: read notices, attend to major defect decisions, understand the capital plan and make sure completed work is documented. The owner's view is in [strata risks for owners](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/strata-risks-for-owners).

> Note: Newer buildings reward documentary discipline. Keep approvals, defect reports, warranty material, repairs and scheme records together, and update the file as the building changes.

> Important: Do not assume current building-code provisions, warranty periods or cladding programs apply to a property without checking the building type, jurisdiction and relevant dates.

## Frequently asked questions
### Is a house built in 2015 a 7-star home?
Not necessarily. Most states required 6 stars for new homes from around 2010–11; the 7-star minimum came with NCC 2022, with energy provisions taking effect from October 2023 and state variations. Check the energy rating certificate or stamped plans.

### Do new homes have problems too?
Yes. Newer homes can have workmanship, waterproofing, drainage, façade, condensation, termite-management, service or approval issues. Apartments add shared-building defects, fire systems, cladding, governance and funding.

### What are builder defects?
Issues attributed to original design, materials or construction. Diagnosis, responsibility and available warranty or statutory paths are jurisdiction- and time-specific, so trace reports, notices, completed work and remaining rights.

### Why do modern bathrooms and balconies leak?
Wet areas and balconies depend on coordinated falls, drainage, membranes, flashings, joints and penetrations. A visible leak may result from several interfaces, so diagnosis should identify the complete water path before repair scope is set.

### Can I tell whether waterproofing is compliant by looking at the bathroom?
Usually not. Much of the system is concealed. Present-condition evidence, renovation date, approvals/inspection records where available and the requirements that applied when the work was done are all relevant.

### Is cladding a risk on a newer apartment?
It can be. Obtain the external-wall assessment, authority records, rectification and funding status, fire advice and insurance information, then use the current state program or legal pathway for that building.

### Why does condensation matter in a modern home?
Condensation can occur when warm moist air meets cold surfaces or within building assemblies. Repeated moisture can support mould or damage materials, so ventilation, humidity, insulation, thermal bridges and drying paths need to be considered together.

### Do newer homes need termite inspections?
Where termite risk applies, yes. A management system reduces risk only when it remains intact, inspectable and maintained. Later landscaping, paving and alterations can compromise inspection zones or barriers.

### Does an occupation or completion certificate prove there are no defects?
No. It is evidence in the approval/completion pathway, not a guarantee of present condition or freedom from concealed defects.

### Is a newer apartment safer because the sinking/capital fund has money in it?
Not necessarily. Read the fund balance against planned work, known defects, liabilities, special levies and recovery prospects. The funding gap matters more than the headline balance.

### Is a newer home lower-maintenance?
It may have fewer age-related renewals at first, but waterproofing, seals, roofing, services, drainage, termite systems and finishes begin ageing from handover. A maintenance plan belongs in the first year of ownership.

## Method
We split the modern era into two risk systems: the newer detached house and the shared apartment building, then trace each issue from record to current condition to responsibility and funding.

## Limitations
Warranty periods, defect regimes, cladding programs and compliance pathways differ by state, building type and date. Current NCC provisions explain present building principles but do not automatically establish whether older work was compliant when built.

guides.question: How do I prepare my home for storms, floods and bushfire?
guides.title: How to prepare your home for storms, floods, bushfire and heat
guides.summary: A safer home starts with the people in it. Make the plan, know where warnings come from and plan to act early, then work through the property risks that apply to your address.
guides.answer: Prepare a household plan before severe weather, including safe destinations, transport, communication and individual needs. Plan to act early; do not assume an official warning will arrive before flash flooding. Follow current local emergency directions. Assess storm, flood, bushfire and heat risks for the particular home, arranging competent property work in calm conditions. Confirm any proposed insurance benefit with the insurer.
guides.methodology: A hazard-specific preparation guide separating household safety, building assessment, early decisions and recovery. Property examples are illustrative; current local emergency directions govern an event.
guides.limitations: This is a national resilience guide. During an event, follow your emergency service. BAL ratings, flood levels and engineering require site-specific assessment.
guides.researchNote: Official emergency and health guidance supports the safety passages linked above. The property examples illustrate questions for competent assessment, not hazard ratings or instructions to undertake dangerous work. Follow current local authority information during an event.

cluster.label: Own, maintain and change
cluster.blurb: Keep useful records, maintain the fabric safely and plan works without over-promising what condition can prove.

sections.heading: Opening
sections.markdown:
### Protect people first
- **People:** A household plan: people, pets, medication, and when to leave
- **Warnings:** One source of truth: your local emergency authority
- **Property:** Then the property, with hazard-specific advice and competent hands

_Plan to act early. Do not assume a warning will arrive before flash flooding; follow current local emergency guidance._

sections.heading: The order is people, warnings, property
sections.markdown:
1. **People:** decide who does what, where you will go, when you will leave and how children, older people, disability, medication and pets are supported.
2. **Warnings:** use the official emergency service and hazard authority for your location; understand warning levels before the event.
3. **Property:** assess the specific storm, flood or bushfire mechanism and complete competent work in calm conditions.
4. **Records and insurance:** keep photographs and invoices, update the rebuild basis, and ask the insurer about cover, excesses and recognised mitigation.

The [NSW Rural Fire Service survival plan](https://www.rfs.nsw.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0003/36597/BFSP-Complete.pdf) says leaving early is the safest option and calls for a prepared plan. Follow the current authority for your state or territory during an event.

sections.heading: Storm and wind
sections.markdown:
Before storm season, use safe ground-level observation and competent inspection to identify loose roof material, deteriorated flashings, [blocked or failing rainwater goods](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/the-maintenance-that-prevents-the-big-bills), vulnerable openings, hazardous trees and unsecured outdoor objects. [VICSES advises maintaining the home and yard, clearing gutters and securing loose items](https://www.ses.vic.gov.au/plan-and-stay-safe/emergencies/storm). Use trained, equipped people for roof access. Stay clear of fallen powerlines and floodwater.

**Who should check each part of the home before a storm**

| Signal | Action in calm weather | Who may be needed |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Roof movement, leaks or damaged flashings | Arrange condition assessment and repair scope | Roof plumber, builder or engineer as appropriate |
| Overflowing gutters or failed downpipes | Clear safely; repair falls, joints and lawful discharge | Roof plumber or drainage professional |
| Tree defect or contact risk | Obtain risk-based pruning or removal advice | Qualified arborist; council/utility where relevant |
| Vulnerable garage door, shutters or openings | Assess against local wind region and product suitability | Engineer, builder or product specialist |

sections.heading: Flood
sections.markdown:
Flood depth, velocity, duration, contamination and access vary by location. Start with the council or state flood authority and property-specific information. [VICSES warns that flash flooding can develop without an official warning](https://www.ses.vic.gov.au/plan-and-stay-safe/emergencies/flood). Plan early and never enter floodwater. Discuss property measures, service vulnerabilities and lawful drainage with qualified professionals before an event; no measure guarantees that a home will remain dry or accessible.

Stay out of floodwater and follow official power-safety advice. After inundation, treat water and affected materials as potentially contaminated and follow emergency, electrical and public-health instructions before re-entry.

sections.heading: Bushfire and ember attack
sections.markdown:
Begin with a survival plan and the local fire authority. Determine whether the property is in bushfire-prone land and whether a Bushfire Attack Level or planning control applies. Building measures depend on the assessed exposure, construction and local rules.

Preparation can include lawful fuel and vegetation management, clear gutters, maintained decks and subfloors, sealed gaps and compliant non-combustible mesh at openings. Keep required ventilation paths, cavity drainage and weep holes clear. On catastrophic or extreme conditions, follow official advice and leave early.

### What a Bushfire Attack Level means

In bushfire-prone areas, new building work is designed to a Bushfire Attack Level (BAL) under [AS 3959](https://store.standards.org.au/product/as-3959-2018). The BAL rates a site's likely exposure to embers, radiant heat and flame, and sets the construction requirements. A BAL certificate or assessment for an existing home tells you what the site was assessed as, which matters for renovations and extensions.

**The six Bushfire Attack Levels**

| Level | Risk | Predicted attack |
| --- | --- | --- |
| BAL-LOW | Very low | Insufficient risk to warrant specific bushfire construction requirements |
| BAL-12.5 | Low | Ember attack |
| BAL-19 | Moderate | Increasing ember attack and burning debris, with radiant heat up to 19 kW/m² |
| BAL-29 | High | Increasing ember attack and burning debris, with radiant heat up to 29 kW/m² |
| BAL-40 | Very high | Increasing ember attack, radiant heat up to 40 kW/m² and some likelihood of flame contact |
| BAL-FZ | Extreme (flame zone) | Direct exposure to flames from the fire front, as well as heat and embers |

Older homes built before the current requirements may not meet the BAL their site would attract today. Ember protection, such as sealed gaps, screened vents and clear gutters, is usually the most practical improvement. Councils and fire agencies, such as the [Shire of Harvey in WA](https://www.harvey.wa.gov.au/build-and-develop/building/bushfire-prone-areas) and [Mitcham Council in SA](https://www.mitchamcouncil.sa.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0043/879865/Bushfire-Attack-Levels.pdf), publish local guidance on BAL assessments.

sections.heading: Confirm insurance outcomes in writing
sections.markdown: Before major resilience work, ask the insurer or broker what evidence it requires (see [home condition and insurance](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/home-condition-and-insurance)), whether the measure changes cover or excess, and whether construction must be notified. Review flood, storm, bushfire, actions-of-the-sea and temporary-accommodation definitions using [Moneysmart's hazard insurance guide](https://moneysmart.gov.au/home-insurance/storm-flood-and-fire-insurance).

sections.heading: The property record to keep
sections.markdown:
- Official hazard maps, BAL or flood information and the date accessed.
- Emergency plan, contacts, routes, medication and pet arrangements.
- Dated photographs of roof, elevations, drainage, openings, yard and critical equipment.
- Inspection reports, design advice, approvals, invoices, product specifications and warranties for resilience work.
- Insurance schedule, PDS version, endorsements and written insurer responses about mitigation.

sections.heading: Heat is a building and household risk too
sections.markdown:
A home can become difficult to occupy without visible storm damage. [Victoria's health department](https://www.health.vic.gov.au/environmental-health/extreme-heat-and-heatwaves) identifies extreme heat as a health risk that can also disrupt power and services. Include a plan for vulnerable household members and follow current health guidance. An air conditioner is useful equipment, but it is not a complete plan if electricity or transport fails.

Before hot weather, identify which rooms overheat, when direct sun enters and whether shading and cooling equipment function. Consider access to a cooler safe place and how you will get there if normal arrangements fail. For lasting improvements, have a competent designer assess shading, insulation, ventilation and the particular construction. Opening windows is not always helpful when outside conditions are hotter or smoke-affected; the strategy must respond to actual conditions.

sections.heading: Read the address, not just the hazard label
sections.markdown:
A map is a starting point for property questions. Ask which hazard and scenario it represents, its date, whether it describes land or floor exposure, and how access might be affected. A home above a mapped flood extent may still have a vulnerable access route or local overland-flow problem. An omitted area is not a professional finding that every hazard is absent.

Construction changes the questions. A raised timber home may have habitable rooms clear of ground water while services or enclosed spaces below remain exposed. An apartment can depend on basement pumps, lifts and shared electrical equipment. A lightweight extension and the original masonry home may behave differently in wind and heat. Use these distinctions to commission assessment, not to assign a safety rating from era or listing photographs.

**Separate three different kinds of preparation**

| Stage | Useful decision | Limit |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Well before an event | Assess the property, arrange competent repairs and practise the household plan | A maintenance checklist is not an engineering assessment |
| When conditions threaten | Act on the prepared plan and current official information while safe options remain | Do not delay leaving to finish property work |
| After an event | Confirm safe access and obtain the appropriate damage and service checks | A dry-looking room does not establish that concealed materials or electricity are safe |

sections.heading: Plan for a failure of the first plan
sections.markdown:
List the assumptions behind your preparations. Does a garage door need power to open? Does the household rely on one driver, one mobile network or a lift? Does a pump require electricity during the same event that might interrupt it? Review these dependencies in calm conditions with the appropriate professional or service provider. Do not improvise electrical connections or generator arrangements during an emergency.

Discuss access and responsibilities in a strata scheme before the season. An owner may be able to secure items on their balcony while roof repairs, tree work or drainage alterations require scheme decisions. Record outstanding work and who has responsibility for it. Link this to the [strata risks for owners](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/strata-risks-for-owners) guide; a shared system is not maintained simply because each owner has checked their own unit.

sections.heading: Recovery starts with safe access and a clear chronology
sections.markdown:
Use the relevant emergency authority's advice before re-entry, and competent assessment for damaged structures or services. Document the event and visible damage only where safe, then retain the records of emergency work and insurer directions. Explain what existed before the event, what was first seen afterwards and what remains uncertain. An event occurring before a symptom is evidence of timing; it does not by itself establish the full cause or insurance outcome. Keep that chronology with the original files using the [home-record guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/keeping-a-record-of-your-home).

A repair plan should distinguish immediate protection, drying or contamination assessment, permanent repairs and the evidence needed before finishes close the affected area. Discuss the scope with the insurer and the responsible professionals. Repainting alone cannot establish that a concealed moisture problem has been resolved. The [moisture guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/damp-and-moisture-in-your-home) helps frame the investigation questions without turning a photograph into a diagnosis.

sections.heading: Worked example: a clean gutter and water at the door
sections.markdown:
**Illustrative reasoning example, not an inspected property.** A household has recently cleaned its gutters. During heavy rain, water reaches a rear doorway and a nearby street becomes difficult to access. The owners conclude that larger gutters will solve the problem.

Cleaning is evidence of one maintenance task, not proof of the capacity or operation of the entire drainage system. Roof discharge, surface falls and wider water movement are separate possibilities. During the event, household safety and official instructions take priority; no one should enter floodwater to test the theory.

Later, a drainage professional can examine the property and lawful discharge, while local flood information helps explain wider exposure and access. A defined finding may support gutter work, another intervention or several measures. The household plan also needs review, because keeping the floor dry would not necessarily keep the access route usable.

Keep conclusions at the level the evidence supports: observed, reported, inferred or confirmed. An unavailable document is a gap in the record; it does not prove the work was never done.

> Important: Follow current official warnings and call emergency services where life or property is in immediate danger. Use property-specific engineering, flood or bushfire assessment for building work.

faqs.question: What does BAL-29 mean?
faqs.answer: BAL-29 is the third-highest of six Bushfire Attack Levels under AS 3959. It indicates a high risk, with increasing ember attack and burning debris and radiant heat up to 29 kW/m², and sets specific construction requirements for new work.

faqs.question: Does an older house meet bushfire construction standards?
faqs.answer: Often not. Homes built before current bushfire construction requirements may not meet the Bushfire Attack Level their site would attract today. Sealing gaps, screening vents and keeping gutters clear are usually the most practical ember-protection improvements.

faqs.question: What is the first step in extreme-weather preparation?
faqs.answer: Prepare the household plan, destinations and official information sources before the building checklist. Include transport, communication, medication, disability needs and pets. Plan to act early; flash flooding may develop without an official warning. Follow current local emergency guidance.

faqs.question: What should I do before storm season?
faqs.answer: From safe locations, check for roof, drainage, tree, opening and loose-object risks; arrange competent inspection and repair where needed. Never work on a roof during a storm or approach fallen powerlines.

faqs.question: Should I install flood barriers?
faqs.answer: Only after property-specific flood and professional advice. Depth, velocity, duration, contamination and drainage interactions matter, and a barrier can redirect water or fail if misapplied.

faqs.question: How do I protect vents and weep holes from embers?
faqs.answer: Use bushfire-compliant, non-combustible mesh and details suited to the assessed exposure without blocking required drainage or ventilation. Confirm the applicable BAL, standard and local requirements.

faqs.question: Will resilience work lower my insurance premium?
faqs.answer: Ask the insurer what it recognises, what evidence it needs and whether cover or excess changes before spending for an insurance outcome.

faqs.question: Should I wait for a flood warning before acting?
faqs.answer: No. Flash flooding can develop without an official warning. Prepare early, know local conditions and follow current emergency guidance; never enter floodwater.

faqs.question: Does an air conditioner complete my heatwave preparation?
