guides.contentMarkdown:
# How to prepare your home for storms, floods, bushfire and heat

Prepare a household plan before severe weather, including safe destinations, transport, communication and individual needs. Plan to act early; do not assume an official warning will arrive before flash flooding. Follow current local emergency directions. Assess storm, flood, bushfire and heat risks for the particular home, arranging competent property work in calm conditions. Confirm any proposed insurance benefit with the insurer.

## Research note
Official emergency and health guidance supports the safety passages linked above. The property examples illustrate questions for competent assessment, not hazard ratings or instructions to undertake dangerous work. Follow current local authority information during an event.

## Opening
### Protect people first
- **People:** A household plan: people, pets, medication, and when to leave
- **Warnings:** One source of truth: your local emergency authority
- **Property:** Then the property, with hazard-specific advice and competent hands

_Plan to act early. Do not assume a warning will arrive before flash flooding; follow current local emergency guidance._

## The order is people, warnings, property
1. **People:** decide who does what, where you will go, when you will leave and how children, older people, disability, medication and pets are supported.
2. **Warnings:** use the official emergency service and hazard authority for your location; understand warning levels before the event.
3. **Property:** assess the specific storm, flood or bushfire mechanism and complete competent work in calm conditions.
4. **Records and insurance:** keep photographs and invoices, update the rebuild basis, and ask the insurer about cover, excesses and recognised mitigation.

The [NSW Rural Fire Service survival plan](https://www.rfs.nsw.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0003/36597/BFSP-Complete.pdf) says leaving early is the safest option and calls for a prepared plan. Follow the current authority for your state or territory during an event.

## Storm and wind
Before storm season, use safe ground-level observation and competent inspection to identify loose roof material, deteriorated flashings, [blocked or failing rainwater goods](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/the-maintenance-that-prevents-the-big-bills), vulnerable openings, hazardous trees and unsecured outdoor objects. [VICSES advises maintaining the home and yard, clearing gutters and securing loose items](https://www.ses.vic.gov.au/plan-and-stay-safe/emergencies/storm). Use trained, equipped people for roof access. Stay clear of fallen powerlines and floodwater.

**Who should check each part of the home before a storm**

| Signal | Action in calm weather | Who may be needed |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Roof movement, leaks or damaged flashings | Arrange condition assessment and repair scope | Roof plumber, builder or engineer as appropriate |
| Overflowing gutters or failed downpipes | Clear safely; repair falls, joints and lawful discharge | Roof plumber or drainage professional |
| Tree defect or contact risk | Obtain risk-based pruning or removal advice | Qualified arborist; council/utility where relevant |
| Vulnerable garage door, shutters or openings | Assess against local wind region and product suitability | Engineer, builder or product specialist |

## Flood
Flood depth, velocity, duration, contamination and access vary by location. Start with the council or state flood authority and property-specific information. [VICSES warns that flash flooding can develop without an official warning](https://www.ses.vic.gov.au/plan-and-stay-safe/emergencies/flood). Plan early and never enter floodwater. Discuss property measures, service vulnerabilities and lawful drainage with qualified professionals before an event; no measure guarantees that a home will remain dry or accessible.

Stay out of floodwater and follow official power-safety advice. After inundation, treat water and affected materials as potentially contaminated and follow emergency, electrical and public-health instructions before re-entry.

## Bushfire and ember attack
Begin with a survival plan and the local fire authority. Determine whether the property is in bushfire-prone land and whether a Bushfire Attack Level or planning control applies. Building measures depend on the assessed exposure, construction and local rules.

Preparation can include lawful fuel and vegetation management, clear gutters, maintained decks and subfloors, sealed gaps and compliant non-combustible mesh at openings. Keep required ventilation paths, cavity drainage and weep holes clear. On catastrophic or extreme conditions, follow official advice and leave early.

### What a Bushfire Attack Level means

In bushfire-prone areas, new building work is designed to a Bushfire Attack Level (BAL) under [AS 3959](https://store.standards.org.au/product/as-3959-2018). The BAL rates a site's likely exposure to embers, radiant heat and flame, and sets the construction requirements. A BAL certificate or assessment for an existing home tells you what the site was assessed as, which matters for renovations and extensions.

**The six Bushfire Attack Levels**

| Level | Risk | Predicted attack |
| --- | --- | --- |
| BAL-LOW | Very low | Insufficient risk to warrant specific bushfire construction requirements |
| BAL-12.5 | Low | Ember attack |
| BAL-19 | Moderate | Increasing ember attack and burning debris, with radiant heat up to 19 kW/m² |
| BAL-29 | High | Increasing ember attack and burning debris, with radiant heat up to 29 kW/m² |
| BAL-40 | Very high | Increasing ember attack, radiant heat up to 40 kW/m² and some likelihood of flame contact |
| BAL-FZ | Extreme (flame zone) | Direct exposure to flames from the fire front, as well as heat and embers |

Older homes built before the current requirements may not meet the BAL their site would attract today. Ember protection, such as sealed gaps, screened vents and clear gutters, is usually the most practical improvement. Councils and fire agencies, such as the [Shire of Harvey in WA](https://www.harvey.wa.gov.au/build-and-develop/building/bushfire-prone-areas) and [Mitcham Council in SA](https://www.mitchamcouncil.sa.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0043/879865/Bushfire-Attack-Levels.pdf), publish local guidance on BAL assessments.

## Confirm insurance outcomes in writing
Before major resilience work, ask the insurer or broker what evidence it requires (see [home condition and insurance](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/home-condition-and-insurance)), whether the measure changes cover or excess, and whether construction must be notified. Review flood, storm, bushfire, actions-of-the-sea and temporary-accommodation definitions using [Moneysmart's hazard insurance guide](https://moneysmart.gov.au/home-insurance/storm-flood-and-fire-insurance).

## The property record to keep
- Official hazard maps, BAL or flood information and the date accessed.
- Emergency plan, contacts, routes, medication and pet arrangements.
- Dated photographs of roof, elevations, drainage, openings, yard and critical equipment.
- Inspection reports, design advice, approvals, invoices, product specifications and warranties for resilience work.
- Insurance schedule, PDS version, endorsements and written insurer responses about mitigation.

## Heat is a building and household risk too
A home can become difficult to occupy without visible storm damage. [Victoria's health department](https://www.health.vic.gov.au/environmental-health/extreme-heat-and-heatwaves) identifies extreme heat as a health risk that can also disrupt power and services. Include a plan for vulnerable household members and follow current health guidance. An air conditioner is useful equipment, but it is not a complete plan if electricity or transport fails.

Before hot weather, identify which rooms overheat, when direct sun enters and whether shading and cooling equipment function. Consider access to a cooler safe place and how you will get there if normal arrangements fail. For lasting improvements, have a competent designer assess shading, insulation, ventilation and the particular construction. Opening windows is not always helpful when outside conditions are hotter or smoke-affected; the strategy must respond to actual conditions.

## Read the address, not just the hazard label
A map is a starting point for property questions. Ask which hazard and scenario it represents, its date, whether it describes land or floor exposure, and how access might be affected. A home above a mapped flood extent may still have a vulnerable access route or local overland-flow problem. An omitted area is not a professional finding that every hazard is absent.

Construction changes the questions. A raised timber home may have habitable rooms clear of ground water while services or enclosed spaces below remain exposed. An apartment can depend on basement pumps, lifts and shared electrical equipment. A lightweight extension and the original masonry home may behave differently in wind and heat. Use these distinctions to commission assessment, not to assign a safety rating from era or listing photographs.

**Separate three different kinds of preparation**

| Stage | Useful decision | Limit |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Well before an event | Assess the property, arrange competent repairs and practise the household plan | A maintenance checklist is not an engineering assessment |
| When conditions threaten | Act on the prepared plan and current official information while safe options remain | Do not delay leaving to finish property work |
| After an event | Confirm safe access and obtain the appropriate damage and service checks | A dry-looking room does not establish that concealed materials or electricity are safe |

## Plan for a failure of the first plan
List the assumptions behind your preparations. Does a garage door need power to open? Does the household rely on one driver, one mobile network or a lift? Does a pump require electricity during the same event that might interrupt it? Review these dependencies in calm conditions with the appropriate professional or service provider. Do not improvise electrical connections or generator arrangements during an emergency.

Discuss access and responsibilities in a strata scheme before the season. An owner may be able to secure items on their balcony while roof repairs, tree work or drainage alterations require scheme decisions. Record outstanding work and who has responsibility for it. Link this to the [strata risks for owners](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/strata-risks-for-owners) guide; a shared system is not maintained simply because each owner has checked their own unit.

## Recovery starts with safe access and a clear chronology
Use the relevant emergency authority's advice before re-entry, and competent assessment for damaged structures or services. Document the event and visible damage only where safe, then retain the records of emergency work and insurer directions. Explain what existed before the event, what was first seen afterwards and what remains uncertain. An event occurring before a symptom is evidence of timing; it does not by itself establish the full cause or insurance outcome. Keep that chronology with the original files using the [home-record guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/keeping-a-record-of-your-home).

A repair plan should distinguish immediate protection, drying or contamination assessment, permanent repairs and the evidence needed before finishes close the affected area. Discuss the scope with the insurer and the responsible professionals. Repainting alone cannot establish that a concealed moisture problem has been resolved. The [moisture guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/damp-and-moisture-in-your-home) helps frame the investigation questions without turning a photograph into a diagnosis.

## Worked example: a clean gutter and water at the door
**Illustrative reasoning example, not an inspected property.** A household has recently cleaned its gutters. During heavy rain, water reaches a rear doorway and a nearby street becomes difficult to access. The owners conclude that larger gutters will solve the problem.

Cleaning is evidence of one maintenance task, not proof of the capacity or operation of the entire drainage system. Roof discharge, surface falls and wider water movement are separate possibilities. During the event, household safety and official instructions take priority; no one should enter floodwater to test the theory.

Later, a drainage professional can examine the property and lawful discharge, while local flood information helps explain wider exposure and access. A defined finding may support gutter work, another intervention or several measures. The household plan also needs review, because keeping the floor dry would not necessarily keep the access route usable.

Keep conclusions at the level the evidence supports: observed, reported, inferred or confirmed. An unavailable document is a gap in the record; it does not prove the work was never done.

> Important: Follow current official warnings and call emergency services where life or property is in immediate danger. Use property-specific engineering, flood or bushfire assessment for building work.

## Frequently asked questions
### What does BAL-29 mean?
BAL-29 is the third-highest of six Bushfire Attack Levels under AS 3959. It indicates a high risk, with increasing ember attack and burning debris and radiant heat up to 29 kW/m², and sets specific construction requirements for new work.

### Does an older house meet bushfire construction standards?
Often not. Homes built before current bushfire construction requirements may not meet the Bushfire Attack Level their site would attract today. Sealing gaps, screening vents and keeping gutters clear are usually the most practical ember-protection improvements.

### What is the first step in extreme-weather preparation?
Prepare the household plan, destinations and official information sources before the building checklist. Include transport, communication, medication, disability needs and pets. Plan to act early; flash flooding may develop without an official warning. Follow current local emergency guidance.

### What should I do before storm season?
From safe locations, check for roof, drainage, tree, opening and loose-object risks; arrange competent inspection and repair where needed. Never work on a roof during a storm or approach fallen powerlines.

### Should I install flood barriers?
Only after property-specific flood and professional advice. Depth, velocity, duration, contamination and drainage interactions matter, and a barrier can redirect water or fail if misapplied.

### How do I protect vents and weep holes from embers?
Use bushfire-compliant, non-combustible mesh and details suited to the assessed exposure without blocking required drainage or ventilation. Confirm the applicable BAL, standard and local requirements.

### Will resilience work lower my insurance premium?
Ask the insurer what it recognises, what evidence it needs and whether cover or excess changes before spending for an insurance outcome.

### Should I wait for a flood warning before acting?
No. Flash flooding can develop without an official warning. Prepare early, know local conditions and follow current emergency guidance; never enter floodwater.

### Does an air conditioner complete my heatwave preparation?
No. Include household needs and a safe alternative if power or cooling fails, following current health advice. Building improvements and equipment maintenance are longer-term parts of the plan.

### Does being outside a mapped hazard area mean my home is safe?
A map has a defined purpose, coverage and scenario. Check property and access conditions; absence from one map does not establish absence of every hazard.

## Method
A hazard-specific preparation guide separating household safety, building assessment, early decisions and recovery. Property examples are illustrative; current local emergency directions govern an event.

## Limitations
This is a national resilience guide. During an event, follow your emergency service. BAL ratings, flood levels and engineering require site-specific assessment.

## Sources
- [Bush Fire Survival Plan](https://www.rfs.nsw.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0003/36597/BFSP-Complete.pdf) — NSW Rural Fire Service; accessed 2026-07-19
- [Plan and stay safe in a storm](https://www.ses.vic.gov.au/plan-and-stay-safe/emergencies/storm) — Victoria State Emergency Service; accessed 2026-07-19
- [Flood preparation and safety](https://www.ses.vic.gov.au/plan-and-stay-safe/emergencies/flood) — Victoria State Emergency Service; accessed 2026-09-07
- [Storm, flood and fire insurance](https://moneysmart.gov.au/home-insurance/storm-flood-and-fire-insurance) — Moneysmart, Australian Securities and Investments Commission; accessed 2026-07-19
- [Extreme heat and heatwaves](https://www.health.vic.gov.au/environmental-health/extreme-heat-and-heatwaves) — Victorian Department of Health; accessed 2026-09-07
- [AS 3959:2018 Construction of buildings in bushfire-prone areas](https://store.standards.org.au/product/as-3959-2018) — Standards Australia; accessed 2026-10-14
- [Bushfire prone areas and Bushfire Attack Levels](https://www.harvey.wa.gov.au/build-and-develop/building/bushfire-prone-areas) — Shire of Harvey (WA); accessed 2026-10-14
- [Bushfire Attack Levels](https://www.mitchamcouncil.sa.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0043/879865/Bushfire-Attack-Levels.pdf) — City of Mitcham (SA); accessed 2026-10-14

guides.question: What does a 1980s–90s home need?
guides.title: 1980s–90s homes: what to expect and what they need
guides.summary: Homes from the 1980s and 1990s sit across changes in materials, waterproofing practice, insulation, termite systems and renovation expectations. Separate the original build from later upgrades, then test what is actually installed.
guides.answer: For a 1980s or 1990s home, first establish which systems are original and which have been renewed. The pre-1990 asbestos screen still matters to early-1980s fabric and renovations. Then focus on wet areas, roof and windows, insulation and condensation clues, services, drainage, termite management, footings and later alterations. Do not assume a system is sound because it looks comparatively modern; use dates, records and current condition.
guides.methodology: We map each major system by installation date, then test the physical evidence: wet areas, envelope, roof, services, termite management, drainage and later alterations.
guides.limitations: A build year does not establish the age or compliance of a later bathroom, roof, service or retrofit. Assess the installed system and the requirements relevant to the date of that work.
guides.researchNote: Homes from the 1980s and 1990s span changing materials and several generations of later renovation. The pre-1990 asbestos screen still matters to the earlier part of the era, while wet areas, roofs, aluminium windows, insulation, termite systems, drainage and services need their own installation dates and current-condition evidence.

cluster.label: Read the building
cluster.blurb: Use age and construction as a starting hypothesis, then test it against evidence and physical inspection.

sections.heading: Opening
sections.markdown:
### A time of mixed materials and systems
- **Materials:** Identify the installed materials and systems
- **Wet areas:** Age, renewal history and evidence of leaks
- **Envelope:** The roof, windows and joints as they stand today

_The waterproofing membrane is the quiet one to ask about._

sections.heading: The transition era
sections.markdown:
The 1980s and 1990s sit in an awkwardly useful middle ground. The houses often look familiar and relatively modern, yet many original systems are now old enough to have been repaired, replaced or renovated at least once. Brick veneer, slab-on-ground construction, concrete or metal roofing, aluminium-framed windows and varied wet-area systems are common, but the exact mix changes by region, builder and year.

If the exact year matters, for example for asbestos or wet-area questions, [working out when a house was built](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/when-was-my-house-built) shows how to confirm it from records and aerial photographs.

The practical inspection task is to **separate the original systems from later work and identify the evidence for each change.** A 1987 bathroom and a 2019 bathroom in the same house belong to completely different evidence timelines. [How to tell which wall system you have](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/brick-veneer-vs-double-brick#tell) helps when the listing is vague about construction.

sections.heading: Map the original and later systems
sections.markdown:
**A useful system map for 1980s–90s homes**

| System | Questions | Evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Wet areas | Original or renovated? Any leak, swelling, loose finishes or staining? | Renovation date, invoices, inspection records where available, moisture evidence and repair history |
| Roof and rainwater | Original covering? Repointed/recoated/re-sheeted? Gutters and downpipes working? | Roof work invoices, leak history, visible condition, stormwater route |
| Windows and doors | Original aluminium/timber or replacement? Condensation, failed seals, leaks or difficult operation? | Installation date, glazing type, flashing/seal evidence and current condition |
| Electrical | Original circuits, later switchboard, solar or major appliance upgrades? | Licensed inspection, invoices/certificates where applicable and system specifications |
| Plumbing/hot water | Pipework and heater age? Leak or drainage history? | Invoices, service records, pressure/drainage observations and licensed assessment where needed |
| Termite management | What barrier or system exists, and is it still inspectable/maintained? | Termite notice if present, pest reports, treatment records, visible inspection zones |
| Insulation/ventilation | Original, retrofitted or unknown? Any roof-space moisture or condensation? | Roof-space inspection, product/installation records, ventilation and condensation evidence |

### Signs worth following in a 1980s–90s home
- **Wet areas:** Loose or hollow-sounding tiles, mould low on shower walls, swollen vanity panels
- **Windows:** Condensation on aluminium frames and mould in the corners of sills
- **Ceilings:** Stains below valleys or roof penetrations, and sagging plasterboard

_A sign in a renovated room belongs to the renovation’s age, not the house’s._

sections.heading: Inspection priorities
sections.markdown:
### The pre-1990 asbestos screen still matters

The [national householders' guide](https://www.newaste.org.au/asbestos/assets/asbestos-guide-for-householders.pdf) says homes built or renovated before 1990 may contain asbestos products, and all uses were prohibited nationally from 31 December 2003. That makes the early part of this era important to screen. Later renovation history matters too. Identify suspect material before drilling, sanding, cutting or demolition rather than treating the year as proof of presence or absence. [Which homes may contain asbestos](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/asbestos-in-the-home#which-homes) explains the build and renovation dates to check.

### Wet areas: current performance and renovation date both matter

Bathrooms, laundries and balconies can be original or later replacements, and the decorative finish does not tell you the membrane history. Look for staining, swelling, loose finishes, cracked grout or tiles, deteriorated sealants, poor falls, ponding and moisture to adjoining areas. Where the evidence matters to the purchase, use [suitable moisture investigation](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/damp-and-moisture-in-your-home) and establish when the work was done.

Current [NCC guidance on waterproofing in houses](https://ncc.abcb.gov.au/ncc-navigator/waterproofing-houses) is useful because it shows how modern wet areas depend on coordinated waterproof and water-resistant materials, junctions, penetrations and drainage. It should not be used to declare an original 1980s bathroom non-compliant simply because today's provisions differ. Existing-work compliance turns on the requirements and approvals applicable when the work was carried out.

### Roofs and rainwater systems

Concrete tile and metal roofs can both perform well, but condition is in the details: broken or displaced elements, flashings, valleys, penetrations, bedding/pointing where applicable, gutters, downpipes and whether water actually gets away from the footings. A cosmetic roof coating is not the same thing as a documented repair to the underlying cause of leakage.

### Aluminium windows, glazing and condensation

Many homes from this era use aluminium-framed windows. Aluminium is highly conductive, and [YourHome](https://www.yourhome.gov.au/passive-design/condensation) notes that conventional aluminium frames can act as thermal bridges and be prone to condensation in suitable conditions. Condensation does not automatically mean the window is defective, but repeated moisture at frames, reveals or adjacent finishes deserves a ventilation, humidity, glazing and envelope assessment rather than repeated repainting.

### Insulation and roof-space changes

A home from this era may have original insulation, later top-ups, patchy coverage or several products layered together. [YourHome's insulation guidance](https://www.yourhome.gov.au/passive-design/insulation) stresses electrical and installation safety in roof spaces. Ask what is installed, whether it has been displaced by trades, whether clearances around heat-producing fittings and equipment are appropriate, and whether there are signs of roof-space condensation or leaks.

### Termite management needs an actual system history

These decades include both raised and slab-on-ground homes, and termite management can be easy to overlook because the building looks 'new enough'. Risk depends on location, moisture, access, landscaping and construction details. [QBCC guidance](https://www.qbcc.qld.gov.au/home-owner-hub/maintain-protect/protect-against-termites) explains that later paths, gardens, patios and renovations can reduce the effectiveness or inspectability of a termite system. Look for any termite-management notice, treatment history and recent pest report, then confirm that inspection zones remain visible. [Finding the durable notice](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/termites-in-australian-homes#durable-notice) shows where the original system is usually recorded.

### Movement, drainage and slab edges

Reactive soils, leaking services, trees and uneven moisture around footings can affect homes of this era. Record crack pattern, width, distortion and whether movement has changed. Also check where downpipes discharge, whether surface water falls away from the building, whether garden beds bridge slab edges or damp-proofing, and whether later paving has changed drainage. Use [the crack guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/cracks-structural-or-cosmetic) for escalation clues.

### This era straddles the key safety milestones

A house built in 1985 and one built in 1999 can sit on different sides of several requirements. Check the approval date, not just the decade.

**Milestones that fall inside this era**

| Milestone | Built before it | Built after it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Wet-area waterproofing standard (AS 3740, 1989, revised 1994) | Original showers rely on older waterproofing methods; leaks are common as they age ([guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/bathroom-waterproofing-and-leaking-showers#by-era)) | Built to a published waterproofing standard, though workmanship still varies |
| Asbestos screen: homes built or renovated before 1990 | May contain asbestos in sheeting, eaves, flues or floor coverings | Asbestos unlikely in original construction, but later imports and repairs can vary |
| Safety switches on power circuits (around 1991) | May have no safety switch unless retrofitted ([guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/switchboards-wiring-and-safety-switches)) | Power points protected; lighting often not until around 2000–01 |
| Mains-powered smoke alarms (around 1997) | May rely on battery alarms | Hard-wired alarms, usually not interconnected (that came in 2014) |

sections.heading: Renovation date can matter more than build date
sections.markdown:
These homes are now old enough that kitchens, bathrooms, roofs, hot-water units, heating/cooling, windows and electrical systems may each belong to different decades. This creates a common mistake: buyers see a renovated interior and mentally reset the whole house to the renovation year. Do not. The slab, drainage, frame, roof structure and concealed wall systems may still be original.

**Common renovation claims and the evidence behind them**

| Claim | What to verify | What can remain unknown |
| --- | --- | --- |
| “New bathroom” | Date, installer, approvals/inspection where relevant, leak history and present moisture evidence | Membrane detailing is concealed once finishes are complete. |
| “Rewired” | Scope of electrical work, switchboard changes and licensed documentation | Whether every circuit and concealed cable was replaced. |
| “New roof” | Covering, flashings, sarking/membrane, gutters, valleys and date | Whether roof framing or all water-entry details were renewed. |
| “Double glazed” | Which openings, frame type, product details and installation date | Whether surrounding wall insulation, sealing or flashings were changed. |
| “Termite protected” | System type, installation/treatment date, maintenance and latest inspection | Whether later landscaping or building work compromised the system. |

sections.heading: Energy upgrades can alter moisture behaviour
sections.markdown: Draught sealing, added insulation and replacement glazing can make a home more comfortable, but the building still needs a safe drying and ventilation strategy. [YourHome](https://www.yourhome.gov.au/passive-design/ventilation-airtightness) warns that improving airtightness without considering condensation can increase moisture risk. If the house has been progressively sealed and insulated, look for mould, recurrent window condensation and roof-space moisture, and consider how bathrooms, laundries and cooking moisture are exhausted.

sections.heading: What to ask before you buy
sections.markdown:
1. **Original systems:** list wet areas, roof covering, windows, wiring, plumbing, hot water, heating/cooling and insulation as renewed, original or explicitly unknown.
2. **Pre-1990 work:** identify it so hazardous-material screening can be focused before disturbance.
3. **Water history:** ask about bathroom leaks, roof leaks, stormwater, plumbing and any repaired staining.
4. **Termite system:** find the notice or treatment history if available and verify current inspection access.
5. **Envelope changes:** record windows, recladding, insulation, roofing and extensions that may have altered drainage or condensation behaviour.
6. **Budget-changing evidence:** prioritise invoices, permits, reports and specialist inspection over a generic “renovated” label.

sections.heading: Worked example: the restored roof and ceiling stain
sections.markdown:
**Illustrative reasoning example, not an inspected property.** A 1992 house has a recently coated tile roof and a ceiling stain below a valley. The coating is visible; the valley’s condition and the stain’s history are not established. Ask whether the restoration included the valley, what caused the stain and whether it has changed since relevant rainfall. A roofer’s documented diagnosis and repair scope can distinguish a resolved historic event from an ongoing leak.

This changes the budget. A coating invoice is not a reason to assume the whole roof is new, and a stain is not enough to assume the whole roof needs replacing. Keep the unresolved water-entry question explicit until the relevant components and any damage beneath have been assessed.

sections.heading: Confirm the property’s current condition
sections.markdown:
The build date gives you a useful first list of questions. The records and the home itself provide the answers. Separate original work from later renovations, then assess each element by material, exposure, maintenance and present condition. The overview is [what your home needs by decade](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/what-your-home-needs-by-decade), and the eras either side are [postwar homes](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/postwar-homes-1950s-70s) and [modern homes](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/modern-homes-2000s-on).

> Note: For 1980s–90s homes, the most useful document is often a timeline: original build, each major renovation, each service renewal and each known leak or repair.

faqs.question: What inspection issues are common in late-1990s homes?
faqs.answer: Typical findings include ageing original showers and wet areas, early safety switch coverage that may not protect lighting, concrete tile roofs needing ridge and pointing work, aluminium window seals and condensation, and termite systems whose servicing has lapsed. Most are maintenance-level, but each is worth confirming.

faqs.question: Does a 1990s house have safety switches?
faqs.answer: Probably on the power-point circuits if it was built after around 1991, but lighting circuits were usually not required to have them until around 2000–01. Check the switchboard: safety switches have a test button.

faqs.question: Were 1980s bathrooms waterproofed?
faqs.answer: Often by older methods. The first Australian Standard for waterproofing residential wet areas, AS 3740, was published in 1989 and revised in 1994. Original showers from before then are a common source of leaks as they age.

faqs.question: What problems do 1980s–90s homes have?
faqs.answer: Priority checks include pre-1990 hazardous materials where relevant, wet areas, roof-water disposal, aluminium windows and condensation, insulation, services, termite management, drainage and movement. Later renovations can be as important as the original build.

faqs.question: Does a 1980s home have asbestos?
faqs.answer: It may. Australian household guidance treats homes built or renovated before 1990 as potentially containing asbestos products. Identify suspect material before disturbance rather than assuming from age alone.

faqs.question: Does a 1990s home have no asbestos risk?
faqs.answer: Do not use the decade as a guarantee. The strongest household screening rule is pre-1990, while all uses were not prohibited nationally until 31 December 2003. Property-specific material identification is the appropriate route where suspect material may be disturbed.

faqs.question: Why do bathrooms from this era leak?
faqs.answer: Potential causes include plumbing, junctions, drainage, screens, finishes and waterproofing. Establish whether the room is original or renovated and investigate the current moisture evidence.

faqs.question: Do concrete tile roofs need maintenance?
faqs.answer: Yes. Roof coverings, flashings, valleys, gutters and related details age in place. Inspect their current condition and repair history rather than relying on the roof’s appearance from the street.

faqs.question: Why do aluminium windows get condensation?
faqs.answer: Conventional aluminium is highly conductive and can form a thermal bridge. Condensation depends on indoor humidity, surface temperature, glazing, ventilation and climate, so repeated moisture should be investigated as a building-system issue rather than treated only as a cleaning problem.

faqs.question: How do I know whether a termite system still works?
faqs.answer: Identify the system, installation or treatment date, maintenance requirements and recent inspection history. Also check whether landscaping, paving or later building work has hidden slab edges or inspection zones.

faqs.question: What makes an 1980s–90s home a sound purchase?
faqs.answer: Clear evidence about wet areas, roof and drainage, windows, services, termite management, alterations and any relevant pre-1990 materials makes future work easier to budget. The aim is not a defect-free house but a well-understood one.

guides.contentMarkdown:
# 1980s–90s homes: what to expect and what they need

For a 1980s or 1990s home, first establish which systems are original and which have been renewed. The pre-1990 asbestos screen still matters to early-1980s fabric and renovations. Then focus on wet areas, roof and windows, insulation and condensation clues, services, drainage, termite management, footings and later alterations. Do not assume a system is sound because it looks comparatively modern; use dates, records and current condition.

## Research note
Homes from the 1980s and 1990s span changing materials and several generations of later renovation. The pre-1990 asbestos screen still matters to the earlier part of the era, while wet areas, roofs, aluminium windows, insulation, termite systems, drainage and services need their own installation dates and current-condition evidence.

## Opening
### A time of mixed materials and systems
- **Materials:** Identify the installed materials and systems
- **Wet areas:** Age, renewal history and evidence of leaks
- **Envelope:** The roof, windows and joints as they stand today

_The waterproofing membrane is the quiet one to ask about._

## The transition era
The 1980s and 1990s sit in an awkwardly useful middle ground. The houses often look familiar and relatively modern, yet many original systems are now old enough to have been repaired, replaced or renovated at least once. Brick veneer, slab-on-ground construction, concrete or metal roofing, aluminium-framed windows and varied wet-area systems are common, but the exact mix changes by region, builder and year.

If the exact year matters, for example for asbestos or wet-area questions, [working out when a house was built](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/when-was-my-house-built) shows how to confirm it from records and aerial photographs.

The practical inspection task is to **separate the original systems from later work and identify the evidence for each change.** A 1987 bathroom and a 2019 bathroom in the same house belong to completely different evidence timelines. [How to tell which wall system you have](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/brick-veneer-vs-double-brick#tell) helps when the listing is vague about construction.

## Map the original and later systems
**A useful system map for 1980s–90s homes**

| System | Questions | Evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Wet areas | Original or renovated? Any leak, swelling, loose finishes or staining? | Renovation date, invoices, inspection records where available, moisture evidence and repair history |
| Roof and rainwater | Original covering? Repointed/recoated/re-sheeted? Gutters and downpipes working? | Roof work invoices, leak history, visible condition, stormwater route |
| Windows and doors | Original aluminium/timber or replacement? Condensation, failed seals, leaks or difficult operation? | Installation date, glazing type, flashing/seal evidence and current condition |
| Electrical | Original circuits, later switchboard, solar or major appliance upgrades? | Licensed inspection, invoices/certificates where applicable and system specifications |
| Plumbing/hot water | Pipework and heater age? Leak or drainage history? | Invoices, service records, pressure/drainage observations and licensed assessment where needed |
| Termite management | What barrier or system exists, and is it still inspectable/maintained? | Termite notice if present, pest reports, treatment records, visible inspection zones |
| Insulation/ventilation | Original, retrofitted or unknown? Any roof-space moisture or condensation? | Roof-space inspection, product/installation records, ventilation and condensation evidence |

### Signs worth following in a 1980s–90s home
- **Wet areas:** Loose or hollow-sounding tiles, mould low on shower walls, swollen vanity panels
- **Windows:** Condensation on aluminium frames and mould in the corners of sills
- **Ceilings:** Stains below valleys or roof penetrations, and sagging plasterboard

_A sign in a renovated room belongs to the renovation’s age, not the house’s._

## Inspection priorities
### The pre-1990 asbestos screen still matters

The [national householders' guide](https://www.newaste.org.au/asbestos/assets/asbestos-guide-for-householders.pdf) says homes built or renovated before 1990 may contain asbestos products, and all uses were prohibited nationally from 31 December 2003. That makes the early part of this era important to screen. Later renovation history matters too. Identify suspect material before drilling, sanding, cutting or demolition rather than treating the year as proof of presence or absence. [Which homes may contain asbestos](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/asbestos-in-the-home#which-homes) explains the build and renovation dates to check.

### Wet areas: current performance and renovation date both matter

Bathrooms, laundries and balconies can be original or later replacements, and the decorative finish does not tell you the membrane history. Look for staining, swelling, loose finishes, cracked grout or tiles, deteriorated sealants, poor falls, ponding and moisture to adjoining areas. Where the evidence matters to the purchase, use [suitable moisture investigation](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/damp-and-moisture-in-your-home) and establish when the work was done.

Current [NCC guidance on waterproofing in houses](https://ncc.abcb.gov.au/ncc-navigator/waterproofing-houses) is useful because it shows how modern wet areas depend on coordinated waterproof and water-resistant materials, junctions, penetrations and drainage. It should not be used to declare an original 1980s bathroom non-compliant simply because today's provisions differ. Existing-work compliance turns on the requirements and approvals applicable when the work was carried out.

### Roofs and rainwater systems

Concrete tile and metal roofs can both perform well, but condition is in the details: broken or displaced elements, flashings, valleys, penetrations, bedding/pointing where applicable, gutters, downpipes and whether water actually gets away from the footings. A cosmetic roof coating is not the same thing as a documented repair to the underlying cause of leakage.

### Aluminium windows, glazing and condensation

Many homes from this era use aluminium-framed windows. Aluminium is highly conductive, and [YourHome](https://www.yourhome.gov.au/passive-design/condensation) notes that conventional aluminium frames can act as thermal bridges and be prone to condensation in suitable conditions. Condensation does not automatically mean the window is defective, but repeated moisture at frames, reveals or adjacent finishes deserves a ventilation, humidity, glazing and envelope assessment rather than repeated repainting.

### Insulation and roof-space changes

A home from this era may have original insulation, later top-ups, patchy coverage or several products layered together. [YourHome's insulation guidance](https://www.yourhome.gov.au/passive-design/insulation) stresses electrical and installation safety in roof spaces. Ask what is installed, whether it has been displaced by trades, whether clearances around heat-producing fittings and equipment are appropriate, and whether there are signs of roof-space condensation or leaks.

### Termite management needs an actual system history

These decades include both raised and slab-on-ground homes, and termite management can be easy to overlook because the building looks 'new enough'. Risk depends on location, moisture, access, landscaping and construction details. [QBCC guidance](https://www.qbcc.qld.gov.au/home-owner-hub/maintain-protect/protect-against-termites) explains that later paths, gardens, patios and renovations can reduce the effectiveness or inspectability of a termite system. Look for any termite-management notice, treatment history and recent pest report, then confirm that inspection zones remain visible. [Finding the durable notice](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/termites-in-australian-homes#durable-notice) shows where the original system is usually recorded.

### Movement, drainage and slab edges

Reactive soils, leaking services, trees and uneven moisture around footings can affect homes of this era. Record crack pattern, width, distortion and whether movement has changed. Also check where downpipes discharge, whether surface water falls away from the building, whether garden beds bridge slab edges or damp-proofing, and whether later paving has changed drainage. Use [the crack guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/cracks-structural-or-cosmetic) for escalation clues.

### This era straddles the key safety milestones

A house built in 1985 and one built in 1999 can sit on different sides of several requirements. Check the approval date, not just the decade.

**Milestones that fall inside this era**

| Milestone | Built before it | Built after it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Wet-area waterproofing standard (AS 3740, 1989, revised 1994) | Original showers rely on older waterproofing methods; leaks are common as they age ([guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/bathroom-waterproofing-and-leaking-showers#by-era)) | Built to a published waterproofing standard, though workmanship still varies |
| Asbestos screen: homes built or renovated before 1990 | May contain asbestos in sheeting, eaves, flues or floor coverings | Asbestos unlikely in original construction, but later imports and repairs can vary |
| Safety switches on power circuits (around 1991) | May have no safety switch unless retrofitted ([guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/switchboards-wiring-and-safety-switches)) | Power points protected; lighting often not until around 2000–01 |
| Mains-powered smoke alarms (around 1997) | May rely on battery alarms | Hard-wired alarms, usually not interconnected (that came in 2014) |

## Renovation date can matter more than build date
These homes are now old enough that kitchens, bathrooms, roofs, hot-water units, heating/cooling, windows and electrical systems may each belong to different decades. This creates a common mistake: buyers see a renovated interior and mentally reset the whole house to the renovation year. Do not. The slab, drainage, frame, roof structure and concealed wall systems may still be original.

**Common renovation claims and the evidence behind them**

| Claim | What to verify | What can remain unknown |
| --- | --- | --- |
| “New bathroom” | Date, installer, approvals/inspection where relevant, leak history and present moisture evidence | Membrane detailing is concealed once finishes are complete. |
| “Rewired” | Scope of electrical work, switchboard changes and licensed documentation | Whether every circuit and concealed cable was replaced. |
| “New roof” | Covering, flashings, sarking/membrane, gutters, valleys and date | Whether roof framing or all water-entry details were renewed. |
| “Double glazed” | Which openings, frame type, product details and installation date | Whether surrounding wall insulation, sealing or flashings were changed. |
| “Termite protected” | System type, installation/treatment date, maintenance and latest inspection | Whether later landscaping or building work compromised the system. |

## Energy upgrades can alter moisture behaviour
Draught sealing, added insulation and replacement glazing can make a home more comfortable, but the building still needs a safe drying and ventilation strategy. [YourHome](https://www.yourhome.gov.au/passive-design/ventilation-airtightness) warns that improving airtightness without considering condensation can increase moisture risk. If the house has been progressively sealed and insulated, look for mould, recurrent window condensation and roof-space moisture, and consider how bathrooms, laundries and cooking moisture are exhausted.

## What to ask before you buy
1. **Original systems:** list wet areas, roof covering, windows, wiring, plumbing, hot water, heating/cooling and insulation as renewed, original or explicitly unknown.
2. **Pre-1990 work:** identify it so hazardous-material screening can be focused before disturbance.
3. **Water history:** ask about bathroom leaks, roof leaks, stormwater, plumbing and any repaired staining.
4. **Termite system:** find the notice or treatment history if available and verify current inspection access.
5. **Envelope changes:** record windows, recladding, insulation, roofing and extensions that may have altered drainage or condensation behaviour.
6. **Budget-changing evidence:** prioritise invoices, permits, reports and specialist inspection over a generic “renovated” label.

## Worked example: the restored roof and ceiling stain
**Illustrative reasoning example, not an inspected property.** A 1992 house has a recently coated tile roof and a ceiling stain below a valley. The coating is visible; the valley’s condition and the stain’s history are not established. Ask whether the restoration included the valley, what caused the stain and whether it has changed since relevant rainfall. A roofer’s documented diagnosis and repair scope can distinguish a resolved historic event from an ongoing leak.

This changes the budget. A coating invoice is not a reason to assume the whole roof is new, and a stain is not enough to assume the whole roof needs replacing. Keep the unresolved water-entry question explicit until the relevant components and any damage beneath have been assessed.

## Confirm the property’s current condition
The build date gives you a useful first list of questions. The records and the home itself provide the answers. Separate original work from later renovations, then assess each element by material, exposure, maintenance and present condition. The overview is [what your home needs by decade](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/what-your-home-needs-by-decade), and the eras either side are [postwar homes](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/postwar-homes-1950s-70s) and [modern homes](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/modern-homes-2000s-on).

> Note: For 1980s–90s homes, the most useful document is often a timeline: original build, each major renovation, each service renewal and each known leak or repair.

## Frequently asked questions
### What inspection issues are common in late-1990s homes?
Typical findings include ageing original showers and wet areas, early safety switch coverage that may not protect lighting, concrete tile roofs needing ridge and pointing work, aluminium window seals and condensation, and termite systems whose servicing has lapsed. Most are maintenance-level, but each is worth confirming.

### Does a 1990s house have safety switches?
Probably on the power-point circuits if it was built after around 1991, but lighting circuits were usually not required to have them until around 2000–01. Check the switchboard: safety switches have a test button.

### Were 1980s bathrooms waterproofed?

### What problems do 1980s–90s homes have?
Priority checks include pre-1990 hazardous materials where relevant, wet areas, roof-water disposal, aluminium windows and condensation, insulation, services, termite management, drainage and movement. Later renovations can be as important as the original build.

### Does a 1980s home have asbestos?
It may. Australian household guidance treats homes built or renovated before 1990 as potentially containing asbestos products. Identify suspect material before disturbance rather than assuming from age alone.

### Does a 1990s home have no asbestos risk?
Do not use the decade as a guarantee. The strongest household screening rule is pre-1990, while all uses were not prohibited nationally until 31 December 2003. Property-specific material identification is the appropriate route where suspect material may be disturbed.

### Why do bathrooms from this era leak?
Potential causes include plumbing, junctions, drainage, screens, finishes and waterproofing. Establish whether the room is original or renovated and investigate the current moisture evidence.

### Do concrete tile roofs need maintenance?
Yes. Roof coverings, flashings, valleys, gutters and related details age in place. Inspect their current condition and repair history rather than relying on the roof’s appearance from the street.

### Why do aluminium windows get condensation?
Conventional aluminium is highly conductive and can form a thermal bridge. Condensation depends on indoor humidity, surface temperature, glazing, ventilation and climate, so repeated moisture should be investigated as a building-system issue rather than treated only as a cleaning problem.

### How do I know whether a termite system still works?

### What makes an 1980s–90s home a sound purchase?
Clear evidence about wet areas, roof and drainage, windows, services, termite management, alterations and any relevant pre-1990 materials makes future work easier to budget. The aim is not a defect-free house but a well-understood one.

## Method
We map each major system by installation date, then test the physical evidence: wet areas, envelope, roof, services, termite management, drainage and later alterations.

## Limitations
A build year does not establish the age or compliance of a later bathroom, roof, service or retrofit. Assess the installed system and the requirements relevant to the date of that work.

guides.question: What should I check in a weatherboard home?
guides.title: Weatherboard homes: read the whole water-shedding system
guides.summary: The paint is part of the weatherproofing, and the small junctions do the quiet work. Read the boards, flashings, openings, drainage and subfloor as one connected system.
guides.answer: Start with the boards and coating, then follow every place water can get in or linger: end grain, fixings, joints, windows, doors, penetrations, roof and gutter junctions, ground clearance and splashback. Check the wall wrap or sarking where it can be seen, and identify the footing and subfloor arrangement. Repaint timing depends on preparation, product, colour, orientation and exposure, so the most weathered side usually tells the story first.
guides.methodology: We follow each elevation from exposure to water entry, concealed damage and a defined repair scope, with a fictional example showing which evidence changes that scope.
guides.limitations: Weatherboard homes may use stump, pier, strip footing or slab systems. Confirm the actual assembly and safe access before work.
guides.researchNote: Use the actual cladding assembly and repair history to frame the inspection. [YourHome's cladding guidance](https://www.yourhome.gov.au/materials/cladding-systems) explains the role of the layers behind the outer finish.

cluster.label: Read the building
cluster.blurb: Use age and construction as a starting hypothesis, then test it against evidence and physical inspection.

sections.heading: Opening
sections.markdown:
### The paint is part of the weatherproofing
- **Face:** The boards and their coat, down to the end grain
- **Junctions:** The corners, openings and flashings where water tries first
- **Below:** Clearance from the ground, and air moving underneath

_Paint starts the job. Flashings and drainage finish it._

sections.heading: What you'll notice
sections.markdown:
Weatherboard problems start small and visible. These are the signs to look for, walking each side of the house.

**Signs by sense**

| Sense | Sign | Where to read next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| See | Paint peeling, blistering or cracking, often worst on the weather side | [Paint and weatherproofing](#paint) |
| See | Dark staining, gaps or open joints at board ends, corners and around windows | [The envelope checklist](#envelope) |
| See | Soil, mulch or paving against the bottom boards | [Ground clearance and termites](#ground-and-pests) |
| Feel | Soft or spongy timber when pressed gently at the bottom boards or sills | Decay; see the FAQ on where rot starts |
| See | Boards bowing, splitting or pulling away from the frame | [Movement and decay](#movement) |
| See | Mud tubes on stumps or along the base of walls | [Termites](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/termites-in-australian-homes) |

sections.heading: Start with exposure and condition
sections.markdown: North- and west-facing walls, coastal salt, shade, wind-driven rain, garden irrigation and low clearances can make one elevation deteriorate much faster than another. Walk every side in consistent light and compare the bottom boards, corners, window sills, meter boxes, decks, pipes and roof-to-wall junctions.

sections.heading: The envelope checklist
sections.markdown:
**What each layer is doing**

| Layer | Look for | Why it matters |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Boards and coating | Peeling, checking, open laps, splitting, softness, exposed end grain and failed filler | The outer layer sheds weather and protects the substrate |
| Openings and penetrations | Missing or failed flashings, sealant-only repairs, sill damage and staining | Water concentrates at interruptions in the wall |
| Wrap / sarking and cavity | Records, visible edges at alterations, blocked drainage or incompatible additions | The secondary drainage and air-control layer may be concealed |
| Ground and paving | Low boards, soil contact, mulch, splashback and paving falling toward walls | Persistent wetting raises decay, pest and concealed-moisture risk |
| Subfloor or footing | Actual slab, stump, pier or strip system; ventilation, damp and movement evidence | Confirm the foundation separately from the cladding |
| Roof and rainwater goods | Overflow paths, downpipes, apron flashings and staining | Many wall problems begin above the wall |

sections.heading: Paint within the weatherproofing system
sections.markdown:
A compatible, well-prepared coating protects timber from ultraviolet and moisture cycling. Missing flashing, soil contact, failed joints and trapped water need their own repairs. Repeated early paint failure usually points to an underlying moisture, preparation or detailing problem. Find the cause before repainting.

Manufacturer guidance, coating type, preparation, timber or sheet substrate, colour and exposure determine inspection and recoating. Record the product and colour, inspect the most exposed elevation first, and plan work from current condition.

sections.heading: Movement and decay need different questions
sections.markdown: Gaps, sticking openings and out-of-level floors can relate to footings, moisture, alterations or local timber damage. Soft boards, fungal decay or pest evidence relate to material and moisture pathways. Use [the movement guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/cracks-structural-or-cosmetic) and a competent building inspection where associated distortion or progression exists.

sections.heading: Renovating older weatherboards
sections.markdown:
Before sanding, drilling or removing cladding on a home built or renovated before 1990, screen for asbestos-containing sheet products and older lead paint. Later recladding may also hide mixed substrates, missing wrap or non-compliant junctions. Identify the assembly before specifying repair.

For ongoing care, follow the water-path approach in [the maintenance guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/the-maintenance-that-prevents-the-big-bills) and keep the product, repair and photo record described in [the home record](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/keeping-a-record-of-your-home).

sections.heading: Establish what the boards actually are
sections.markdown:
Weatherboard describes a profile or appearance as much as a material. Solid timber, reconstituted timber and fibre-cement boards need different preparation, fixing and repair methods. A painted elevation may include original boards, later sheet infill and replacement window trims. Ask for recladding invoices and product information, then have uncertain material identified before disturbing it. A listing photograph can show the profile and visible coating failure; it cannot establish every layer behind the paint.

[YourHome's cladding guidance](https://www.yourhome.gov.au/materials/cladding-systems) treats the outer boards, membrane, framing and insulation as an assembly. Older direct-fixed boards may have no modern drainage cavity or membrane. Record that arrangement accurately: an old assembly needs a suitable repair design, and its age alone does not establish a current leak or a legal compliance failure.

**Common board materials and what each means for the inspection**

| Material | Where you find it | Practical tells | What it changes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Older solid timber boards | Much pre-war and early post-war housing | Solid timber, often under many coats of paint, sometimes with original profiles | Often durable, but older coatings may contain lead; follow end grain and joints for decay |
| Western red cedar | Mid-century onward, often stained or clear-finished | Light, aromatic, soft enough to dent with a fingernail | Needs regular finish renewal; weathers grey when coatings lapse |
| Treated softwood (pine) | Later housing and repairs | Lighter, sometimes with a treatment tag or greenish tint on cut ends | Cut ends must be resealed; check the treatment suits exposure |
| Fibre-cement planks | From the post-war period onward | Hard, brittle, uniform texture, sometimes a faux wood grain | Products made before 1990 may contain asbestos; do not drill, sand or cut to identify |
| Aluminium or vinyl over-cladding | Renovations from the 1960s to the 1990s | Hollow sound, uniform pressed profile, visible end caps | Can hide decayed original boards and old moisture problems behind |

Fibre-cement and over-cladding deserve particular care. The [Asbestos and Silica Safety and Eradication Agency](https://www.asbestossafety.gov.au/about-asbestos/finding-asbestos/home) advises that homes built or renovated before 1990 may contain asbestos, and that only testing confirms it. Over-cladding is not a defect in itself, but it means the condition of the original boards and framing beneath is unknown until opened up.

sections.heading: Ground clearance, subfloors and termites
sections.markdown:
Most weatherboard homes sit on stumps or piers, which makes the subfloor both their weak point and their best inspection opportunity. Keep soil, mulch, paving and garden beds well clear of the bottom boards so they can dry and so termite activity is visible rather than hidden. [CSIRO's building technology resource on managing termites](https://research.csiro.au/infratech/btr/) explains why visible inspection zones and regular professional inspection matter more than any single barrier.

**Below the floor**

| Look for | What it can mean | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Mud tubes on stumps, piers or walls | Possible termite activity | Do not disturb them; arrange a licensed timber pest inspection |
| Soil, mulch or garden beds against the bottom boards | Hidden termite entry and moisture held against timber | Restore clearance and check the bottom boards and framing for decay |
| Damp, musty subfloor or no cross-ventilation | Blocked vents, poor drainage or plumbing leaks | Clear vents, check drainage and plumbing, and see the damp guide |
| Leaning, packed or mixed stumps | Earlier partial restumping, settlement or decay | Ask for restumping records and check floor levels across rooms |

sections.heading: Use the differences between elevations
sections.markdown:
**Comparisons that make a weatherboard inspection more informative**

| Observation | Question it raises | Evidence that helps |
| --- | --- | --- |
| One freshly painted wall; three weathered walls | Was it routine staged maintenance or a response to damage? | Earlier photographs, painting scope and any board or flashing replacement invoices. |
| Repeated failure below one window | Does water arrive from the opening, above it or behind the cladding? | Window installation details, rainfall history and targeted inspection of the junction. |
| Sound upper boards; deteriorated bottom courses | What maintains wetting at ground level? | Paving falls, garden levels, irrigation, clearance and accessible framing condition. |
| A gap where an extension joins the house | Is this an intended joint, local timber movement or movement between structures? | Plans, supports on each side, dated changes and associated distortion. |

Close-up photographs should retain enough surrounding detail to locate the defect. A photograph of peeling paint with no window, corner or ground reference is much less useful for understanding the water path.

sections.heading: Separate board repair from the work behind it
sections.markdown:
A quote to replace visibly damaged boards may leave the main uncertainty untouched. Ask whether the scope includes opening enough of the affected area to assess framing, repairing the entry point, matching the board profile, treating exposed cut ends as specified, reinstating flashings and preparing adjoining paint. Where concealed work is unknown, ask for a defined opening-up stage and a method for agreeing additional work.

The reverse also matters: a few damaged boards do not establish a need to reclad the entire house. A building inspector or carpenter can define the accessible defect and recommend further investigation; suspected structural timber damage or movement may need engineering input. Pest evidence needs a timber-pest professional. The scope should state which person answers each unresolved question.

sections.heading: Read the shell and each upgrade separately
sections.markdown:
A [1930s weatherboard](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/interwar-homes-1920s-40s) with a recent extension has at least two construction histories. sections.heading: Worked example: the freshly painted wall below a deck
sections.markdown:
**Illustrative reasoning example, not an inspected property.** A 1940s house has one freshly painted elevation, and the seller reports replacing three boards below a deck. # Weatherboard homes: read the whole water-shedding system

Start with the boards and coating, then follow every place water can get in or linger: end grain, fixings, joints, windows, doors, penetrations, roof and gutter junctions, ground clearance and splashback. ### The paint is part of the weatherproofing
- **Face:** The boards and their coat, down to the end grain
- **Junctions:** The corners, openings and flashings where water tries first

**Signs by sense**

| Sense | Sign | Where to read next |
| --- | --- | --- |

| See | Soil, mulch or paving against the bottom boards | [Ground clearance and termites](#ground-and-pests) |
| Feel | Soft or spongy timber when pressed gently at the bottom boards or sills | Decay; see the FAQ on where rot starts |
| See | Boards bowing, splitting or pulling away from the frame | [Movement and decay](#movement) |
| See | Mud tubes on stumps or along the base of walls | [Termites](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/termites-in-australian-homes) |

North- and west-facing walls, coastal salt, shade, wind-driven rain, garden irrigation and low clearances can make one elevation deteriorate much faster than another.
