guides.question: How do I tell if a roof needs repair, restoration or replacement?
guides.title: Roofs: tiles, metal and where leaks really start
guides.summary: How to read a tiled or metal roof, where leaks really start, what to check in the roof space, gutters and box gutters, chimneys and solar panels, what to do after hail, and how to judge a restoration quote.
guides.answer: Most roof leaks start at the junctions, not in the middle of the tiles or sheets: valleys, ridge and hip capping, flashings at walls and chimneys, penetrations such as flues and vents, and box gutters. A restoration that cleans, repoints and coats a tiled roof treats surface wear; it does not fix a failing valley, flashing or sagging frame.
guides.methodology: We identify the roof material, follow water to the junctions where it most often enters, then separate repair, restoration and replacement scopes, with a fictional example.
guides.limitations: Roof access is hazardous. Material identification from the ground is indicative; asbestos and concealed defects need testing and safe professional access.
guides.researchNote: Roof materials and leak points draw on QBCC's maintenance guidance and manufacturer guidance on incompatible metals. Asbestos screening follows the national agency's pre-1990 advice. The leak table reflects common inspection experience and should be confirmed on site.

cluster.label: Read the building
cluster.blurb: Use age and construction as a starting hypothesis, then test it against evidence and physical inspection.

sections.heading: Opening
sections.markdown:
### Water tries the junctions first
- **Covering:** Tiles, sheet or slate shed most of the rain
- **Junctions:** Valleys, ridges, flashings and penetrations are where leaks begin
- **Drainage:** Gutters, box gutters and downpipes carry it away, or back inside

_A coating refreshes a surface. It does not fix a valley._

Identify the material first, whether terracotta or concrete tiles, metal sheet, slate or older asbestos-cement sheeting, then look from the ground and, where safe, the roof space for slipped or cracked tiles, failed ridge pointing, rust at laps and fixings, and water stains on timbers.

sections.heading: What you'll notice
sections.markdown:
Roof problems usually announce themselves inside or from the ground first. Follow the sign to the part of the roof that causes it.

**Signs by sense**

| Sense | Sign | Where to read next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| See | Stains or bubbling paint on ceilings, often near internal corners or below the ridge | [Where roofs leak](#leak-points) |
| See | Slipped, cracked or missing tiles, or gaps along the ridge capping, from the ground | [Where roofs leak](#leak-points) |
| See | Rust streaks on metal sheets, gutters or around screws | [Metal roofs](#metal) |
| See | Water overflowing gutters or spilling down walls in heavy rain | [Site drainage](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/site-drainage-and-stormwater) |
| Hear | Dripping in the ceiling during rain, or rattling or banging sheets in wind | [The roof space](#roof-space) |
| Feel | Damp or compressed insulation, or drips on cold mornings under a metal roof | [Condensation under metal roofs](#metal) |

sections.heading: Start by identifying the roof
sections.markdown:
The material sets the questions. A roof can also be mixed: a tiled original house with a metal-roofed extension, or a slate front with later sheeting at the rear. Record each section separately.

**Common Australian roof materials**

| Material | Where you find it | How to recognise it | What usually needs attention |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Terracotta tiles | Much pre-war and many later homes | Fired clay, colour through the tile, often orange or red; glazed versions exist | Ridge and hip bedding and pointing, cracked or slipped tiles, valleys |
| Concrete tiles | Very common from the post-war decades onward | Thicker, heavier tiles with a surface coating that wears to expose a sandy texture | Surface wear, pointing, cracked tiles and valleys |
| Metal sheet | All eras; older galvanised iron, later coated steel | Corrugated or trimdeck profiles, fixed with screws or nails through the sheet | Rust at laps, fixings and gutters, incompatible metals, low-pitch drainage, condensation |
| Slate | Period homes | Thin natural stone, often blue-grey, fixed with nails | Slipped or cracked slates and corroded fixing nails; specialist repair |
| Asbestos-cement sheeting | Homes, sheds and carports built or altered before 1990 | Grey fibre-cement corrugated sheets, often weathered with lichen | Do not walk on, drill, cut or water-blast; testing and specialist advice first |

The [Asbestos and Silica Safety and Eradication Agency](https://www.asbestossafety.gov.au/about-asbestos/finding-asbestos/home) advises that homes built or renovated before 1990 may contain asbestos, and only testing confirms it. Weathered asbestos-cement roofing is brittle as well as hazardous, so nobody should walk on it.

sections.heading: How a roof is put together
sections.markdown:
Every pitched roof has the same basic layers. A frame of rafters or factory-made trusses carries timber or steel battens. On newer roofs, and many re-roofed older ones, a layer of sarking or a roofing blanket sits under the battens. The covering of tiles, sheet or slate is fixed to the battens, and gutters and downpipes take the water away. Knowing the names helps you read quotes and reports, because most problems belong to one layer or one junction.

**Roof parts you will hear about**

| Part | What it is | Why it matters |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Rafters or trusses | The sloping frame members that carry the roof | Sagging, cut or overloaded framing shows as a dip in the roof line |
| Battens | Timber or steel strips the tiles or sheets are fixed to | Decayed or loose battens let tiles slip and sheets lift in wind |
| Sarking or roofing blanket | A reflective foil or membrane under the covering | Catches wind-driven rain and dust; many older tiled roofs have none |
| Ridge and hip capping | Curved tiles or metal caps along the top and the external corners | Held by bedding and pointing on tiled roofs; a common leak point |
| Valley | The internal corner where two roof slopes meet, lined with a metal valley iron | Collects the most water and debris on the roof |
| Flashing | Shaped metal that seals the roof to walls, chimneys and penetrations | Lifted, cracked or corroded flashings are a frequent cause of leaks |
| Barge and fascia | The trims along the gable edges and the eaves | Decay here can loosen gutters and let water into the eaves |
| Box gutter | An internal gutter between roofs or behind a parapet | If it blocks or overflows, water goes into the building |

Roof shape matters too. A simple gable or hip roof sheds water easily. Every valley, change of level, parapet or roof-to-wall junction adds a place where water has to be turned, and that is where leaks cluster. A complicated roof on an extended house deserves a closer look than a plain one.

sections.heading: Where roofs actually leak
sections.markdown:
**Junctions are where water tries first**

| Location | What goes wrong | Signs inside or below |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Valleys | Debris blocks the valley iron, water backs up under the tiles, or the valley iron corrodes | Stains on ceilings near internal corners of the roof |
| Ridge and hip capping | Bedding cracks and pointing fails, letting wind-driven rain in | Damp spots along the line of the ridge after storms |
| Flashings at walls, chimneys and skylights | Flashings lift, crack, corrode or were never properly installed | Stains where the roof meets a wall or around a chimney breast |
| Penetrations | Seals around flues, vents, aerials and air-conditioning fail | Localised stains below the penetration |
| Box gutters and parapets | Internal gutters overflow into the building when blocked or undersized | Sudden heavy leaks in storms, often well inside the house |
| Eaves gutters | Blocked or sagging gutters overflow back into the eaves and wall | Stained eaves linings, damp walls below, overflow during rain |

[QBCC's maintenance guide](https://www.qbcc.qld.gov.au/sites/default/files/documents/guide-essential-home-maintenance.pdf) notes that many roof leak complaints turn out to be maintenance rather than defective work, and lists the basics: keep leaves out of gutters and downpipes, clean valley gutters regularly, and repair cracked or broken tiles, guttering and flashings promptly.

sections.heading: Tiled roofs in more detail
sections.markdown:
On a tiled roof the ridge and hip capping traditionally sits on a bed of sand and cement mortar, finished with a thin layer of pointing. Over time the bedding cracks and the pointing comes away, and capping tiles can work loose. Re-pointing renews the surface layer. Re-bedding lifts the capping and lays it on fresh bedding, which is the bigger job and the right one when the bedding itself has failed. Many roofers now use flexible pointing compounds, which cope better with the small movements of a roof.

Individual tiles crack, most often from people walking on them, from hail or falling branches, or from slipping out of place. A cracked tile can usually be swapped for a matching one, which is why it is worth keeping a few spare tiles of the right profile. Terracotta and concrete tiles also age differently. Concrete tiles lose their surface coating and become more porous, so a coating can help them. Terracotta keeps its colour, but some older tiles can flake or laminate in exposed or salty conditions, and a coating will not repair that.

Wind is the other test. Tiles rely on their weight, their interlock and their fixings to stay put. Older roofs, and tiles relaid during repairs, may not be fixed the way current practice expects, so a roof that has lost tiles in a storm is worth checking for fixing as well as for replacement tiles.

sections.heading: Metal roofs: fixings, laps and incompatible metals
sections.markdown:
Coated steel roofs usually fail at the details rather than across the sheet: corroded fixings, laps where water sits, cut edges, and anywhere debris holds moisture. One cause is often missed: some metals accelerate corrosion of coated steel. [BlueScope's Lysaght compatibility bulletin](https://cdn.dcs.lysaght.com/download/lysaght-product-advisory-bulletin-pab02-design-metal-and-timber-compatibility) lists copper and lead as incompatible with ZINCALUME® and COLORBOND® steel, both in direct contact and where water drains from one onto the other. Look for copper hot-water or air-conditioning pipes discharging onto a steel roof, and old lead flashings left in place when a roof was renewed.

Under a metal roof, condensation can form on the underside of the sheet on cold nights and drip into the roof space. Look for drip marks on insulation or ceilings in a pattern rather than at one point. Newer homes are subject to the condensation provisions introduced with [NCC 2022](https://cpd.nccb.gov.au/news/2022/overview-changes-energy-efficiency-and-condensation); older roofs may have no insulation blanket or sarking under the sheet.

Older metal roofs are often galvanised iron, which rusts first at laps, nail holes and anywhere water lingers. Most metal roofs installed in recent decades are aluminium-zinc coated or pre-painted steel, which lasts much longer in normal conditions but still suffers at the details, and much faster near the coast or in industrial air. Each sheet profile also has a minimum roof pitch set by the manufacturer. A sheet laid flatter than intended can hold water at the laps and leak in heavy rain, so it is worth asking what profile and pitch a low-slope roof uses.

Watch for small rust spots scattered across an otherwise sound roof. They are often left by swarf: tiny metal filings from drilling or cutting that were not swept off after installation work, including solar and air-conditioning installs. Swarf rusts quickly and stains or damages the coating, so ask any trade working on a metal roof to sweep it clean before they leave.

sections.heading: What the roof space can tell you
sections.markdown:
Only enter a roof space where it is safe: good lighting, solid footing on joists, no exposed wiring, and no suspicion of asbestos-containing material. From the access hatch you can often see enough.

**Roof-space checks**

| Look for | What it can mean |
| --- | --- |
| Daylight through tiles or at the ridge | Gaps that can let in wind-driven rain; normal in small amounts under some unsarked tile roofs |
| Water stains or tide marks on rafters, battens or sarking | Past or present leaks; note the location against the roof above |
| Damp, compressed or stained insulation | An active or recent leak, or condensation |
| Rusted nails and fixings | Persistent moisture or condensation |
| Sagging, cracked or altered rafters and purlins | Overloading, decay, removed supports or a heavier roof covering added later |
| Exhaust fans venting into the roof space | Moisture being pumped into the roof, which can cause condensation and mould |

sections.heading: Gutters, box gutters and downpipes
sections.markdown:
A roof only works if the water it sheds is carried away. Eaves gutters need enough size and fall, and enough downpipes, to keep up with heavy rain. When they overflow towards the house, water runs into the eaves and down the wall, and can soak the ground beside the footings. The [site drainage guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/site-drainage-and-stormwater) follows the water from the downpipe onwards.

Box gutters deserve special attention because they sit inside the line of the building. A blocked or undersized box gutter overflows into the ceiling or walls rather than onto the garden. Well-designed box gutters have an overflow, such as a rainhead or an overflow outlet, so that a blockage spills outside where you can see it. Older box gutters often lack one, and leaf litter, a dead bird or a tennis ball can be enough to cause a serious leak in a storm.

**Gutter and downpipe checks from the ground**

| Look for | What it can mean | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Water spilling over the front of the gutter in heavy rain | Blocked gutter or downpipe, too little fall, or a gutter too small for the roof area | Clean first; if it still overflows, ask a roof plumber about capacity |
| Stained or peeling eaves linings | Overflow back into the eaves, or a leaking gutter joint | Check the gutter above and its joints |
| Downpipes that end above the ground or discharge against the wall | Water soaking the ground beside the footings | Connect to stormwater or take the water well away from the house |
| Sagging gutters or pooled water after rain | Lost fall or failed brackets | Re-hang or replace the affected run |
| Rust holes along the gutter base | Gutter at the end of its life, often first at joints and outlets | Replace the run and check the fascia behind |

Gutter guards can reduce cleaning, especially under trees, but they are not maintenance-free. Fine debris can still build up, some guards trap leaves on top, and they make it harder to see what is happening in the gutter. In bushfire-prone areas, keeping gutters clear of leaves matters for ember attack too; the [extreme weather guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/preparing-your-home-for-extreme-weather) covers that.

sections.heading: Chimneys, skylights and solar panels
sections.markdown:
Anything that passes through the roof needs its own seal, and each one is a place where leaks start. Chimneys need sound flashings where they meet the roof and an intact mortar cap (flaunching) on top. A chimney that leans, has loose bricks or cracked flaunching is a safety question as well as a leak risk, so keep clear and have it checked. Disused chimneys are often capped; a capped flue still needs some ventilation to avoid trapping moisture.

Skylights and roof windows rely on their flashing kit and on the seals around the frame. Leaks often show as staining on the light-well lining rather than at the glass. Solar panels add brackets that pass through or hook under the covering. On tiled roofs, tiles can crack when installers walk on them or when brackets are fitted; on metal roofs, screws through the sheet need proper sealing. Ask the installer how the brackets are fixed and sealed, for photos of the roof before and after, and who is responsible if a leak appears. Remember that future roof work may mean removing and refitting the panels, so ask about that before you re-roof.

sections.heading: Repair, restoration or replacement
sections.markdown:
These are three different jobs, and quotes often blur them. A **repair** fixes a defined defect, such as a valley iron, a flashing or a set of cracked tiles. A **restoration** on a tiled roof usually means cleaning, replacing broken tiles, re-bedding and re-pointing ridges and hips, and often a coating. A **replacement** renews the covering, and sometimes the battens, sarking and flashings.

Ask every quote to name the sections of roof covered, what happens to valleys and flashings, whether battens and sarking are inspected, and what the coating actually does. A coating can refresh the surface of worn concrete tiles; it does not repair a corroded valley, a failed flashing or a sagging frame. On metal roofs, overpainting is a specialist system with its own preparation requirements, not a cure for corroded sheets.

sections.heading: After hail or a storm
sections.markdown:
Hail can crack tiles, dent and scratch metal sheets and gutters, and damage skylights and solar panels. Wind can lift capping, tiles and sheets, and falling branches can hole a roof. After a storm, look from the ground and from inside: missing or displaced tiles, bent sheets, debris in valleys and gutters, and new stains on ceilings. Photograph what you see before anything is moved, and contact your insurer early. Do not climb onto the roof. In an emergency, the State Emergency Service in your state can help make a damaged roof safe. The [extreme weather guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/preparing-your-home-for-extreme-weather) covers storm preparation and recovery.

Hail damage is not always obvious from the ground. Cracked tiles may only leak in the next heavy rain, and damage to a coating on metal can take months to show as rust. If a hailstorm has passed over your street, a roof inspection by a licensed roof plumber or roofer is worth arranging while the claim window is open.

sections.heading: A roof maintenance rhythm
sections.markdown:
**Simple, safe roof care**

| When | What to do | Who |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Regularly, and more often under trees | Check gutters, valleys and downpipes are clear; look over the roof from the ground | You, from the ground; a gutter cleaner or roof plumber for access |
| Before winter and before bushfire season | Clear gutters and valleys, and check overflow from box gutters | Roof plumber or gutter cleaner |
| After major storms or hail | Look for displaced tiles, damage and new stains; photograph and report | You, from the ground; then a roof plumber or roofer |
| Every few years, or when buying | Have the roof and roof space inspected, including valleys, flashings, fixings and box gutters | Licensed roof plumber or roofer |
| When any trade works on the roof | Ask for before and after photos, and for metal roofs to be swept of swarf | The trade concerned |

### What a good roof quote names

**Compare quotes on the same scope**

| Item | What to look for |
| --- | --- |
| Roof sections | Which slopes, additions and verandahs are included, marked on a sketch or photo |
| Valleys and flashings | Whether they are inspected, repaired or replaced, and with what material |
| Ridge and hip capping | Re-pointing only, or full re-bedding where the bedding has failed |
| Broken tiles or damaged sheets | How many are allowed for, and the rate for extras |
| Battens, sarking and fixings | Whether they are inspected and what happens if they are found to be failing |
| Coatings | The product, preparation, number of coats and what the warranty actually covers |
| Gutters, downpipes and box gutters | Whether they are cleaned, repaired or replaced, and how overflow is handled |
| Access and safety | Scaffolding or edge protection, and who provides it |
| Asbestos | Whether any material has been tested, and what happens if asbestos is suspected |

sections.heading: Common misreads
sections.markdown:
**Things often said about roofs**

| What people say | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| "No stains on the ceiling, so the roof is fine" | Water can run along timbers and sarking before showing, and insulation can absorb it. Check the roof space. |
| "The roof was restored, so it is as good as new" | A restoration treats surface wear. Ask what happened to valleys, flashings, battens and sarking. |
| "Leaks come through broken tiles" | Most leaks start at junctions: valleys, ridges, flashings, penetrations and box gutters. |
| "A metal roof will last forever" | Fixings, laps, cut edges and incompatible metals can corrode long before the sheet itself. |
| "The gutters were cleaned, so overflow is solved" | Overflow can also come from undersized gutters, poor falls, blocked downpipes or missing overflow provisions. |

sections.heading: What to ask before you buy
sections.markdown: Ask for invoices for any roof work with a defined scope and roof sections, as set out in [keeping a record of your home](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/keeping-a-record-of-your-home). A standard building inspection usually excludes the adequacy of roof drainage and concealed roof areas, so read the report's limitations, covered in [inspection before auction](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/building-inspection-before-auction). For older homes, the era guides show which roof materials to expect: [pre-1920s](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/period-homes-pre-1920s), [interwar](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/interwar-homes-1920s-40s) and [post-war](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/postwar-homes-1950s-70s).

sections.heading: Worked example: a restored roof and a new ceiling stain
sections.markdown:
**Illustrative reasoning example, not an inspected property.** A 1960s concrete-tile roof was "restored" two years ago: cleaned, ridges re-pointed and coated. A new stain appears near an internal corner after a storm. The invoice lists ridge work and coating, but says nothing about the valley.

The stain sits below a valley, and the restoration scope did not include it. The next step is a roof plumber to inspect the valley iron and the tiles alongside it, not another coating. If the valley iron is corroded or debris has been backing water under the tiles, the repair is local and defined. Record the outcome against the right section of roof.

> Note: Do not walk on roofs yourself. Use a licensed roof plumber or roofer for access, and stop if any material might contain asbestos.

faqs.question: What is sarking?
faqs.answer: Sarking is a reflective foil or membrane laid under the tiles or sheets. It catches wind-driven rain and dust that gets past the covering and helps with heat. Many older tiled roofs have no sarking, so some daylight and dust in the roof space is normal there.

faqs.question: What is the difference between re-pointing and re-bedding?
faqs.answer: Re-pointing renews the thin surface layer that finishes the ridge and hip capping. Re-bedding lifts the capping tiles and lays them on fresh bedding. Re-bedding is the right job when the bedding underneath has cracked or come loose.

faqs.question: How long does a roof last?
faqs.answer: It depends on the material, the exposure, the quality of the original work and how well it has been maintained. Junctions, fixings, flashings and gutters usually need attention long before the main covering does. Judge a roof by its condition and records rather than by age alone.

faqs.question: Is a roof restoration worth it?
faqs.answer: It can be for a sound tiled roof with worn surfaces and tired ridge capping. It is poor value if valleys, flashings, battens or framing are failing and are left out of the scope. Ask what each quote does about those parts.

faqs.question: Can solar panels cause roof leaks?
faqs.answer: They can if brackets are poorly fixed or sealed, or if tiles are cracked during installation. Ask the installer how the panels are fixed, for before and after photos, and who is responsible for any leak.

faqs.question: What should I do after hail?
faqs.answer: Check from the ground and inside for damaged tiles or sheets and new stains, photograph what you see and contact your insurer. Do not climb onto the roof. Arrange an inspection by a licensed roof plumber or roofer, since hail damage is not always visible from the ground.

faqs.question: Why does my box gutter overflow inside?
faqs.answer: Box gutters sit within the building, so a blockage or a gutter too small for the roof sends water into the ceiling or walls. Older box gutters often have no overflow. A roof plumber can clean it, check its capacity and advise on adding an overflow.

faqs.question: Are gutter guards worth it?
faqs.answer: They can reduce cleaning under trees, but fine debris still builds up and some guards trap leaves on top. They still need checking, and they make it harder to see the gutter itself.

faqs.question: Where do most roof leaks start?
faqs.answer: At junctions rather than in the middle of the tiles or sheets: valleys, ridge and hip capping, flashings at walls and chimneys, penetrations such as flues and vents, and box gutters.

faqs.question: How can I tell terracotta from concrete roof tiles?
faqs.answer: Terracotta is fired clay with its colour right through, often orange or red. Concrete tiles are thicker and heavier, with a surface coating that wears to expose a sandy texture.

faqs.question: Is a roof restoration the same as a new roof?
faqs.answer: No. A tiled-roof restoration usually means cleaning, replacing broken tiles, re-pointing ridges and coating. It treats surface wear but does not fix corroded valleys, failed flashings or a sagging frame unless those are in the scope.

faqs.question: Can copper pipes damage a Colorbond or Zincalume roof?
faqs.answer: Yes. BlueScope advises that copper and lead should not contact ZINCALUME® or COLORBOND® steel and that water from copper pipes should not run onto it, because it accelerates corrosion.

faqs.question: Could my old roof contain asbestos?
faqs.answer: If the home or shed was built or altered before 1990, grey fibre-cement roof sheeting may contain asbestos. Only testing confirms it. Do not walk on, drill, cut or water-blast it.

faqs.question: What should I look for in the roof space?
faqs.answer: Water stains on timbers or sarking, damp or compressed insulation, rusted fixings, sagging or altered framing, daylight at the ridge and exhaust fans venting into the roof. Only enter where it is safe.

faqs.question: Why does my metal roof drip on cold nights?
faqs.answer: Likely condensation forming on the underside of the sheet. Older metal roofs may lack an insulation blanket or sarking. Look for drip marks in a pattern rather than at a single point.

faqs.question: Does a building inspection check the roof properly?
faqs.answer: A standard inspection looks at safely accessible roof areas, but commonly excludes the adequacy of roof drainage and concealed sections. Read the limitations and get a roof plumber for specific concerns.

guides.contentMarkdown:
# Roofs: tiles, metal and where leaks really start

Most roof leaks start at the junctions, not in the middle of the tiles or sheets: valleys, ridge and hip capping, flashings at walls and chimneys, penetrations such as flues and vents, and box gutters. A restoration that cleans, repoints and coats a tiled roof treats surface wear; it does not fix a failing valley, flashing or sagging frame.

## Research note
Roof materials and leak points draw on QBCC's maintenance guidance and manufacturer guidance on incompatible metals. Asbestos screening follows the national agency's pre-1990 advice. The leak table reflects common inspection experience and should be confirmed on site.

## Opening
### Water tries the junctions first
- **Covering:** Tiles, sheet or slate shed most of the rain
- **Junctions:** Valleys, ridges, flashings and penetrations are where leaks begin
- **Drainage:** Gutters, box gutters and downpipes carry it away, or back inside

_A coating refreshes a surface. It does not fix a valley._

Identify the material first, whether terracotta or concrete tiles, metal sheet, slate or older asbestos-cement sheeting, then look from the ground and, where safe, the roof space for slipped or cracked tiles, failed ridge pointing, rust at laps and fixings, and water stains on timbers.

## What you'll notice
Roof problems usually announce themselves inside or from the ground first. Follow the sign to the part of the roof that causes it.

**Signs by sense**

| Sense | Sign | Where to read next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| See | Stains or bubbling paint on ceilings, often near internal corners or below the ridge | [Where roofs leak](#leak-points) |
| See | Slipped, cracked or missing tiles, or gaps along the ridge capping, from the ground | [Where roofs leak](#leak-points) |
| See | Rust streaks on metal sheets, gutters or around screws | [Metal roofs](#metal) |
| See | Water overflowing gutters or spilling down walls in heavy rain | [Site drainage](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/site-drainage-and-stormwater) |
| Hear | Dripping in the ceiling during rain, or rattling or banging sheets in wind | [The roof space](#roof-space) |
| Feel | Damp or compressed insulation, or drips on cold mornings under a metal roof | [Condensation under metal roofs](#metal) |

## Start by identifying the roof
The material sets the questions. A roof can also be mixed: a tiled original house with a metal-roofed extension, or a slate front with later sheeting at the rear. Record each section separately.

**Common Australian roof materials**

| Material | Where you find it | How to recognise it | What usually needs attention |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Terracotta tiles | Much pre-war and many later homes | Fired clay, colour through the tile, often orange or red; glazed versions exist | Ridge and hip bedding and pointing, cracked or slipped tiles, valleys |
| Concrete tiles | Very common from the post-war decades onward | Thicker, heavier tiles with a surface coating that wears to expose a sandy texture | Surface wear, pointing, cracked tiles and valleys |
| Metal sheet | All eras; older galvanised iron, later coated steel | Corrugated or trimdeck profiles, fixed with screws or nails through the sheet | Rust at laps, fixings and gutters, incompatible metals, low-pitch drainage, condensation |
| Slate | Period homes | Thin natural stone, often blue-grey, fixed with nails | Slipped or cracked slates and corroded fixing nails; specialist repair |
| Asbestos-cement sheeting | Homes, sheds and carports built or altered before 1990 | Grey fibre-cement corrugated sheets, often weathered with lichen | Do not walk on, drill, cut or water-blast; testing and specialist advice first |

The [Asbestos and Silica Safety and Eradication Agency](https://www.asbestossafety.gov.au/about-asbestos/finding-asbestos/home) advises that homes built or renovated before 1990 may contain asbestos, and only testing confirms it. Weathered asbestos-cement roofing is brittle as well as hazardous, so nobody should walk on it.

## How a roof is put together
Every pitched roof has the same basic layers. A frame of rafters or factory-made trusses carries timber or steel battens. On newer roofs, and many re-roofed older ones, a layer of sarking or a roofing blanket sits under the battens. The covering of tiles, sheet or slate is fixed to the battens, and gutters and downpipes take the water away. Knowing the names helps you read quotes and reports, because most problems belong to one layer or one junction.

**Roof parts you will hear about**

| Part | What it is | Why it matters |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Rafters or trusses | The sloping frame members that carry the roof | Sagging, cut or overloaded framing shows as a dip in the roof line |
| Battens | Timber or steel strips the tiles or sheets are fixed to | Decayed or loose battens let tiles slip and sheets lift in wind |
| Sarking or roofing blanket | A reflective foil or membrane under the covering | Catches wind-driven rain and dust; many older tiled roofs have none |
| Ridge and hip capping | Curved tiles or metal caps along the top and the external corners | Held by bedding and pointing on tiled roofs; a common leak point |
| Valley | The internal corner where two roof slopes meet, lined with a metal valley iron | Collects the most water and debris on the roof |
| Flashing | Shaped metal that seals the roof to walls, chimneys and penetrations | Lifted, cracked or corroded flashings are a frequent cause of leaks |
| Barge and fascia | The trims along the gable edges and the eaves | Decay here can loosen gutters and let water into the eaves |
| Box gutter | An internal gutter between roofs or behind a parapet | If it blocks or overflows, water goes into the building |

Roof shape matters too. A simple gable or hip roof sheds water easily. Every valley, change of level, parapet or roof-to-wall junction adds a place where water has to be turned, and that is where leaks cluster. A complicated roof on an extended house deserves a closer look than a plain one.

## Where roofs actually leak
**Junctions are where water tries first**

| Location | What goes wrong | Signs inside or below |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Valleys | Debris blocks the valley iron, water backs up under the tiles, or the valley iron corrodes | Stains on ceilings near internal corners of the roof |
| Ridge and hip capping | Bedding cracks and pointing fails, letting wind-driven rain in | Damp spots along the line of the ridge after storms |
| Flashings at walls, chimneys and skylights | Flashings lift, crack, corrode or were never properly installed | Stains where the roof meets a wall or around a chimney breast |
| Penetrations | Seals around flues, vents, aerials and air-conditioning fail | Localised stains below the penetration |
| Box gutters and parapets | Internal gutters overflow into the building when blocked or undersized | Sudden heavy leaks in storms, often well inside the house |
| Eaves gutters | Blocked or sagging gutters overflow back into the eaves and wall | Stained eaves linings, damp walls below, overflow during rain |

[QBCC's maintenance guide](https://www.qbcc.qld.gov.au/sites/default/files/documents/guide-essential-home-maintenance.pdf) notes that many roof leak complaints turn out to be maintenance rather than defective work, and lists the basics: keep leaves out of gutters and downpipes, clean valley gutters regularly, and repair cracked or broken tiles, guttering and flashings promptly.

## Tiled roofs in more detail
On a tiled roof the ridge and hip capping traditionally sits on a bed of sand and cement mortar, finished with a thin layer of pointing. Over time the bedding cracks and the pointing comes away, and capping tiles can work loose. Re-pointing renews the surface layer. Re-bedding lifts the capping and lays it on fresh bedding, which is the bigger job and the right one when the bedding itself has failed. Many roofers now use flexible pointing compounds, which cope better with the small movements of a roof.

Individual tiles crack, most often from people walking on them, from hail or falling branches, or from slipping out of place. A cracked tile can usually be swapped for a matching one, which is why it is worth keeping a few spare tiles of the right profile. Terracotta and concrete tiles also age differently. Concrete tiles lose their surface coating and become more porous, so a coating can help them. Terracotta keeps its colour, but some older tiles can flake or laminate in exposed or salty conditions, and a coating will not repair that.

Wind is the other test. Tiles rely on their weight, their interlock and their fixings to stay put. Older roofs, and tiles relaid during repairs, may not be fixed the way current practice expects, so a roof that has lost tiles in a storm is worth checking for fixing as well as for replacement tiles.

## Metal roofs: fixings, laps and incompatible metals
Coated steel roofs usually fail at the details rather than across the sheet: corroded fixings, laps where water sits, cut edges, and anywhere debris holds moisture. One cause is often missed: some metals accelerate corrosion of coated steel. [BlueScope's Lysaght compatibility bulletin](https://cdn.dcs.lysaght.com/download/lysaght-product-advisory-bulletin-pab02-design-metal-and-timber-compatibility) lists copper and lead as incompatible with ZINCALUME® and COLORBOND® steel, both in direct contact and where water drains from one onto the other. Look for copper hot-water or air-conditioning pipes discharging onto a steel roof, and old lead flashings left in place when a roof was renewed.

Under a metal roof, condensation can form on the underside of the sheet on cold nights and drip into the roof space. Look for drip marks on insulation or ceilings in a pattern rather than at one point. Newer homes are subject to the condensation provisions introduced with [NCC 2022](https://cpd.nccb.gov.au/news/2022/overview-changes-energy-efficiency-and-condensation); older roofs may have no insulation blanket or sarking under the sheet.

Older metal roofs are often galvanised iron, which rusts first at laps, nail holes and anywhere water lingers. Most metal roofs installed in recent decades are aluminium-zinc coated or pre-painted steel, which lasts much longer in normal conditions but still suffers at the details, and much faster near the coast or in industrial air. Each sheet profile also has a minimum roof pitch set by the manufacturer. A sheet laid flatter than intended can hold water at the laps and leak in heavy rain, so it is worth asking what profile and pitch a low-slope roof uses.

Watch for small rust spots scattered across an otherwise sound roof. They are often left by swarf: tiny metal filings from drilling or cutting that were not swept off after installation work, including solar and air-conditioning installs. Swarf rusts quickly and stains or damages the coating, so ask any trade working on a metal roof to sweep it clean before they leave.

## What the roof space can tell you
Only enter a roof space where it is safe: good lighting, solid footing on joists, no exposed wiring, and no suspicion of asbestos-containing material. From the access hatch you can often see enough.

**Roof-space checks**

| Look for | What it can mean |
| --- | --- |
| Daylight through tiles or at the ridge | Gaps that can let in wind-driven rain; normal in small amounts under some unsarked tile roofs |
| Water stains or tide marks on rafters, battens or sarking | Past or present leaks; note the location against the roof above |
| Damp, compressed or stained insulation | An active or recent leak, or condensation |
| Rusted nails and fixings | Persistent moisture or condensation |
| Sagging, cracked or altered rafters and purlins | Overloading, decay, removed supports or a heavier roof covering added later |
| Exhaust fans venting into the roof space | Moisture being pumped into the roof, which can cause condensation and mould |

## Gutters, box gutters and downpipes
A roof only works if the water it sheds is carried away. Eaves gutters need enough size and fall, and enough downpipes, to keep up with heavy rain. When they overflow towards the house, water runs into the eaves and down the wall, and can soak the ground beside the footings. The [site drainage guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/site-drainage-and-stormwater) follows the water from the downpipe onwards.

Box gutters deserve special attention because they sit inside the line of the building. A blocked or undersized box gutter overflows into the ceiling or walls rather than onto the garden. Well-designed box gutters have an overflow, such as a rainhead or an overflow outlet, so that a blockage spills outside where you can see it. Older box gutters often lack one, and leaf litter, a dead bird or a tennis ball can be enough to cause a serious leak in a storm.

**Gutter and downpipe checks from the ground**

| Look for | What it can mean | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Water spilling over the front of the gutter in heavy rain | Blocked gutter or downpipe, too little fall, or a gutter too small for the roof area | Clean first; if it still overflows, ask a roof plumber about capacity |
| Stained or peeling eaves linings | Overflow back into the eaves, or a leaking gutter joint | Check the gutter above and its joints |
| Downpipes that end above the ground or discharge against the wall | Water soaking the ground beside the footings | Connect to stormwater or take the water well away from the house |
| Sagging gutters or pooled water after rain | Lost fall or failed brackets | Re-hang or replace the affected run |
| Rust holes along the gutter base | Gutter at the end of its life, often first at joints and outlets | Replace the run and check the fascia behind |

Gutter guards can reduce cleaning, especially under trees, but they are not maintenance-free. Fine debris can still build up, some guards trap leaves on top, and they make it harder to see what is happening in the gutter. In bushfire-prone areas, keeping gutters clear of leaves matters for ember attack too; the [extreme weather guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/preparing-your-home-for-extreme-weather) covers that.

## Chimneys, skylights and solar panels
Anything that passes through the roof needs its own seal, and each one is a place where leaks start. Chimneys need sound flashings where they meet the roof and an intact mortar cap (flaunching) on top. A chimney that leans, has loose bricks or cracked flaunching is a safety question as well as a leak risk, so keep clear and have it checked. Disused chimneys are often capped; a capped flue still needs some ventilation to avoid trapping moisture.

Skylights and roof windows rely on their flashing kit and on the seals around the frame. Leaks often show as staining on the light-well lining rather than at the glass. Solar panels add brackets that pass through or hook under the covering. On tiled roofs, tiles can crack when installers walk on them or when brackets are fitted; on metal roofs, screws through the sheet need proper sealing. Ask the installer how the brackets are fixed and sealed, for photos of the roof before and after, and who is responsible if a leak appears. Remember that future roof work may mean removing and refitting the panels, so ask about that before you re-roof.

## Repair, restoration or replacement
These are three different jobs, and quotes often blur them. A **repair** fixes a defined defect, such as a valley iron, a flashing or a set of cracked tiles. A **restoration** on a tiled roof usually means cleaning, replacing broken tiles, re-bedding and re-pointing ridges and hips, and often a coating. A **replacement** renews the covering, and sometimes the battens, sarking and flashings.

Ask every quote to name the sections of roof covered, what happens to valleys and flashings, whether battens and sarking are inspected, and what the coating actually does. A coating can refresh the surface of worn concrete tiles; it does not repair a corroded valley, a failed flashing or a sagging frame. On metal roofs, overpainting is a specialist system with its own preparation requirements, not a cure for corroded sheets.

## After hail or a storm
Hail can crack tiles, dent and scratch metal sheets and gutters, and damage skylights and solar panels. Wind can lift capping, tiles and sheets, and falling branches can hole a roof. After a storm, look from the ground and from inside: missing or displaced tiles, bent sheets, debris in valleys and gutters, and new stains on ceilings. Photograph what you see before anything is moved, and contact your insurer early. Do not climb onto the roof. In an emergency, the State Emergency Service in your state can help make a damaged roof safe. The [extreme weather guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/preparing-your-home-for-extreme-weather) covers storm preparation and recovery.

Hail damage is not always obvious from the ground. Cracked tiles may only leak in the next heavy rain, and damage to a coating on metal can take months to show as rust. If a hailstorm has passed over your street, a roof inspection by a licensed roof plumber or roofer is worth arranging while the claim window is open.

## A roof maintenance rhythm
**Simple, safe roof care**

| When | What to do | Who |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Regularly, and more often under trees | Check gutters, valleys and downpipes are clear; look over the roof from the ground | You, from the ground; a gutter cleaner or roof plumber for access |
| Before winter and before bushfire season | Clear gutters and valleys, and check overflow from box gutters | Roof plumber or gutter cleaner |
| After major storms or hail | Look for displaced tiles, damage and new stains; photograph and report | You, from the ground; then a roof plumber or roofer |
| Every few years, or when buying | Have the roof and roof space inspected, including valleys, flashings, fixings and box gutters | Licensed roof plumber or roofer |
| When any trade works on the roof | Ask for before and after photos, and for metal roofs to be swept of swarf | The trade concerned |

### What a good roof quote names

**Compare quotes on the same scope**

| Item | What to look for |
| --- | --- |
| Roof sections | Which slopes, additions and verandahs are included, marked on a sketch or photo |
| Valleys and flashings | Whether they are inspected, repaired or replaced, and with what material |
| Ridge and hip capping | Re-pointing only, or full re-bedding where the bedding has failed |
| Broken tiles or damaged sheets | How many are allowed for, and the rate for extras |
| Battens, sarking and fixings | Whether they are inspected and what happens if they are found to be failing |
| Coatings | The product, preparation, number of coats and what the warranty actually covers |
| Gutters, downpipes and box gutters | Whether they are cleaned, repaired or replaced, and how overflow is handled |
| Access and safety | Scaffolding or edge protection, and who provides it |
| Asbestos | Whether any material has been tested, and what happens if asbestos is suspected |

## Common misreads
**Things often said about roofs**

| What people say | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| "No stains on the ceiling, so the roof is fine" | Water can run along timbers and sarking before showing, and insulation can absorb it. Check the roof space. |
| "The roof was restored, so it is as good as new" | A restoration treats surface wear. Ask what happened to valleys, flashings, battens and sarking. |
| "Leaks come through broken tiles" | Most leaks start at junctions: valleys, ridges, flashings, penetrations and box gutters. |
| "A metal roof will last forever" | Fixings, laps, cut edges and incompatible metals can corrode long before the sheet itself. |
| "The gutters were cleaned, so overflow is solved" | Overflow can also come from undersized gutters, poor falls, blocked downpipes or missing overflow provisions. |

## What to ask before you buy
Ask for invoices for any roof work with a defined scope and roof sections, as set out in [keeping a record of your home](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/keeping-a-record-of-your-home). A standard building inspection usually excludes the adequacy of roof drainage and concealed roof areas, so read the report's limitations, covered in [inspection before auction](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/building-inspection-before-auction). For older homes, the era guides show which roof materials to expect: [pre-1920s](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/period-homes-pre-1920s), [interwar](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/interwar-homes-1920s-40s) and [post-war](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/postwar-homes-1950s-70s).

## Worked example: a restored roof and a new ceiling stain
**Illustrative reasoning example, not an inspected property.** A 1960s concrete-tile roof was "restored" two years ago: cleaned, ridges re-pointed and coated. A new stain appears near an internal corner after a storm. The invoice lists ridge work and coating, but says nothing about the valley.

The stain sits below a valley, and the restoration scope did not include it. The next step is a roof plumber to inspect the valley iron and the tiles alongside it, not another coating. If the valley iron is corroded or debris has been backing water under the tiles, the repair is local and defined. Record the outcome against the right section of roof.

> Note: Do not walk on roofs yourself. Use a licensed roof plumber or roofer for access, and stop if any material might contain asbestos.

## Frequently asked questions
### What is sarking?
Sarking is a reflective foil or membrane laid under the tiles or sheets. It catches wind-driven rain and dust that gets past the covering and helps with heat. Many older tiled roofs have no sarking, so some daylight and dust in the roof space is normal there.

### What is the difference between re-pointing and re-bedding?
Re-pointing renews the thin surface layer that finishes the ridge and hip capping. Re-bedding lifts the capping tiles and lays them on fresh bedding. Re-bedding is the right job when the bedding underneath has cracked or come loose.

### How long does a roof last?
It depends on the material, the exposure, the quality of the original work and how well it has been maintained. Junctions, fixings, flashings and gutters usually need attention long before the main covering does. Judge a roof by its condition and records rather than by age alone.

### Is a roof restoration worth it?
It can be for a sound tiled roof with worn surfaces and tired ridge capping. It is poor value if valleys, flashings, battens or framing are failing and are left out of the scope. Ask what each quote does about those parts.

### Can solar panels cause roof leaks?
They can if brackets are poorly fixed or sealed, or if tiles are cracked during installation. Ask the installer how the panels are fixed, for before and after photos, and who is responsible for any leak.

### What should I do after hail?
Check from the ground and inside for damaged tiles or sheets and new stains, photograph what you see and contact your insurer. Do not climb onto the roof. Arrange an inspection by a licensed roof plumber or roofer, since hail damage is not always visible from the ground.

### Why does my box gutter overflow inside?
Box gutters sit within the building, so a blockage or a gutter too small for the roof sends water into the ceiling or walls. Older box gutters often have no overflow. A roof plumber can clean it, check its capacity and advise on adding an overflow.

### Are gutter guards worth it?
They can reduce cleaning under trees, but fine debris still builds up and some guards trap leaves on top. They still need checking, and they make it harder to see the gutter itself.

### Where do most roof leaks start?
At junctions rather than in the middle of the tiles or sheets: valleys, ridge and hip capping, flashings at walls and chimneys, penetrations such as flues and vents, and box gutters.

### How can I tell terracotta from concrete roof tiles?
Terracotta is fired clay with its colour right through, often orange or red. Concrete tiles are thicker and heavier, with a surface coating that wears to expose a sandy texture.

### Is a roof restoration the same as a new roof?
No. A tiled-roof restoration usually means cleaning, replacing broken tiles, re-pointing ridges and coating. It treats surface wear but does not fix corroded valleys, failed flashings or a sagging frame unless those are in the scope.

### Can copper pipes damage a Colorbond or Zincalume roof?
Yes. BlueScope advises that copper and lead should not contact ZINCALUME® or COLORBOND® steel and that water from copper pipes should not run onto it, because it accelerates corrosion.

### Could my old roof contain asbestos?
If the home or shed was built or altered before 1990, grey fibre-cement roof sheeting may contain asbestos. Only testing confirms it. Do not walk on, drill, cut or water-blast it.

### What should I look for in the roof space?
Water stains on timbers or sarking, damp or compressed insulation, rusted fixings, sagging or altered framing, daylight at the ridge and exhaust fans venting into the roof. Only enter where it is safe.

### Why does my metal roof drip on cold nights?
Likely condensation forming on the underside of the sheet. Older metal roofs may lack an insulation blanket or sarking. Look for drip marks in a pattern rather than at a single point.

### Does a building inspection check the roof properly?

We identify the roof material, follow water to the junctions where it most often enters, then separate repair, restoration and replacement scopes, with a fictional example.

sections.heading: Opening
sections.markdown:

sections.heading: Tiles are not the waterproofing
sections.markdown: Tiles and grout shed most water, but grout is porous and water reaches the bed behind them. sections.heading: What you'll notice: signs of a leaking shower
sections.markdown:
**What you see, and what it often means**

| Sign | Often means | Check next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Swollen or stained skirting, door frame or vanity near the shower | Water escaping sideways through the wall or floor | Moisture readings along the wall; whether it worsens after showers |
| Loose, cracked or hollow-sounding tiles | Water behind the tiles has weakened the bed or adhesive | The extent of drummy tiles, and the membrane underneath |
| Crumbling or missing grout, failed silicone at corners and the base | An entry point for water; may be the start of a bigger problem | Whether staining appears beyond the shower |
| Mould or stains on the other side of the shower wall | Long-term leakage into the wall | Framing condition, and whether it is a plumbing leak |
| Stain on the ceiling below an upstairs bathroom | A leaking floor membrane, waste or pipe | Whether it follows shower use or is constant |
| White powdery deposits on tiles or grout | Moisture moving through the bed and leaving salts behind | Membrane condition and fall to the drain |
| Musty smell that persists after airing | Moisture trapped in the structure | Hidden areas such as cupboards backing onto the bathroom |

[QBCC's maintenance guide](https://www.qbcc.qld.gov.au/sites/default/files/documents/guide-essential-home-maintenance.pdf) suggests checking the silicone at the base of the shower and where screens meet walls, and looking inside cupboards and behind fittings on walls that back onto wet areas for signs of water seeping through.

### Waterproofing or plumbing?

A simple pattern helps. If staining appears or grows after the shower is used and stays dry otherwise, suspect the shower floor, walls or seals. If it is wet regardless of use, suspect a supply pipe under pressure, and call a plumber promptly. An unexplained increase in your water bill points the same way. A plumber can pressure-test the pipes, and a leak detection specialist can help separate the two.

sections.heading: How the age of the bathroom changes the question
sections.markdown:
**Waterproofing by the bathroom’s date**

| When the bathroom was built | What to expect | What to ask |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Before 1989 | Built before the first national wet-area standard ([AS 3740](https://store.standards.org.au/product/as-3740-1994)), using older methods that are now well past their likely life | When was it last renovated? Original showers of this age are a common leak source |
| 1989 to the 2000s | Built to an early edition of AS 3740; workmanship varied widely | Is there a waterproofing certificate? Who did the work? |
| From 2012 onward | The NCC set out where waterproofing is required, with AS 3740 as the technical solution | Ask for the waterproofing certificate and the membrane product used |
| From NCC 2022 | The ABCB Housing Provisions offer detailed wet-area construction as an alternative to AS 3740 | Same: a certificate, the product and the installer |

The bathroom’s date matters more than the house’s. A 1950s house can have a 2018 bathroom, and a 1990s house can still have its original shower. See the [dated milestones table](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/red-flags-by-era#milestones) for how this fits with other changes.

sections.heading: What current rules require
sections.markdown: For new work, the National Construction Code sets out which parts of a wet area must be waterproof or water resistant. Under NCC 2022, the [ABCB explains](https://ncc.abcb.gov.au/ncc-navigator/waterproofing-houses) that the walls of the shower area must be waterproofed to a height of 1800 mm, and that where a floor waste is installed, the floor must be graded to fall towards it. These rules apply to new building work, so an older bathroom built to earlier rules is not automatically defective, but they are a useful benchmark when you renovate.

sections.heading: How a membrane is put in
sections.markdown:
Most membranes are either liquid-applied, painted or rolled on in coats to a set thickness, or sheet membranes bonded to the substrate. Good installation is about the details as much as the product.

**Waterproofing details worth asking about**

| Detail | What it does | What goes wrong |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Bond breakers at corners and junctions | Let the membrane flex where walls and floor meet | Membrane tears at the corner as the building moves |
| Upturns at walls and the doorway | Turn the membrane up so water cannot spill out at the edges | Water escapes under the wall or doorway |
| Puddle flange at the floor waste | Seals the membrane into the drain | Water tracks around the outside of the waste |
| Water stop angle at the shower entry or door | Holds water within the wet area at hobless showers and doorways | Water runs under the tiles into the next room |
| Sealed penetrations | Seals around taps, shower roses and pipes through the wall | Water enters the wall cavity at each penetration |
| Fall to the waste | Moves water to the drain instead of pooling | Water sits on the membrane and finds any weakness |

Ask the waterproofer to photograph the membrane before tiling, including the corners, the waste and the doorway. Those photos are the only practical way to show later what was done.

sections.heading: Ventilation, condensation and mould
sections.markdown: Many bathroom mould problems are caused by condensation rather than leaks. Steam settles on cool ceilings and walls and, without enough air movement, mould follows. An exhaust fan that runs during and for a while after showers, and that discharges outside rather than into the roof space, does most of the work. [Western Australia's building regulator](https://www.wa.gov.au/government/announcements/be-aware-of-the-signs-of-stressed-ceiling) advises that exhaust fans should discharge to the outside, not into the ceiling space. The [condensation guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/insulation-ventilation-and-condensation) covers this in more detail.

sections.heading: Laundries, toilets and balconies
sections.markdown:
Showers get the attention, but laundries, toilets and balconies leak too. A laundry floor takes spills from washing machines and tubs, and a failed hose can flood it in minutes. A balcony or deck above a living space is effectively a roof, and it needs a membrane, falls and outlets designed for that job; leaks there often show as stains or bubbling paint on the ceiling below. The [decks and balconies guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/decks-balconies-and-balustrades) covers balconies in more detail.

sections.heading: From regrouting to a full strip-out
sections.markdown:
**Repair options, from least to most invasive**

| Option | What it does | When it suits |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Regrout and reseal | Replaces failed grout and silicone at the surface | Routine maintenance where the membrane is sound and no water is escaping |
| Surface sealers and grout-injection products | Attempts to seal the tiled surface from above | Sometimes a short-term measure; does not replace a failed membrane, so ask what warranty and evidence support it |
| Partial strip-out | Removes tiles in one area, such as the shower floor, to renew the membrane there | A defined, localised failure with sound surroundings |
| Full strip-out and re-waterproofing | Removes tiles and bed, renews the membrane and retiles | A failed or missing membrane, widespread drummy tiles, or water damage to framing |

Whatever the scope, ask for the membrane product, the installer’s licence and a waterproofing certificate, and photographs of the membrane before tiling. Those records are what a buyer, insurer or future owner will ask for, as covered in [keeping a record of your home](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/keeping-a-record-of-your-home).

### What a waterproofing quote and certificate should show

**Records worth having**

| Item | Why it matters |
| --- | --- |
| The membrane product and system | Shows what was used and whether it suits the substrate |
| Areas waterproofed, with heights | Confirms the shower walls, floor and doorway were covered |
| The installer's licence or registration where your state requires one | Shows who is accountable for the work |
| Photos of the membrane before tiling | The only practical evidence of the hidden work |
| Certificate or warranty | What a buyer or insurer will ask for |

sections.heading: Checking a shower before you buy
sections.markdown: A building inspector can look for the signs in this guide, take moisture readings around the shower and note drummy tiles, but cannot see the membrane. Ask the seller for the waterproofing certificate and the date of the last renovation. If the signs are there, a specialist leak detection test can narrow down whether water is escaping from the floor, walls or pipes before you commit.

sections.heading: In an apartment, a leak is a neighbour issue
sections.markdown: In strata buildings, a failed shower can damage the lot below and common property. Who is responsible for the membrane and the repair depends on your state, the by-laws and where the failure is. Report it early, keep photographs, and use the owners corporation process; see [strata risks for owners](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/strata-risks-for-owners).

sections.heading: Common misreads
sections.markdown:
**Things often said about showers**

| What people say | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| "The tiles are fine, so the shower is fine" | Tiles can look perfect over a failed membrane. Check the walls, skirting and rooms around it. |
| "Regrouting will fix the leak" | Only if the leak is at the surface. It will not fix a failed or missing membrane. |
| "Mould in the bathroom means a leak" | Often it is condensation from poor ventilation. Leaks show as damage outside the shower. |
| "It is a new bathroom, so it is waterproofed" | Ask for the certificate. Workmanship varies, and some renovations skip proper membranes. |

sections.heading: Worked example: a swollen door frame next to the ensuite
sections.markdown:
**Illustrative reasoning example, not an inspected property.** A 1990s house has an original ensuite. The bedroom door frame beside it has swollen at the base, and the shower grout was replaced a year ago. The tiles look sound.

The new grout and the swelling together suggest water is escaping below the surface. The next step is moisture readings along the wall and skirting, then a plumber to rule out the supply pipes. If the pipes test sound and the moisture follows shower use, the likely scope is the shower floor membrane. Get a defined quote for that area, with a certificate on completion, rather than another regrout.

> Note: Persistent leaks near electrical fittings, or a sagging ceiling below a bathroom, need prompt attention from a licensed electrician or plumber. Keep clear of the affected area.

faqs.question: How high should shower waterproofing go?
faqs.answer: For new work under NCC 2022, the walls of the shower area must be waterproofed to a height of 1800 mm. Older bathrooms were built to earlier rules, so check what your bathroom has before assuming it meets that benchmark.

faqs.question: Should a bathroom exhaust fan vent into the roof?
faqs.answer: No. Exhaust air should be discharged outside. Venting it into the roof space puts moisture there, which can cause condensation, mould and damage to the ceiling.

faqs.question: Does a laundry need waterproofing?
faqs.answer: Laundry floors take spills and appliance leaks, and the NCC sets water-resistance requirements for them in new work. A failed washing machine hose can flood a laundry quickly, so check hoses and the floor waste.

faqs.question: Can you waterproof over existing tiles?
faqs.answer: Some surface products are applied over tiles, but they do not replace a failed membrane underneath. Ask what evidence and warranty support the product, and treat it as a short-term measure if the membrane has failed.

faqs.question: Why is there mould on my bathroom ceiling?
faqs.answer: Usually condensation from steam and too little ventilation. Run an exhaust fan that discharges outside during and after showers. Mould or damage outside the shower area, such as swollen skirting, points more to a leak.

faqs.question: What is a water stop angle?
faqs.answer: A metal or plastic angle set at the edge of the shower or at the bathroom doorway that holds water within the wet area. Without one, water can run under the tiles into the next room.

faqs.question: How do I know if my shower is leaking?
faqs.answer: Look outside the shower: swollen or stained skirting, door frames or vanities, loose or hollow tiles, crumbling grout, mould on the other side of the wall, or a stain on the ceiling below. Damage that appears after showers points to the shower; damage that is constant points to a pipe.

faqs.question: When did bathroom waterproofing become a standard in Australia?
faqs.answer: The first Australian Standard for waterproofing residential wet areas, AS 3740, was published in 1989 and revised in 1994. Original bathrooms from before then rely on older methods.

faqs.question: Will regrouting stop a shower leak?
faqs.answer: Only if the problem is at the surface. Regrouting and resealing maintain a sound shower, but they will not fix a failed or missing waterproofing membrane under the tiles.

faqs.question: Do grout sealers or injection products fix leaking showers?
faqs.answer: Sometimes as a short-term measure, but they do not replace a failed membrane. Ask what evidence and warranty support the product before relying on it.

faqs.question: What documents should I ask for after a bathroom renovation?
faqs.answer: A waterproofing certificate, the membrane product used, the installer’s licence details and photographs of the membrane before tiling.

faqs.question: Is bathroom mould a sign of a leak?
faqs.answer: Not always. Mould on ceilings and corners is often condensation from poor ventilation. Leaks tend to show as damage outside the shower area, such as swollen skirting or stains in adjacent rooms.

faqs.question: Who pays for a leaking shower in an apartment?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state, the by-laws and where the failure is. Report it to the owners corporation early with photographs and follow the scheme’s process.

In strata buildings, a failed shower can damage the lot below and common property. Who is responsible for the membrane and the repair depends on your state, the by-laws and where the failure is. Report it early, keep photographs, and use the owners corporation process; see [strata risks for owners](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/strata-risks-for-owners).

## Common misreads
**Things often said about showers**

| What people say | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| "The tiles are fine, so the shower is fine" | Tiles can look perfect over a failed membrane. Check the walls, skirting and rooms around it. |
| "Regrouting will fix the leak" | Only if the leak is at the surface. It will not fix a failed or missing membrane. |
| "Mould in the bathroom means a leak" | Often it is condensation from poor ventilation. Leaks show as damage outside the shower. |
| "It is a new bathroom, so it is waterproofed" | Ask for the certificate. Workmanship varies, and some renovations skip proper membranes. |

## Worked example: a swollen door frame next to the ensuite
**Illustrative reasoning example, not an inspected property.** A 1990s house has an original ensuite. The bedroom door frame beside it has swollen at the base, and the shower grout was replaced a year ago. The tiles look sound.

The new grout and the swelling together suggest water is escaping below the surface. The next step is moisture readings along the wall and skirting, then a plumber to rule out the supply pipes. If the pipes test sound and the moisture follows shower use, the likely scope is the shower floor membrane. Get a defined quote for that area, with a certificate on completion, rather than another regrout.

> Note: Persistent leaks near electrical fittings, or a sagging ceiling below a bathroom, need prompt attention from a licensed electrician or plumber. Keep clear of the affected area.

## Frequently asked questions
### How high should shower waterproofing go?
For new work under NCC 2022, the walls of the shower area must be waterproofed to a height of 1800 mm. Older bathrooms were built to earlier rules, so check what your bathroom has before assuming it meets that benchmark.

### Should a bathroom exhaust fan vent into the roof?
No. Exhaust air should be discharged outside. Venting it into the roof space puts moisture there, which can cause condensation, mould and damage to the ceiling.

### Does a laundry need waterproofing?
Laundry floors take spills and appliance leaks, and the NCC sets water-resistance requirements for them in new work. A failed washing machine hose can flood a laundry quickly, so check hoses and the floor waste.

### Can you waterproof over existing tiles?
Some surface products are applied over tiles, but they do not replace a failed membrane underneath. Ask what evidence and warranty support the product, and treat it as a short-term measure if the membrane has failed.

### Why is there mould on my bathroom ceiling?
Usually condensation from steam and too little ventilation. Run an exhaust fan that discharges outside during and after showers. Mould or damage outside the shower area, such as swollen skirting, points more to a leak.

### What is a water stop angle?
A metal or plastic angle set at the edge of the shower or at the bathroom doorway that holds water within the wet area. Without one, water can run under the tiles into the next room.

### How do I know if my shower is leaking?
Look outside the shower: swollen or stained skirting, door frames or vanities, loose or hollow tiles, crumbling grout, mould on the other side of the wall, or a stain on the ceiling below. Damage that appears after showers points to the shower; damage that is constant points to a pipe.

### When did bathroom waterproofing become a standard in Australia?
The first Australian Standard for waterproofing residential wet areas, AS 3740, was published in 1989 and revised in 1994. Original bathrooms from before then rely on older methods.

### Will regrouting stop a shower leak?
Only if the problem is at the surface. Regrouting and resealing maintain a sound shower, but they will not fix a failed or missing waterproofing membrane under the tiles.

### Do grout sealers or injection products fix leaking showers?
Sometimes as a short-term measure, but they do not replace a failed membrane. Ask what evidence and warranty support the product before relying on it.

### What documents should I ask for after a bathroom renovation?
A waterproofing certificate, the membrane product used, the installer’s licence details and photographs of the membrane before tiling.

### Is bathroom mould a sign of a leak?
Not always. Mould on ceilings and corners is often condensation from poor ventilation. Leaks tend to show as damage outside the shower area, such as swollen skirting or stains in adjacent rooms.

### Who pays for a leaking shower in an apartment?
It depends on the state, the by-laws and where the failure is. Report it to the owners corporation early with photographs and follow the scheme’s process.

## Method
We separate surface seals, the membrane and plumbing as distinct water paths, date the bathroom rather than the house, and order repair options from least to most invasive, with a fictional example.

## Limitations
A membrane cannot be inspected without removing tiles. Moisture readings and leak testing narrow the cause; strata responsibility depends on state law and by-laws.

guides.question: How do I know if a house needs restumping, and what should I check under the floor?
guides.title: Subfloors, stumps and restumping: what to check under the floor
guides.summary: How raised timber floors work, the signs of failing stumps and framing, why subfloors get damp and how to fix it, insulating without trapping moisture, and what a restumping job and quote should cover.
guides.answer: Houses with raised timber floors sit on stumps or piers, and the subfloor beneath is where decay, termites and movement usually start. Signs of trouble include uneven or sloping floors, springy or bouncy areas, doors that stick or swing, cracked plaster and gaps under skirting. Restumping, also called reblocking, replaces failed stumps; in Victoria it needs a building permit and a registered builder.
