guides.limitations: Older homes may predate current clearance requirements. Permit and licensing rules vary by state; confirm with your regulator or council.
guides.researchNote: Clearance and ventilation figures follow the [ABCB Housing Provisions](https://www.abcb.gov.au/editions/ncc-2022/adopted/housing-provisions/6-framing/part-62-subfloor-ventilation). Victorian permit requirements draw on council guidance; other states differ.

cluster.label: Read the building
cluster.blurb: Use age and construction as a starting hypothesis, then test it against evidence and physical inspection.

sections.heading: Opening
sections.markdown:
### Stumps, air and room to look
- **Support:** Stumps carry bearers, bearers carry joists, joists carry the floor
- **Air:** Cross-ventilation lets ground moisture escape
- **Clearance:** 150 mm minimum, 400 mm where termite inspection is needed

_A floor that slopes is telling you something about what holds it up._

Check the subfloor for clearance, ventilation, damp, decayed or leaning stumps and termite mud tubes; current housing provisions require at least 150 mm of ground clearance, and 400 mm where termite inspection is required.

sections.heading: How a raised floor works
sections.markdown:
In a raised timber floor, stumps or piers carry timber bearers, the bearers carry joists, and the joists carry the floorboards. Older homes often stand on timber stumps, many of red gum; later homes use concrete, brick piers or adjustable steel stumps. The subfloor space below needs air moving through it and enough clearance for someone to inspect it, because that is where moisture, decay and termites do their damage unseen.

**Stump and pier types**

| Type | Where you find it | What to watch for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Timber stumps | Much pre-war and early post-war housing | Decay at and below ground level, termite attack, settlement |
| Concrete stumps | Common from the post-war decades and in restumping | Cracking, spalling, and timber packers between stump and bearer that decay |
| Brick or masonry piers | Many older and mid-century homes | Cracked or leaning piers, loose mortar, missing ant caps |
| Adjustable steel stumps | Newer homes and restumping | Corrosion in damp subfloors and coastal areas, and loose adjustment fittings |

sections.heading: What you'll notice above the floor
sections.markdown:
**Above-floor symptoms and what they raise**

| Symptom | What it can mean | Check next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sloping or uneven floors | Settled, decayed or sunken stumps, or ground movement | Floor levels across rooms, and stump condition below the low area |
| Springy or bouncy floor areas | Decayed joists or bearers, missing supports or overspanning | Framing condition and support spacing below |
| Doors sticking, swinging open or out of square | Frame movement from stump or footing movement | Whether it is seasonal, and floor levels at the door |
| Cracked plaster, especially diagonal cracks from door corners | Movement in the frame | The pattern, read with the [cracks guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/cracks-structural-or-cosmetic) |
| Gaps between skirting and floor | The floor dropping away from the walls | Stumps and bearers along that wall |
| Creaking or hollow sounds underfoot | Loose or decayed floor framing, or missing supports | Framing and supports below the noisy area |
| Musty smell or damp underfloor | Poor ventilation, drainage or leaking plumbing | Vents, drainage and pipes; see the [damp guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/damp-and-moisture-in-your-home) |

sections.heading: The timber above the stumps
sections.markdown:
Stumps get the attention, but the bearers, joists and floorboards above them fail too, and their problems can look like stump problems from inside the house. Bearers are the heavy beams that sit on the stumps; joists run across the bearers; floorboards are fixed to the joists. Moisture, insects and later building work are the usual causes of trouble.

**Floor framing problems and how they show**

| Problem | Common cause | How it shows above |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Decay at bearer and joist ends | Damp subfloor, leaking plumbing, timber in contact with soil or masonry | Soft or sinking floor near walls or wet areas |
| Joists notched, drilled or cut | Plumbers, electricians or renovators cutting through framing to run services | A local dip or spring in the floor, often near a bathroom or kitchen |
| Sagging bearers | Supports too far apart, a removed stump, or an extra load such as a heavy bath or masonry wall | A gradual dip across the room |
| Termite damage | Termites entering through the ground, a stump or a bypassed barrier | Hollow-sounding or soft timber; see the [termites guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/termites-in-australian-homes) |
| Borer in floorboards | Wood-boring beetles, more common in older softwood boards | Small round holes and fine dust on or under the boards |
| Cupped or buckled boards | Moisture from below, or boards laid without room to expand | Board edges higher than their centres, or boards lifting |

A springy patch often means a framing problem close to the surface, while a slope across a whole room or house more often points to the supports or the ground beneath. Both need someone to look underneath before any repair is priced.

sections.heading: Clearance and ventilation: the numbers
sections.markdown:
The [ABCB Housing Provisions](https://www.abcb.gov.au/editions/ncc-2022/adopted/housing-provisions/6-framing/part-62-subfloor-ventilation) set minimum ground clearances under suspended floors: at least **150 mm** where termite inspection is not required, and at least **400 mm** where a termite management system needs to be inspected. On sloping sites, the 400 mm may reduce to 150 mm within 2 metres of the external walls. The same provisions require cross-ventilation through openings in the walls, because ground moisture in a still subfloor encourages rot, fungus and termites.

Older homes were not always built to these clearances, and later work often reduces them: soil and paving built up against walls, garden beds, blocked vents, or storage pushed into the subfloor. Restoring clearance and airflow is often the cheapest improvement available.

**Subfloor checklist, where access is safe**

| Check | Good sign | Concern |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Clearance | Room to inspect; ground well below bearers | Ground or debris close to timbers |
| Ventilation | Clear vents on opposite sides; air moving | Blocked, painted-over or missing vents; still, humid air |
| Ground moisture | Dry soil | Damp soil, ponding, or water entering after rain |
| Stumps and piers | Plumb, sound, bearing evenly | Leaning, decayed, cracked or packed stumps; gaps to the bearer |
| Termites | No mud tubes; ant caps intact | Mud tubes on stumps or walls; damaged or bypassed ant caps |
| Plumbing and services | Dry pipes and connections | Leaks, wet patches below wet areas, sagging pipes; see the [plumbing guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/plumbing-hot-water-and-leaks) |

Do not disturb termite mud tubes; leave them for a licensed timber pest inspector. [CSIRO's building technology resource on managing termites](https://research.csiro.au/infratech/btr/) explains why visible, inspectable subfloors matter.

Ant caps, the metal plates on top of stumps and piers, do not stop termites. They force termites to build their mud tubes around the edge of the cap, where an inspector can see them. A cap that is bent, missing or bridged by timber, packing or debris no longer does that job. The [termites guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/termites-in-australian-homes) explains inspection and treatment.

sections.heading: Why subfloors get damp, and what fixes it
sections.markdown:
Most damp subfloors have a source you can find. Fixing the source almost always works better than treating the symptoms. The [damp guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/damp-and-moisture-in-your-home) covers moisture throughout the house; under the floor, these are the usual suspects.

**Common sources of subfloor moisture**

| Source | What you may see | What usually helps |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Downpipes discharging at the wall or into the subfloor | Wet soil along one side, worst after rain | Connect downpipes to stormwater or carry water well away; see [site drainage](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/site-drainage-and-stormwater) |
| Ground that falls towards the house | Water running under the floor in heavy rain | Regrade, add surface drains, or both |
| Leaking pipes under bathrooms, laundries and kitchens | A wet patch under one area, rotting framing, a constant musty smell | Find and fix the leak; check the framing around it |
| Blocked or too few vents | Still, humid air; mould on timbers | Clear vents, add more where needed, and keep cross-flow open on opposite sides |
| Garden beds or paving built up against the walls | Vents covered, soil close to or above the floor level | Lower the ground and keep vents and weep holes clear |
| A naturally damp or poorly drained site | Persistently damp soil even in dry weather | Specialist advice; options include better drainage, a ground cover membrane or mechanical ventilation |

Avoid quick fixes that hide the problem. Sealing vents, laying plastic over damp soil without fixing the source, or spraying fungicide on timbers that stay wet will not stop decay. Once the source is dealt with, give the subfloor time to dry and check the framing that was affected.

sections.heading: Insulating a raised floor without trapping moisture
sections.markdown: Raised timber floors can lose a lot of heat in winter, and insulating between the joists can make a real difference to comfort. It needs care, though. Insulation should be fitted under the floor without blocking the subfloor vents or reducing the clearance needed for inspection. It should be kept off damp soil, and fitted so that a termite inspector can still see stumps, piers and the edges of the walls. Fix any damp problem before insulating, because insulation over a wet subfloor can hold moisture against the timbers. The [insulation and ventilation guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/insulation-ventilation-and-condensation) covers the wider picture.

sections.heading: Restumping and reblocking
sections.markdown:
Restumping (often called reblocking) replaces failed stumps and re-levels the floor. It can be partial, replacing only failed stumps, or full. In Victoria, councils and the VBA list reblocking or restumping as work that needs a building permit, and it must be carried out by a registered builder; [Macedon Ranges Shire's permit guideline](https://www.mrsc.vic.gov.au/files/assets/public/build-amp-plan/build-renovate-amp-extend/restumping-guidelines.pdf) also notes that domestic building insurance is required for registered builders where the work is over $16,000. Requirements differ elsewhere, so check with your state regulator or council.

Two things are worth knowing before you start. First, re-levelling a floor that has settled over decades can crack plaster, jam doors or open gaps that need making good, so budget for it. Second, "restumped" on a listing can mean anything from a few stumps to the whole house. Ask for the permit, the builder, the date and a plan showing which stumps were replaced.

### What a restumping job involves

A typical job runs in a clear order. The builder assesses which stumps have failed, takes floor levels and arranges the permit. The floor is then supported on temporary props while old stumps are dug out, new footings are formed and new stumps set in place. The bearers are packed to the new levels, termite barriers such as ant caps are fitted where needed, and the floor is re-checked. Afterwards come the making-good works inside, such as plaster repairs, door adjustments and gaps at skirtings.

**Stump choices when restumping**

| Option | Strengths | Watch for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Concrete stumps | Durable, widely used, not food for termites | Need a sound footing and correct packing; timber packers above can still decay |
| Adjustable steel stumps | Can be fine-tuned for level; quick to install | Corrosion in damp or coastal subfloors; protective coating and drainage matter |
| Partial restumping | Lower cost where only some stumps have failed | Old and new stumps can settle differently, so the rest of the floor needs assessing |

### What a restumping quote should name

**Compare restumping quotes on the same basis**

| Item | What to look for |
| --- | --- |
| Extent | How many stumps, which ones, marked on a plan |
| Permit and builder | Who arranges the permit, and the builder's registration |
| Stump type and footings | Concrete or steel, footing size and depth |
| Bearers and joists | What happens if decayed framing is found, and the rate for extra work |
| Re-levelling | How far the floor will be brought back towards level, and how levels are recorded |
| Termite protection | Ant caps or other barriers, and access left for inspection |
| Making good | Plaster, doors, skirtings and other repairs inside, or whether these are excluded |
| Warranty and insurance | The warranty on the work and any domestic building insurance required in your state |

sections.heading: Houses on more than one kind of footing
sections.markdown: Many homes have a raised timber floor in the original house and a concrete slab under a later extension. The two parts move differently with the seasons and over time, so the junction between them is a common place for cracks, sticking doors and a step or dip in the floor. Treat each part separately when reading symptoms, and look closely at the junction. The [cracks guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/cracks-structural-or-cosmetic) covers junction cracking, and [working out when a house was built](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/when-was-my-house-built) helps you date each part.

sections.heading: Common misreads
sections.markdown:
**Things often said about subfloors**

| What people say | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| "It has been restumped" | Ask how many stumps, where, when, with what material, and under which permit. |
| "The floor is level now, so the problem is fixed" | Levelling treats the symptom. Drainage, plumbing leaks and termites can keep causing movement. |
| "Concrete stumps cannot fail" | They can crack or settle, and the timber packers and bearers above them can still decay. |
| "Sealing the vents keeps the house warmer" | It also traps moisture under the floor. Insulate the floor instead of blocking the vents. |

sections.heading: Worked example: restumped, but the back room still slopes
sections.markdown:
**Illustrative reasoning example, not an inspected property.** A 1930s weatherboard was advertised as restumped. The front rooms are level, but the rear room slopes and its door sticks. The vendor provides an invoice for "restumping".

The invoice lists 24 stumps at the front of the house. The rear room is a later addition on its own stumps, with a downpipe discharging against the wall beside it. The next steps are a subfloor inspection of the addition, a check of the drainage, and a quote for that area alone. The front restumping is real evidence for the front of the house, not for the whole of it. See the [interwar homes guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/interwar-homes-1920s-40s) for the wider pattern.

> Note: Only enter a subfloor where it is safe: adequate clearance, no standing water, no exposed wiring, and no suspicion of asbestos-containing debris. Otherwise leave it to an inspector.

faqs.question: How long do timber stumps last?
faqs.answer: It depends on the timber, the soil, how wet the subfloor is and whether termites have reached them. Many older homes still stand on original stumps, while others failed decades ago. Judge by condition: probe at and below ground level and check floor levels.

faqs.question: Should I choose concrete or steel stumps?
faqs.answer: Both are common. Concrete stumps are durable and are not attacked by termites. Adjustable steel stumps make fine levelling easier but need protection from corrosion in damp or coastal subfloors. The builder should explain why they recommend one for your site.

faqs.question: Can I insulate under a raised timber floor?
faqs.answer: Yes, and it can make a real difference to comfort. Fix any damp first, keep vents and inspection clearances open, keep insulation off the soil, and leave stumps and wall edges visible for termite inspections.

faqs.question: Why are my floorboards cupping?
faqs.answer: Cupping, where board edges sit higher than the middle, usually means moisture from below. Check subfloor ventilation, drainage and any plumbing leaks under the area before repairing the boards.

faqs.question: What does an ant cap do?
faqs.answer: An ant cap is a metal plate on a stump or pier that forces termites to build their mud tubes around its edge where they can be seen. It does not stop termites by itself, and it only works if it is intact and not bridged.

faqs.question: Is a bouncy floor dangerous?
faqs.answer: A springy area usually means framing below is decayed, damaged, cut or under-supported. It should be inspected from underneath before it gets worse, and sooner if it is getting softer or sits near a wet area.

faqs.question: Do I need to restump if the floor slopes a little?
faqs.answer: Not necessarily. Many older floors have a gentle, long-standing slope. What matters is whether it is getting worse, whether the stumps and framing are sound and whether doors and walls show new movement. An inspection under the floor answers that.

faqs.question: What are the signs of moisture under a house?
faqs.answer: A musty smell inside, cupping or soft floorboards, damp or ponding soil under the floor, fungus or mould on bearers and joists, rusting fixings and condensation on pipes. Clear vents, check drainage and plumbing, and have the subfloor inspected.

faqs.question: How do I know if my house needs restumping?
faqs.answer: Common signs are sloping or uneven floors, springy areas, doors that stick or swing, diagonal cracks in plaster from door corners and gaps under skirting. A subfloor inspection showing decayed, leaning or sunken stumps confirms it.

faqs.question: What is the minimum subfloor clearance in Australia?
faqs.answer: Current ABCB Housing Provisions require at least 150 mm ground clearance under suspended floors where termite inspection is not required, and at least 400 mm where a termite management system needs to be inspected. On sloping sites, 400 mm may reduce to 150 mm within 2 metres of external walls.

faqs.question: Do I need a permit to restump a house in Victoria?
faqs.answer: Yes. Victorian councils and the VBA list restumping or reblocking as building work requiring a building permit, carried out by a registered builder. Domestic building insurance is also required for registered builders where the work is over $16,000.

faqs.question: What is the difference between restumping and reblocking?
faqs.answer: They usually mean the same thing: replacing failed stumps and re-levelling the floor. Restumping is common in some states and reblocking in others.

faqs.question: Can restumping cause cracks?
faqs.answer: Yes. Re-levelling a floor that has settled over many years can crack plaster, jam doors or open gaps, so allow for making good afterwards.

faqs.question: Should I block the subfloor vents to keep the house warm?
faqs.answer: No. Vents let ground moisture escape; blocking them encourages rot, fungus and termites. Insulating the floor is the better way to improve comfort.

faqs.question: What do termite mud tubes look like under a house?
faqs.answer: Pencil-width earthen tubes running up stumps, piers or walls. Do not break them open; arrange a licensed timber pest inspection.

| Type | Where you find it | What to watch for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Timber stumps | Much pre-war and early post-war housing | Decay at and below ground level, termite attack, settlement |
| Concrete stumps | Common from the post-war decades and in restumping | Cracking, spalling, and timber packers between stump and bearer that decay |
| Brick or masonry piers | Many older and mid-century homes | Cracked or leaning piers, loose mortar, missing ant caps |
| Adjustable steel stumps | Newer homes and restumping | Corrosion in damp subfloors and coastal areas, and loose adjustment fittings |

## What you'll notice above the floor
**Above-floor symptoms and what they raise**

| Symptom | What it can mean | Check next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sloping or uneven floors | Settled, decayed or sunken stumps, or ground movement | Floor levels across rooms, and stump condition below the low area |
| Springy or bouncy floor areas | Decayed joists or bearers, missing supports or overspanning | Framing condition and support spacing below |
| Doors sticking, swinging open or out of square | Frame movement from stump or footing movement | Whether it is seasonal, and floor levels at the door |
| Cracked plaster, especially diagonal cracks from door corners | Movement in the frame | The pattern, read with the [cracks guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/cracks-structural-or-cosmetic) |
| Gaps between skirting and floor | The floor dropping away from the walls | Stumps and bearers along that wall |
| Creaking or hollow sounds underfoot | Loose or decayed floor framing, or missing supports | Framing and supports below the noisy area |
| Musty smell or damp underfloor | Poor ventilation, drainage or leaking plumbing | Vents, drainage and pipes; see the [damp guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/damp-and-moisture-in-your-home) |

## The timber above the stumps
Stumps get the attention, but the bearers, joists and floorboards above them fail too, and their problems can look like stump problems from inside the house. Bearers are the heavy beams that sit on the stumps; joists run across the bearers; floorboards are fixed to the joists. Moisture, insects and later building work are the usual causes of trouble.

**Floor framing problems and how they show**

| Problem | Common cause | How it shows above |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Decay at bearer and joist ends | Damp subfloor, leaking plumbing, timber in contact with soil or masonry | Soft or sinking floor near walls or wet areas |
| Joists notched, drilled or cut | Plumbers, electricians or renovators cutting through framing to run services | A local dip or spring in the floor, often near a bathroom or kitchen |
| Sagging bearers | Supports too far apart, a removed stump, or an extra load such as a heavy bath or masonry wall | A gradual dip across the room |
| Termite damage | Termites entering through the ground, a stump or a bypassed barrier | Hollow-sounding or soft timber; see the [termites guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/termites-in-australian-homes) |
| Borer in floorboards | Wood-boring beetles, more common in older softwood boards | Small round holes and fine dust on or under the boards |
| Cupped or buckled boards | Moisture from below, or boards laid without room to expand | Board edges higher than their centres, or boards lifting |

A springy patch often means a framing problem close to the surface, while a slope across a whole room or house more often points to the supports or the ground beneath. Both need someone to look underneath before any repair is priced.

## Clearance and ventilation: the numbers
The [ABCB Housing Provisions](https://www.abcb.gov.au/editions/ncc-2022/adopted/housing-provisions/6-framing/part-62-subfloor-ventilation) set minimum ground clearances under suspended floors: at least **150 mm** where termite inspection is not required, and at least **400 mm** where a termite management system needs to be inspected. On sloping sites, the 400 mm may reduce to 150 mm within 2 metres of the external walls. The same provisions require cross-ventilation through openings in the walls, because ground moisture in a still subfloor encourages rot, fungus and termites.

Older homes were not always built to these clearances, and later work often reduces them: soil and paving built up against walls, garden beds, blocked vents, or storage pushed into the subfloor. Restoring clearance and airflow is often the cheapest improvement available.

**Subfloor checklist, where access is safe**

| Check | Good sign | Concern |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Clearance | Room to inspect; ground well below bearers | Ground or debris close to timbers |
| Ventilation | Clear vents on opposite sides; air moving | Blocked, painted-over or missing vents; still, humid air |
| Ground moisture | Dry soil | Damp soil, ponding, or water entering after rain |
| Stumps and piers | Plumb, sound, bearing evenly | Leaning, decayed, cracked or packed stumps; gaps to the bearer |
| Termites | No mud tubes; ant caps intact | Mud tubes on stumps or walls; damaged or bypassed ant caps |
| Plumbing and services | Dry pipes and connections | Leaks, wet patches below wet areas, sagging pipes; see the [plumbing guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/plumbing-hot-water-and-leaks) |

Do not disturb termite mud tubes; leave them for a licensed timber pest inspector. [CSIRO's building technology resource on managing termites](https://research.csiro.au/infratech/btr/) explains why visible, inspectable subfloors matter.

Ant caps, the metal plates on top of stumps and piers, do not stop termites. They force termites to build their mud tubes around the edge of the cap, where an inspector can see them. A cap that is bent, missing or bridged by timber, packing or debris no longer does that job. The [termites guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/termites-in-australian-homes) explains inspection and treatment.

## Why subfloors get damp, and what fixes it
Most damp subfloors have a source you can find. Fixing the source almost always works better than treating the symptoms. The [damp guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/damp-and-moisture-in-your-home) covers moisture throughout the house; under the floor, these are the usual suspects.

**Common sources of subfloor moisture**

| Source | What you may see | What usually helps |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Downpipes discharging at the wall or into the subfloor | Wet soil along one side, worst after rain | Connect downpipes to stormwater or carry water well away; see [site drainage](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/site-drainage-and-stormwater) |
| Ground that falls towards the house | Water running under the floor in heavy rain | Regrade, add surface drains, or both |
| Leaking pipes under bathrooms, laundries and kitchens | A wet patch under one area, rotting framing, a constant musty smell | Find and fix the leak; check the framing around it |
| Blocked or too few vents | Still, humid air; mould on timbers | Clear vents, add more where needed, and keep cross-flow open on opposite sides |
| Garden beds or paving built up against the walls | Vents covered, soil close to or above the floor level | Lower the ground and keep vents and weep holes clear |
| A naturally damp or poorly drained site | Persistently damp soil even in dry weather | Specialist advice; options include better drainage, a ground cover membrane or mechanical ventilation |

Avoid quick fixes that hide the problem. Sealing vents, laying plastic over damp soil without fixing the source, or spraying fungicide on timbers that stay wet will not stop decay. Once the source is dealt with, give the subfloor time to dry and check the framing that was affected.

## Insulating a raised floor without trapping moisture
Raised timber floors can lose a lot of heat in winter, and insulating between the joists can make a real difference to comfort. It needs care, though. Insulation should be fitted under the floor without blocking the subfloor vents or reducing the clearance needed for inspection. It should be kept off damp soil, and fitted so that a termite inspector can still see stumps, piers and the edges of the walls. Fix any damp problem before insulating, because insulation over a wet subfloor can hold moisture against the timbers. The [insulation and ventilation guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/insulation-ventilation-and-condensation) covers the wider picture.

## Restumping and reblocking
Restumping (often called reblocking) replaces failed stumps and re-levels the floor. It can be partial, replacing only failed stumps, or full. In Victoria, councils and the VBA list reblocking or restumping as work that needs a building permit, and it must be carried out by a registered builder; [Macedon Ranges Shire's permit guideline](https://www.mrsc.vic.gov.au/files/assets/public/build-amp-plan/build-renovate-amp-extend/restumping-guidelines.pdf) also notes that domestic building insurance is required for registered builders where the work is over $16,000. Requirements differ elsewhere, so check with your state regulator or council.

Two things are worth knowing before you start. First, re-levelling a floor that has settled over decades can crack plaster, jam doors or open gaps that need making good, so budget for it. Second, "restumped" on a listing can mean anything from a few stumps to the whole house. Ask for the permit, the builder, the date and a plan showing which stumps were replaced.

### What a restumping job involves

A typical job runs in a clear order. The builder assesses which stumps have failed, takes floor levels and arranges the permit. The floor is then supported on temporary props while old stumps are dug out, new footings are formed and new stumps set in place. The bearers are packed to the new levels, termite barriers such as ant caps are fitted where needed, and the floor is re-checked. Afterwards come the making-good works inside, such as plaster repairs, door adjustments and gaps at skirtings.

**Stump choices when restumping**

| Option | Strengths | Watch for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Concrete stumps | Durable, widely used, not food for termites | Need a sound footing and correct packing; timber packers above can still decay |
| Adjustable steel stumps | Can be fine-tuned for level; quick to install | Corrosion in damp or coastal subfloors; protective coating and drainage matter |
| Partial restumping | Lower cost where only some stumps have failed | Old and new stumps can settle differently, so the rest of the floor needs assessing |

### What a restumping quote should name

**Compare restumping quotes on the same basis**

| Item | What to look for |
| --- | --- |
| Extent | How many stumps, which ones, marked on a plan |
| Permit and builder | Who arranges the permit, and the builder's registration |
| Stump type and footings | Concrete or steel, footing size and depth |
| Bearers and joists | What happens if decayed framing is found, and the rate for extra work |
| Re-levelling | How far the floor will be brought back towards level, and how levels are recorded |
| Termite protection | Ant caps or other barriers, and access left for inspection |
| Making good | Plaster, doors, skirtings and other repairs inside, or whether these are excluded |
| Warranty and insurance | The warranty on the work and any domestic building insurance required in your state |

## Houses on more than one kind of footing
Many homes have a raised timber floor in the original house and a concrete slab under a later extension. The two parts move differently with the seasons and over time, so the junction between them is a common place for cracks, sticking doors and a step or dip in the floor. Treat each part separately when reading symptoms, and look closely at the junction. The [cracks guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/cracks-structural-or-cosmetic) covers junction cracking, and [working out when a house was built](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/when-was-my-house-built) helps you date each part.

## Common misreads
**Things often said about subfloors**

| What people say | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| "It has been restumped" | Ask how many stumps, where, when, with what material, and under which permit. |
| "The floor is level now, so the problem is fixed" | Levelling treats the symptom. Drainage, plumbing leaks and termites can keep causing movement. |
| "Concrete stumps cannot fail" | They can crack or settle, and the timber packers and bearers above them can still decay. |
| "Sealing the vents keeps the house warmer" | It also traps moisture under the floor. Insulate the floor instead of blocking the vents. |

## Worked example: restumped, but the back room still slopes
**Illustrative reasoning example, not an inspected property.** A 1930s weatherboard was advertised as restumped. The front rooms are level, but the rear room slopes and its door sticks. The vendor provides an invoice for "restumping".

The invoice lists 24 stumps at the front of the house. The rear room is a later addition on its own stumps, with a downpipe discharging against the wall beside it. The next steps are a subfloor inspection of the addition, a check of the drainage, and a quote for that area alone. The front restumping is real evidence for the front of the house, not for the whole of it. See the [interwar homes guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/interwar-homes-1920s-40s) for the wider pattern.

> Note: Only enter a subfloor where it is safe: adequate clearance, no standing water, no exposed wiring, and no suspicion of asbestos-containing debris. Otherwise leave it to an inspector.

## Frequently asked questions
### How long do timber stumps last?
It depends on the timber, the soil, how wet the subfloor is and whether termites have reached them. Many older homes still stand on original stumps, while others failed decades ago. Judge by condition: probe at and below ground level and check floor levels.

### Should I choose concrete or steel stumps?
Both are common. Concrete stumps are durable and are not attacked by termites. Adjustable steel stumps make fine levelling easier but need protection from corrosion in damp or coastal subfloors. The builder should explain why they recommend one for your site.

### Can I insulate under a raised timber floor?
Yes, and it can make a real difference to comfort. Fix any damp first, keep vents and inspection clearances open, keep insulation off the soil, and leave stumps and wall edges visible for termite inspections.

### Why are my floorboards cupping?
Cupping, where board edges sit higher than the middle, usually means moisture from below. Check subfloor ventilation, drainage and any plumbing leaks under the area before repairing the boards.

### What does an ant cap do?
An ant cap is a metal plate on a stump or pier that forces termites to build their mud tubes around its edge where they can be seen. It does not stop termites by itself, and it only works if it is intact and not bridged.

### Is a bouncy floor dangerous?
A springy area usually means framing below is decayed, damaged, cut or under-supported. It should be inspected from underneath before it gets worse, and sooner if it is getting softer or sits near a wet area.

### Do I need to restump if the floor slopes a little?
Not necessarily. Many older floors have a gentle, long-standing slope. What matters is whether it is getting worse, whether the stumps and framing are sound and whether doors and walls show new movement. An inspection under the floor answers that.

### What are the signs of moisture under a house?
A musty smell inside, cupping or soft floorboards, damp or ponding soil under the floor, fungus or mould on bearers and joists, rusting fixings and condensation on pipes. Clear vents, check drainage and plumbing, and have the subfloor inspected.

### How do I know if my house needs restumping?
Common signs are sloping or uneven floors, springy areas, doors that stick or swing, diagonal cracks in plaster from door corners and gaps under skirting. A subfloor inspection showing decayed, leaning or sunken stumps confirms it.

### What is the minimum subfloor clearance in Australia?
Current ABCB Housing Provisions require at least 150 mm ground clearance under suspended floors where termite inspection is not required, and at least 400 mm where a termite management system needs to be inspected. On sloping sites, 400 mm may reduce to 150 mm within 2 metres of external walls.

### Do I need a permit to restump a house in Victoria?
Yes. Victorian councils and the VBA list restumping or reblocking as building work requiring a building permit, carried out by a registered builder. Domestic building insurance is also required for registered builders where the work is over $16,000.

### What is the difference between restumping and reblocking?
They usually mean the same thing: replacing failed stumps and re-levelling the floor. Restumping is common in some states and reblocking in others.

### Can restumping cause cracks?
Yes. Re-levelling a floor that has settled over many years can crack plaster, jam doors or open gaps, so allow for making good afterwards.

### Should I block the subfloor vents to keep the house warm?
No. Vents let ground moisture escape; blocking them encourages rot, fungus and termites. Insulating the floor is the better way to improve comfort.

### What do termite mud tubes look like under a house?
Pencil-width earthen tubes running up stumps, piers or walls. Do not break them open; arrange a licensed timber pest inspection.

## Method
We work from above-floor symptoms to subfloor evidence, set out current clearance and ventilation requirements, and separate partial from full restumping scope, with a fictional example.

## Limitations
Older homes may predate current clearance requirements. Permit and licensing rules vary by state; confirm with your regulator or council.

- [Restumping or re-blocking a building: permit application guideline](https://www.mrsc.vic.gov.au/files/assets/public/build-amp-plan/build-renovate-amp-extend/restumping-guidelines.pdf) — Macedon Ranges Shire Council; accessed 2026-10-14

guides.question: Could my older house contain asbestos, and where should I look?
guides.title: Asbestos in older homes: where it hides and what to do
guides.summary: Which homes may contain asbestos, where it is usually found and how to spot suspect products, bonded versus friable material, how to read its condition, and what to do before renovating, after a storm, when buying and when disposing of it.
guides.answer: Homes built or renovated before 1990 may contain asbestos, and products containing it were banned nationally from 31 December 2003. You cannot tell by looking: only laboratory testing of a sample confirms it. Material in good condition and left undisturbed is low risk; the danger is cutting, drilling, sanding, breaking or water-blasting it.
guides.methodology: We date the home and each renovation, map common locations room by room, separate bonded from friable material, and set out a test-before-disturbance sequence, with a fictional example.
guides.limitations: Only laboratory testing confirms asbestos. State licensing and removal thresholds differ; check your regulator before any work.
guides.researchNote: Locations and dates follow the [national asbestos agency](https://www.asbestossafety.gov.au/about-asbestos/finding-asbestos/home) and Queensland Government guidance. Removal rules differ by state; the NSW example comes from the NSW EPA.

cluster.label: Read the building
cluster.blurb: Use age and construction as a starting hypothesis, then test it against evidence and physical inspection.

sections.heading: Opening
sections.markdown:
### Date it, find it, test it
- **Date:** Built or renovated before 1990 means it may be present
- **Find:** Eaves, wet areas, floors, roofs, fences and sheds are the usual places
- **Test:** Only a laboratory sample confirms it

_Sound and undisturbed is low risk. Cutting, drilling and sanding are not._

It is most often found as fibre-cement sheeting in eaves, wet-area walls and floors, roofing and fences, and in vinyl floor tiles and the backing of sheet vinyl, with less common friable forms in older heater and stove insulation.

sections.heading: Which homes may contain it: build date and renovation date
sections.markdown: Asbestos was used in thousands of building products in Australia. The [Asbestos and Silica Safety and Eradication Agency](https://www.asbestossafety.gov.au/about-asbestos/finding-asbestos/home) advises that homes built or renovated before 1990 may contain it, and the [national ban](https://www.asbestos.nsw.gov.au/safety/safety-in-the-home/when-was-asbestos-banned-in-australia) on its use and import took effect on 31 December 2003. The renovation date matters as much as the build date: a 1995 house can have a 1980s shed, and a 1950s house may have had its bathroom relined in 2010.

sections.heading: Where it hides in an older house
sections.markdown:
**Common locations, room by room**

| Area | Typical asbestos-containing materials |
| --- | --- |
| Outside | Roof sheeting, ridge capping, gutters and downpipes, eaves and soffit linings, wall sheeting, imitation brick cladding |
| Bathroom, toilet and laundry | Wall and ceiling sheeting, sheeting behind wall tiles, sheeting under floor tiles, vinyl floor tiles |
| Kitchen | Wall and ceiling panels, backing for splashbacks, vinyl floor tiles, the backing of sheet vinyl, insulation in old stoves |
| Living areas | Wall and ceiling panels, textured ceilings, carpet underlay, insulation in old heaters |
| Backyard | Fences, sheds, garages, carports, outdoor toilets and buried or dumped building waste |
| Other | Electrical switchboard backing, hot water pipe lagging, textured paint and older plaster patching compounds, wood heater door rope |

This summary follows the agency's [Where is asbestos in the home](https://www.asbestossafety.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/Where_is_asbestos_in_the_home_diagram.pdf) diagram and [Queensland's guide to common locations](https://www.asbestos.qld.gov.au/sites/default/files/common-locations-materials-containing-asbestos-concrete-clay-tiled-roof.pdf). Many of these products look identical to their asbestos-free successors.

sections.heading: Suspect products and how to spot them
sections.markdown:
You cannot confirm asbestos by looking, but you can learn which materials deserve a test. Most asbestos in homes is in fibre cement products, and those have recognisable forms. Treat anything below as suspect in a home built or renovated before 1990 until it has been tested.

**Common suspect products**

| Product | What it looks like | Where it turns up |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Flat fibre cement sheeting | Thin, hard grey sheets, often painted, with nail heads in rows and sometimes cover strips over the joints | Eaves, wall linings in wet areas, external cladding, sheds and extensions |
| Corrugated fibre cement roofing | Grey wavy sheets, often weathered and covered in lichen | Roofs of homes, garages, sheds and carports |
| Imitation brick or stone cladding | Pressed sheets made to look like brick or stone | External walls, often on older weatherboard homes |
| Vinyl floor tiles and sheet vinyl | Small square vinyl tiles, or sheet vinyl with a fibrous backing | Kitchens, laundries, bathrooms and hallways, sometimes under newer flooring |
| Textured ceilings and coatings | Sprayed or trowelled textured finishes | Living rooms and bedrooms |
| Insulation and lagging | Wrapping on old hot water pipes, or insulation inside old heaters and stoves | Roof spaces, subfloors, old appliances |

Asbestos-free fibre cement replaced the older products and looks almost identical, so a match in this table is a reason to test, not a conclusion. The renovation history matters as much as the build date: a 1960s home may have a 2010 bathroom, and a 1995 home may have an older shed or fence moved onto the site.

sections.heading: Bonded and friable: why the difference matters
sections.markdown:
**Two kinds of asbestos material**

|  | Bonded (non-friable) | Friable |
| --- | --- | --- |
| What it is | Asbestos fibres locked into a solid material such as cement sheet or vinyl | Loose material that can be crumbled by hand, releasing fibres easily |
| Examples | Fibro sheeting, corrugated roofing, vinyl floor tiles | Some older heater and stove insulation, pipe lagging, and the backing of some sheet vinyl ([Queensland Government](https://asbestos.qld.gov.au/node/2)) |
| How common in homes | By far the most common | Less common, but far more hazardous |
| Who may remove it | Rules vary by state; licensed removalists are recommended for any amount | Licensed friable (Class A) removalists only |

In NSW, for example, the [EPA's homeowner fact sheet](https://epa.nsw.gov.au/sites/default/files/19p1498-AA-factsheet-homeowners.pdf) explains that licensed removal is required for friable asbestos and for more than 10 square metres of bonded asbestos. Other states set their own rules, so check with your state's work health and safety regulator before anyone touches it.

sections.heading: Reading the condition
sections.markdown:
The risk from asbestos depends on whether fibres can be released. Material that is sound, painted and left alone is low risk. Material that is weathered, cracked, broken or crumbling is a different matter, and so is any material about to be cut, drilled, sanded or demolished.

**Condition and what to do**

| Condition | What it means | What to do |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sound, painted and undisturbed | Fibres are locked in | Leave it alone, record where it is and keep it painted |
| Weathered or with a rough surface | The surface is breaking down, more so outdoors | Get advice on sealing or removal; do not water-blast or scrub |
| Cracked or broken pieces | Damaged material can release fibres | Keep people away, do not sweep or vacuum, get advice from a licensed professional |
| Crumbling or soft material | Possibly friable, which is far more hazardous | Stop, keep clear and contact a licensed asbestos assessor |
| About to be disturbed by work | Cutting, drilling or demolishing releases fibres | Test before work starts, and arrange licensed removal if positive |

sections.heading: Why disturbance is the danger
sections.markdown: Asbestos causes harm when its fibres are breathed in. The diseases linked to it, including mesothelioma, asbestosis and lung cancer, usually appear many years after exposure. That is why the advice focuses on not creating dust in the first place. If you are worried about past exposure, talk to your GP, who can advise on what, if anything, to do.

sections.heading: How to find out safely
sections.markdown:
**Steps before any work**

| Step | What to do |
| --- | --- |
| 1. Check the dates | When was the house built, and when was each part renovated? |
| 2. Look without touching | Note suspect materials room by room, and their condition: intact, weathered, cracked or broken |
| 3. Test what will be disturbed | Have a licensed asbestos assessor or competent person take samples for laboratory testing |
| 4. Plan around the result | Leave sound material alone, manage it, or arrange licensed removal before work starts |
| 5. Keep the paperwork | Test results, removal records and clearance certificates belong in the home record |

A standard pre-purchase building inspection does not test for asbestos. It may note suspect materials, but confirming them needs sampling. See [what an inspection typically leaves out](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/building-inspection-before-auction), and keep results with your [home record](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/keeping-a-record-of-your-home).

sections.heading: Asbestos and renovations
sections.markdown:
Renovation is when most home asbestos exposure happens, because it is when material gets cut, drilled and broken. Build the asbestos step into the start of the project, before demolition quotes are finalised.

**A safe renovation sequence**

| Step | What happens | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Identify | A licensed assessor or competent person samples anything that will be disturbed | Results change the scope, cost and order of work |
| Plan | Decide what stays, what is sealed and what is removed | Leaving sound material in place is sometimes the safest choice |
| Remove | A licensed removalist removes positive material under controlled conditions | Licensing rules depend on the state, the type and the amount |
| Clear | A clearance inspection, and air monitoring where required, before other trades return | Shows the area is safe to work in |
| Record | Keep test results, removal records and the clearance certificate | A future buyer, insurer or builder will ask for them |

sections.heading: After a storm, fire or other damage
sections.markdown: Storms, hail and fire can break fibre cement roofing, eaves and fences and scatter pieces around a property. Keep people and pets away from damaged material, do not try to clean it up yourself, and do not use a leaf blower, broom or household vacuum on it. Tell your insurer and arrange a licensed professional. State governments often publish specific advice after major disasters. The [extreme weather guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/preparing-your-home-for-extreme-weather) covers recovery more generally.

sections.heading: Asbestos when buying
sections.markdown: For most buyers the question is not whether a pre-1990 home has some asbestos, but where it is, what condition it is in and whether your plans will disturb it. A building inspection may note suspect materials but will not test them. If you are planning renovations, ask the vendor for any test results or an asbestos register, and consider arranging sampling of the areas you plan to change before committing. Disclosure rules differ between states, so ask your conveyancer what the vendor must tell you.

sections.heading: Disposal and dumped asbestos
sections.markdown: Asbestos waste must go to a facility licensed to accept it, packaged as the rules require. It cannot go in household bins or skips. Illegal dumping is common enough that councils and regulators warn about it, and older properties sometimes have buried building waste in the garden. If you find broken fibre cement while digging, stop, keep the area damp and undisturbed, and get advice before going further.

sections.heading: Common misreads
sections.markdown:
**Things often said about asbestos**

| What people say | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| "It looks like fibro, so it is asbestos" | Asbestos-free fibre cement looks the same. Only testing confirms it. |
| "Asbestos in the house is an emergency" | Sound, undisturbed bonded material is low risk. The risk comes with damage and disturbance. |
| "Painting it makes it safe to drill" | Paint can help seal weathered sheeting, but drilling, cutting and sanding still release fibres. |
| "A newer house cannot have any" | Unlikely in original construction after 1990, but older sheds, fences, renovations and imported products can still be a source. |
| "Water-blasting the roof will tidy it up" | Water-blasting asbestos-cement roofs releases fibres and is commonly prohibited. Do not do it. |

sections.heading: Worked example: a bathroom renovation in a 1970s house
sections.markdown:
**Illustrative reasoning example, not an inspected property.** An owner plans to retile a 1970s bathroom. The walls are sheeted behind the tiles, and there is vinyl in the adjoining laundry. Nothing records whether either contains asbestos.

Before any tile comes off, the sheeting behind the tiles and the laundry vinyl and its backing are sampled. guides.contentMarkdown:
# Asbestos in older homes: where it hides and what to do

Homes built or renovated before 1990 may contain asbestos, and products containing it were banned nationally from 31 December 2003. You cannot tell by looking: only laboratory testing of a sample confirms it. Material in good condition and left undisturbed is low risk; the danger is cutting, drilling, sanding, breaking or water-blasting it.

## Research note
Locations and dates follow the [national asbestos agency](https://www.asbestossafety.gov.au/about-asbestos/finding-asbestos/home) and Queensland Government guidance. Removal rules differ by state; the NSW example comes from the NSW EPA.

## Opening
### Date it, find it, test it
- **Date:** Built or renovated before 1990 means it may be present
- **Find:** Eaves, wet areas, floors, roofs, fences and sheds are the usual places
- **Test:** Only a laboratory sample confirms it

_Sound and undisturbed is low risk. Cutting, drilling and sanding are not._

It is most often found as fibre-cement sheeting in eaves, wet-area walls and floors, roofing and fences, and in vinyl floor tiles and the backing of sheet vinyl, with less common friable forms in older heater and stove insulation.

## Which homes may contain it: build date and renovation date
Asbestos was used in thousands of building products in Australia. The [Asbestos and Silica Safety and Eradication Agency](https://www.asbestossafety.gov.au/about-asbestos/finding-asbestos/home) advises that homes built or renovated before 1990 may contain it, and the [national ban](https://www.asbestos.nsw.gov.au/safety/safety-in-the-home/when-was-asbestos-banned-in-australia) on its use and import took effect on 31 December 2003. The renovation date matters as much as the build date: a 1995 house can have a 1980s shed, and a 1950s house may have had its bathroom relined in 2010.

## Where it hides in an older house
**Common locations, room by room**

| Area | Typical asbestos-containing materials |
| --- | --- |
| Outside | Roof sheeting, ridge capping, gutters and downpipes, eaves and soffit linings, wall sheeting, imitation brick cladding |
| Bathroom, toilet and laundry | Wall and ceiling sheeting, sheeting behind wall tiles, sheeting under floor tiles, vinyl floor tiles |
| Kitchen | Wall and ceiling panels, backing for splashbacks, vinyl floor tiles, the backing of sheet vinyl, insulation in old stoves |
| Living areas | Wall and ceiling panels, textured ceilings, carpet underlay, insulation in old heaters |
| Backyard | Fences, sheds, garages, carports, outdoor toilets and buried or dumped building waste |
| Other | Electrical switchboard backing, hot water pipe lagging, textured paint and older plaster patching compounds, wood heater door rope |

This summary follows the agency's [Where is asbestos in the home](https://www.asbestossafety.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/Where_is_asbestos_in_the_home_diagram.pdf) diagram and [Queensland's guide to common locations](https://www.asbestos.qld.gov.au/sites/default/files/common-locations-materials-containing-asbestos-concrete-clay-tiled-roof.pdf). Many of these products look identical to their asbestos-free successors.

## Suspect products and how to spot them
You cannot confirm asbestos by looking, but you can learn which materials deserve a test. Most asbestos in homes is in fibre cement products, and those have recognisable forms. Treat anything below as suspect in a home built or renovated before 1990 until it has been tested.

**Common suspect products**

| Product | What it looks like | Where it turns up |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Flat fibre cement sheeting | Thin, hard grey sheets, often painted, with nail heads in rows and sometimes cover strips over the joints | Eaves, wall linings in wet areas, external cladding, sheds and extensions |
| Corrugated fibre cement roofing | Grey wavy sheets, often weathered and covered in lichen | Roofs of homes, garages, sheds and carports |
| Imitation brick or stone cladding | Pressed sheets made to look like brick or stone | External walls, often on older weatherboard homes |
| Vinyl floor tiles and sheet vinyl | Small square vinyl tiles, or sheet vinyl with a fibrous backing | Kitchens, laundries, bathrooms and hallways, sometimes under newer flooring |
| Textured ceilings and coatings | Sprayed or trowelled textured finishes | Living rooms and bedrooms |
| Insulation and lagging | Wrapping on old hot water pipes, or insulation inside old heaters and stoves | Roof spaces, subfloors, old appliances |

Asbestos-free fibre cement replaced the older products and looks almost identical, so a match in this table is a reason to test, not a conclusion. The renovation history matters as much as the build date: a 1960s home may have a 2010 bathroom, and a 1995 home may have an older shed or fence moved onto the site.

## Bonded and friable: why the difference matters
**Two kinds of asbestos material**

|  | Bonded (non-friable) | Friable |
| --- | --- | --- |
| What it is | Asbestos fibres locked into a solid material such as cement sheet or vinyl | Loose material that can be crumbled by hand, releasing fibres easily |
| Examples | Fibro sheeting, corrugated roofing, vinyl floor tiles | Some older heater and stove insulation, pipe lagging, and the backing of some sheet vinyl ([Queensland Government](https://asbestos.qld.gov.au/node/2)) |
| How common in homes | By far the most common | Less common, but far more hazardous |
| Who may remove it | Rules vary by state; licensed removalists are recommended for any amount | Licensed friable (Class A) removalists only |

In NSW, for example, the [EPA's homeowner fact sheet](https://epa.nsw.gov.au/sites/default/files/19p1498-AA-factsheet-homeowners.pdf) explains that licensed removal is required for friable asbestos and for more than 10 square metres of bonded asbestos. Other states set their own rules, so check with your state's work health and safety regulator before anyone touches it.

## Reading the condition
The risk from asbestos depends on whether fibres can be released. Material that is sound, painted and left alone is low risk. Material that is weathered, cracked, broken or crumbling is a different matter, and so is any material about to be cut, drilled, sanded or demolished.

**Condition and what to do**

| Condition | What it means | What to do |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sound, painted and undisturbed | Fibres are locked in | Leave it alone, record where it is and keep it painted |
| Weathered or with a rough surface | The surface is breaking down, more so outdoors | Get advice on sealing or removal; do not water-blast or scrub |
| Cracked or broken pieces | Damaged material can release fibres | Keep people away, do not sweep or vacuum, get advice from a licensed professional |
| Crumbling or soft material | Possibly friable, which is far more hazardous | Stop, keep clear and contact a licensed asbestos assessor |
| About to be disturbed by work | Cutting, drilling or demolishing releases fibres | Test before work starts, and arrange licensed removal if positive |

## Why disturbance is the danger
Asbestos causes harm when its fibres are breathed in. The diseases linked to it, including mesothelioma, asbestosis and lung cancer, usually appear many years after exposure. That is why the advice focuses on not creating dust in the first place. If you are worried about past exposure, talk to your GP, who can advise on what, if anything, to do.

## How to find out safely
**Steps before any work**

| Step | What to do |
| --- | --- |
| 1. Check the dates | When was the house built, and when was each part renovated? |
| 2. Look without touching | Note suspect materials room by room, and their condition: intact, weathered, cracked or broken |
| 3. Test what will be disturbed | Have a licensed asbestos assessor or competent person take samples for laboratory testing |
| 4. Plan around the result | Leave sound material alone, manage it, or arrange licensed removal before work starts |
| 5. Keep the paperwork | Test results, removal records and clearance certificates belong in the home record |

A standard pre-purchase building inspection does not test for asbestos. It may note suspect materials, but confirming them needs sampling. See [what an inspection typically leaves out](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/building-inspection-before-auction), and keep results with your [home record](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/keeping-a-record-of-your-home).

## Asbestos and renovations
Renovation is when most home asbestos exposure happens, because it is when material gets cut, drilled and broken. Build the asbestos step into the start of the project, before demolition quotes are finalised.

**A safe renovation sequence**

| Step | What happens | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Identify | A licensed assessor or competent person samples anything that will be disturbed | Results change the scope, cost and order of work |
| Plan | Decide what stays, what is sealed and what is removed | Leaving sound material in place is sometimes the safest choice |
| Remove | A licensed removalist removes positive material under controlled conditions | Licensing rules depend on the state, the type and the amount |
| Clear | A clearance inspection, and air monitoring where required, before other trades return | Shows the area is safe to work in |
| Record | Keep test results, removal records and the clearance certificate | A future buyer, insurer or builder will ask for them |

## After a storm, fire or other damage
Storms, hail and fire can break fibre cement roofing, eaves and fences and scatter pieces around a property. Keep people and pets away from damaged material, do not try to clean it up yourself, and do not use a leaf blower, broom or household vacuum on it. Tell your insurer and arrange a licensed professional. State governments often publish specific advice after major disasters. The [extreme weather guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/preparing-your-home-for-extreme-weather) covers recovery more generally.

## Asbestos when buying
For most buyers the question is not whether a pre-1990 home has some asbestos, but where it is, what condition it is in and whether your plans will disturb it. A building inspection may note suspect materials but will not test them. If you are planning renovations, ask the vendor for any test results or an asbestos register, and consider arranging sampling of the areas you plan to change before committing. Disclosure rules differ between states, so ask your conveyancer what the vendor must tell you.

## Disposal and dumped asbestos
Asbestos waste must go to a facility licensed to accept it, packaged as the rules require. It cannot go in household bins or skips. Illegal dumping is common enough that councils and regulators warn about it, and older properties sometimes have buried building waste in the garden. If you find broken fibre cement while digging, stop, keep the area damp and undisturbed, and get advice before going further.

## Common misreads
**Things often said about asbestos**

| What people say | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| "It looks like fibro, so it is asbestos" | Asbestos-free fibre cement looks the same. Only testing confirms it. |
| "Asbestos in the house is an emergency" | Sound, undisturbed bonded material is low risk. The risk comes with damage and disturbance. |
| "Painting it makes it safe to drill" | Paint can help seal weathered sheeting, but drilling, cutting and sanding still release fibres. |
| "A newer house cannot have any" | Unlikely in original construction after 1990, but older sheds, fences, renovations and imported products can still be a source. |
| "Water-blasting the roof will tidy it up" | Water-blasting asbestos-cement roofs releases fibres and is commonly prohibited. Do not do it. |

## Worked example: a bathroom renovation in a 1970s house
**Illustrative reasoning example, not an inspected property.** An owner plans to retile a 1970s bathroom. The walls are sheeted behind the tiles, and there is vinyl in the adjoining laundry. Nothing records whether either contains asbestos.

Before any tile comes off, the sheeting behind the tiles and the laundry vinyl and its backing are sampled. If either tests positive, the quote changes: licensed removal goes in before the waterproofing and tiling, with a clearance certificate before the next trade starts. The renovation sequence is set out in [planning a renovation](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/planning-a-renovation), and the bathroom itself in the [waterproofing guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/bathroom-waterproofing-and-leaking-showers).

> Important: If you think asbestos has been damaged or disturbed, stop work, keep people away from the area, avoid spreading dust, and get advice from a licensed asbestos professional or your state regulator.

## Frequently asked questions
### What does asbestos fibro look like?
Usually thin, hard grey sheets, often painted, with nail heads in rows and sometimes cover strips over the joints. Asbestos-free fibre cement looks almost identical, so only laboratory testing confirms it.

### Can I paint asbestos sheeting?
Painting sound, weathered fibre cement can help seal its surface, but preparation must not involve sanding, scraping, water-blasting or wire-brushing. Get advice first, and never drill or cut it.

### What should I do with asbestos damaged in a storm?

### Do old vinyl floor tiles contain asbestos?

### Where do I dispose of asbestos?

### Should I buy a house with asbestos?

### Which Australian homes contain asbestos?

### Where is asbestos usually found in a house?

### Can you tell asbestos by looking at it?
No. Asbestos-free fibre cement looks the same. Only laboratory testing of a sample confirms it, so treat suspect material as asbestos until tested.

### What is the difference between bonded and friable asbestos?

No. A standard pre-purchase inspection may note suspect materials but does not sample or test them. Use a licensed asbestos assessor if it matters to your decision or planned work.

## Method
We date the home and each renovation, map common locations room by room, separate bonded from friable material, and set out a test-before-disturbance sequence, with a fictional example.

## Limitations
Only laboratory testing confirms asbestos. State licensing and removal thresholds differ; check your regulator before any work.
