guides.question: How do termites get into a house, and does the way it is built change the risk?
guides.title: Termites by construction type: signs and protection
guides.summary: The signs of termites, the conditions that invite them, how risk varies across Australia, how protection systems and timber pest inspections work, what to do if termites are found, and the renovations that quietly break protection.
guides.answer: Subterranean termites reach timber from the ground, usually unseen, through mud tubes, cracks and anything that bridges the inspection zone. Signs include mud tubes on stumps, walls or slab edges, timber that sounds hollow or crumbles, mud packed into cracks or joints, and swarms of winged termites. No system stops termites reaching a site; protection relies on a barrier or monitoring system, an inspection zone kept visible, and inspection at least every 12 months.
guides.methodology: We start from visible signs, list the conditions that invite activity, explain what each system type can and cannot do, and show where to find the installation record, with a fictional example.
guides.limitations: Termite risk varies by region and species. Only a licensed timber pest inspection confirms activity or damage.
guides.researchNote: System requirements and the durable notice follow the [ABCB Housing Provisions](https://www.abcb.gov.au/editions/ncc-2022/adopted/housing-provisions/3-site-preparation/part-34-termite-risk-management). Inspection practice references AS 3660.2 and AS 4349.3, and the clearance rules come from QBCC guidance.

cluster.label: Read the building
cluster.blurb: Use age and construction as a starting hypothesis, then test it against evidence and physical inspection.

sections.heading: Opening
sections.markdown:
### Stop them entering unseen
- **System:** A barrier or monitoring system around the building
- **Zone:** A visible inspection zone, kept clear of soil and paving
- **Inspect:** A licensed inspection at least every 12 months

_No system stops termites reaching a site. Inspection is what catches them._

In newer homes a durable notice, usually in the meter box, records the system installed.

sections.heading: What you'll notice: signs of termite activity
sections.markdown:
**What to look for, and what to do**

| Sign | Where | What to do |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Mud tubes, about pencil width | Stumps, piers, walls, slab edges, behind cladding | Do not break them; arrange a licensed timber pest inspection |
| Hollow-sounding or crumbling timber | Skirting, architraves, door frames, floorboards, decks | Leave it undisturbed for the inspector |
| Mud packed into cracks or joints | Plaster cracks, cornices, timber joints | Note the location and arrange inspection |
| Swarms of winged termites | Around lights and windows on warm, humid evenings | Collect a few if you can; arrange inspection |
| Sagging floors or jamming doors and windows | Throughout | Rule out termite damage alongside other causes of movement |

Disturbing an active nest or workings can drive termites elsewhere in the building and make treatment harder. Leave suspected activity alone and get it inspected.

sections.heading: How termite risk varies across Australia
sections.markdown:
Subterranean termites, which travel from a nest in the ground or a tree, cause most of the damage to Australian homes. Risk is not the same everywhere. The [ABCB Housing Provisions](https://www.abcb.gov.au/editions/ncc-2022/adopted/housing-provisions/3-site-preparation/part-34-termite-risk-management) note that termites are not considered a risk in Tasmania and are a lesser risk in parts of Victoria, and they add extra measures where the giant northern termite, *Mastotermes darwiniensis*, is prevalent. Warm, humid areas and sites with bushland, old tree stumps or damp ground tend to carry higher risk. Your council or a local pest manager can tell you what is typical for your area.

Low risk is not no risk. Homes in lower-risk areas can still be attacked, especially where timber touches the ground or the subfloor stays damp, so the basic habits in this guide apply almost everywhere.

sections.heading: Conditions that invite termites
sections.markdown:
**Conducive conditions and the simple fix**

| Condition | Why it matters | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Soil, mulch or garden beds against walls | Hides entry and bridges the inspection zone | Keep the slab edge or wall base visible |
| Paving laid over the slab edge or weep holes | Termites can enter unseen beneath it | Keep paths at least 75 mm below the termite barrier |
| Leaking pipes, hot water overflows or air-conditioner drips | Moist soil attracts termites | Fix leaks; drain overflows away from the house |
| Timber in contact with the ground | A direct food source and pathway | Remove or isolate timber, sleepers and stored wood; check [deck posts](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/decks-balconies-and-balustrades) and [sleeper walls](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/retaining-walls) |
| Poor subfloor ventilation | Damp timber is more attractive and decays | Clear vents; see the subfloor guide |
| Stumps of old trees near the house | A common nest site | Have them inspected; consider removal |

The path and clearance rules come from [QBCC's maintenance guide](https://www.qbcc.qld.gov.au/sites/default/files/documents/guide-essential-home-maintenance.pdf). For raised floors, the clearance and ventilation numbers are in [subfloors, stumps and restumping](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/subfloors-stumps-and-restumping).

sections.heading: Where termites get in: slabs, stumps and walls
sections.markdown:
Termites look for a hidden route from the soil to timber. The table shows the common ones; most are places where the original protection has been covered, cracked or bypassed.

**Common termite entry points**

| Entry point | Why it works for termites | What helps |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Slab edge covered by soil, paving or garden beds | The edge is the inspection zone; covering it hides any mud tubes | Keep the slab edge exposed and paths below the barrier |
| Pipes and cables through the slab | Gaps around penetrations give concealed access | Protect penetrations with collars or other treatment when they are installed |
| Cracks and joints in the slab | Termites can pass through cracks wider than a hair | Note cracking, and keep inspection access around affected areas |
| Weep holes and cavities in brick walls | A route up inside the wall cavity, out of sight | Keep weep holes above ground and clear of soil and paving |
| Stumps and piers under raised floors | A direct path to the bearers if ant caps are missing or bridged | Intact ant caps, clear subfloor access and regular inspection |
| Attached decks, pergolas and fences | Timber touching the ground and the house links soil to the building | Separate timber from the house or protect it, and inspect the junction |
| Behind cladding and render to ground level | Cladding taken down to the soil hides activity behind it | Maintain clearance between cladding and finished ground |

Older homes on stumps can be easier to inspect than slab homes, because the subfloor is open to view, provided the clearance and access are maintained. Slab homes depend more on the edge staying exposed and on protection around penetrations. The [subfloor guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/subfloors-stumps-and-restumping) and [wall-system guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/brick-veneer-vs-double-brick) show how construction changes the inspection.

sections.heading: How termite management systems work
sections.markdown:
The [ABCB Housing Provisions](https://www.abcb.gov.au/editions/ncc-2022/adopted/housing-provisions/3-site-preparation/part-34-termite-risk-management) make the key point plainly: a termite management system will not stop termite activity on a site. Its job is to stop termites entering the building unseen, forcing them into the open where an inspection can find them. Its effectiveness relies on regular maintenance and competent inspection.

**Common system types**

| Type | How it works | What it needs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Chemical soil barrier | Treated soil around and under the building deters or kills termites | Periodic re-treatment; some use reticulation pipes for top-ups |
| Physical barrier | Stainless steel mesh, graded stone or termite shields block concealed entry | An intact barrier, not bridged by later work |
| Baiting and monitoring | Stations around the house detect activity and deliver bait to the colony | Regular servicing to the provider’s schedule |
| Inspection zone | A visible strip, such as an exposed slab edge, where tubes can be seen | Kept clear of soil, paving and garden beds |

### Find the durable notice

Where a termite management system is required in a new building, a durable notice must be permanently fixed in a prominent location, such as the meter box, recording the system used and advising that it should be inspected and maintained. Look for it in the meter box, and sometimes in a kitchen cupboard. If it is missing, faded or out of date, ask the vendor or owner for treatment records, and have a licensed technician confirm what is installed.

sections.heading: How often to inspect
sections.markdown: Most termite management systems need a licensed pest controller to inspect and service them at least every 12 months, more often in high-risk areas. Inspections of existing buildings follow [AS 3660.2](https://store.standards.org.au/product/as-3660-2-2017), and pre-purchase timber pest inspections follow AS 4349.3. Read the timber pest report alongside the building report, as described in [how to read a building and pest report](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/how-to-read-a-building-and-pest-report).

sections.heading: What a timber pest inspection involves
sections.markdown:
A timber pest inspection is a visual inspection of the readily accessible parts of the house and site: the interior, the roof space and subfloor where safe access exists, the exterior and the grounds, including fences, trees and outbuildings. Inspectors usually tap timbers and may use a moisture meter, and some use a thermal camera to look for clues behind linings. Pre-purchase timber pest inspections follow AS 4349.3, and inspections of existing buildings follow AS 3660.2.

**What the report should tell you**

| Section | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| Active termites | Whether live termites were found, and where |
| Damage | Timber damage seen, and whether a builder should assess it |
| Conducive conditions | Things that make attack more likely, such as damp, soil against walls or timber on the ground |
| Areas not inspected | Rooms, roof or subfloor areas that could not be reached, and why |
| Recommendations | Treatment, a protection system, invasive inspection or more frequent inspection |

The areas not inspected matter as much as the findings. Furniture, stored goods, fixed linings, low subfloors and covered slab edges all limit what can be seen. Read the list of limitations and ask whether a return visit or further access would change the picture. The [report-reading guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/how-to-read-a-building-and-pest-report) covers this in more detail.

sections.heading: If termites are found
sections.markdown:
Do not disturb them. A licensed pest manager will usually aim to eliminate the colony first, using methods such as baiting or treating the termites in the workings so they carry the treatment back to the nest. Once activity has stopped, the next step is a protection system to reduce the risk of future attack, such as a soil barrier or ongoing monitoring stations. Damaged timber is then assessed and repaired by a builder, since a pest manager treats the termites, not the building.

**A sensible order after a find**

| Step | Who | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Leave the workings alone and book an inspection | You | Disturbance can drive termites elsewhere |
| Identify the species and extent, and treat the colony | Licensed pest manager | Stops the current attack |
| Install or renew a protection system | Licensed pest manager | Reduces the risk of future attack |
| Assess and repair damaged framing | Builder, sometimes with an engineer | Restores the structure |
| Update the durable notice and records | Pest manager and you | Future owners and inspectors can see what was done |

Many home insurance policies exclude termite damage, so check your policy rather than assuming it is covered. This is one reason regular inspection is good value.

sections.heading: Renovations that break termite protection
sections.markdown: Protection that worked when the house was built is easily undone by later work. Extensions, new decks and verandahs, paving laid over a slab edge, garden beds against the walls, new plumbing or cables through the slab and timber stored under the house can all bridge a barrier or hide the inspection zone. Tell your pest manager before work starts, ask the builder how protection will be kept or extended, and have the system checked when the work is finished. The [renovation guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/planning-a-renovation) covers the checks to make before building.

sections.heading: Common misreads
sections.markdown:
**Things often said about termites**

| What people say | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| "The house is on a slab, so termites cannot get in" | Termites can enter through slab edges, joints and penetrations. A slab alone is not a complete system. |
| "It has a barrier, so I do not need inspections" | Barriers can be bridged or expire. Inspection at least every 12 months is what catches activity. |
| "Double brick houses are termite-proof" | Roof framing, floors, door frames and joinery are usually timber. |
| "I sprayed the mud tubes, so they are gone" | Surface sprays can drive termites elsewhere. Professional treatment targets the colony. |
| "No activity found means no problem" | A report can find no activity and still list serious conducive conditions. Fix them. |

sections.heading: Worked example: a new garden bed and an old notice
sections.markdown:
**Illustrative reasoning example, not an inspected property.** A 2008 brick-veneer house on a slab has a durable notice in the meter box for a chemical barrier, last treated in 2015. A new garden bed now covers the slab edge along one side.

The record shows a system was installed, not that it is current. The garden bed has buried the inspection zone. The next steps are to pull the bed back to expose the slab edge, have a licensed technician inspect and advise on re-treatment, and update the notice and records. See [keeping a record of your home](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/keeping-a-record-of-your-home).

guides.contentMarkdown:
# Termites by construction type: signs and protection

Subterranean termites reach timber from the ground, usually unseen, through mud tubes, cracks and anything that bridges the inspection zone. Signs include mud tubes on stumps, walls or slab edges, timber that sounds hollow or crumbles, mud packed into cracks or joints, and swarms of winged termites. No system stops termites reaching a site; protection relies on a barrier or monitoring system, an inspection zone kept visible, and inspection at least every 12 months.

## Research note
System requirements and the durable notice follow the [ABCB Housing Provisions](https://www.abcb.gov.au/editions/ncc-2022/adopted/housing-provisions/3-site-preparation/part-34-termite-risk-management). Inspection practice references AS 3660.2 and AS 4349.3, and the clearance rules come from QBCC guidance.

## Opening
### Stop them entering unseen
- **System:** A barrier or monitoring system around the building
- **Zone:** A visible inspection zone, kept clear of soil and paving
- **Inspect:** A licensed inspection at least every 12 months

_No system stops termites reaching a site. Inspection is what catches them._

In newer homes a durable notice, usually in the meter box, records the system installed.

## What you'll notice: signs of termite activity
**What to look for, and what to do**

| Sign | Where | What to do |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Mud tubes, about pencil width | Stumps, piers, walls, slab edges, behind cladding | Do not break them; arrange a licensed timber pest inspection |
| Hollow-sounding or crumbling timber | Skirting, architraves, door frames, floorboards, decks | Leave it undisturbed for the inspector |
| Mud packed into cracks or joints | Plaster cracks, cornices, timber joints | Note the location and arrange inspection |
| Swarms of winged termites | Around lights and windows on warm, humid evenings | Collect a few if you can; arrange inspection |
| Sagging floors or jamming doors and windows | Throughout | Rule out termite damage alongside other causes of movement |

Disturbing an active nest or workings can drive termites elsewhere in the building and make treatment harder. Leave suspected activity alone and get it inspected.

## How termite risk varies across Australia
Subterranean termites, which travel from a nest in the ground or a tree, cause most of the damage to Australian homes. Risk is not the same everywhere. The [ABCB Housing Provisions](https://www.abcb.gov.au/editions/ncc-2022/adopted/housing-provisions/3-site-preparation/part-34-termite-risk-management) note that termites are not considered a risk in Tasmania and are a lesser risk in parts of Victoria, and they add extra measures where the giant northern termite, *Mastotermes darwiniensis*, is prevalent. Warm, humid areas and sites with bushland, old tree stumps or damp ground tend to carry higher risk. Your council or a local pest manager can tell you what is typical for your area.

Low risk is not no risk. Homes in lower-risk areas can still be attacked, especially where timber touches the ground or the subfloor stays damp, so the basic habits in this guide apply almost everywhere.

## Conditions that invite termites
**Conducive conditions and the simple fix**

| Condition | Why it matters | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Soil, mulch or garden beds against walls | Hides entry and bridges the inspection zone | Keep the slab edge or wall base visible |
| Paving laid over the slab edge or weep holes | Termites can enter unseen beneath it | Keep paths at least 75 mm below the termite barrier |
| Leaking pipes, hot water overflows or air-conditioner drips | Moist soil attracts termites | Fix leaks; drain overflows away from the house |
| Timber in contact with the ground | A direct food source and pathway | Remove or isolate timber, sleepers and stored wood; check [deck posts](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/decks-balconies-and-balustrades) and [sleeper walls](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/retaining-walls) |
| Poor subfloor ventilation | Damp timber is more attractive and decays | Clear vents; see the subfloor guide |
| Stumps of old trees near the house | A common nest site | Have them inspected; consider removal |

The path and clearance rules come from [QBCC's maintenance guide](https://www.qbcc.qld.gov.au/sites/default/files/documents/guide-essential-home-maintenance.pdf). For raised floors, the clearance and ventilation numbers are in [subfloors, stumps and restumping](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/subfloors-stumps-and-restumping).

## Where termites get in: slabs, stumps and walls
Termites look for a hidden route from the soil to timber. The table shows the common ones; most are places where the original protection has been covered, cracked or bypassed.

**Common termite entry points**

| Entry point | Why it works for termites | What helps |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Slab edge covered by soil, paving or garden beds | The edge is the inspection zone; covering it hides any mud tubes | Keep the slab edge exposed and paths below the barrier |
| Pipes and cables through the slab | Gaps around penetrations give concealed access | Protect penetrations with collars or other treatment when they are installed |
| Cracks and joints in the slab | Termites can pass through cracks wider than a hair | Note cracking, and keep inspection access around affected areas |
| Weep holes and cavities in brick walls | A route up inside the wall cavity, out of sight | Keep weep holes above ground and clear of soil and paving |
| Stumps and piers under raised floors | A direct path to the bearers if ant caps are missing or bridged | Intact ant caps, clear subfloor access and regular inspection |
| Attached decks, pergolas and fences | Timber touching the ground and the house links soil to the building | Separate timber from the house or protect it, and inspect the junction |
| Behind cladding and render to ground level | Cladding taken down to the soil hides activity behind it | Maintain clearance between cladding and finished ground |

Older homes on stumps can be easier to inspect than slab homes, because the subfloor is open to view, provided the clearance and access are maintained. Slab homes depend more on the edge staying exposed and on protection around penetrations. The [subfloor guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/subfloors-stumps-and-restumping) and [wall-system guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/brick-veneer-vs-double-brick) show how construction changes the inspection.

## How termite management systems work
The [ABCB Housing Provisions](https://www.abcb.gov.au/editions/ncc-2022/adopted/housing-provisions/3-site-preparation/part-34-termite-risk-management) make the key point plainly: a termite management system will not stop termite activity on a site. Its job is to stop termites entering the building unseen, forcing them into the open where an inspection can find them. Its effectiveness relies on regular maintenance and competent inspection.

**Common system types**

| Type | How it works | What it needs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Chemical soil barrier | Treated soil around and under the building deters or kills termites | Periodic re-treatment; some use reticulation pipes for top-ups |
| Physical barrier | Stainless steel mesh, graded stone or termite shields block concealed entry | An intact barrier, not bridged by later work |
| Baiting and monitoring | Stations around the house detect activity and deliver bait to the colony | Regular servicing to the provider’s schedule |
| Inspection zone | A visible strip, such as an exposed slab edge, where tubes can be seen | Kept clear of soil, paving and garden beds |

### Find the durable notice

Where a termite management system is required in a new building, a durable notice must be permanently fixed in a prominent location, such as the meter box, recording the system used and advising that it should be inspected and maintained. Look for it in the meter box, and sometimes in a kitchen cupboard. If it is missing, faded or out of date, ask the vendor or owner for treatment records, and have a licensed technician confirm what is installed.

Read the timber pest report alongside the building report, as described in [how to read a building and pest report](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/how-to-read-a-building-and-pest-report).

## Renovations that break termite protection

## Common misreads

| What people say | What is closer to right |

guides.question: How can I tell if a house has old wiring or needs a switchboard upgrade?
guides.title: Switchboards, wiring and safety switches in older homes
guides.summary: How to read a switchboard and what is inside the meter box, what safety switches do and when they became required, the signs of old or failing wiring, what rewiring involves, capacity for solar, batteries and EV chargers, and the electrical certificates to keep.
guides.answer: Start at the switchboard. Old ceramic fuses rather than circuit breakers, no safety switches (devices with a test button, also called RCDs), scorch marks, a warm cover or a board with no spare space all point to an upgrade. Older rubber-insulated wiring becomes brittle with age. Any electrical work must be done by a licensed electrician, who issues a compliance certificate.
guides.methodology: We read the switchboard first, date the likely safety switch coverage by the age of the home, list warning signs of failing wiring, and separate what an owner can observe from what an electrician must test.
guides.limitations: Do not open switchboards or handle wiring. Requirements were introduced state by state; dates are national reference points.
guides.researchNote: Safety switch dates follow [Master Electricians Australia's](https://treasury.gov.au/sites/default/files/2020-09/115786_MASTER_ELECTRICIANS_AUSTRALIA.pdf) account of the wiring rules. Switchboard and wiring signs are general indicators for a licensed electrician to confirm.

sections.heading: Opening
sections.markdown:
### The switchboard tells the story
- **Fuses or breakers:** Ceramic fuses point to an original or early board
- **Safety switches:** Required on power circuits of new homes from around 1991
- **Wiring:** Older rubber-insulated cable becomes brittle with age

_Look, test the button, and leave the rest to a licensed electrician._

Safety switches have been required on the power-point circuits of new homes since around 1991, on lighting circuits since around 2000–01, and on all circuits in new installations under the 2018 wiring rules, so older homes may have none unless retrofitted.

sections.heading: Read the switchboard first
sections.markdown:
The switchboard, usually in or near the meter box, tells you more about a home’s electrical history than anything else you can safely see. Look, but do not touch anything inside it.

**What you might see at the board**

| What you see | What it suggests | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Ceramic fuse holders with fuse wire | An original or early board; overload protection only, and slow | An electrician’s assessment; an upgrade is usually recommended |
| Circuit breakers but no device with a test button | Overload protection, but no safety switch protecting people from shock | Ask an electrician about adding safety switches |
| One or two safety switches, some circuits unprotected | Typical of homes from the 1990s and 2000s | Check which circuits are covered |
| Safety switches or combined RCBOs on every circuit | A modern or upgraded board | Test the safety switches regularly |
| Scorch marks, a burning smell or a warm cover | Overheating connections | Turn off at the main switch if safe and call an electrician promptly |
| An old dark backing board | Older boards can have backing panels containing asbestos | Do not drill or cut it; see the [asbestos guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/asbestos-in-the-home) |

sections.heading: What is inside the meter box
sections.markdown:
A typical meter box holds the network's equipment and your own. Knowing the parts helps you describe what you see to an electrician and read an upgrade quote.

**Parts of a typical meter box**

| Part | What it does | Who looks after it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Service fuse | Protects the supply cable coming into the property | The network distributor; do not touch |
| Meter | Measures the electricity you use, and any solar you export | The metering provider |
| Main switch | Turns off power to the whole house | You, in an emergency |
| Circuit breakers or fuses | Protect each circuit's wiring from overload and short circuits | Your electrician |
| Safety switches (RCDs) | Cut power when current leaks to earth, such as through a person | Test them yourself regularly |
| RCBOs | A circuit breaker and safety switch combined, one per circuit | Your electrician |
| Surge protection | Limits voltage spikes reaching appliances | Your electrician |

Good boards have every circuit labelled. If the labels are missing or wrong, ask your electrician to fix them at the next visit, because a clearly labelled board makes emergencies and future work much easier.

sections.heading: Safety switches: what they do and when they became required
sections.markdown:
A circuit breaker or fuse protects the wiring from overload. A safety switch, or residual current device (RCD), protects people: it cuts power in a fraction of a second when current leaks to earth, such as through a person. They are not interchangeable. According to [Master Electricians Australia](https://treasury.gov.au/sites/default/files/2020-09/115786_MASTER_ELECTRICIANS_AUSTRALIA.pdf), safety switches have been required on power-point circuits in new homes since around 1991 and on lighting circuits since around 2000–01, and the 2018 wiring rules require them on all final circuits in new installations.

**What a home of each age is likely to have, unless upgraded**

| Built | Likely protection |
| --- | --- |
| Before around 1991 | Possibly no safety switch at all |
| Around 1991 to 2000 | Power-point circuits protected; lighting often not |
| Around 2001 to 2018 | Power and lighting protected; some circuits such as ovens or hot water may not be |
| From the 2018 wiring rules | All final circuits protected in new installations |

Press the test button on each safety switch regularly; it should trip immediately. If it does not, call an electrician. The [dated milestones table](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/red-flags-by-era#milestones) puts these dates alongside other safety changes.

sections.heading: What you'll notice: signs of old or failing wiring
sections.markdown:
**Warning signs around the house**

| Sign | Why it matters |
| --- | --- |
| Original round-pin outlets or old brown switches and fittings | Often a sign the original wiring behind them is still in place |
| Rubber-insulated cable visible in the roof space or subfloor | Older rubber insulation becomes brittle and can crack, exposing live conductors |
| Lights that flicker or dim when appliances start | Possible loose connections or an overloaded circuit |
| Warm or discoloured outlets and switches | Overheating at the connection |
| Fuses blowing or breakers tripping often | Overload or a fault; not something to keep resetting |
| Tingles from taps, appliances or metal fittings | A possible earth fault; turn off and call an electrician urgently |
| Extension leads and double adaptors everywhere | Too few outlets for modern use, and a sign of overloading |

Do not enter a roof space or subfloor to inspect wiring yourself if cables are damaged, loose or you are unsure; old cable can be live and brittle. An electrician can test insulation and earthing properly. Homes from the [interwar](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/interwar-homes-1920s-40s) and [period](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/period-homes-pre-1920s) eras are the most likely to still have original-era wiring somewhere.

sections.heading: When a safety switch keeps tripping
sections.markdown: A safety switch that trips is doing its job: it has detected current leaking to earth. Common causes are a faulty appliance, water getting into an outdoor power point or light, or damaged wiring. A simple check is to unplug everything on the affected circuits, reset the switch, then plug appliances back in one at a time. If it trips when one appliance goes back in, that appliance is the likely culprit. If it trips with nothing plugged in, or keeps tripping, call a licensed electrician. Do not keep resetting it or try to bypass it.

sections.heading: Rewiring: partial or full
sections.markdown:
When an electrician finds old or deteriorated wiring, the options range from replacing a few circuits to rewiring the whole house. A full rewire usually means new cable through the roof space and walls, new power points and switches, a new or upgraded switchboard and some patching of plaster afterwards. It is far easier and cheaper when walls are already open, so it pairs naturally with a renovation.

**Partial or full rewiring**

| Approach | When it suits | Watch for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Replace specific circuits | Only some circuits are old or damaged, often after earlier partial upgrades | Old and new wiring side by side; ask for a clear record of which circuits were done |
| Switchboard upgrade only | The board is old but the wiring tests well | An upgrade does not renew the cable in the walls |
| Full rewire | Widespread old rubber-insulated cable, failed insulation tests, or a major renovation | Making good afterwards, and access through heritage or solid masonry walls |

sections.heading: Capacity for solar, batteries, EV chargers and electric appliances
sections.markdown: Homes are asking more of their electrical systems: solar panels and batteries, electric vehicle chargers, induction cooktops and heat pump hot water and heating. Each can need space on the switchboard, extra circuits and sometimes a bigger supply. Older boards often have no spare space, and some homes are on a supply that limits how much can be added. Solar and battery systems also usually need approval from the local network before connection. Have an electrician assess the board and supply before you buy the equipment, so the upgrade is part of the plan rather than a surprise.

sections.heading: Outdoors, sheds and pools
sections.markdown: Outdoor power points and lights need to be rated for the weather and protected by a safety switch. Power run to a shed, garage or pool equipment is often added later, sometimes by people who were not licensed, so it deserves a check by an electrician. Before digging anywhere in the garden, find out where underground services run; [Before You Dig Australia](https://www.byda.com.au/) provides information on underground networks, and private cables to sheds may not appear on any plan.

sections.heading: The certificate to keep
sections.markdown: Electrical work in Australia must be done by a licensed electrician, who must provide a certificate for most work. The name differs by state: in Victoria it is a Certificate of Electrical Safety, in New South Wales a Certificate of Compliance for Electrical Work, and in Queensland a certificate of testing and safety. Ask for it every time, and keep it with the date and a description of what was done in your [home record](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/keeping-a-record-of-your-home). When buying, certificates are the best evidence that a switchboard upgrade or rewire actually happened.

sections.heading: What to ask before you buy or renovate
sections.markdown: A standard building inspection does not test electrical services. If the home is older, ask when it was rewired, whether the switchboard has been upgraded, and for the electrical compliance certificate for that work (each state names it differently). Before adding insulation, solar, batteries, air-conditioning or an EV charger, have an electrician check the switchboard and wiring, because new loads often need an upgrade first. Keep the certificates in your [home record](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/keeping-a-record-of-your-home).

sections.heading: Common misreads
sections.markdown:
**Things often said about wiring**

| What people say | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| "The lights work, so the wiring is fine" | Wiring can work while its insulation is degraded. Only testing shows its condition. |
| "Circuit breakers are the same as safety switches" | Breakers protect wiring from overload; safety switches protect people from shock. |
| "It has a safety switch, so everything is protected" | Many homes have one or two covering only some circuits. Check which. |
| "I can replace a power point myself" | In Australia, fixed electrical work must be done by a licensed electrician. |

sections.heading: Worked example: a renovated kitchen and an old board
sections.markdown:
**Illustrative reasoning example, not an inspected property.** A 1950s house has a newly renovated kitchen with modern power points, but the switchboard still has ceramic fuses and one safety switch. The listing says "fully renovated".

guides.question: How do I check the plumbing and hot water in an older house?
guides.title: Plumbing in older homes: pipes, drains, hot water and leaks
guides.summary: How to spot hidden water leaks, where to turn the water off in an emergency, what older pipes and sewer drains tell you, how the main hot water systems compare, the safe temperatures for hot water, and the plumbing records worth keeping.
guides.answer: Hidden leaks are the costliest plumbing problem, and the cheapest check is the water meter: turn every tap off, note the reading, and check again later. An unexplained rise in your water bill points the same way. Look under sinks and vanities, at flexible tap hoses and around the hot water system. Older galvanised steel pipes can corrode inside, and plumbing work must be done by a licensed plumber.
guides.methodology: We start with the cheapest diagnostic, the water meter, then read pipe materials, hot water temperatures and system checks, and separate owner observation from licensed plumbing work.
guides.limitations: The 5 August 1998 tempering date is Victorian; other states differ. All plumbing and gas work must be done by licensed practitioners.

sections.heading: Opening
sections.markdown:
### The meter finds what you cannot see
- **Leaks:** Taps off, read the meter, wait, read it again
- **Stored:** At least 60°C, to control Legionella
- **Delivered:** No more than 50°C to bathrooms

_A rising bill with a dry house usually means a hidden leak._

Hot water should be stored at 60°C or more to control Legionella and delivered at no more than 50°C to bathrooms; in Victoria, systems installed before 5 August 1998 are unlikely to be tempered.

sections.heading: What you'll notice
sections.markdown:
Most plumbing faults are heard, smelled or felt before they are found. Each sign below points to the check that narrows it down.

**Signs by sense**

| Sense | Sign | Where to read next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Hear | Running water when every tap is off, or a toilet that keeps refilling | [Finding hidden leaks](#leaks) |
| Hear | Banging or shuddering pipes when a tap closes (water hammer) | A plumber can fit an arrestor or adjust the pressure |
| Smell | Sewer smell inside, or gurgling drains | Possible blocked or cracked sewer; see [pipes](#pipes) |
| See | Rust-coloured water when a tap first runs, or damp cupboard floors | [What the pipes tell you](#pipes) |
| See | A water bill that jumps with no change in use | [The meter test](#leaks) |
| Feel | Low pressure at some taps, or hot water that runs lukewarm or scalding | [Hot water](#hot-water) |

sections.heading: Know where to turn the water off
sections.markdown:
Before anything goes wrong, find the main stop tap. It is usually beside the water meter, near the front boundary, though some homes have it in a meter box or under the house. Turning it clockwise shuts off water to the whole property. Most toilets, basins, sinks and appliances also have their own small isolation valves on the pipe underneath, and storage hot water systems have a cold-water isolation valve on the inlet.

If a pipe or flexible hose bursts, turn off the main stop tap first, then switch off power to any electrical fittings the water has reached, and call a licensed plumber. Take photos before you clean up, and note the time. Those details help with any insurance claim.

**Where the shut-offs usually are**

| Shut-off | Usual location | What it isolates |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Main stop tap | Beside the water meter, often near the front boundary | The water supply to the whole property |
| Isolation valves | On the pipe under toilets, basins, sinks and some appliances | That one fitting |
| Hot water cold-inlet valve | On the cold pipe going into a storage hot water unit | Water into the hot water system |
| Gas isolation valve | Near the gas meter, and at gas appliances | Gas to the house or to one appliance |

sections.heading: Finding hidden leaks
sections.markdown:
Many expensive water problems start as a slow leak nobody sees: under a vanity, inside a wall, under a slab or in the garden. [QBCC's maintenance guide](https://www.qbcc.qld.gov.au/sites/default/files/documents/guide-essential-home-maintenance.pdf) suggests watching for an unexplained increase in your water bill, checking under sinks and around taps, and inspecting flexible hoses, which can fail and flood a home.

**Simple leak checks**

| Check | How | What a fault looks like |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Water meter test | Turn off every tap and appliance, read the meter, wait an hour without using water, read it again | The reading has moved, or the meter’s leak indicator is turning |
| Water bills | Compare usage with the same period last year | An unexplained jump |
| Under sinks and vanities | Look and feel for damp, swelling and staining | Damp cupboard floors, swollen panels, drips at connections |
| Flexible tap hoses | Check the braided hoses under sinks and basins | Rust, fraying, kinks or bulges; replace before they burst |
| Toilets | Listen for running water; add food colouring to the cistern | Colour appears in the bowl without flushing |
| Outside | Walk the garden and the base of walls | Persistent wet patches, lush growth or sinking in dry weather; see [site drainage](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/site-drainage-and-stormwater) |

A leak near the house can also wet the soil under footings, which matters for reactive clay and termites. Read it with the [cracks](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/cracks-structural-or-cosmetic) and [termites](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/termites-in-australian-homes) guides.

sections.heading: What the pipes tell you about the house
sections.markdown:
**Common supply pipe materials**

| Material | Where you find it | What to know |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Galvanised steel | Older homes, often pre-war and early post-war | Corrodes from the inside, reducing flow and causing leaks and discoloured water |
| Copper | Very common from the mid-twentieth century onward | Durable, but joints can leak and pinhole corrosion occurs in some water conditions |
| Plastic (PEX and similar) | Newer homes and repairs | Flexible; check fittings and that it is protected from sunlight |

Low pressure at some taps, rust-coloured water when a tap first runs, or many patched joints suggest ageing pipework. A licensed plumber can tell you whether to repair sections or replace runs. Sewer and stormwater pipes are a separate system; older clay sewer pipes can be cracked or blocked by tree roots, which a CCTV drain camera can confirm.

sections.heading: Sewer and drains: older clay pipes and tree roots
sections.markdown:
The pipes that bring water in are only half the system. Waste water leaves through the sewer drain, and rain water through a separate stormwater system; the two must never be connected to each other. Older homes often have clay sewer pipes with joints every metre or so, and tree roots find their way in through those joints. Newer drains are usually PVC, which has fewer joints but can still crack, sag or be damaged by roots and digging.

**Signs of a drain problem**

| Sign | What it can mean | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Slow-draining basins, showers or toilets in several rooms | A partial blockage further down the main drain | A plumber with a drain camera |
| Gurgling from drains when another fixture empties | Air being pulled through traps by a partly blocked or poorly vented drain | Have the drain and its vents checked |
| Sewage smell inside or in the garden | A dry trap, a cracked pipe or a blockage | Run water into rarely used drains; if it persists, call a plumber |
| Overflow from the grated gully outside | The sewer is blocked; the overflow relief gully is doing its job | Stop using water and call a plumber promptly |
| Lush, wet patches in the garden along the line of the drain | A leaking or broken drain | Drain camera and pressure test |

A camera inspection shows the inside of the drain, where roots, cracks and collapses are, and often where the pipe runs. Your water authority may also hold a plan of the property's sewer connection. The private drain is generally the owner's responsibility up to the point where it joins the water authority's sewer, but where that point sits varies, so check with your local water authority before assuming who pays. The [site drainage guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/site-drainage-and-stormwater) covers the overflow relief gully and stormwater.

sections.heading: Hot water: temperatures and the system itself
sections.markdown:
Victoria's [Building and Plumbing Commission](https://www.bpc.vic.gov.au/resource-hub/safety-guides/hot-water-safety) (formerly the Victorian Building Authority) explains the two temperatures that matter. Hot water must be stored above 60°C to prevent Legionella bacteria growing, and delivered at no more than 50°C to showers, baths and basins in homes, because water at 60°C can scald in about a second. A tempering valve blends cold water in to bring the delivered temperature down. In Victoria, systems installed before 5 August 1998 are unlikely to be tempered.

**Hot water system checks**

| Check | What to look for |
| --- | --- |
| Age and type | The compliance plate shows the manufacture date; storage, continuous flow, heat pump or solar |
| Leaks and rust | Water around the base, rust streaks or a damp floor |
| Relief valve and drain | The pressure and temperature relief valve and overflow drain discharge safely, not against the house footings |
| Tempering valve | Whether one is fitted for bathrooms, especially on older systems |
| Gas systems | Flue condition and clearances; servicing by a licensed gasfitter |

Many manufacturers recommend operating the relief valve lever periodically, and servicing the system to their schedule. Check the manufacturer’s instructions for your unit, and leave adjustment and repairs to a licensed plumber.

sections.heading: Hot water systems compared
sections.markdown:
The type of system shapes what to check and what tends to go wrong. Whatever the type, the compliance plate on the unit shows the manufacture date and model, which is the first thing a plumber will want to know.

**Common hot water systems**

| Type | How it works | What to watch for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Electric storage | A tank heated by an electric element, often on an off-peak tariff | Leaks at the base, a corroding tank, element or thermostat failure |
| Gas storage | A tank heated by a gas burner with a flue | Flue condition and clearances, leaks, burner servicing |
| Continuous flow (instantaneous) | Heats water only as it is used, usually by gas | Flow and temperature settings, servicing, and whether it suits the number of outlets |
| Heat pump | Uses a compressor to move heat from the air into a tank | Noise, condensate drainage and clearances around the unit |
| Solar with a booster | Roof collectors heat a tank, with gas or electric backup | Roof collector condition, frost protection, pump and booster function |

Storage tanks usually rely on a sacrificial anode, a metal rod inside the tank that corrodes in place of the tank lining. Checking and replacing it at the intervals the manufacturer recommends can extend the life of the tank. Rust-coloured hot water, or water around the base of the unit, are signs the tank itself may be near the end of its life.

sections.heading: Water pressure, noise and hammer
sections.markdown: Pressure that is too low makes showers weak and some appliances struggle; common causes are corroded galvanised pipes, a partly closed valve, a failing pressure-limiting valve or high demand in the street. Pressure that is too high wears tap washers and fittings, causes water hammer and can shorten the life of hoses and appliances. A licensed plumber can measure the pressure and fit or adjust a pressure-limiting valve if needed.

sections.heading: Plumbing in a renovation
sections.markdown: Plumbing work in Australia must be done by a licensed plumber, and most states require a certificate or notice for the work. Keep it with the waterproofing certificate and photos of pipes before the walls were closed, in your [home record](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/keeping-a-record-of-your-home). When a kitchen, bathroom or laundry is renovated, it is usually the cheapest time to replace old supply pipes in that area, fit isolation valves and add a tempering valve if the hot water has none.

sections.heading: Leaks and insurance
sections.markdown: Home insurance policies commonly treat a sudden burst differently from a slow leak or wear and tear, and many exclude gradual damage. Read your policy's wording on escape of liquid, act quickly when you find a leak, and keep the meter readings, photos and plumber's report. The [home condition and insurance guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/home-condition-and-insurance) explains why evidence matters.

sections.heading: What to ask before you buy
sections.markdown: A standard building inspection does not test plumbing. Ask the age of the hot water system, whether there have been leaks or insurance claims, and for plumbing compliance certificates for any bathroom or kitchen renovation. If the home is older or has large trees near the sewer line, consider a drain camera inspection. For the bathroom itself, see the [waterproofing guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/bathroom-waterproofing-and-leaking-showers).

sections.heading: Common misreads
sections.markdown:
**Things often said about plumbing**

| What people say | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| "No visible water, so no leak" | Leaks inside walls, under slabs or in the garden often show only on the meter or the bill. |
| "Turning the hot water down saves money safely" | Storage below 60°C risks Legionella. Lower the delivered temperature with a tempering valve instead. |
| "The relief valve dripping means it is broken" | Some discharge can be normal operation; constant flow or none at all needs a plumber’s check. |
| "Old pipes are fine if the water runs" | Galvanised pipes can be heavily corroded inside while still flowing. |

sections.heading: Worked example: a rising bill and a dry house
sections.markdown:
**Illustrative reasoning example, not an inspected property.** A household’s water bill has risen by a third with no change in use. There are no visible leaks inside.

A meter test with every tap off shows the reading moving. Shutting off the supply to the house at the main tap stops the meter, so the leak is inside the house rather than on the garden line. A plumber pressure-tests the system and finds a failing joint under the slab near the laundry. The repair is defined and the insurer can be told early, with the meter readings and bills as evidence.

faqs.question: Where is the main water shut-off?
faqs.answer: Usually beside the water meter, near the front boundary of the property. Turning the main stop tap clockwise shuts off water to the whole house. Most fittings also have their own isolation valve underneath.

faqs.question: Who is responsible for a blocked sewer?
faqs.answer: The private drain from the house is generally the owner's responsibility up to the point where it joins the water authority's sewer. Where that point sits varies, so check with your water authority.

faqs.question: How long does a hot water system last?
faqs.answer: It depends on the type, water quality, how hard it works and how well it is serviced. Check the manufacture date on the compliance plate, look for leaks and rust, and follow the manufacturer's servicing schedule.

faqs.question: What is a sacrificial anode?
faqs.answer: A metal rod inside a storage hot water tank that corrodes in place of the tank lining. Checking and replacing it at the manufacturer's recommended intervals can extend the life of the tank.

faqs.question: Why is my water pressure low?
faqs.answer: Common causes are corroded galvanised pipes, a partly closed valve, a failing pressure-limiting valve or high demand in the street. A plumber can measure the pressure and find the cause.

faqs.question: Does home insurance cover leaking pipes?
faqs.answer: It depends on the policy. Many cover sudden bursts but exclude gradual leaks and wear. Read the wording on escape of liquid, act quickly and keep evidence such as meter readings and photos.

faqs.question: How do I check for a hidden water leak?
faqs.answer: Turn off every tap and water-using appliance, read the water meter, wait an hour without using water, and read it again. If it has moved, there is likely a leak. An unexplained rise in your water bill is another sign.

faqs.question: What temperature should hot water be in Australia?
faqs.answer: Stored at 60°C or more to prevent Legionella, and delivered at no more than 50°C to showers, baths and basins in homes. A tempering valve blends in cold water to lower the delivered temperature.

faqs.question: Do older hot water systems have tempering valves?
faqs.answer: Often not. In Victoria, systems installed before 5 August 1998 are unlikely to be tempered. A licensed plumber can fit a tempering valve or thermostatic mixing valve.

faqs.question: Should flexible tap hoses be replaced?
faqs.answer: Inspect them regularly and replace any with rust, fraying, kinks or bulges. Failed flexible hoses are a common cause of sudden flooding.

faqs.question: What are the problems with galvanised water pipes?
faqs.answer: Galvanised steel pipes, common in older homes, corrode from the inside, reducing water pressure and causing leaks and discoloured water.

faqs.question: Does a building inspection check plumbing?
faqs.answer: No. A standard pre-purchase inspection does not test plumbing services. Use a licensed plumber, and consider a drain camera inspection for older sewer lines.

A plumber pressure-tests the system and finds a failing joint under the slab near the laundry. The repair is defined and the insurer can be told early, with the meter readings and bills as evidence.

## Frequently asked questions
### Where is the main water shut-off?
Usually beside the water meter, near the front boundary of the property. Turning the main stop tap clockwise shuts off water to the whole house. Most fittings also have their own isolation valve underneath.

### Who is responsible for a blocked sewer?
The private drain from the house is generally the owner's responsibility up to the point where it joins the water authority's sewer. Where that point sits varies, so check with your water authority.

### How long does a hot water system last?
It depends on the type, water quality, how hard it works and how well it is serviced. Check the manufacture date on the compliance plate, look for leaks and rust, and follow the manufacturer's servicing schedule.

### What is a sacrificial anode?
A metal rod inside a storage hot water tank that corrodes in place of the tank lining. Checking and replacing it at the manufacturer's recommended intervals can extend the life of the tank.

### Why is my water pressure low?
Common causes are corroded galvanised pipes, a partly closed valve, a failing pressure-limiting valve or high demand in the street. A plumber can measure the pressure and find the cause.

### Does home insurance cover leaking pipes?
It depends on the policy. Many cover sudden bursts but exclude gradual leaks and wear. Read the wording on escape of liquid, act quickly and keep evidence such as meter readings and photos.

### How do I check for a hidden water leak?
Turn off every tap and water-using appliance, read the water meter, wait an hour without using water, and read it again. If it has moved, there is likely a leak. An unexplained rise in your water bill is another sign.

### What temperature should hot water be in Australia?
Stored at 60°C or more to prevent Legionella, and delivered at no more than 50°C to showers, baths and basins in homes. A tempering valve blends in cold water to lower the delivered temperature.

### Do older hot water systems have tempering valves?
Often not. In Victoria, systems installed before 5 August 1998 are unlikely to be tempered. A licensed plumber can fit a tempering valve or thermostatic mixing valve.

### Should flexible tap hoses be replaced?
Inspect them regularly and replace any with rust, fraying, kinks or bulges. Failed flexible hoses are a common cause of sudden flooding.

### What are the problems with galvanised water pipes?
Galvanised steel pipes, common in older homes, corrode from the inside, reducing water pressure and causing leaks and discoloured water.

### Does a building inspection check plumbing?
No. A standard pre-purchase inspection does not test plumbing services. Use a licensed plumber, and consider a drain camera inspection for older sewer lines.

## Method
We start with the cheapest diagnostic, the water meter, then read pipe materials, hot water temperatures and system checks, and separate owner observation from licensed plumbing work.

## Limitations
The 5 August 1998 tempering date is Victorian; other states differ. All plumbing and gas work must be done by licensed practitioners.

guides.title: Site drainage and stormwater: where the water goes

cluster.label: Read the building
cluster.blurb: Use age and construction as a starting hypothesis, then test it against evidence and physical inspection.

sections.heading: Opening
sections.markdown:
### Water away, and kept away
- **Fall:** Ground slopes away, 50 mm over the first metre
- **Height:** Slab 150 mm above ground, 50 mm above paving
- **Discharge:** Every downpipe into stormwater, not the soil

_Many cracks and damp walls start in the garden._

Ponding, damp walls, cracking near downpipes and water under the floor all point to drainage problems, which are usually cheaper to fix than the damage they cause.

sections.heading: Why drainage sits behind so many problems
sections.markdown: Water that collects against a house wets the soil under the footings, which moves on reactive clay. It feeds damp walls, decays timber and attracts termites. Poor drainage is a root cause in many of the issues covered in the [cracks](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/cracks-structural-or-cosmetic), [damp](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/damp-and-moisture-in-your-home) and [termites](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/termites-in-australian-homes) guides, so it is worth reading the site before reading the building.

sections.heading: What you'll notice
sections.markdown:
Drainage problems are easiest to spot during or just after rain. Walk the house then and note what you see.

**Signs by sense**

| Sense | Sign | Where to read next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| See | Water pooling against walls or across paths after rain | [Levels and slopes](#numbers) |
| See | Downpipes ending on the ground, or water spilling from gutters and pits | [Stormwater](#stormwater) |
| See | Garden beds or paving at or above the slab edge or weep holes | [Levels and slopes](#numbers) |
| See | Cracks at one corner of the house, near a downpipe or low point | [Cracks](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/cracks-structural-or-cosmetic) |
| Smell | Musty smell or damp air rising from under the floor after rain | [Subfloors](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/subfloors-stumps-and-restumping) |
| Hear | Gurgling drains, especially in storms | Possible blocked sewer or stormwater; a plumber and drain camera |

sections.heading: The levels and slopes that matter
sections.markdown:
The [ABCB Housing Provisions](https://www.abcb.gov.au/editions/ncc-2022/adopted/housing-provisions/3-site-preparation/part-33-drainage) set the basic requirements for new homes. Older homes were not always built to them, and later landscaping often undoes them.

**Key drainage requirements for slab-on-ground homes**

| Requirement | Minimum | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Ground slope away from the building | 50 mm over the first metre in most cases (less in some low-rainfall areas with impermeable paving) | Surface water flows away rather than towards the footings |
| Slab height above unpaved ground | 150 mm (100 mm in low-rainfall or sandy, well-drained areas) | Keeps water, splash and termites away from the building edge |
| Slab height above paving that slopes away | 50 mm | Paving sheds water but must not trap it at the wall |
| Ground under suspended floors | Graded so it sits above the outside ground and does not pond | Keeps the subfloor dry |
| Overflow relief gully | At least 150 mm below the lowest sanitary fixture | A blocked sewer overflows outside, not into the house |

[QBCC's maintenance guide](https://www.qbcc.qld.gov.au/sites/default/files/documents/guide-essential-home-maintenance.pdf) adds the everyday rules: never let soil or paving cover weep holes, keep paths at least 75 mm below the termite barrier, and do not run sprinklers against the walls.

sections.heading: Roof water and the stormwater system
sections.markdown:
A typical roof sheds a large volume of water in a storm, and all of it arrives at a few downpipes. Each downpipe should connect into a stormwater pipe that carries it to the street, a legal point of discharge or a tank, not onto the ground beside the house. Look for downpipes discharging onto the soil, broken or disconnected pipes at ground level, and pits full of silt or leaves.

**Signs of drainage trouble**

| Sign | What it can mean | Check next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Ponding near walls after rain | Ground falls towards the house, or the soil is saturated | Ground levels and where the water comes from |
| Downpipe discharging onto soil | A disconnected or missing stormwater connection | Whether a stormwater pipe exists and is clear |
| Cracking near a downpipe or corner | Wet, moving soil under the footing | Read with the [cracks guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/cracks-structural-or-cosmetic) |
| Water entering the subfloor after rain | Surface water draining under the house | Grading, ag drains and the [subfloor guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/subfloors-stumps-and-restumping) |
| Damp, mould or salts at the base of walls | Ground or paving too high, or water pooling | Slab or floor height against finished ground |
| Gurgling drains or sewage smells | A partly blocked sewer, often tree roots in older clay pipes | A plumber and a drain camera |

sections.heading: Courtyards, driveways and garages
sections.markdown:
Some of the worst drainage problems come from small details. An enclosed courtyard surrounded by walls has nowhere to send its water unless a grated drain or outlet is built in, and in a storm it can fill until water finds its way under a door. A driveway that falls towards a garage or the house carries water from the street straight to the building. A garage slab poured level with the driveway, or a back door threshold set at paving level, has no margin when water builds up.

**Small details that cause big problems**

| Detail | What happens in heavy rain | What helps |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Enclosed courtyard with no outlet | Water pools and enters under doors | A grated drain connected to stormwater, sized for the area |
| Driveway falling towards the garage or house | Street and driveway water runs to the building | A strip drain across the driveway, connected to stormwater |
| Door thresholds level with paving | Water runs straight inside once it builds up | Regrade the paving, add a strip drain, or raise the threshold where practical |
| Paving joined to the house without a fall | Water sits against the wall and soaks the edge of the slab | Relay paving with a fall away from the building |
| Roof of a carport or pergola draining towards the house | Extra water arrives at one wall | Gutters and downpipes on the structure, discharging away from the house |

sections.heading: Subsoil and agricultural drains
sections.markdown:
Not all water arrives on the surface. On sloping or poorly drained sites, water also moves through the soil and arrives at footings, basements and retaining walls from underneath. A subsoil drain, often called an ag drain, intercepts it: a slotted pipe laid in a trench of gravel, usually wrapped in a filter fabric so silt does not block it, with a fall to an outlet. The [ABCB Housing Provisions](https://www.abcb.gov.au/editions/ncc-2022/adopted/housing-provisions/3-site-preparation/part-33-drainage) include subsoil drainage where site conditions call for water to be diverted away from footings and walls.

**Subsoil drains: what to check**

| Check | Good sign | Concern |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Outlet | The drain discharges into a stormwater pit or line you can find | No visible outlet, or it ends in the garden near the house |
| Flow after rain | Clear water runs from the outlet during and after rain | Nothing flows even when the ground is saturated |
| Silt and roots | Pits and outlets clear | Silt or roots in the pit, suggesting the pipe is blocking up |
| Location | Behind retaining walls and on the uphill side of the house | A drain laid where it collects water and delivers it towards the house |

sections.heading: Pits, grates and where the water ends up
sections.markdown:
Every stormwater system has to end somewhere legal. Councils set the point of discharge for a property, which may be the street kerb, a council drain or an easement at the rear, and some sites also need on-site detention. Stormwater must never be connected into the sewer, and sewer must never be connected into stormwater. If you are not sure where your water goes, look for pits in the garden, kerb outlets at the front and any drainage easement on the title, and ask your council or water authority what plans they hold.

Grated strip drains across a garage entry or at the edge of a large paved area catch water that would otherwise run to the house. They only work if they are clear, connected and set at the right level, so lift a grate and check after rain.

sections.heading: Rainwater tanks and soakage pits
sections.markdown: A rainwater tank catches roof water, but in a big storm it fills and overflows. The overflow needs to go into the stormwater system or another approved outlet; an overflow pipe that dumps water beside the house simply moves the problem. Some properties, especially without a street drain, rely on a soakage pit to let water soak into the ground. On reactive clay that is a poor match for a location close to the house, because the pit keeps one patch of ground wet beside the footings. Ask where any soakage pit is and how far it sits from the building, and check local council requirements before adding one.

sections.heading: Read the site in the rain
sections.markdown:
The best drainage inspection happens during or just after heavy rain. A dry day hides almost everything. If you are buying, ask to revisit in wet weather; if you own the home, take a walk with an umbrella and a phone camera.

**A wet-weather walk**

| Where | What to look for |
| --- | --- |
| Gutters and downpipes | Overflow at the front of gutters, water spilling from joints, downpipes ending on the ground |
| Ground beside the walls | Water flowing towards the house, ponding against the slab or base of the walls |
| Paths and paving | Water sitting on paving at the wall, or running towards the house |
| Pits and grates | Pits overflowing or not taking water, strip drains bypassed |
| Under raised floors | Water entering or ponding under the house |
| The boundary | Water arriving from a neighbour or the street, and where it flows |

sections.heading: Common fixes and what each one solves
sections.markdown:
**Match the fix to the problem**

| Fix | What it solves | What it does not |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Connecting downpipes to stormwater | Roof water dumped beside the footings | Surface water from the garden or neighbours |
| Regrading soil and garden beds to fall away | Surface water flowing towards the house | Water arriving through the soil from uphill |
| Lowering paving or adding a strip drain | Water trapped against the wall by paving | A blocked or missing stormwater connection |
| Subsoil or cut-off drain on the uphill side | Ground water moving towards the house on a slope | Roof water or surface ponding elsewhere |
| Clearing or relining the stormwater line | Pipes blocked by roots or silt | Ground that falls the wrong way |
| Larger gutters or more downpipes | Gutters that overflow even when clean | Poor discharge further down the system |

Connecting to stormwater and altering drains is generally licensed plumbing or drainage work, so use a licensed plumber or drainer and keep the certificate and a sketch of where the pipes run. Regrading and garden changes can be done by a landscaper, but check the finished levels against the slab and weep holes before the work is signed off.

sections.heading: Sloping sites and neighbours
sections.markdown: On a slope, water from higher ground arrives at the uphill wall. A cut-off or agricultural drain behind the house, or behind a [retaining wall](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/retaining-walls), intercepts it before it reaches the building. Water flowing between properties is also a neighbour issue, with rules that vary by state, so keep photographs and records if it causes damage.

sections.heading: Common misreads
sections.markdown:
**Things often said about drainage**

| What people say | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| "New paving will keep the area dry" | Paving laid too high or falling towards the house traps water at the wall and can cover weep holes. |
| "The downpipe goes into the ground, so it is connected" | It may run into a broken pipe or soakage pit beside the footings. Check where it ends up. |
| "Garden beds against the house are fine" | They raise ground levels, hold water and hide termite entry. |
| "It only floods in big storms" | Big storms reveal the design limits; small repeated wetting often does the slow damage. |

sections.heading: Worked example: cracks at one corner only
sections.markdown:
**Illustrative reasoning example, not an inspected property.** A 1970s brick-veneer house has stepped cracking at one rear corner and nowhere else. A downpipe at that corner discharges onto a garden bed that is level with the slab.

The location points to drainage before footing failure. The first steps are to reconnect the downpipe to the stormwater system, lower the bed below the slab and regrade it to fall away, then monitor the crack through a full wet and dry season. If it stabilises, the repair is drainage and making good. If it keeps moving, an engineer assesses the footing with the drainage already corrected.

faqs.question: What is an ag drain?
faqs.answer: An agricultural or subsoil drain is a slotted pipe laid in a gravel trench, usually wrapped in filter fabric, that collects water moving through the soil and carries it to an outlet. It is common behind retaining walls and on the uphill side of houses on slopes.

faqs.question: Can downpipes be connected to the sewer?
faqs.answer: No. Stormwater and sewer systems must be kept separate. Roof water goes to the stormwater system, a tank or another approved point of discharge.

faqs.question: Is a soakage pit near the house a problem?
faqs.answer: It can be, especially on reactive clay, because it keeps one area of ground wet beside the footings. Ask how far it is from the building, and check council requirements before adding one.

faqs.question: How do I find out where my stormwater goes?
faqs.answer: Look for pits, kerb outlets and any drainage easement on the title, then ask your council or water authority what plans they hold. A plumber with a drain camera can trace the pipes.

faqs.question: What should I do about water coming from a neighbour's property?
faqs.answer: Keep dated photos and notes of when and where the water arrives, talk to your neighbour, and check your state's rules and your council's advice, since the rules on water flowing between properties vary.

faqs.question: When is the best time to check drainage?
faqs.answer: During or just after heavy rain. A wet-weather walk shows overflowing gutters, ponding, water flowing towards the house and pits that are not working.

faqs.question: How much should the ground slope away from a house?
faqs.answer: Current housing provisions require the ground around a slab to slope away by at least 50 mm over the first metre in most cases, with a smaller fall allowed in some low-rainfall areas with impermeable paving.

faqs.question: How high should a slab be above the ground?
faqs.answer: At least 150 mm above finished ground in most cases, 100 mm in low-rainfall or sandy, well-drained areas, and 50 mm above paving that slopes away from the building.

faqs.question: Where should downpipes discharge?
faqs.answer: Into a stormwater system that carries water to the street, a legal point of discharge or a tank, not onto the soil beside the house.

faqs.question: Can poor drainage cause cracks in a house?
faqs.answer: Yes. Water collecting beside footings wets the soil, and reactive clay soils swell and shrink with moisture, which can move footings and crack walls.

faqs.question: What is an overflow relief gully?
faqs.answer: A grated outlet on the sewer line outside the house, set at least 150 mm below the lowest sanitary fixture, so a blocked sewer overflows outside rather than into the house.

faqs.question: Why does water get under my house after rain?
faqs.answer: Usually because surface water flows towards the building instead of away. Regrading the ground, connecting downpipes and adding an agricultural drain on the uphill side often fixes it.
