| --- | --- | --- |
| Outlet | The drain discharges into a stormwater pit or line you can find | No visible outlet, or it ends in the garden near the house |
| Flow after rain | Clear water runs from the outlet during and after rain | Nothing flows even when the ground is saturated |
| Silt and roots | Pits and outlets clear | Silt or roots in the pit, suggesting the pipe is blocking up |
| Location | Behind retaining walls and on the uphill side of the house | A drain laid where it collects water and delivers it towards the house |

## Pits, grates and where the water ends up
Every stormwater system has to end somewhere legal. Councils set the point of discharge for a property, which may be the street kerb, a council drain or an easement at the rear, and some sites also need on-site detention. Stormwater must never be connected into the sewer, and sewer must never be connected into stormwater. If you are not sure where your water goes, look for pits in the garden, kerb outlets at the front and any drainage easement on the title, and ask your council or water authority what plans they hold.

Grated strip drains across a garage entry or at the edge of a large paved area catch water that would otherwise run to the house. They only work if they are clear, connected and set at the right level, so lift a grate and check after rain.

## Rainwater tanks and soakage pits
A rainwater tank catches roof water, but in a big storm it fills and overflows. The overflow needs to go into the stormwater system or another approved outlet; an overflow pipe that dumps water beside the house simply moves the problem. Some properties, especially without a street drain, rely on a soakage pit to let water soak into the ground. On reactive clay that is a poor match for a location close to the house, because the pit keeps one patch of ground wet beside the footings. Ask where any soakage pit is and how far it sits from the building, and check local council requirements before adding one.

## Read the site in the rain
The best drainage inspection happens during or just after heavy rain. A dry day hides almost everything. If you are buying, ask to revisit in wet weather; if you own the home, take a walk with an umbrella and a phone camera.

**A wet-weather walk**

| Where | What to look for |
| --- | --- |
| Gutters and downpipes | Overflow at the front of gutters, water spilling from joints, downpipes ending on the ground |
| Ground beside the walls | Water flowing towards the house, ponding against the slab or base of the walls |
| Paths and paving | Water sitting on paving at the wall, or running towards the house |
| Pits and grates | Pits overflowing or not taking water, strip drains bypassed |
| Under raised floors | Water entering or ponding under the house |
| The boundary | Water arriving from a neighbour or the street, and where it flows |

## Common fixes and what each one solves
**Match the fix to the problem**

| Fix | What it solves | What it does not |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Connecting downpipes to stormwater | Roof water dumped beside the footings | Surface water from the garden or neighbours |
| Regrading soil and garden beds to fall away | Surface water flowing towards the house | Water arriving through the soil from uphill |
| Lowering paving or adding a strip drain | Water trapped against the wall by paving | A blocked or missing stormwater connection |
| Subsoil or cut-off drain on the uphill side | Ground water moving towards the house on a slope | Roof water or surface ponding elsewhere |
| Clearing or relining the stormwater line | Pipes blocked by roots or silt | Ground that falls the wrong way |
| Larger gutters or more downpipes | Gutters that overflow even when clean | Poor discharge further down the system |

Connecting to stormwater and altering drains is generally licensed plumbing or drainage work, so use a licensed plumber or drainer and keep the certificate and a sketch of where the pipes run. Regrading and garden changes can be done by a landscaper, but check the finished levels against the slab and weep holes before the work is signed off.

## Sloping sites and neighbours
On a slope, water from higher ground arrives at the uphill wall. A cut-off or agricultural drain behind the house, or behind a [retaining wall](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/retaining-walls), intercepts it before it reaches the building. Water flowing between properties is also a neighbour issue, with rules that vary by state, so keep photographs and records if it causes damage.

## Common misreads
**Things often said about drainage**

| What people say | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| "New paving will keep the area dry" | Paving laid too high or falling towards the house traps water at the wall and can cover weep holes. |
| "The downpipe goes into the ground, so it is connected" | It may run into a broken pipe or soakage pit beside the footings. Check where it ends up. |
| "Garden beds against the house are fine" | They raise ground levels, hold water and hide termite entry. |
| "It only floods in big storms" | Big storms reveal the design limits; small repeated wetting often does the slow damage. |

## Worked example: cracks at one corner only
**Illustrative reasoning example, not an inspected property.** A 1970s brick-veneer house has stepped cracking at one rear corner and nowhere else. A downpipe at that corner discharges onto a garden bed that is level with the slab.

The location points to drainage before footing failure. The first steps are to reconnect the downpipe to the stormwater system, lower the bed below the slab and regrade it to fall away, then monitor the crack through a full wet and dry season. If it stabilises, the repair is drainage and making good. If it keeps moving, an engineer assesses the footing with the drainage already corrected.

## Frequently asked questions
### What is an ag drain?
An agricultural or subsoil drain is a slotted pipe laid in a gravel trench, usually wrapped in filter fabric, that collects water moving through the soil and carries it to an outlet. It is common behind retaining walls and on the uphill side of houses on slopes.

### Can downpipes be connected to the sewer?
No. Stormwater and sewer systems must be kept separate. Roof water goes to the stormwater system, a tank or another approved point of discharge.

### Is a soakage pit near the house a problem?
It can be, especially on reactive clay, because it keeps one area of ground wet beside the footings. Ask how far it is from the building, and check council requirements before adding one.

### How do I find out where my stormwater goes?
Look for pits, kerb outlets and any drainage easement on the title, then ask your council or water authority what plans they hold. A plumber with a drain camera can trace the pipes.

### What should I do about water coming from a neighbour's property?
Keep dated photos and notes of when and where the water arrives, talk to your neighbour, and check your state's rules and your council's advice, since the rules on water flowing between properties vary.

### When is the best time to check drainage?
During or just after heavy rain. A wet-weather walk shows overflowing gutters, ponding, water flowing towards the house and pits that are not working.

### How much should the ground slope away from a house?
Current housing provisions require the ground around a slab to slope away by at least 50 mm over the first metre in most cases, with a smaller fall allowed in some low-rainfall areas with impermeable paving.

### How high should a slab be above the ground?
At least 150 mm above finished ground in most cases, 100 mm in low-rainfall or sandy, well-drained areas, and 50 mm above paving that slopes away from the building.

### Where should downpipes discharge?
Into a stormwater system that carries water to the street, a legal point of discharge or a tank, not onto the soil beside the house.

### Can poor drainage cause cracks in a house?
Yes. Water collecting beside footings wets the soil, and reactive clay soils swell and shrink with moisture, which can move footings and crack walls.

### What is an overflow relief gully?
A grated outlet on the sewer line outside the house, set at least 150 mm below the lowest sanitary fixture, so a blocked sewer overflows outside rather than into the house.

### Why does water get under my house after rain?
Usually because surface water flows towards the building instead of away. Regrading the ground, connecting downpipes and adding an agricultural drain on the uphill side often fixes it.

## Method
We read the site before the building: where water arrives, where it should go, the levels that keep it away, and the symptoms that show it is not, with a fictional example.

## Limitations
Older homes may predate current requirements. Stormwater discharge and neighbour rules vary by council and state.

sections.heading: Opening
sections.markdown:
### Soil pushes; wet soil pushes harder
- **Wall:** Sleepers, masonry, blocks or concrete, on a proper footing
- **Drainage:** Gravel, an ag pipe and weep holes let water out
- **Approval:** Permits and engineering for taller and boundary walls

_A lean that is growing is movement. Date it and photograph it._

In Victoria a building permit is generally required for retaining walls of 1 metre or more, or near boundaries and other buildings; Queensland and other states have their own thresholds.

sections.heading: What a retaining wall is really holding back
sections.markdown:
Soil pushes sideways on a retaining wall, and wet soil pushes much harder. That is why a well-built wall has drainage behind it: free-draining gravel, an agricultural pipe at the base carrying water away, and weep holes or gaps letting water out. Without drainage, water builds up behind the wall after rain and adds load the wall was never designed to carry.

**Common wall types**

| Type | Typical use | What to watch for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Timber sleepers | Garden and low walls | Decay at ground level and at posts; posts leaning; sleepers bowing |
| Concrete sleepers with steel posts | Low to medium walls, often on boundaries | Rusting posts, cracked sleepers, posts not deep or plumb enough |
| Masonry (brick, block or stone) | All heights, older and newer homes | Cracking, bulging, blocked weep holes, mortar loss |
| Segmental blocks | Landscaped and stepped walls | Blocks sliding or bulging, missing geogrid on taller walls |
| Reinforced concrete | Taller walls and walls supporting buildings or driveways | Cracking, rust staining from reinforcement, blocked drainage |

sections.heading: How the drainage behind a wall should work
sections.markdown:
Most retaining wall failures are really drainage failures. Water that cannot escape builds up behind the wall and pushes far harder than dry soil. A well-built wall manages water at three levels: on the surface above, in the soil behind, and out through the base.

**Parts of a working drainage system**

| Part | What it does | What goes wrong |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Surface or spoon drain along the top | Catches water running towards the wall before it soaks in | Missing, blocked with leaves, or falling the wrong way |
| Free-draining gravel behind the wall | Lets water move down instead of building up | Replaced with soil, or clogged with silt over time |
| Filter fabric around the gravel | Stops fine soil washing into the gravel and pipe | Left out, so the drainage silts up |
| Slotted ag pipe at the base | Collects the water and carries it along the wall | Crushed, blocked or with no outlet |
| Outlet to stormwater | Takes the water somewhere it can safely go | Discharging onto a neighbour, a path or the base of the house |
| Weep holes or gaps in the face | Relieve water pressure through the wall itself | Blocked by soil, paint or mortar |

After heavy rain, water should run from the outlet and weep holes. A wall that stays dry at its base while the ground behind it is saturated is a warning sign. The [site drainage guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/site-drainage-and-stormwater) covers where that water should end up.

sections.heading: What you'll notice: signs a wall is moving or failing
sections.markdown:
**Warning signs and next steps**

| Sign | What it can mean | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Leaning outward or bulging | The wall is yielding to soil and water pressure | Keep clear and get an engineer’s assessment |
| Gaps opening between the wall and the soil above | The wall is rotating or sliding forward | Monitor with dated photos; engineer if growing |
| Cracks, especially stepped or horizontal | Movement or overload in masonry or concrete | Measure and photograph; engineer for structural walls |
| Soil or water escaping at the base | Drainage failing or the base being undermined | Check the drainage outlet and pipe |
| No drainage holes, or blocked ones | Water may be building up behind the wall | Clear outlets; ask how the wall drains |
| Rotting sleepers or posts | Timber decay, often worst at ground level | Probe gently; plan replacement before it fails |
| Cracks in paving, fences or buildings above the wall | The retained ground is moving | Engineer, especially near the house; see the [cracks guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/cracks-structural-or-cosmetic) |

A wall that is leaning, cracked and holding back a driveway or a house is a safety issue, not just maintenance. Keep people and vehicles clear and get professional advice promptly.

sections.heading: What sits on top changes everything
sections.markdown:
A retaining wall is designed for the soil behind it and for whatever sits on that soil. Engineers call extra loads on top a surcharge. A driveway, parked cars, a swimming pool, a shed, a garage slab, a heavy fence or even soil and garden beds built up behind the wall all add load. A wall that was fine holding back a lawn can start to move once a driveway or pool is built above it.

**Common surcharges and why they matter**

| Load on top | Why it matters |
| --- | --- |
| Driveways and parked cars | Heavy, repeated loads close to the wall |
| Pools and spas | Large, constant loads plus water if they leak |
| Sheds, garages and slabs | Concentrated loads near the edge |
| Fences fixed to or near the wall | Wind on the fence adds overturning force |
| Extra soil or garden beds | More weight, and more water held against the wall |
| Large trees | Root growth can push walls, and removal can change soil moisture |

Before adding anything near the top of an existing wall, ask whether the wall was designed for it. If there are no drawings, an engineer can advise.

sections.heading: Timber sleeper walls in more detail
sections.markdown: Timber sleeper walls are common and affordable, but they have a limited life. Timber in contact with the ground must be treated for in-ground use, and the posts carry most of the load, so their condition at and just below ground level matters most. Cut ends left untreated decay faster. Look for posts leaning or rotating, sleepers bowing between posts, and soft timber when you press a screwdriver gently into the base of a post. Concrete sleepers last longer but rely on steel posts, which can rust where they enter the ground.

sections.heading: Permits, engineering and boundaries
sections.markdown:
Requirements differ by state and council. In Victoria, councils such as the [City of Greater Bendigo](https://www.bendigo.vic.gov.au/building-and-business/building/building-retaining-walls) advise that a building permit is required for a retaining wall 1 metre or more in height, for walls on or near boundaries, and where excavation or filling could affect the stability of the site, an adjoining building or an adjoining lot. In Queensland, councils such as [Livingstone Shire](https://www.livingstone.qld.gov.au/downloads/file/3737/retaining-walls) advise that walls over 1 metre need a building permit from a certifier. Check with your council before building, replacing or significantly repairing a wall.

Any wall supporting a house, driveway, pool or a neighbour’s land should be designed by an engineer, whatever its height. Walls on a boundary raise questions of who owns and maintains them, which depend on state law and the title, so get advice before work that affects the neighbour.

sections.heading: Walls on or near a boundary
sections.markdown: Retaining walls on a boundary are a common source of neighbour disputes. Who is responsible usually depends on who changed the ground levels, who built the wall and the rules in your state, and it is not always the person whose land the wall stands on. A retaining wall is also different from a dividing fence, and fence laws may not apply to it. If a boundary wall is failing, keep dated photos, find any permits or plans, talk to your neighbour early and get advice on your state's rules before starting work. Do not dig beside a neighbour's wall or footings without advice.

sections.heading: Repair or replace
sections.markdown:
**Options, from simplest to most involved**

| Option | When it suits | Limits |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Clear and repair the drainage | The wall is sound but water is building up | Will not fix a wall that is already leaning or decayed |
| Replace individual sleepers | A few sleepers have decayed on an otherwise sound low wall | Posts must be sound; mixing old and new timber shortens the repair's life |
| Add or replace posts | Posts have rotted or rusted but the infill is sound | Needs a proper footing for each post |
| Rebuild with proper drainage | The wall is near the end of its life or poorly built | Major work; may need a permit |
| Engineered replacement | The wall is tall, supports a structure or is moving | Engineer design, permit and often staged work with temporary support |

If a wall is moving, do not wait for a perfect plan. Keep people and vehicles clear, remove extra load from the top where you safely can, and get an engineer to advise on temporary support while the permanent repair is designed.

sections.heading: What to ask before you buy
sections.markdown: Ask when each wall was built or replaced, whether permits and engineering exist, and how it drains. A standard building inspection may comment on visible condition but often excludes walls beyond a set distance from the house. On sloping blocks, read this alongside [site drainage and stormwater](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/site-drainage-and-stormwater), and record the answers in your [home record](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/keeping-a-record-of-your-home).

sections.heading: Common misreads
sections.markdown:
**Things often said about retaining walls**

| What people say | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| "It has stood for years, so it is fine" | Timber decays and drainage clogs slowly; failure often follows a wet season. |
| "Concrete sleepers last forever" | The steel posts can rust, and a wall is only as good as its footings and drainage. |
| "Under 1 metre, so no rules apply" | Lower walls can still need permits near boundaries or buildings, and must still be built properly. |
| "A small lean is normal" | A lean that is increasing is movement. Photograph it with a level and date it. |

sections.heading: Worked example: a sleeper wall below the driveway
sections.markdown:
**Illustrative reasoning example, not an inspected property.** A 1.2 metre treated-pine sleeper wall supports the edge of a driveway. Two posts lean outward, and a crack has opened in the driveway slab parallel to the wall. There are no drainage holes.

This is beyond maintenance. The wall carries vehicle loads, exceeds 1 metre and is moving. The next steps are to stop parking near the edge, get an engineer to assess and design a replacement with proper drainage, and lodge any required permit. Replacing sleepers like for like would repeat the original problem.

faqs.question: What is a surcharge on a retaining wall?
faqs.answer: Any extra load sitting on the ground behind the wall, such as a driveway, cars, a pool, a shed or a fence. Walls are designed for particular loads, so adding a surcharge can overload an existing wall.

faqs.question: Can I build a fence on top of a retaining wall?
faqs.answer: Only if the wall was designed for it. A fence adds weight and catches wind, which pushes on the wall. Check the drawings or ask an engineer, and check council rules on combined wall and fence heights.

faqs.question: Who is responsible for a retaining wall on the boundary?
faqs.answer: It depends on who changed the ground levels, who built the wall and your state's rules. It is not always the owner of the land it sits on. Keep records, talk to your neighbour early and get advice.

faqs.question: Do I need an engineer for a wall under 1 metre?
faqs.answer: Not always, but any wall supporting a house, driveway, pool or a neighbour's land should be engineered regardless of height, and lower walls can still need permits near boundaries or buildings.

faqs.question: What is a spoon drain?
faqs.answer: A shallow, dish-shaped surface drain that catches water running across the ground, often along the top of a retaining wall, and carries it to a pit or outlet before it soaks in behind the wall.

faqs.question: How can I tell if a sleeper wall is rotting?
faqs.answer: Look for leaning or rotating posts, sleepers bowing between posts and soft or crumbling timber at ground level. Gently probing the base of posts with a screwdriver shows whether the timber is still firm.

faqs.question: How do I know if a retaining wall is failing?
faqs.answer: Warning signs include leaning or bulging, gaps opening between the wall and the soil above, cracks, soil or water escaping at the base, blocked or missing drainage holes, rotting sleepers, and cracks in paving or buildings above the wall.

faqs.question: Do I need a permit for a retaining wall in Victoria?
faqs.answer: Generally yes for walls 1 metre or more in height, and for walls on or near boundaries or where excavation could affect a building or adjoining land. Check with your council before building or replacing one.

faqs.question: Why do retaining walls need drainage?
faqs.answer: Wet soil pushes much harder than dry soil. Free-draining gravel, an agricultural pipe and weep holes stop water building up behind the wall and overloading it.

faqs.question: How long do timber sleeper retaining walls last?
faqs.answer: It varies with timber type, treatment, drainage and soil contact. Decay usually starts at ground level and around posts, so inspect them regularly and plan replacement before failure.

faqs.question: Who is responsible for a retaining wall on a boundary?
faqs.answer: It depends on state law, the title and which side the retained soil came from. Get advice before work that affects a neighbour.

faqs.question: Does a retaining wall need an engineer?
faqs.answer: Any wall supporting a house, driveway, pool or a neighbour’s land should be designed by an engineer, and taller walls usually need engineering for a permit.

Timber sleeper walls are common and affordable, but they have a limited life. Timber in contact with the ground must be treated for in-ground use, and the posts carry most of the load, so their condition at and just below ground level matters most. Cut ends left untreated decay faster. Look for posts leaning or rotating, sleepers bowing between posts, and soft timber when you press a screwdriver gently into the base of a post. Concrete sleepers last longer but rely on steel posts, which can rust where they enter the ground.

## Permits, engineering and boundaries
Requirements differ by state and council. In Victoria, councils such as the [City of Greater Bendigo](https://www.bendigo.vic.gov.au/building-and-business/building/building-retaining-walls) advise that a building permit is required for a retaining wall 1 metre or more in height, for walls on or near boundaries, and where excavation or filling could affect the stability of the site, an adjoining building or an adjoining lot. In Queensland, councils such as [Livingstone Shire](https://www.livingstone.qld.gov.au/downloads/file/3737/retaining-walls) advise that walls over 1 metre need a building permit from a certifier. Check with your council before building, replacing or significantly repairing a wall.

Any wall supporting a house, driveway, pool or a neighbour’s land should be designed by an engineer, whatever its height. Walls on a boundary raise questions of who owns and maintains them, which depend on state law and the title, so get advice before work that affects the neighbour.

## Walls on or near a boundary
Retaining walls on a boundary are a common source of neighbour disputes. Who is responsible usually depends on who changed the ground levels, who built the wall and the rules in your state, and it is not always the person whose land the wall stands on. A retaining wall is also different from a dividing fence, and fence laws may not apply to it. If a boundary wall is failing, keep dated photos, find any permits or plans, talk to your neighbour early and get advice on your state's rules before starting work. Do not dig beside a neighbour's wall or footings without advice.

## Repair or replace
**Options, from simplest to most involved**

| Option | When it suits | Limits |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Clear and repair the drainage | The wall is sound but water is building up | Will not fix a wall that is already leaning or decayed |
| Replace individual sleepers | A few sleepers have decayed on an otherwise sound low wall | Posts must be sound; mixing old and new timber shortens the repair's life |
| Add or replace posts | Posts have rotted or rusted but the infill is sound | Needs a proper footing for each post |
| Rebuild with proper drainage | The wall is near the end of its life or poorly built | Major work; may need a permit |
| Engineered replacement | The wall is tall, supports a structure or is moving | Engineer design, permit and often staged work with temporary support |

If a wall is moving, do not wait for a perfect plan. Keep people and vehicles clear, remove extra load from the top where you safely can, and get an engineer to advise on temporary support while the permanent repair is designed.

## What to ask before you buy
Ask when each wall was built or replaced, whether permits and engineering exist, and how it drains. A standard building inspection may comment on visible condition but often excludes walls beyond a set distance from the house. On sloping blocks, read this alongside [site drainage and stormwater](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/site-drainage-and-stormwater), and record the answers in your [home record](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/keeping-a-record-of-your-home).

## Common misreads
**Things often said about retaining walls**

| What people say | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| "It has stood for years, so it is fine" | Timber decays and drainage clogs slowly; failure often follows a wet season. |
| "Concrete sleepers last forever" | The steel posts can rust, and a wall is only as good as its footings and drainage. |
| "Under 1 metre, so no rules apply" | Lower walls can still need permits near boundaries or buildings, and must still be built properly. |
| "A small lean is normal" | A lean that is increasing is movement. Photograph it with a level and date it. |

## Worked example: a sleeper wall below the driveway
**Illustrative reasoning example, not an inspected property.** A 1.2 metre treated-pine sleeper wall supports the edge of a driveway. Two posts lean outward, and a crack has opened in the driveway slab parallel to the wall. There are no drainage holes.

This is beyond maintenance. The wall carries vehicle loads, exceeds 1 metre and is moving. The next steps are to stop parking near the edge, get an engineer to assess and design a replacement with proper drainage, and lodge any required permit. Replacing sleepers like for like would repeat the original problem.

## Frequently asked questions
### What is a surcharge on a retaining wall?
Any extra load sitting on the ground behind the wall, such as a driveway, cars, a pool, a shed or a fence. Walls are designed for particular loads, so adding a surcharge can overload an existing wall.

### Can I build a fence on top of a retaining wall?
Only if the wall was designed for it. A fence adds weight and catches wind, which pushes on the wall. Check the drawings or ask an engineer, and check council rules on combined wall and fence heights.

### Who is responsible for a retaining wall on the boundary?
It depends on who changed the ground levels, who built the wall and your state's rules. It is not always the owner of the land it sits on. Keep records, talk to your neighbour early and get advice.

### Do I need an engineer for a wall under 1 metre?
Not always, but any wall supporting a house, driveway, pool or a neighbour's land should be engineered regardless of height, and lower walls can still need permits near boundaries or buildings.

### What is a spoon drain?
A shallow, dish-shaped surface drain that catches water running across the ground, often along the top of a retaining wall, and carries it to a pit or outlet before it soaks in behind the wall.

### How can I tell if a sleeper wall is rotting?
Look for leaning or rotating posts, sleepers bowing between posts and soft or crumbling timber at ground level. Gently probing the base of posts with a screwdriver shows whether the timber is still firm.

### How do I know if a retaining wall is failing?
Warning signs include leaning or bulging, gaps opening between the wall and the soil above, cracks, soil or water escaping at the base, blocked or missing drainage holes, rotting sleepers, and cracks in paving or buildings above the wall.

### Do I need a permit for a retaining wall in Victoria?
Generally yes for walls 1 metre or more in height, and for walls on or near boundaries or where excavation could affect a building or adjoining land. Check with your council before building or replacing one.

### Why do retaining walls need drainage?
Wet soil pushes much harder than dry soil. Free-draining gravel, an agricultural pipe and weep holes stop water building up behind the wall and overloading it.

### How long do timber sleeper retaining walls last?
It varies with timber type, treatment, drainage and soil contact. Decay usually starts at ground level and around posts, so inspect them regularly and plan replacement before failure.

### Who is responsible for a retaining wall on a boundary?
It depends on state law, the title and which side the retained soil came from. Get advice before work that affects a neighbour.

### Does a retaining wall need an engineer?
Any wall supporting a house, driveway, pool or a neighbour’s land should be designed by an engineer, and taller walls usually need engineering for a permit.

## Method
We explain the soil and water loads, list warning signs with next steps, and set out where permits and engineering typically apply, with a fictional example.

## Limitations
Permit rules differ by state and council and change over time. A leaning or cracked wall supporting a structure needs an engineer.

sections.heading: Opening
sections.markdown:
### Frame first, then the barrier
- **Frame:** Posts, bearers, joists and the fixing to the house
- **Barrier:** 1 m high, gaps under 125 mm, nothing to climb
- **Water:** Balconies over rooms need a membrane and clear outlets

_New boards say nothing about the frame beneath them._

Where someone could fall more than 1 metre, current housing provisions require a balustrade at least 1 metre high with gaps that will not let a 125 mm sphere pass, and where the fall exceeds 4 metres, no climbable horizontal elements between 150 mm and 760 mm above the floor. Many older decks predate these rules.

sections.heading: What you'll notice
sections.markdown:
Decks and balconies warn before they fail. Take any of these signs seriously, and keep people off a deck that moves.

**Signs by sense**

| Sense | Sign | Where to read next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Feel | A bouncy or springy deck, especially near the house | [The structure](#structure) |
| See | A gap opening between the deck and the house wall | Keep people off; see the structure checks |
| See | Soft, dark or crumbling timber at post bases, bearer ends or joist tops | [The structure](#structure) |
| See | Rust on bolts, brackets and nails, especially near the coast | [The structure](#structure) |
| Feel | A balustrade that moves or flexes when pushed | [Balustrades](#balustrades) |
| See | Stains on the ceiling below a balcony, or water ponding on its surface | [Balconies over rooms](#balconies) |

sections.heading: Check the structure first
sections.markdown:
A deck is a small structure exposed to weather on every side. Water sitting on and between timbers drives decay, and decay often starts where you cannot easily see it: the tops of joists under the boards, the ends of bearers, and post bases.

**Structural checks, where safely accessible**

| Check | Good sign | Concern |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Posts and post bases | Sound timber or steel, clear of soil, on stirrups or footings | Soft or crumbling timber at the base, rust, posts buried in soil |
| Bearers and joists | Firm when probed; dry between rains | Soft spots, fungal growth, splits at fixings, sagging |
| Connection to the house | Bolted to the house frame or slab as designed, with flashing above | Nails only, fixings into brick veneer alone, rot or water staining at the junction |
| Fixings and brackets | Galvanised or stainless, tight | Rust, especially near the coast, loose bolts, missing nails |
| Decking boards | Firm underfoot, gaps for drainage | Bouncy or springy boards, rot, cupping from poor ventilation |
| Under the deck | Ventilated, clear of debris | Low and enclosed, damp, leaves and soil packed against timber |

A deck attached to the house must be fixed to the structure, not just the outer leaf of brick veneer, which is cladding rather than structure; see [brick veneer vs double brick](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/brick-veneer-vs-double-brick). A bouncy deck, a gap opening between the deck and the house, or rot at the connection are reasons to keep people off until it has been assessed.

sections.heading: The connection to the house
sections.markdown:
The point where a deck meets the house is where the most serious failures happen. A deck can be attached to the house frame or slab, or be freestanding with its own posts along the house side. Where it is attached, the fixing must go into the structure, with a flashing above it so rain running down the wall does not soak the timber behind. Water trapped here rots the deck framing and can rot the house frame too.

**Checks at the house connection**

| Look for | What it can mean |
| --- | --- |
| A gap opening between the deck and the wall | The connection is pulling away; keep people off |
| Bolts or brackets that are rusted or loose | Fixings losing their grip |
| Staining, soft timber or mould where the deck meets the wall | Water getting behind the fixing |
| No flashing above the connection | Water is likely running into the junction |
| Fixings only into the outer leaf of brick veneer | The deck may be held by cladding rather than structure |

sections.heading: Spas, planters and parties
sections.markdown: A deck is designed for certain loads. A spa full of water and people, large planter boxes full of wet soil, an outdoor kitchen or a crowd at a party can exceed what an ordinary deck was built for. Before adding a spa or heavy features, have an engineer or builder confirm the deck can carry them or design extra support. Large gatherings are a good reason to check the structure, especially on older or elevated decks.

sections.heading: Balustrades: heights, gaps and climbing
sections.markdown:
The [ABCB Housing Provisions](https://abcb.gov.au/editions/ncc-2022/adopted/housing-provisions/11-safe-movement-and-access/part-113-barriers-and-handrails) set the rules for barriers where people could fall, and councils such as [Darebin](https://www.darebin.vic.gov.au/Planning-and-building/Building-and-renovations/Other-building-works/Handrails-and-balustrades) summarise them for owners.

**Key balustrade requirements for new work**

| Requirement | Rule | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| When a barrier is needed | Where it is possible to fall more than 1 metre | Falls from this height cause serious injury |
| Height on decks, balconies and landings | At least 1 metre above the floor | Stops adults toppling over |
| Height on stairs | At least 865 mm above the stair nosings | Matched to the stair geometry |
| Gaps | Must not let a 125 mm sphere pass through | Stops a small child slipping through |
| Climbing | Where the fall exceeds 4 metres, no climbable horizontal elements between 150 mm and 760 mm above the floor | Stops children climbing over |

Many older decks and balconies predate these rules: low balustrades, wide gaps, horizontal rails or decorative infill a child can climb. They are not automatically illegal, but they are a safety question for any household with children, and replacing a balustrade usually means meeting the current rules. Wire balustrades have specific spacing and tension requirements and slacken over time.

sections.heading: Making an older balustrade safer
sections.markdown: If an older balustrade is too low, has wide gaps or has climbable rails, there are usually practical fixes. A builder can raise the top rail, add infill such as vertical balusters or panels to close the gaps, or replace climbable horizontal rails. Glass balustrades must use safety glass suited to the purpose and be fixed as designed. Whatever the fix, it should be firm when pushed and suited to the height of the drop, and work on a balustrade where people could fall is not a job to improvise. Check with your council whether the work needs approval.

sections.heading: Balconies over rooms: waterproofing and drainage
sections.markdown:
A balcony built over a room or garage is a roof as well as a floor. Its membrane, falls and outlets must carry water away, and a blocked outlet can flood the balcony and push water into the room below. Look for ceiling stains below, efflorescence or cracking on the balcony surface, blocked outlets and missing overflows. The water paths are similar to those in the [bathroom waterproofing guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/bathroom-waterproofing-and-leaking-showers).

In apartments, balconies, balustrades and their waterproofing are often common property, with repairs organised through the owners corporation; see [strata risks for owners](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/strata-risks-for-owners).

sections.heading: Decking materials and how they age
sections.markdown:
**Common decking materials**

| Material | Strengths | What to watch |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Hardwood boards | Strong and attractive, many species are naturally durable | Greying and checking in the sun, cupping if poorly ventilated, needs regular oiling to keep its colour |
| Treated pine boards and framing | Affordable and widely used | Decay at unsealed cut ends and where water sits; splitting and movement |
| Composite boards | Low maintenance, consistent appearance | Heat in full sun, expansion gaps, fixings and the frame underneath still need checking |
| Steel or aluminium framing | Not eaten by termites or subject to decay | Corrosion near the coast or where water sits; check coatings and fixings |

Near the coast, fixings matter as much as timber. Galvanised fixings can rust within years in salty air, and stainless steel fixings last much longer. Rust stains around nails and screws are an early sign.

sections.heading: Keeping a deck sound
sections.markdown:
**A simple deck maintenance rhythm**

| When | What to do |
| --- | --- |
| Regularly | Sweep leaves and dirt from the boards and the gaps between them so water can drain |
| Every year or as the product requires | Clean and re-oil or re-coat timber boards |
| Once a year | Check fixings, balustrade firmness and the connection to the house |
| After a wet season | Look under the deck for damp, soil against posts and soft timber |
| Always | Keep garden beds, soil and mulch away from posts and framing, and keep the space under the deck ventilated |

sections.heading: What to ask before you buy
sections.markdown: Ask when the deck or balcony was built, whether it had a building permit, and whether it has been maintained or re-stained. Many councils require permits for decks above certain heights, and an unapproved deck can affect insurance and resale. Coastal and high-exposure sites need closer attention to fixings. Record what you learn in your [home record](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/keeping-a-record-of-your-home).

sections.heading: Common misreads
sections.markdown:
**Things often said about decks**

| What people say | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| "The boards look new, so the deck is sound" | Re-decking can hide decayed joists and bearers beneath. Check the frame. |
| "Treated pine does not rot" | Treated timber still decays where water sits, especially at cut ends left unsealed. |
| "The balustrade was fine when it was built" | It may predate current rules on height, gaps and climbing. |
| "It is only a small deck, so no permit was needed" | Permit rules depend on height, size and location; check with your council. |

sections.heading: Worked example: a bouncy deck after re-decking
sections.markdown:
**Illustrative reasoning example, not an inspected property.** A 1990s deck about 1.5 metres off the ground was re-decked with new boards last year. It now feels bouncy near the house, and the balustrade has horizontal rails with 140 mm gaps.

The new boards say nothing about the frame. The bounce near the house points to the connection or the joists beneath, which need inspecting before anyone holds a party on it. The balustrade fails today’s gap rule, which matters for a household with young children and will matter when it is replaced. The scope is a structural inspection, then a defined repair to the connection and frame, and a compliant balustrade.

> Important: If a deck or balcony moves, sags, or has a gap opening at the house, keep people off it until a builder or engineer has assessed it.

faqs.question: How often should I oil my deck?
faqs.answer: Usually every year or so for timber decks, or as the product's instructions say. Exposed, sunny decks may need it more often. Clean the boards first and let them dry.

faqs.question: Can I put a spa on my deck?
faqs.answer: Only if the deck is designed to carry it. A filled spa with people in it is very heavy. Have an engineer or builder confirm the structure or design additional support before installing one.

faqs.question: What fixings should a coastal deck use?
faqs.answer: Stainless steel fixings last much longer than galvanised ones in salty air. Rust stains around nails and screws are an early sign of fixings failing.

faqs.question: What is the most important part of a deck to check?
faqs.answer: The connection to the house, where most serious failures start. Look for gaps opening, rusted or loose bolts, staining and soft timber, and a missing flashing.

faqs.question: Is a glass balustrade safe?
faqs.answer: It can be when it uses safety glass suited to the purpose and is installed as designed. Check that it is firm, that fixings are intact and that there is no damage to the glass.

faqs.question: Can I fix a loose balustrade myself?
faqs.answer: Have a builder do it where people could fall from a height. A balustrade must resist people leaning and pushing on it, and a poor repair can fail when it matters most.

faqs.question: How high does a balustrade need to be in Australia?
faqs.answer: Under current housing provisions, at least 1 metre above the floor on decks, balconies and landings where it is possible to fall more than 1 metre, and at least 865 mm above the stair nosings on stairs.

faqs.question: What is the maximum gap in a balustrade?
faqs.answer: Openings must not allow a 125 mm sphere to pass through, so a small child cannot slip through.

faqs.question: What is the non-climbable zone?
faqs.answer: Where it is possible to fall more than 4 metres, balustrades must have no climbable horizontal elements between 150 mm and 760 mm above the floor, so children cannot climb over.

faqs.question: How do I check if a deck is safe?
faqs.answer: Check posts, bearers and joists for soft or decayed timber, fixings for rust, how the deck is attached to the house, and whether it feels bouncy. Keep people off a deck that moves or has a gap opening at the house.

faqs.question: Can a deck be fixed to brick veneer?
faqs.answer: Not to the brick veneer alone. Brick veneer is cladding rather than structure, so a deck must be fixed to the house frame or slab as designed, or be freestanding.

faqs.question: Do older decks have to meet current balustrade rules?
faqs.answer: Existing decks are not automatically non-compliant because rules changed, but replacing a balustrade generally means meeting current requirements, and older designs can be a real risk for children.

| Requirement | Rule | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| When a barrier is needed | Where it is possible to fall more than 1 metre | Falls from this height cause serious injury |
| Height on decks, balconies and landings | At least 1 metre above the floor | Stops adults toppling over |
| Height on stairs | At least 865 mm above the stair nosings | Matched to the stair geometry |
| Gaps | Must not let a 125 mm sphere pass through | Stops a small child slipping through |
| Climbing | Where the fall exceeds 4 metres, no climbable horizontal elements between 150 mm and 760 mm above the floor | Stops children climbing over |

Many older decks and balconies predate these rules: low balustrades, wide gaps, horizontal rails or decorative infill a child can climb. They are not automatically illegal, but they are a safety question for any household with children, and replacing a balustrade usually means meeting the current rules. Wire balustrades have specific spacing and tension requirements and slacken over time.

## Making an older balustrade safer
If an older balustrade is too low, has wide gaps or has climbable rails, there are usually practical fixes. A builder can raise the top rail, add infill such as vertical balusters or panels to close the gaps, or replace climbable horizontal rails. Glass balustrades must use safety glass suited to the purpose and be fixed as designed. Whatever the fix, it should be firm when pushed and suited to the height of the drop, and work on a balustrade where people could fall is not a job to improvise. Check with your council whether the work needs approval.

## Balconies over rooms: waterproofing and drainage
A balcony built over a room or garage is a roof as well as a floor. Its membrane, falls and outlets must carry water away, and a blocked outlet can flood the balcony and push water into the room below. Look for ceiling stains below, efflorescence or cracking on the balcony surface, blocked outlets and missing overflows. The water paths are similar to those in the [bathroom waterproofing guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/bathroom-waterproofing-and-leaking-showers).

In apartments, balconies, balustrades and their waterproofing are often common property, with repairs organised through the owners corporation; see [strata risks for owners](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/strata-risks-for-owners).

## Decking materials and how they age
**Common decking materials**

| Material | Strengths | What to watch |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Hardwood boards | Strong and attractive, many species are naturally durable | Greying and checking in the sun, cupping if poorly ventilated, needs regular oiling to keep its colour |
| Treated pine boards and framing | Affordable and widely used | Decay at unsealed cut ends and where water sits; splitting and movement |
| Composite boards | Low maintenance, consistent appearance | Heat in full sun, expansion gaps, fixings and the frame underneath still need checking |
| Steel or aluminium framing | Not eaten by termites or subject to decay | Corrosion near the coast or where water sits; check coatings and fixings |

Near the coast, fixings matter as much as timber. Galvanised fixings can rust within years in salty air, and stainless steel fixings last much longer. Rust stains around nails and screws are an early sign.

## Keeping a deck sound
**A simple deck maintenance rhythm**

| When | What to do |
| --- | --- |
| Regularly | Sweep leaves and dirt from the boards and the gaps between them so water can drain |
| Every year or as the product requires | Clean and re-oil or re-coat timber boards |
| Once a year | Check fixings, balustrade firmness and the connection to the house |
| After a wet season | Look under the deck for damp, soil against posts and soft timber |
| Always | Keep garden beds, soil and mulch away from posts and framing, and keep the space under the deck ventilated |

## What to ask before you buy
Ask when the deck or balcony was built, whether it had a building permit, and whether it has been maintained or re-stained. Many councils require permits for decks above certain heights, and an unapproved deck can affect insurance and resale. Coastal and high-exposure sites need closer attention to fixings. Record what you learn in your [home record](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/keeping-a-record-of-your-home).

## Common misreads
**Things often said about decks**

| What people say | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| "The boards look new, so the deck is sound" | Re-decking can hide decayed joists and bearers beneath. Check the frame. |
| "Treated pine does not rot" | Treated timber still decays where water sits, especially at cut ends left unsealed. |
| "The balustrade was fine when it was built" | It may predate current rules on height, gaps and climbing. |
| "It is only a small deck, so no permit was needed" | Permit rules depend on height, size and location; check with your council. |

## Worked example: a bouncy deck after re-decking
**Illustrative reasoning example, not an inspected property.** A 1990s deck about 1.5 metres off the ground was re-decked with new boards last year. It now feels bouncy near the house, and the balustrade has horizontal rails with 140 mm gaps.

The new boards say nothing about the frame. The bounce near the house points to the connection or the joists beneath, which need inspecting before anyone holds a party on it. The balustrade fails today’s gap rule, which matters for a household with young children and will matter when it is replaced. The scope is a structural inspection, then a defined repair to the connection and frame, and a compliant balustrade.

> Important: If a deck or balcony moves, sags, or has a gap opening at the house, keep people off it until a builder or engineer has assessed it.

## Frequently asked questions
### How often should I oil my deck?
Usually every year or so for timber decks, or as the product's instructions say. Exposed, sunny decks may need it more often. Clean the boards first and let them dry.

### Can I put a spa on my deck?
Only if the deck is designed to carry it. A filled spa with people in it is very heavy. Have an engineer or builder confirm the structure or design additional support before installing one.

### What fixings should a coastal deck use?
Stainless steel fixings last much longer than galvanised ones in salty air. Rust stains around nails and screws are an early sign of fixings failing.

### What is the most important part of a deck to check?
The connection to the house, where most serious failures start. Look for gaps opening, rusted or loose bolts, staining and soft timber, and a missing flashing.

### Is a glass balustrade safe?
It can be when it uses safety glass suited to the purpose and is installed as designed. Check that it is firm, that fixings are intact and that there is no damage to the glass.

### Can I fix a loose balustrade myself?
Have a builder do it where people could fall from a height. A balustrade must resist people leaning and pushing on it, and a poor repair can fail when it matters most.

### How high does a balustrade need to be in Australia?
Under current housing provisions, at least 1 metre above the floor on decks, balconies and landings where it is possible to fall more than 1 metre, and at least 865 mm above the stair nosings on stairs.

### What is the maximum gap in a balustrade?
Openings must not allow a 125 mm sphere to pass through, so a small child cannot slip through.

### What is the non-climbable zone?
Where it is possible to fall more than 4 metres, balustrades must have no climbable horizontal elements between 150 mm and 760 mm above the floor, so children cannot climb over.

### How do I check if a deck is safe?
Check posts, bearers and joists for soft or decayed timber, fixings for rust, how the deck is attached to the house, and whether it feels bouncy. Keep people off a deck that moves or has a gap opening at the house.

### Can a deck be fixed to brick veneer?
Not to the brick veneer alone. Brick veneer is cladding rather than structure, so a deck must be fixed to the house frame or slab as designed, or be freestanding.

### Do older decks have to meet current balustrade rules?
Existing decks are not automatically non-compliant because rules changed, but replacing a balustrade generally means meeting current requirements, and older designs can be a real risk for children.

## Method
We check the structure first, then the balustrade rules for new work, then waterproofing for balconies over rooms, with a fictional example.

## Limitations
Rules shown are for new work under current provisions; older decks may predate them. Structural condition needs safe access and professional assessment.

sections.heading: Opening
sections.markdown:
### Photoelectric, interconnected, everywhere people sleep
- **Type:** Photoelectric alarms to AS 3786:2014
- **Connected:** When one sounds, they all sound
- **Kept:** Tested monthly, replaced every 10 years

_A hallway alarm may not hear a fire behind a closed bedroom door._

Rules differ by state: in Queensland, every home must have interconnected photoelectric alarms by 1 January 2027, while Victoria requires an alarm on every storey and hardwired alarms in homes built after 1 August 1997.

sections.heading: What you'll notice
sections.markdown:
Most smoke alarm problems are easy to miss until they matter. These are the signs worth acting on.

**Signs by sense**

| Sense | Sign | What to do |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Hear | A short chirp every minute or so | Usually a low battery or an alarm reaching the end of its life; replace the battery or the unit |
| See | A manufacture date more than 10 years ago, or no date at all | Replace the alarm; see [testing and replacement](#maintenance) |
| See | Yellowed, painted-over or dusty alarms | Clean gently or replace; paint can block the sensor |
| See | No alarm in bedrooms, or only one alarm on a level | Add alarms; see [placement](#placement) |
| Hear | Only the alarm near the fire sounds when tested | The alarms are not interconnected; see [types and power](#types) |
| See | An apartment entry door that no longer closes by itself | A possible fire safety breach; see [apartments and fire doors](#apartments) |

sections.heading: Types of alarm and how they are powered
sections.markdown:
There are two main sensing types. **Photoelectric** alarms detect visible smoke particles and respond earlier to slow, smouldering fires, which are common in homes; **ionisation** alarms respond to the small particles of fast, flaming fires. Victorian fire services and the [Queensland Fire Department](https://fire.qld.gov.au/smokealarms) recommend photoelectric alarms that meet AS 3786:2014. Queensland's rules now require them and prohibit alarms with an ionisation sensor.

**Power and connection options**

| Option | How it works | What to know |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Hardwired (mains) with backup battery | Connected to the house wiring, with a battery for power cuts | Must be installed by a licensed electrician; required in many newer homes |
| Sealed 10-year lithium battery | Battery lasts the life of the alarm and cannot be removed | No yearly battery change; replace the whole unit at 10 years |
| Replaceable 9-volt battery | Battery changed by the owner | Change the battery every year; the least reliable option |
| Interconnected | All alarms sound together, by wiring or wirelessly | The single biggest improvement: a fire in a closed bedroom may not set off a hallway alarm |

[Victoria's fire services note](https://www.wodonga.vic.gov.au/Newsroom/Archive/ArtMID/1777/ArticleID/10355) that in Fire and Rescue NSW tests where a fire started in a bedroom with the door closed, the hallway alarms did not activate at all. That is why interconnected alarms in bedrooms matter.

sections.heading: Where alarms should go
sections.markdown: As a minimum, most states require an alarm on every storey, between sleeping areas and the rest of the home, in the path people would use to escape. Fire services recommend going further: interconnected alarms in every bedroom, hallway and living area. Alarms go on the ceiling, kept clear of the corner where wall meets ceiling; [Boroondara Council](https://www.boroondara.vic.gov.au/node/89306) gives at least 30 cm from the wall. Avoid spots near kitchens, bathrooms and air-conditioning vents that cause false alarms.

sections.heading: Kitchens, bathrooms and garages
sections.markdown:
Smoke alarms placed too close to a cooktop, toaster or bathroom door go off from cooking fumes and steam, and that is the most common reason people disable them. Place alarms in the hallway or living area outside these rooms, rather than right next to them, and follow the manufacturer's spacing advice. A photoelectric alarm with a hush button lets you silence a cooking false alarm for a few minutes without disabling it.

Heat alarms respond to a rise in temperature rather than smoke, so they suit kitchens and garages where smoke alarms would false alarm. They react later than smoke alarms and are not a substitute for smoke alarms in bedrooms, hallways and living areas. If you add heat alarms, choose ones that can be interconnected with the smoke alarms so the whole house hears them.

sections.heading: Alarms for people who are deaf or hard of hearing
sections.markdown: A standard alarm may not wake someone who is deaf or hard of hearing, or someone who removes hearing aids at night. Specialised alarm systems add a strobe light and a vibrating pad that goes under the pillow or mattress, triggered when the smoke alarms sound. Several states and fire services run programs that help with the cost or the installation, so ask your state fire service what is available.

sections.heading: The rules in Queensland and Victoria
sections.markdown:
**Key requirements and dates**

| State | Requirement |
| --- | --- |
| Queensland | New and substantially renovated homes since 1 January 2017, and homes sold or leased since 1 January 2022, need photoelectric, interconnected alarms in every bedroom, in hallways connecting bedrooms and on every storey. From **1 January 2027 this applies to every home**, owner-occupied included ([Queensland Fire Department](https://fire.qld.gov.au/prepare/fire/smoke-alarms/faq)) |
| Victoria | Smoke alarms are compulsory in every home, on every storey. Homes built after 1 August 1997 must have mains-powered alarms with battery backup, and new homes since 1 May 2014 must have interconnected alarms ([Boroondara Council](https://www.boroondara.vic.gov.au/node/89306), [Master Electricians Australia](https://www.masterelectricians.com.au/?p=12756)) |
| Other states | Each sets its own rules, usually at least one working alarm on every storey, with extra requirements for rentals and new homes; check your state fire service |

Landlords have extra obligations in every state, and when a home is renovated or extended, newer requirements can apply to the new work. The [dated milestones table](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/red-flags-by-era#milestones) shows when mains-powered and interconnected alarms began for new homes nationally.

sections.heading: Testing, cleaning and replacing
sections.markdown:
**Smoke alarm maintenance**

| How often | Task |
| --- | --- |
| Monthly | Press the test button on every alarm; with interconnected alarms, check they all sound |
| Every year | Replace 9-volt batteries, if your alarms use them |
| Regularly | Gently vacuum the vents to clear dust and insects |
| Every 10 years | Replace every alarm, including hardwired ones; check the date on the base |

These intervals follow [Victoria's fire services](https://www.cfa.vic.gov.au/plan-prepare/fires-in-the-home/home-fire-safety-communications-kit/smoke-alarms) and Victorian council guidance. Hardwired alarms must be replaced by a licensed electrician; sealed 10-year battery alarms can usually be fitted by the owner. Never disconnect an alarm because of false alarms; move it or replace it with the right type.

sections.heading: Rentals
sections.markdown: Landlords in every state have obligations to install and maintain working smoke alarms, and several states also set testing and replacement duties before and during a tenancy. Tenants usually need to test alarms and report faults promptly, and must not remove batteries or disable alarms. Rules and timeframes vary, so landlords should check with their state's consumer affairs or tenancy regulator and keep records of each check and repair.

sections.heading: Apartments: fire doors and shared safety systems
sections.markdown:
In many apartment buildings, each unit's entry door is part of the building's fire safety system: a fire-rated or solid-core door that must close and latch by itself. A fire door usually carries a metal tag on its hinge edge. A door that no longer self-closes, a removed closer, a painted-over tag, an unapproved lock change or a security screen fitted to the door can all compromise it, as [strata fire safety specialists explain](https://www.lookupstrata.com.au/nsw-fire-door-not-self-closing/).

Shared systems, such as fire doors, alarms, extinguishers, exit signs and emergency lighting, are maintained by the owners corporation under state rules, such as Victoria's essential safety measures and NSW's annual fire safety statement. Ask before altering your entry door, and report one that will not close. See [strata risks for owners](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/strata-risks-for-owners).

sections.heading: Beyond alarms: the rest of home fire safety
sections.markdown: Alarms give warning; the house still needs a way out and fewer ways for fire to start. Agree a home escape plan with everyone in the household, keep keys near deadlocked doors, and keep exits clear. Old wiring, overloaded power boards and faulty heaters are common causes of house fires, so read the [switchboards and wiring guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/switchboards-wiring-and-safety-switches), and have gas heaters serviced, as set out in [heating, cooling and gas safety](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/heating-cooling-and-gas-safety). In bushfire-prone areas, see [preparing your home for extreme weather](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/preparing-your-home-for-extreme-weather).

sections.heading: A simple home escape plan
sections.markdown:
Alarms buy time; a plan turns that time into a safe exit. Fire services recommend every household agrees and practises a plan.

**Making a home escape plan**

| Step | What to do |
| --- | --- |
| Draw the home | Mark every room, door and window, and two ways out of each room where possible |
| Keep exits usable | Keep keys in deadlocks or close by, and keep hallways and doors clear |
| Agree a meeting place | Choose a safe spot outside, such as the letterbox, where everyone gathers |
| Plan for everyone | Decide who helps young children, older people, people with disability and pets |
| Practise | Walk through the plan with the household, including at night |
| Get out and stay out | Once outside, call 000 and do not go back in |

A fire blanket and a fire extinguisher in or near the kitchen are worth having, provided everyone knows how to use them and understands that getting out comes first. Never use water on a fat or oil fire.

sections.heading: Common misreads
sections.markdown:
**Things often said about smoke alarms**

| What people say | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| "The alarm works, the light is on" | The light shows power, not that the sensor works. Press the test button monthly. |
| "Hardwired alarms last forever" | All smoke alarms, hardwired included, should be replaced every 10 years. |
| "One alarm in the hallway is enough" | A fire behind a closed bedroom door may not reach it. Interconnected alarms in bedrooms close that gap. |
| "It keeps going off when I cook, so I took the battery out" | Move the alarm or replace it with the right type; a disabled alarm protects no one. |

sections.heading: Worked example: a 1990s house with two hardwired alarms
sections.markdown:
**Illustrative reasoning example, not an inspected property.** A 1998 Victorian house has two hardwired alarms in the hallways, dated 2009. The bedrooms have none, and pressing one alarm's test button does not set off the other.

The house meets the requirement it was built to, but the alarms are past 10 years and are not interconnected. The practical upgrade is a licensed electrician replacing them with photoelectric alarms, adding interconnected alarms in each bedroom and the living area. The electrician's certificate goes in the [home record](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/keeping-a-record-of-your-home).

faqs.question: Should I put a smoke alarm in the kitchen?
faqs.answer: Usually not right in the kitchen, because cooking causes false alarms. Place smoke alarms in the hallway or living area outside it, and consider an interconnected heat alarm in the kitchen itself.

faqs.question: What is a heat alarm?
faqs.answer: An alarm that responds to a rise in temperature rather than smoke. It suits kitchens and garages, but reacts later than a smoke alarm and does not replace smoke alarms in bedrooms, hallways and living areas.

faqs.question: Are there smoke alarms for people who are deaf?
faqs.answer: Yes. Specialised systems add a strobe light and a vibrating pad under the pillow or mattress, triggered by the smoke alarms. Ask your state fire service about programs that help with cost or installation.

faqs.question: Who is responsible for smoke alarms in a rental?
faqs.answer: Landlords must install and maintain working smoke alarms, and several states set testing and replacement duties. Tenants should test alarms, report faults and never disable them. Check your state's tenancy rules for the details.

faqs.question: What should a home fire escape plan include?
faqs.answer: Two ways out of each room where possible, keys kept near deadlocks, a meeting place outside, who helps whom, and practice. Once outside, call 000 and do not go back in.

faqs.question: What type of smoke alarm is best?
faqs.answer: Fire services recommend photoelectric smoke alarms meeting AS 3786:2014, interconnected so they all sound together, and either mains-powered with a backup battery or fitted with a sealed 10-year battery.

faqs.question: Where should smoke alarms be installed?
faqs.answer: At least on every storey, between sleeping areas and the rest of the home, on the ceiling and clear of the wall-to-ceiling corner. Fire services recommend interconnected alarms in every bedroom, hallway and living area.

faqs.question: What are the new Queensland smoke alarm rules?
faqs.answer: From 1 January 2027, every Queensland home must have photoelectric, interconnected smoke alarms in every bedroom, in hallways connecting bedrooms and on every storey, either hardwired with backup or with a sealed 10-year battery. Homes sold or leased have needed them since 2022.

faqs.question: What are the smoke alarm rules in Victoria?
faqs.answer: Smoke alarms are compulsory in every Victorian home, on every storey. Homes built after 1 August 1997 need mains-powered alarms with battery backup, and new homes since 1 May 2014 need interconnected alarms. Landlords have additional obligations.

faqs.question: How often should smoke alarms be tested and replaced?
faqs.answer: Test them monthly with the test button, replace 9-volt batteries yearly, and replace every alarm, including hardwired ones, every 10 years.

faqs.question: Why does my smoke alarm chirp?
faqs.answer: Usually because the battery is low or the alarm has reached the end of its life. Replace the battery, or the whole unit if it is near 10 years old or has a sealed battery.

faqs.question: Can I install smoke alarms myself?
faqs.answer: You can usually fit alarms with a sealed 10-year battery yourself. Hardwired alarms must be installed or replaced by a licensed electrician.

faqs.question: Is my apartment front door a fire door?
faqs.answer: Often, yes. Look for a metal tag on the hinge edge. Fire doors must close and latch by themselves; do not remove the closer, paint over the tag, change the lock or fit a screen door without approval from the owners corporation.
