If you add heat alarms, choose ones that can be interconnected with the smoke alarms so the whole house hears them.

## Alarms for people who are deaf or hard of hearing
A standard alarm may not wake someone who is deaf or hard of hearing, or someone who removes hearing aids at night. Specialised alarm systems add a strobe light and a vibrating pad that goes under the pillow or mattress, triggered when the smoke alarms sound. Several states and fire services run programs that help with the cost or the installation, so ask your state fire service what is available.

## The rules in Queensland and Victoria
**Key requirements and dates**

| State | Requirement |
| --- | --- |
| Queensland | New and substantially renovated homes since 1 January 2017, and homes sold or leased since 1 January 2022, need photoelectric, interconnected alarms in every bedroom, in hallways connecting bedrooms and on every storey. From **1 January 2027 this applies to every home**, owner-occupied included ([Queensland Fire Department](https://fire.qld.gov.au/prepare/fire/smoke-alarms/faq)) |
| Victoria | Smoke alarms are compulsory in every home, on every storey. Homes built after 1 August 1997 must have mains-powered alarms with battery backup, and new homes since 1 May 2014 must have interconnected alarms ([Boroondara Council](https://www.boroondara.vic.gov.au/node/89306), [Master Electricians Australia](https://www.masterelectricians.com.au/?p=12756)) |
| Other states | Each sets its own rules, usually at least one working alarm on every storey, with extra requirements for rentals and new homes; check your state fire service |

Landlords have extra obligations in every state, and when a home is renovated or extended, newer requirements can apply to the new work. The [dated milestones table](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/red-flags-by-era#milestones) shows when mains-powered and interconnected alarms began for new homes nationally.

## Testing, cleaning and replacing
**Smoke alarm maintenance**

| How often | Task |
| --- | --- |
| Monthly | Press the test button on every alarm; with interconnected alarms, check they all sound |
| Every year | Replace 9-volt batteries, if your alarms use them |
| Regularly | Gently vacuum the vents to clear dust and insects |
| Every 10 years | Replace every alarm, including hardwired ones; check the date on the base |

These intervals follow [Victoria's fire services](https://www.cfa.vic.gov.au/plan-prepare/fires-in-the-home/home-fire-safety-communications-kit/smoke-alarms) and Victorian council guidance. Hardwired alarms must be replaced by a licensed electrician; sealed 10-year battery alarms can usually be fitted by the owner. Never disconnect an alarm because of false alarms; move it or replace it with the right type.

## Rentals
Landlords in every state have obligations to install and maintain working smoke alarms, and several states also set testing and replacement duties before and during a tenancy. Tenants usually need to test alarms and report faults promptly, and must not remove batteries or disable alarms. Rules and timeframes vary, so landlords should check with their state's consumer affairs or tenancy regulator and keep records of each check and repair.

## Apartments: fire doors and shared safety systems
In many apartment buildings, each unit's entry door is part of the building's fire safety system: a fire-rated or solid-core door that must close and latch by itself. A fire door usually carries a metal tag on its hinge edge. A door that no longer self-closes, a removed closer, a painted-over tag, an unapproved lock change or a security screen fitted to the door can all compromise it, as [strata fire safety specialists explain](https://www.lookupstrata.com.au/nsw-fire-door-not-self-closing/).

Shared systems, such as fire doors, alarms, extinguishers, exit signs and emergency lighting, are maintained by the owners corporation under state rules, such as Victoria's essential safety measures and NSW's annual fire safety statement. Ask before altering your entry door, and report one that will not close. See [strata risks for owners](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/strata-risks-for-owners).

## Beyond alarms: the rest of home fire safety
Alarms give warning; the house still needs a way out and fewer ways for fire to start. Agree a home escape plan with everyone in the household, keep keys near deadlocked doors, and keep exits clear. Old wiring, overloaded power boards and faulty heaters are common causes of house fires, so read the [switchboards and wiring guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/switchboards-wiring-and-safety-switches), and have gas heaters serviced, as set out in [heating, cooling and gas safety](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/heating-cooling-and-gas-safety). In bushfire-prone areas, see [preparing your home for extreme weather](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/preparing-your-home-for-extreme-weather).

## A simple home escape plan
Alarms buy time; a plan turns that time into a safe exit. Fire services recommend every household agrees and practises a plan.

**Making a home escape plan**

| Step | What to do |
| --- | --- |
| Draw the home | Mark every room, door and window, and two ways out of each room where possible |
| Keep exits usable | Keep keys in deadlocks or close by, and keep hallways and doors clear |
| Agree a meeting place | Choose a safe spot outside, such as the letterbox, where everyone gathers |
| Plan for everyone | Decide who helps young children, older people, people with disability and pets |
| Practise | Walk through the plan with the household, including at night |
| Get out and stay out | Once outside, call 000 and do not go back in |

A fire blanket and a fire extinguisher in or near the kitchen are worth having, provided everyone knows how to use them and understands that getting out comes first. Never use water on a fat or oil fire.

## Common misreads
**Things often said about smoke alarms**

| What people say | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| "The alarm works, the light is on" | The light shows power, not that the sensor works. Press the test button monthly. |
| "Hardwired alarms last forever" | All smoke alarms, hardwired included, should be replaced every 10 years. |
| "One alarm in the hallway is enough" | A fire behind a closed bedroom door may not reach it. Interconnected alarms in bedrooms close that gap. |
| "It keeps going off when I cook, so I took the battery out" | Move the alarm or replace it with the right type; a disabled alarm protects no one. |

## Worked example: a 1990s house with two hardwired alarms
**Illustrative reasoning example, not an inspected property.** A 1998 Victorian house has two hardwired alarms in the hallways, dated 2009. The bedrooms have none, and pressing one alarm's test button does not set off the other.

The house meets the requirement it was built to, but the alarms are past 10 years and are not interconnected. The practical upgrade is a licensed electrician replacing them with photoelectric alarms, adding interconnected alarms in each bedroom and the living area. The electrician's certificate goes in the [home record](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/keeping-a-record-of-your-home).

## Frequently asked questions
### Should I put a smoke alarm in the kitchen?
Usually not right in the kitchen, because cooking causes false alarms. Place smoke alarms in the hallway or living area outside it, and consider an interconnected heat alarm in the kitchen itself.

### What is a heat alarm?
An alarm that responds to a rise in temperature rather than smoke. It suits kitchens and garages, but reacts later than a smoke alarm and does not replace smoke alarms in bedrooms, hallways and living areas.

### Are there smoke alarms for people who are deaf?
Yes. Specialised systems add a strobe light and a vibrating pad under the pillow or mattress, triggered by the smoke alarms. Ask your state fire service about programs that help with cost or installation.

### Who is responsible for smoke alarms in a rental?
Landlords must install and maintain working smoke alarms, and several states set testing and replacement duties. Tenants should test alarms, report faults and never disable them. Check your state's tenancy rules for the details.

### What should a home fire escape plan include?
Two ways out of each room where possible, keys kept near deadlocks, a meeting place outside, who helps whom, and practice. Once outside, call 000 and do not go back in.

### What type of smoke alarm is best?
Fire services recommend photoelectric smoke alarms meeting AS 3786:2014, interconnected so they all sound together, and either mains-powered with a backup battery or fitted with a sealed 10-year battery.

### Where should smoke alarms be installed?
At least on every storey, between sleeping areas and the rest of the home, on the ceiling and clear of the wall-to-ceiling corner. Fire services recommend interconnected alarms in every bedroom, hallway and living area.

### What are the new Queensland smoke alarm rules?
From 1 January 2027, every Queensland home must have photoelectric, interconnected smoke alarms in every bedroom, in hallways connecting bedrooms and on every storey, either hardwired with backup or with a sealed 10-year battery. Homes sold or leased have needed them since 2022.

### What are the smoke alarm rules in Victoria?
Smoke alarms are compulsory in every Victorian home, on every storey. Homes built after 1 August 1997 need mains-powered alarms with battery backup, and new homes since 1 May 2014 need interconnected alarms. Landlords have additional obligations.

### How often should smoke alarms be tested and replaced?
Test them monthly with the test button, replace 9-volt batteries yearly, and replace every alarm, including hardwired ones, every 10 years.

### Why does my smoke alarm chirp?
Usually because the battery is low or the alarm has reached the end of its life. Replace the battery, or the whole unit if it is near 10 years old or has a sealed battery.

### Can I install smoke alarms myself?
You can usually fit alarms with a sealed 10-year battery yourself. Hardwired alarms must be installed or replaced by a licensed electrician.

### Is my apartment front door a fire door?
Often, yes. Look for a metal tag on the hinge edge. Fire doors must close and latch by themselves; do not remove the closer, paint over the tag, change the lock or fit a screen door without approval from the owners corporation.

## Method
We start from the signs owners notice, explain alarm types and power, set out placement and the Queensland and Victorian rules with dates, then cover maintenance and apartment fire doors, with a fictional example.

## Limitations
Smoke alarm laws differ by state and change over time; confirm current requirements with your state fire service. Hardwired work must be done by a licensed electrician.

guides.title: Heating, cooling and gas safety: checking older systems
guides.summary: How to identify and check a home’s heating and cooling, tell which type of gas heater you have, how often to service each system, how to avoid carbon monoxide, what to check on ducts, evaporative coolers and wood heaters, and how to think about replacement.

Open-flued gas heaters, which draw air from the room, can spill carbon monoxide if exhaust fans run at the same time or the room lacks ventilation.

guides.limitations: Servicing advice and the 2022 open-flued requirement are Victorian; other states differ. All gas work must be done by a licensed gasfitter.

cluster.blurb: Use age and construction as a starting hypothesis, then test it against evidence and physical inspection.

sections.heading: Opening
sections.markdown:
### Service it, ventilate it, know your heater
- **Service:** Gas heaters at least every two years, with a spillage test
- **Ventilate:** No exhaust fans while an open-flued heater runs
- **Backup:** A carbon monoxide alarm warns; it does not prevent

_Carbon monoxide has no colour and no smell._

Carbon monoxide is colourless and odourless, so headaches, nausea or dizziness that ease away from home deserve attention. An alarm is a backup, never a substitute for servicing.

sections.heading: What you'll notice
sections.markdown:
Heating and cooling faults usually show up as changes in comfort, sound or smell. Some gas warning signs are urgent; treat them that way.

**Signs by sense**

| Sense | Sign | What to do |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Feel | Headaches, nausea, dizziness or drowsiness that ease when you leave the house | Turn the heater off, ventilate, get fresh air and seek medical advice; then have the heater checked |
| See | A yellow or orange gas flame, soot or scorch marks around a heater or flue | Stop using it until a gasfitter has inspected it |
| Smell | Gas | Turn appliances off, avoid switches and flames, ventilate, leave and call your gas emergency line |
| See | A pilot light that keeps going out, or condensation and staining around a heater | Have it serviced; see [gas heaters](#gas) |
| Hear | Rattling, grinding or new noises from a split system or ducted unit | [Systems and servicing](#systems) |
| Feel | Uneven temperatures, weak airflow from vents, or a system that runs constantly | Filters, ducts or refrigerant; see systems and servicing |
| Smell | Musty air from vents or a split system when it starts | Dirty filters or coils, or moisture in ducts; see [damp](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/damp-and-moisture-in-your-home) |

sections.heading: Systems and servicing
sections.markdown:
**Common systems in Australian homes**

| System | How it works | What to check and service |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Split system (reverse-cycle) | An indoor unit and outdoor heat pump heat and cool one area | Clean filters every few months; keep the outdoor unit clear; professional service as the manufacturer recommends |
| Ducted reverse-cycle | One heat pump serves the house through ducts in the roof or floor | Filters, duct condition and insulation, zone controls, outdoor unit clearance |
| Ducted gas heating | A gas furnace heats air and pushes it through ducts | Gas service at least every two years, including the heat exchanger and a carbon monoxide test |
| Gas space heater (wall or freestanding) | Heats one room; may be room-sealed, open-flued or flueless | Gas service at least every two years; know which type it is |
| Hydronic | A boiler heats water piped to radiators or under the floor | Boiler service, pressure, leaks at radiators and valves |
| Wood heater or open fire | Burns wood, venting through a flue or chimney | Annual flue cleaning, dry fuel, clearances to combustibles |
| Evaporative cooler | Cools by evaporating water, usually from a roof unit | Seasonal service, pads, water supply and drainage, roof penetration seals |

Ask for service records for every system when buying, and note its age from the compliance plate. Old systems are not automatically unsafe or inefficient, but a ducted gas heater or split system with no service history deserves a check before you rely on it.

sections.heading: Gas heaters and carbon monoxide
sections.markdown:
[Energy Safe Victoria](https://www.energysafe.vic.gov.au/community-safety/energy-safety-guides/home-safety/heating-your-home-gas) warns that all gas heaters can spill or leak carbon monoxide, and that spillage can be lethal. It recommends that every gas space heater, central heater and gas water heater be serviced at least every two years by a qualified gasfitter, and Victoria's [Department of Health](https://health.vic.gov.au/environmental-health/carbon-monoxide-poisoning-in-the-home) gives the same advice for central heating, wall units and gas log fires.

**Gas heater types and the carbon monoxide risk**

| Type | Where it gets its air | What to know |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Room-sealed | From outside, through a sealed flue | Not affected by room ventilation or exhaust fans; Energy Safe Victoria recommends this type |
| Open-flued | From the room, venting through a flue in the ceiling or wall | Can spill carbon monoxide into the room under negative pressure; needs room ventilation and no exhaust fans running |
| Flueless (unflued) | From the room, venting into the room | Needs generous ventilation; rules on their use vary by state |

**Negative pressure** is the key risk. When a rangehood, bathroom fan or toilet fan runs in a well-sealed home, it can pull air down an open-flued heater's flue and draw carbon monoxide back into the room. Energy Safe Victoria advises not running exhaust fans while an open-flued heater is on, and keeping some ventilation in the room. Since 1 August 2022, any open-flued gas space heater sold or installed in Victoria must shut down automatically if it starts spilling. Ask your gasfitter whether your heater is open-flued, and whether it has that protection.

A service should include a **negative pressure and combustion spillage test**, not only a clean. Victoria's Department of Health has warned specifically against using Vulcan Heritage or Pyrox Heritage gas heaters until they have been tested and serviced.

### Carbon monoxide alarms

Because carbon monoxide has no colour or smell, a carbon monoxide alarm is a sensible backup in homes with gas or wood heating. It is not a substitute for servicing: an alarm warns once carbon monoxide is present, while servicing stops it being produced. Fit it to the manufacturer's instructions and replace it at the end of its stated life.

sections.heading: How to tell which type of gas heater you have
sections.markdown:
The type of gas heater decides how much the room's ventilation matters, so it is worth knowing which one you have. A gasfitter can confirm it, but these clues help.

**Clues to the heater type**

| Type | Clues | Confirm with |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Room-sealed | A flue that runs straight through the external wall behind the heater, often with a terminal visible outside; the heater draws air from outside | The compliance plate or manual, and a gasfitter |
| Open-flued | A flue running up through the ceiling or roof, or into a chimney; the heater draws air from the room | The compliance plate or manual, and a gasfitter |
| Flueless (unflued) | No flue at all; often a portable or freestanding gas heater | The manual; rules on use vary by state |

If you are not sure, treat the heater as open-flued until a gasfitter tells you otherwise: do not run exhaust fans while it is on, and keep some ventilation in the room.

sections.heading: Ducted systems: what lives in the roof or under the floor
sections.markdown:
Ducted heating and cooling depends on ducts you rarely see. Ducts can come apart at joints, be crushed by people walking in the roof space, sag onto the ceiling, or lose their insulation, so warm or cool air is lost before it reaches the room. Look from the roof hatch or subfloor where it is safe, and ask a technician to check ducts at each service. Musty smells from vents can mean moisture or dirt in the ducts.

**Duct problems and their signs**

| Problem | What you notice |
| --- | --- |
| Disconnected or split duct | One room gets little or no air; the roof space feels warm when heating runs |
| Crushed or kinked duct | Weak airflow from one vent |
| Damaged duct insulation | Higher running costs; condensation on ducts in cooling mode |
| Dirty ducts or filters | Musty smells, dust from vents, reduced airflow |

sections.heading: Evaporative coolers
sections.markdown: Evaporative coolers sit on the roof and push cooled, moist air through ducts. They need a seasonal service to clean pads and water reservoirs and check the pump and water supply, and their drainage must not discharge onto the roof or against the house. The roof penetration around the unit is a common leak point, so include it in roof checks. In winter, a duct closer or cover stops warm air escaping through the cooler. The [roofs guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/roofs-tiles-metal-and-leaks) covers penetrations.

sections.heading: Wood heaters and open fires
sections.markdown: Wood heaters and open fires need a clean flue, dry seasoned wood and safe clearances to anything that can burn. Have the flue cleaned at least once a year, or as the manufacturer recommends, because built-up creosote can catch fire. Check that the heater has a compliance plate and was installed with the right clearances and hearth, and that the flue is clear of overhanging trees and roof materials. Carbon monoxide can come from wood heaters too, so a carbon monoxide alarm is sensible in homes that use them.

sections.heading: Replacing an old system
sections.markdown: When an old heater or cooler reaches the end of its life, it is a chance to think about the whole home. Reverse-cycle air conditioners are heat pumps, which are generally efficient for both heating and cooling, and replacing an open-flued gas heater with a room-sealed or electric system removes the carbon monoxide risk from negative pressure. Energy Rating labels help compare models, and sizing matters: an undersized system runs constantly and an oversized one cycles inefficiently. Improving insulation and draught-proofing at the same time, while keeping ventilation that any remaining gas appliance needs, often does more for comfort than the heater alone. The [insulation and ventilation guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/insulation-ventilation-and-condensation) explains how they fit together.

sections.heading: What to ask before you buy or rent
sections.markdown: Ask which heating and cooling systems the home has, their ages, and the date and findings of the last gas service, including whether a carbon monoxide test was done. A standard building inspection does not test gas appliances. For older homes, check gas heaters and flues alongside the wiring in the [switchboards guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/switchboards-wiring-and-safety-switches), and pair heating with a working smoke alarm system from the [fire safety guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/smoke-alarms-and-fire-safety-at-home).

sections.heading: Common misreads
sections.markdown:
**Things often said about heating**

| What people say | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| "It lights and gets warm, so it is fine" | A heater can run while spilling carbon monoxide. Only a gasfitter's spillage test shows it. |
| "A carbon monoxide alarm means I can skip servicing" | The alarm is a backup. Servicing at least every two years prevents the problem. |
| "Sealing up draughts is always good" | In a home with an open-flued heater, sealing without ventilation can raise the carbon monoxide risk. |
| "Ducted heating vents are just dusty" | Musty vents can mean moisture in ducts or dirty coils; have the system checked. |

sections.heading: Worked example: a draught-proofed house with an old wall heater
sections.markdown:
**Illustrative reasoning example, not an inspected property.** An owner has draught-sealed a 1970s house to save energy. The living room has a 1990s gas wall heater with a flue through the ceiling, and a new powerful rangehood in the open kitchen. Family members have had headaches on cold evenings.

The heater is likely open-flued, the house is now tighter, and the rangehood can create negative pressure. The immediate step is to stop using the heater and the rangehood together, ventilate, and see a doctor about the symptoms. Then a gasfitter carries out a negative pressure and spillage test and advises on ventilation, repair or replacing it with a room-sealed heater or reverse-cycle system. See [insulation, ventilation and condensation](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/insulation-ventilation-and-condensation) for balancing a tighter home.

> Important: If you smell gas or suspect carbon monoxide, turn appliances off if safe, open doors and windows, get everyone outside and call your gas emergency line or 000. Do not use switches or naked flames near a gas smell.

faqs.question: How can I tell if my gas heater is open-flued?
faqs.answer: An open-flued heater draws air from the room and usually has a flue running up through the ceiling or into a chimney. A room-sealed heater has a flue straight through the external wall. Check the compliance plate or manual, and ask a gasfitter to confirm.

faqs.question: Should I replace my gas heater with reverse-cycle air conditioning?
faqs.answer: It is worth considering when an old gas heater needs replacing. Reverse-cycle systems are heat pumps that are generally efficient for heating and cooling, and removing an open-flued heater removes its carbon monoxide risk. Compare Energy Rating labels and size the system to the space.

faqs.question: What does a gas heater service include?
faqs.answer: A qualified gasfitter inspects and cleans the heater, checks the installation and flue, and tests for carbon monoxide spillage, including under negative pressure. Ask for a written record of the results.

faqs.question: How often should a wood heater flue be cleaned?
faqs.answer: At least once a year, or as the manufacturer recommends. Built-up creosote in the flue can catch fire.

faqs.question: Why does my evaporative cooler leak into the house?
faqs.answer: Common causes are a failed seal where the unit passes through the roof, blocked drainage or an overflowing reservoir. Have it serviced and the roof penetration checked.

faqs.question: How often should a gas heater be serviced?
faqs.answer: Energy Safe Victoria recommends every gas heater, including central heaters and gas water heaters, be serviced at least every two years by a qualified gasfitter, with a carbon monoxide spillage test.

faqs.question: What is an open-flued gas heater?
faqs.answer: A gas heater that draws its combustion air from the room and vents through a flue in the ceiling or wall. It can spill carbon monoxide into the room if exhaust fans run or the room lacks ventilation. A gasfitter can tell you which type you have.

faqs.question: Can exhaust fans cause carbon monoxide poisoning?
faqs.answer: They can contribute. Rangehoods and bathroom or toilet fans can create negative pressure that draws carbon monoxide from an open-flued heater back into the room. Do not run them while an open-flued heater is on.

faqs.question: What are the symptoms of carbon monoxide poisoning?
faqs.answer: Headaches, nausea, dizziness, tiredness and flu-like symptoms, often easing when you leave the house. Turn the heater off, ventilate, get fresh air and seek medical advice.

faqs.question: Do I need a carbon monoxide alarm?
faqs.answer: It is a sensible backup in homes with gas or wood heating, but it does not replace servicing at least every two years.

faqs.question: How often should I clean split system filters?
faqs.answer: Every few months during regular use, or as the manufacturer recommends. Dirty filters reduce airflow and efficiency and can cause musty smells.

faqs.question: Does a building inspection check the heating?
faqs.answer: Not in any depth. A standard inspection does not test gas appliances or air-conditioning. Ask for service records and use a licensed gasfitter or technician.

## Research note
Gas heater servicing, open-flued risk and negative pressure follow [Energy Safe Victoria](https://www.energysafe.vic.gov.au/community-safety/energy-safety-guides/home-safety/heating-your-home-gas) and Victoria's Department of Health. System descriptions are general; follow each manufacturer's service schedule.

| Feel | Headaches, nausea, dizziness or drowsiness that ease when you leave the house | Turn the heater off, ventilate, get fresh air and seek medical advice; then have the heater checked |
| See | A yellow or orange gas flame, soot or scorch marks around a heater or flue | Stop using it until a gasfitter has inspected it |
| Smell | Gas | Turn appliances off, avoid switches and flames, ventilate, leave and call your gas emergency line |
| See | A pilot light that keeps going out, or condensation and staining around a heater | Have it serviced; see [gas heaters](#gas) |
| Hear | Rattling, grinding or new noises from a split system or ducted unit | [Systems and servicing](#systems) |
| Feel | Uneven temperatures, weak airflow from vents, or a system that runs constantly | Filters, ducts or refrigerant; see systems and servicing |
| Smell | Musty air from vents or a split system when it starts | Dirty filters or coils, or moisture in ducts; see [damp](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/damp-and-moisture-in-your-home) |

## Systems and servicing
**Common systems in Australian homes**

| System | How it works | What to check and service |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Split system (reverse-cycle) | An indoor unit and outdoor heat pump heat and cool one area | Clean filters every few months; keep the outdoor unit clear; professional service as the manufacturer recommends |
| Ducted reverse-cycle | One heat pump serves the house through ducts in the roof or floor | Filters, duct condition and insulation, zone controls, outdoor unit clearance |
| Ducted gas heating | A gas furnace heats air and pushes it through ducts | Gas service at least every two years, including the heat exchanger and a carbon monoxide test |
| Gas space heater (wall or freestanding) | Heats one room; may be room-sealed, open-flued or flueless | Gas service at least every two years; know which type it is |
| Hydronic | A boiler heats water piped to radiators or under the floor | Boiler service, pressure, leaks at radiators and valves |
| Wood heater or open fire | Burns wood, venting through a flue or chimney | Annual flue cleaning, dry fuel, clearances to combustibles |
| Evaporative cooler | Cools by evaporating water, usually from a roof unit | Seasonal service, pads, water supply and drainage, roof penetration seals |

Ask for service records for every system when buying, and note its age from the compliance plate. Old systems are not automatically unsafe or inefficient, but a ducted gas heater or split system with no service history deserves a check before you rely on it.

## Gas heaters and carbon monoxide
[Energy Safe Victoria](https://www.energysafe.vic.gov.au/community-safety/energy-safety-guides/home-safety/heating-your-home-gas) warns that all gas heaters can spill or leak carbon monoxide, and that spillage can be lethal. It recommends that every gas space heater, central heater and gas water heater be serviced at least every two years by a qualified gasfitter, and Victoria's [Department of Health](https://health.vic.gov.au/environmental-health/carbon-monoxide-poisoning-in-the-home) gives the same advice for central heating, wall units and gas log fires.

**Gas heater types and the carbon monoxide risk**

| Type | Where it gets its air | What to know |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Room-sealed | From outside, through a sealed flue | Not affected by room ventilation or exhaust fans; Energy Safe Victoria recommends this type |
| Open-flued | From the room, venting through a flue in the ceiling or wall | Can spill carbon monoxide into the room under negative pressure; needs room ventilation and no exhaust fans running |
| Flueless (unflued) | From the room, venting into the room | Needs generous ventilation; rules on their use vary by state |

**Negative pressure** is the key risk. When a rangehood, bathroom fan or toilet fan runs in a well-sealed home, it can pull air down an open-flued heater's flue and draw carbon monoxide back into the room. Energy Safe Victoria advises not running exhaust fans while an open-flued heater is on, and keeping some ventilation in the room. Since 1 August 2022, any open-flued gas space heater sold or installed in Victoria must shut down automatically if it starts spilling. Ask your gasfitter whether your heater is open-flued, and whether it has that protection.

A service should include a **negative pressure and combustion spillage test**, not only a clean. Victoria's Department of Health has warned specifically against using Vulcan Heritage or Pyrox Heritage gas heaters until they have been tested and serviced.

### Carbon monoxide alarms

Because carbon monoxide has no colour or smell, a carbon monoxide alarm is a sensible backup in homes with gas or wood heating. It is not a substitute for servicing: an alarm warns once carbon monoxide is present, while servicing stops it being produced. Fit it to the manufacturer's instructions and replace it at the end of its stated life.

## How to tell which type of gas heater you have
The type of gas heater decides how much the room's ventilation matters, so it is worth knowing which one you have. A gasfitter can confirm it, but these clues help.

**Clues to the heater type**

| Type | Clues | Confirm with |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Room-sealed | A flue that runs straight through the external wall behind the heater, often with a terminal visible outside; the heater draws air from outside | The compliance plate or manual, and a gasfitter |
| Open-flued | A flue running up through the ceiling or roof, or into a chimney; the heater draws air from the room | The compliance plate or manual, and a gasfitter |
| Flueless (unflued) | No flue at all; often a portable or freestanding gas heater | The manual; rules on use vary by state |

If you are not sure, treat the heater as open-flued until a gasfitter tells you otherwise: do not run exhaust fans while it is on, and keep some ventilation in the room.

## Ducted systems: what lives in the roof or under the floor
Ducted heating and cooling depends on ducts you rarely see. Ducts can come apart at joints, be crushed by people walking in the roof space, sag onto the ceiling, or lose their insulation, so warm or cool air is lost before it reaches the room. Look from the roof hatch or subfloor where it is safe, and ask a technician to check ducts at each service. Musty smells from vents can mean moisture or dirt in the ducts.

**Duct problems and their signs**

| Problem | What you notice |
| --- | --- |
| Disconnected or split duct | One room gets little or no air; the roof space feels warm when heating runs |
| Crushed or kinked duct | Weak airflow from one vent |
| Damaged duct insulation | Higher running costs; condensation on ducts in cooling mode |
| Dirty ducts or filters | Musty smells, dust from vents, reduced airflow |

## Evaporative coolers
Evaporative coolers sit on the roof and push cooled, moist air through ducts. They need a seasonal service to clean pads and water reservoirs and check the pump and water supply, and their drainage must not discharge onto the roof or against the house. The roof penetration around the unit is a common leak point, so include it in roof checks. In winter, a duct closer or cover stops warm air escaping through the cooler. The [roofs guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/roofs-tiles-metal-and-leaks) covers penetrations.

## Wood heaters and open fires
Wood heaters and open fires need a clean flue, dry seasoned wood and safe clearances to anything that can burn. Have the flue cleaned at least once a year, or as the manufacturer recommends, because built-up creosote can catch fire. Check that the heater has a compliance plate and was installed with the right clearances and hearth, and that the flue is clear of overhanging trees and roof materials. Carbon monoxide can come from wood heaters too, so a carbon monoxide alarm is sensible in homes that use them.

## Replacing an old system
When an old heater or cooler reaches the end of its life, it is a chance to think about the whole home. Reverse-cycle air conditioners are heat pumps, which are generally efficient for both heating and cooling, and replacing an open-flued gas heater with a room-sealed or electric system removes the carbon monoxide risk from negative pressure. Energy Rating labels help compare models, and sizing matters: an undersized system runs constantly and an oversized one cycles inefficiently. Improving insulation and draught-proofing at the same time, while keeping ventilation that any remaining gas appliance needs, often does more for comfort than the heater alone. The [insulation and ventilation guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/insulation-ventilation-and-condensation) explains how they fit together.

## What to ask before you buy or rent
Ask which heating and cooling systems the home has, their ages, and the date and findings of the last gas service, including whether a carbon monoxide test was done. A standard building inspection does not test gas appliances. For older homes, check gas heaters and flues alongside the wiring in the [switchboards guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/switchboards-wiring-and-safety-switches), and pair heating with a working smoke alarm system from the [fire safety guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/smoke-alarms-and-fire-safety-at-home).

## Common misreads
**Things often said about heating**

| What people say | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| "It lights and gets warm, so it is fine" | A heater can run while spilling carbon monoxide. Only a gasfitter's spillage test shows it. |
| "A carbon monoxide alarm means I can skip servicing" | The alarm is a backup. Servicing at least every two years prevents the problem. |
| "Sealing up draughts is always good" | In a home with an open-flued heater, sealing without ventilation can raise the carbon monoxide risk. |
| "Ducted heating vents are just dusty" | Musty vents can mean moisture in ducts or dirty coils; have the system checked. |

## Worked example: a draught-proofed house with an old wall heater
**Illustrative reasoning example, not an inspected property.** An owner has draught-sealed a 1970s house to save energy. The living room has a 1990s gas wall heater with a flue through the ceiling, and a new powerful rangehood in the open kitchen. Family members have had headaches on cold evenings.

The heater is likely open-flued, the house is now tighter, and the rangehood can create negative pressure. The immediate step is to stop using the heater and the rangehood together, ventilate, and see a doctor about the symptoms. Then a gasfitter carries out a negative pressure and spillage test and advises on ventilation, repair or replacing it with a room-sealed heater or reverse-cycle system. See [insulation, ventilation and condensation](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/insulation-ventilation-and-condensation) for balancing a tighter home.

> Important: If you smell gas or suspect carbon monoxide, turn appliances off if safe, open doors and windows, get everyone outside and call your gas emergency line or 000. Do not use switches or naked flames near a gas smell.

## Frequently asked questions
### How can I tell if my gas heater is open-flued?
An open-flued heater draws air from the room and usually has a flue running up through the ceiling or into a chimney. A room-sealed heater has a flue straight through the external wall. Check the compliance plate or manual, and ask a gasfitter to confirm.

### Should I replace my gas heater with reverse-cycle air conditioning?
It is worth considering when an old gas heater needs replacing. Reverse-cycle systems are heat pumps that are generally efficient for heating and cooling, and removing an open-flued heater removes its carbon monoxide risk. Compare Energy Rating labels and size the system to the space.

### What does a gas heater service include?
A qualified gasfitter inspects and cleans the heater, checks the installation and flue, and tests for carbon monoxide spillage, including under negative pressure. Ask for a written record of the results.

### How often should a wood heater flue be cleaned?
At least once a year, or as the manufacturer recommends. Built-up creosote in the flue can catch fire.

### Why does my evaporative cooler leak into the house?
Common causes are a failed seal where the unit passes through the roof, blocked drainage or an overflowing reservoir. Have it serviced and the roof penetration checked.

### How often should a gas heater be serviced?
Energy Safe Victoria recommends every gas heater, including central heaters and gas water heaters, be serviced at least every two years by a qualified gasfitter, with a carbon monoxide spillage test.

### What is an open-flued gas heater?
A gas heater that draws its combustion air from the room and vents through a flue in the ceiling or wall. It can spill carbon monoxide into the room if exhaust fans run or the room lacks ventilation. A gasfitter can tell you which type you have.

### Can exhaust fans cause carbon monoxide poisoning?
They can contribute. Rangehoods and bathroom or toilet fans can create negative pressure that draws carbon monoxide from an open-flued heater back into the room. Do not run them while an open-flued heater is on.

### What are the symptoms of carbon monoxide poisoning?
Headaches, nausea, dizziness, tiredness and flu-like symptoms, often easing when you leave the house. Turn the heater off, ventilate, get fresh air and seek medical advice.

### Do I need a carbon monoxide alarm?
It is a sensible backup in homes with gas or wood heating, but it does not replace servicing at least every two years.

### How often should I clean split system filters?
Every few months during regular use, or as the manufacturer recommends. Dirty filters reduce airflow and efficiency and can cause musty smells.

### Does a building inspection check the heating?
Not in any depth. A standard inspection does not test gas appliances or air-conditioning. Ask for service records and use a licensed gasfitter or technician.

## Method
We start from what owners notice, identify each system type and its servicing, then set out the gas heater types, negative pressure and carbon monoxide risk, with a fictional example.

## Limitations
Servicing advice and the 2022 open-flued requirement are Victorian; other states differ. All gas work must be done by a licensed gasfitter.

guides.question: How do I insulate and draught-proof an older home without causing condensation?
guides.title: Insulation, ventilation and condensation: warm and dry
guides.summary: How insulation, draught-proofing, ventilation and condensation work together, how to read the type and condition of existing insulation, what windows and roof spaces contribute, where to start in an older home, and what to check after the work is done.
guides.answer: Warmth, air and moisture are one system. Insulation slows heat loss, draught-sealing stops cold air leaking in, and ventilation removes the moisture a household produces. Start with the ceiling, which is usually the easiest and most effective place to insulate, but have an electrician check older wiring first and keep the required clearances around downlights. A tighter home without ventilation can trap moisture, causing condensation and mould, and can be dangerous with an open-flued gas heater.
guides.methodology: We treat heat, air and moisture as one system: where to insulate first and how to do it safely, how to find and seal draughts, and how to ventilate so condensation does not follow, with a fictional example.
guides.limitations: R-value requirements and installer licensing vary by climate zone and state. Electrical checks and clearances must follow the wiring rules and a licensed electrician.
guides.researchNote: Insulation safety follows [Sustainability Victoria](https://www.sustainability.vic.gov.au/energy-efficiency-and-reducing-emissions/building-or-renovating/build-for-energy-efficiency/key-principles-of-energy-efficient-design/insulation/health-and-safety) and South Australian Government guidance; condensation and design principles follow YourHome and the NCC 2022 condensation provisions.

cluster.label: Read the building
cluster.blurb: Use age and construction as a starting hypothesis, then test it against evidence and physical inspection.

sections.heading: Opening
sections.markdown:
### Insulate, seal, then ventilate
- **Insulate:** Ceiling first, after an electrical check
- **Seal:** Doors, windows, floors and unused chimneys
- **Ventilate:** Bathroom, kitchen and laundry exhausts to outside

_A tighter house needs its moisture taken out on purpose._

Seal draughts around doors, windows and floors, then make sure bathroom, kitchen and laundry exhausts vent outside rather than into the roof space.

sections.heading: What you'll notice
sections.markdown:
Most homes show where heat and moisture are escaping or collecting. These are the common signs.

**Signs by sense**

| Sense | Sign | Where to read next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Feel | Cold rooms despite heating, or rooms that overheat in summer | [Insulation](#insulation) |
| Feel | Cold air around doors, windows, skirting, floorboards or an unused fireplace | [Draughts](#draughts) |
| See | Water running down windows on cold mornings, or wet window frames | [Condensation](#condensation) |
| See | Black mould spots on ceilings, in corners or behind wardrobes | [Condensation](#condensation) |
| See | Bathroom mirrors and walls that stay wet long after a shower | [Ventilation](#ventilation) |
| See | Damp or stained insulation, or rusty nails, in the roof space | [Roof-space condensation](#condensation) |
| Smell | A stuffy or musty smell in a closed-up house | [Ventilation](#ventilation) |

sections.heading: Heat, air and moisture work as one system
sections.markdown: A household adds a lot of moisture to the air every day through showers, cooking, drying clothes and breathing. In a leaky, uninsulated house, cold draughts carry it away, at the cost of comfort and energy. When the same house is insulated and sealed, that moisture has to be removed deliberately, by ventilation, or it condenses on the coldest surfaces. [YourHome](https://www.yourhome.gov.au/passive-design/insulation) treats insulation, sealing and ventilation as parts of the same design, and so should any upgrade.

sections.heading: Insulation: where to start
sections.markdown:
**Where insulation goes in an existing home**

| Location | Ease in an existing home | What to know |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Ceiling | Usually the easiest, from the roof space | Often the biggest gain; check existing depth and condition, and top up rather than compress |
| Underfloor (raised timber floors) | Possible where there is subfloor access | Keep subfloor vents open; see [subfloors](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/subfloors-stumps-and-restumping) |
| Walls | Hard without removing linings or cladding | Best done during renovation or recladding; cavity fills need specialist advice on moisture |
| Roof (under the covering) | Usually only when re-roofing | A reflective or insulating layer is easiest to add when the roof is off |

Insulation performance is measured as its **R-value**: the higher, the better it resists heat flow. Requirements and recommendations vary by climate; the ACT, for example, recommends ceiling insulation of at least R5, and notes that [many homes built before 1997 have little or none](https://www.climatechoices.act.gov.au/policy-programs/home-energy-support-rebates-for-homeowners/ceiling-insulation). Insulation also settles and degrades over time, so an older layer may be thinner than it looks.

### Insulation safety: wiring and downlights

Ceiling insulation work has a history of fires and electrical accidents, so the order matters. [Sustainability Victoria](https://www.sustainability.vic.gov.au/energy-efficiency-and-reducing-emissions/building-or-renovating/build-for-energy-efficiency/key-principles-of-energy-efficient-design/insulation/health-and-safety) and the [South Australian Government](https://www.sa.gov.au/topics/energy-and-environment/energy-efficient-home-design/home-insulation-safety) advise:

**Before insulation goes in**

| Check | Why |
| --- | --- |
| Have a licensed electrician inspect the wiring first | Old wiring can overheat when covered; SA flags wiring installed before 1986 in particular |
| Keep clearances around downlights | Sustainability Victoria gives at least 200 mm above recessed halogen downlights and 50 mm around transformers, under the wiring rules |
| Consider replacing old downlights | Some modern LED downlights are rated to be covered, which reduces the uninsulated gaps |
| Keep foil-faced insulation away from wiring | Foil can become live; never fix it with metal staples |
| Keep clear of flues, exhaust fans and heaters | Hot fittings need clearance from insulation |
| Use a licensed or certified installer | Required in some states, and safer in all |

See the [switchboards and wiring guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/switchboards-wiring-and-safety-switches) for what older wiring looks like. Never enter a roof space with damaged or loose cables, and stop if you suspect asbestos.

sections.heading: Reading the insulation you already have
sections.markdown:
Before adding more, look at what is there. From the roof hatch, where it is safe, note the type, how deep it is, whether it covers the whole ceiling and whether it has been pushed aside by tradespeople or disturbed by rodents.

**Common insulation types**

| Type | What it looks like | What to check |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Glasswool or rockwool batts | Fibrous batts, often yellow, pink, white or grey | Gaps between batts, compressed or displaced batts, damp patches |
| Polyester batts | Soft white synthetic batts | Gaps and displacement, as for other batts |
| Loose-fill | Blown-in fibre or granules spread across the ceiling | Uneven depth, bare patches where it has drifted or been disturbed |
| Reflective foil | Foil sheets or foil-faced blankets | Tears, dust build-up on the shiny side, and clearance from wiring |
| Rigid boards | Foam or composite boards, usually in walls, floors or under roofing | Joins and gaps; usually installed during building or renovation |

> Important: In some homes in the ACT and parts of New South Wales, loose-fill asbestos was blown into roof spaces as insulation decades ago. If you see grey or white fluffy, fibrous insulation in an older roof space and are not sure what it is, do not touch it. Leave the roof space and get advice from your state's asbestos authority before anyone goes back in.

Insulation loses much of its value when it is compressed, wet or full of gaps. A ceiling with insulation over most of it but bare strips around the edges and along trade paths can perform far worse than its rating suggests.

sections.heading: Draughts: find them, then seal them
sections.markdown:
Draughts are often the cheapest comfort improvement. Common leaks are gaps under and around doors, window frames and sashes, gaps between floorboards and at skirting, unused fireplaces and chimneys, wall vents in older homes, and exhaust fans without self-closing dampers. Seal with weather strips, door seals, gap fillers and chimney dampers or balloons.

Two cautions. First, if the home has an **open-flued gas heater**, sealing can reduce the air it needs and raise the carbon monoxide risk; see [heating, cooling and gas safety](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/heating-cooling-and-gas-safety) before sealing that room. Second, some old wall vents provide ventilation the house relies on; ask before blocking them.

sections.heading: Ventilation: remove moisture at its source
sections.markdown:
The most effective ventilation removes moisture where it is made: bathrooms, kitchens and laundries. Exhaust fans and rangehoods must vent **outside**, not into the roof space, where the moisture condenses on the underside of the roof. Since [NCC 2022](https://cpd.nccb.gov.au/news/2022/overview-changes-energy-efficiency-and-condensation), new homes must meet condensation provisions covering exhaust discharge and roof-space ventilation; older homes often do not.

**Ventilation checklist**

| Check | Good sign |
| --- | --- |
| Bathroom exhaust fan | Ducted outside, run during and for a while after showers |
| Kitchen rangehood | Ducted outside, not just recirculating |
| Clothes dryer | Vented outside, or a condenser or heat-pump dryer |
| Subfloor vents | Clear, unblocked, cross-ventilating |
| Daily airing | Windows opened briefly, especially after showers and cooking |

sections.heading: Condensation and mould
sections.markdown:
Condensation forms when moist air meets a surface colder than its dew point: single-glazed or aluminium windows, external corners, poorly insulated ceilings and the underside of metal roofs. Repeated condensation feeds mould. [YourHome](https://www.yourhome.gov.au/passive-design/condensation) explains how moisture, temperature and ventilation interact.

Treat the cause before the mould: reduce moisture at its source, ventilate, keep surfaces warmer with insulation and steady heating, and improve glazing where condensation is severe. Wipe and clean small areas of mould; large or recurring mould needs the moisture source found. For roof-space condensation, see [metal roofs](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/roofs-tiles-metal-and-leaks#metal), and for telling condensation from rising damp or leaks, see [damp and moisture](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/damp-and-moisture-in-your-home).

sections.heading: Windows and glazing
sections.markdown: Windows lose and gain far more heat per square metre than insulated walls and ceilings, and single-glazed or aluminium-framed windows are where condensation forms first on cold mornings. Improving them does not always mean replacing them. Close-fitting curtains with a pelmet, cellular blinds and secondary glazing fitted inside existing frames can all help. Double glazing and thermally improved frames make the biggest difference when windows are being replaced anyway. Wipe condensation from frames and sills each morning in winter, because water left sitting there feeds mould and rots timber frames.

sections.heading: Roof space ventilation
sections.markdown: Roof spaces collect heat in summer and moisture from the house all year. Eave vents, ridge vents and whirlybirds can help warm, moist air escape, but a roof space only needs ventilating to the extent its design calls for, and vents are no substitute for keeping bathroom and kitchen moisture out of it in the first place. Under metal roofs, an insulation blanket or sarking reduces condensation on the underside of the sheeting. The [roofs guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/roofs-tiles-metal-and-leaks) covers condensation under metal roofs.

sections.heading: Where to start in an older home
sections.markdown:
**A sensible order for an older house**

| Step | Why it comes here |
| --- | --- |
| Fix leaks and damp first | Insulation over damp traps moisture; dry the building first |
| Check wiring and downlights | Insulation over old or damaged wiring is a fire risk |
| Seal the obvious draughts | Usually the cheapest comfort gain, provided ventilation stays where it is needed |
| Top up ceiling insulation | Often the biggest single gain in an existing home |
| Insulate under raised floors | Worthwhile where there is subfloor access, keeping vents clear |
| Improve window coverings or glazing | Reduces heat loss and condensation at the coldest surfaces |
| Insulate walls during renovation or recladding | Hard to do well otherwise |

Whatever you do, keep ventilation in the rooms that make moisture and in any room with an open-flued gas heater. A warmer, tighter house that cannot get rid of its moisture swaps cold for mould.

sections.heading: After insulation work
sections.markdown: Ask the installer for photos of the finished roof space, a description of the product and its rating, and confirmation that clearances around downlights, transformers, flues and fans were kept. Check that the roof hatch insulation was replaced and that nothing was left blocking eave vents. Where the installer moved or worked near wiring, an electrician's check is good insurance. Keep the paperwork with your [home record](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/keeping-a-record-of-your-home).

sections.heading: Common misreads
sections.markdown:
**Things often said about insulation and condensation**

| What people say | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| "Seal everything and the house will be warm and healthy" | Sealing without ventilation traps moisture and can cause condensation and mould. |
| "The roof space has insulation, so it is fine" | Old insulation settles and degrades; check its depth, coverage and gaps. |
| "Mould means a leak" | Mould on cold surfaces is often condensation; leaks show as damage beyond the wet area. |
| "The exhaust fan works, so the bathroom is ventilated" | A fan venting into the roof space moves the moisture, it does not remove it. |
| "Insulation can go anywhere in the ceiling" | It needs clearances around downlights, transformers, flues and fans. |

sections.heading: Worked example: mould after new insulation
sections.markdown:
**Illustrative reasoning example, not an inspected property.** A 1960s brick-veneer house had new ceiling insulation and draught seals installed last autumn. This winter, black mould has appeared on the bedroom ceilings and the bathroom stays wet after showers.

The house is now warmer and tighter, but the bathroom fan vents into the roof space and the bedrooms are not aired. The fix is ventilation, not removing the insulation: duct the bathroom fan outside, run it longer, air the bedrooms daily and check the roof space for damp insulation near the fan. Clean the existing mould once the moisture source is under control.

faqs.question: How do I know if my ceiling insulation needs topping up?
faqs.answer: Look from the roof hatch where it is safe. Thin, compressed or patchy insulation, bare strips around edges and trade paths, or damp patches all suggest it needs attention. An installer can measure the depth and advise on adding to it.

faqs.question: Is double glazing worth it?
faqs.answer: It makes the biggest difference when windows are being replaced anyway, especially in cold climates. Close-fitting curtains with pelmets and secondary glazing can improve existing windows at lower cost.

faqs.question: Do whirlybirds help?
faqs.answer: They can help warm, moist air leave the roof space, but they do not replace keeping bathroom and kitchen moisture out of the roof by venting fans outside.

faqs.question: What is loose-fill asbestos insulation?
faqs.answer: A loose, fluffy asbestos product blown into some roof spaces as insulation decades ago, found in some homes in the ACT and parts of New South Wales. If you suspect it, do not enter the roof space and contact your state asbestos authority.

faqs.question: Why did mould appear after I insulated?
faqs.answer: A warmer, tighter house holds more moisture if it is not ventilated. Vent bathroom and kitchen fans outside, air the house daily and keep moisture-producing rooms ventilated.

faqs.question: Where should I insulate an older house first?
faqs.answer: Usually the ceiling: it is the easiest to reach and often gives the biggest improvement. Underfloor insulation suits raised timber floors with subfloor access; walls are best insulated during renovation or recladding.

faqs.question: Is it safe to put insulation over old wiring and downlights?
faqs.answer: Only after a licensed electrician has checked the wiring, and with the required clearances: Sustainability Victoria gives at least 200 mm above recessed halogen downlights and 50 mm around transformers. Keep foil insulation away from wiring.

faqs.question: What R-value should ceiling insulation be?
faqs.answer: It depends on your climate and local requirements. The ACT recommends at least R5 for ceilings, for example. A certified installer can check what you have and what to add.

faqs.question: Can insulation cause condensation and mould?
faqs.answer: Not by itself, but a warmer, tighter house without enough ventilation can trap moisture. Vent bathrooms, kitchens and laundries outside, air the house and keep subfloor vents clear.

faqs.question: Where should a bathroom exhaust fan vent?
faqs.answer: Outside, through a duct. A fan that vents into the roof space moves moisture into the roof, where it can condense on the roof and damage insulation and timber.

faqs.question: Why do my windows drip with condensation in winter?
faqs.answer: Warm, moist indoor air is meeting cold glass and frames, especially single-glazed or aluminium windows. Reduce moisture, ventilate, keep rooms evenly heated and consider better glazing where it is severe.

faqs.question: Should I block old wall vents to stop draughts?
faqs.answer: Ask first. Some older homes rely on wall vents for ventilation, and rooms with open-flued gas heaters need replacement air. Seal draughts elsewhere before closing vents.

guides.contentMarkdown:
# Insulation, ventilation and condensation: warm and dry

Warmth, air and moisture are one system. Insulation slows heat loss, draught-sealing stops cold air leaking in, and ventilation removes the moisture a household produces. Start with the ceiling, which is usually the easiest and most effective place to insulate, but have an electrician check older wiring first and keep the required clearances around downlights. A tighter home without ventilation can trap moisture, causing condensation and mould, and can be dangerous with an open-flued gas heater.

## Research note
Insulation safety follows [Sustainability Victoria](https://www.sustainability.vic.gov.au/energy-efficiency-and-reducing-emissions/building-or-renovating/build-for-energy-efficiency/key-principles-of-energy-efficient-design/insulation/health-and-safety) and South Australian Government guidance; condensation and design principles follow YourHome and the NCC 2022 condensation provisions.

## Opening
### Insulate, seal, then ventilate
- **Insulate:** Ceiling first, after an electrical check
- **Seal:** Doors, windows, floors and unused chimneys
- **Ventilate:** Bathroom, kitchen and laundry exhausts to outside

_A tighter house needs its moisture taken out on purpose._

Seal draughts around doors, windows and floors, then make sure bathroom, kitchen and laundry exhausts vent outside rather than into the roof space.

## What you'll notice
Most homes show where heat and moisture are escaping or collecting. These are the common signs.

**Signs by sense**

| Sense | Sign | Where to read next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Feel | Cold rooms despite heating, or rooms that overheat in summer | [Insulation](#insulation) |
| Feel | Cold air around doors, windows, skirting, floorboards or an unused fireplace | [Draughts](#draughts) |
| See | Water running down windows on cold mornings, or wet window frames | [Condensation](#condensation) |
| See | Black mould spots on ceilings, in corners or behind wardrobes | [Condensation](#condensation) |
| See | Bathroom mirrors and walls that stay wet long after a shower | [Ventilation](#ventilation) |
| See | Damp or stained insulation, or rusty nails, in the roof space | [Roof-space condensation](#condensation) |
| Smell | A stuffy or musty smell in a closed-up house | [Ventilation](#ventilation) |

## Heat, air and moisture work as one system
A household adds a lot of moisture to the air every day through showers, cooking, drying clothes and breathing. In a leaky, uninsulated house, cold draughts carry it away, at the cost of comfort and energy. When the same house is insulated and sealed, that moisture has to be removed deliberately, by ventilation, or it condenses on the coldest surfaces. [YourHome](https://www.yourhome.gov.au/passive-design/insulation) treats insulation, sealing and ventilation as parts of the same design, and so should any upgrade.

## Insulation: where to start
**Where insulation goes in an existing home**

| Location | Ease in an existing home | What to know |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Ceiling | Usually the easiest, from the roof space | Often the biggest gain; check existing depth and condition, and top up rather than compress |
| Underfloor (raised timber floors) | Possible where there is subfloor access | Keep subfloor vents open; see [subfloors](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/subfloors-stumps-and-restumping) |
| Walls | Hard without removing linings or cladding | Best done during renovation or recladding; cavity fills need specialist advice on moisture |
| Roof (under the covering) | Usually only when re-roofing | A reflective or insulating layer is easiest to add when the roof is off |

Insulation performance is measured as its **R-value**: the higher, the better it resists heat flow. Requirements and recommendations vary by climate; the ACT, for example, recommends ceiling insulation of at least R5, and notes that [many homes built before 1997 have little or none](https://www.climatechoices.act.gov.au/policy-programs/home-energy-support-rebates-for-homeowners/ceiling-insulation). Insulation also settles and degrades over time, so an older layer may be thinner than it looks.

### Insulation safety: wiring and downlights

Ceiling insulation work has a history of fires and electrical accidents, so the order matters. [Sustainability Victoria](https://www.sustainability.vic.gov.au/energy-efficiency-and-reducing-emissions/building-or-renovating/build-for-energy-efficiency/key-principles-of-energy-efficient-design/insulation/health-and-safety) and the [South Australian Government](https://www.sa.gov.au/topics/energy-and-environment/energy-efficient-home-design/home-insulation-safety) advise:

**Before insulation goes in**

| Check | Why |
| --- | --- |
| Have a licensed electrician inspect the wiring first | Old wiring can overheat when covered; SA flags wiring installed before 1986 in particular |
| Keep clearances around downlights | Sustainability Victoria gives at least 200 mm above recessed halogen downlights and 50 mm around transformers, under the wiring rules |
| Consider replacing old downlights | Some modern LED downlights are rated to be covered, which reduces the uninsulated gaps |
| Keep foil-faced insulation away from wiring | Foil can become live; never fix it with metal staples |
| Keep clear of flues, exhaust fans and heaters | Hot fittings need clearance from insulation |
| Use a licensed or certified installer | Required in some states, and safer in all |

See the [switchboards and wiring guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/switchboards-wiring-and-safety-switches) for what older wiring looks like. Never enter a roof space with damaged or loose cables, and stop if you suspect asbestos.

## Reading the insulation you already have
Before adding more, look at what is there. From the roof hatch, where it is safe, note the type, how deep it is, whether it covers the whole ceiling and whether it has been pushed aside by tradespeople or disturbed by rodents.

**Common insulation types**

| Type | What it looks like | What to check |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Glasswool or rockwool batts | Fibrous batts, often yellow, pink, white or grey | Gaps between batts, compressed or displaced batts, damp patches |
| Polyester batts | Soft white synthetic batts | Gaps and displacement, as for other batts |
| Loose-fill | Blown-in fibre or granules spread across the ceiling | Uneven depth, bare patches where it has drifted or been disturbed |
| Reflective foil | Foil sheets or foil-faced blankets | Tears, dust build-up on the shiny side, and clearance from wiring |
| Rigid boards | Foam or composite boards, usually in walls, floors or under roofing | Joins and gaps; usually installed during building or renovation |

> Important: In some homes in the ACT and parts of New South Wales, loose-fill asbestos was blown into roof spaces as insulation decades ago. If you see grey or white fluffy, fibrous insulation in an older roof space and are not sure what it is, do not touch it. Leave the roof space and get advice from your state's asbestos authority before anyone goes back in.

Insulation loses much of its value when it is compressed, wet or full of gaps. A ceiling with insulation over most of it but bare strips around the edges and along trade paths can perform far worse than its rating suggests.

## Draughts: find them, then seal them
Draughts are often the cheapest comfort improvement. Common leaks are gaps under and around doors, window frames and sashes, gaps between floorboards and at skirting, unused fireplaces and chimneys, wall vents in older homes, and exhaust fans without self-closing dampers. Seal with weather strips, door seals, gap fillers and chimney dampers or balloons.

Two cautions. First, if the home has an **open-flued gas heater**, sealing can reduce the air it needs and raise the carbon monoxide risk; see [heating, cooling and gas safety](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/heating-cooling-and-gas-safety) before sealing that room. Second, some old wall vents provide ventilation the house relies on; ask before blocking them.

## Ventilation: remove moisture at its source
The most effective ventilation removes moisture where it is made: bathrooms, kitchens and laundries. Exhaust fans and rangehoods must vent **outside**, not into the roof space, where the moisture condenses on the underside of the roof. Since [NCC 2022](https://cpd.nccb.gov.au/news/2022/overview-changes-energy-efficiency-and-condensation), new homes must meet condensation provisions covering exhaust discharge and roof-space ventilation; older homes often do not.

**Ventilation checklist**

| Check | Good sign |
| --- | --- |
| Bathroom exhaust fan | Ducted outside, run during and for a while after showers |
| Kitchen rangehood | Ducted outside, not just recirculating |
| Clothes dryer | Vented outside, or a condenser or heat-pump dryer |
| Subfloor vents | Clear, unblocked, cross-ventilating |
| Daily airing | Windows opened briefly, especially after showers and cooking |

## Condensation and mould
Condensation forms when moist air meets a surface colder than its dew point: single-glazed or aluminium windows, external corners, poorly insulated ceilings and the underside of metal roofs. Repeated condensation feeds mould. [YourHome](https://www.yourhome.gov.au/passive-design/condensation) explains how moisture, temperature and ventilation interact.

Treat the cause before the mould: reduce moisture at its source, ventilate, keep surfaces warmer with insulation and steady heating, and improve glazing where condensation is severe. Wipe and clean small areas of mould; large or recurring mould needs the moisture source found. For roof-space condensation, see [metal roofs](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/roofs-tiles-metal-and-leaks#metal), and for telling condensation from rising damp or leaks, see [damp and moisture](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/damp-and-moisture-in-your-home).

## Windows and glazing
Windows lose and gain far more heat per square metre than insulated walls and ceilings, and single-glazed or aluminium-framed windows are where condensation forms first on cold mornings. Improving them does not always mean replacing them. Close-fitting curtains with a pelmet, cellular blinds and secondary glazing fitted inside existing frames can all help. Double glazing and thermally improved frames make the biggest difference when windows are being replaced anyway. Wipe condensation from frames and sills each morning in winter, because water left sitting there feeds mould and rots timber frames.

## Roof space ventilation
Roof spaces collect heat in summer and moisture from the house all year. Eave vents, ridge vents and whirlybirds can help warm, moist air escape, but a roof space only needs ventilating to the extent its design calls for, and vents are no substitute for keeping bathroom and kitchen moisture out of it in the first place. Under metal roofs, an insulation blanket or sarking reduces condensation on the underside of the sheeting. The [roofs guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/roofs-tiles-metal-and-leaks) covers condensation under metal roofs.

## Where to start in an older home
**A sensible order for an older house**

| Step | Why it comes here |
| --- | --- |
| Fix leaks and damp first | Insulation over damp traps moisture; dry the building first |
| Check wiring and downlights | Insulation over old or damaged wiring is a fire risk |
| Seal the obvious draughts | Usually the cheapest comfort gain, provided ventilation stays where it is needed |
| Top up ceiling insulation | Often the biggest single gain in an existing home |
| Insulate under raised floors | Worthwhile where there is subfloor access, keeping vents clear |
| Improve window coverings or glazing | Reduces heat loss and condensation at the coldest surfaces |
| Insulate walls during renovation or recladding | Hard to do well otherwise |

Whatever you do, keep ventilation in the rooms that make moisture and in any room with an open-flued gas heater. A warmer, tighter house that cannot get rid of its moisture swaps cold for mould.

## After insulation work
Ask the installer for photos of the finished roof space, a description of the product and its rating, and confirmation that clearances around downlights, transformers, flues and fans were kept. Check that the roof hatch insulation was replaced and that nothing was left blocking eave vents. Where the installer moved or worked near wiring, an electrician's check is good insurance. Keep the paperwork with your [home record](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/keeping-a-record-of-your-home).

## Common misreads
**Things often said about insulation and condensation**

| What people say | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| "Seal everything and the house will be warm and healthy" | Sealing without ventilation traps moisture and can cause condensation and mould. |
| "The roof space has insulation, so it is fine" | Old insulation settles and degrades; check its depth, coverage and gaps. |
| "Mould means a leak" | Mould on cold surfaces is often condensation; leaks show as damage beyond the wet area. |
| "The exhaust fan works, so the bathroom is ventilated" | A fan venting into the roof space moves the moisture, it does not remove it. |
| "Insulation can go anywhere in the ceiling" | It needs clearances around downlights, transformers, flues and fans. |

## Worked example: mould after new insulation
**Illustrative reasoning example, not an inspected property.** A 1960s brick-veneer house had new ceiling insulation and draught seals installed last autumn. This winter, black mould has appeared on the bedroom ceilings and the bathroom stays wet after showers.

The house is now warmer and tighter, but the bathroom fan vents into the roof space and the bedrooms are not aired. The fix is ventilation, not removing the insulation: duct the bathroom fan outside, run it longer, air the bedrooms daily and check the roof space for damp insulation near the fan. Clean the existing mould once the moisture source is under control.

## Frequently asked questions
### How do I know if my ceiling insulation needs topping up?
Look from the roof hatch where it is safe. Thin, compressed or patchy insulation, bare strips around edges and trade paths, or damp patches all suggest it needs attention. An installer can measure the depth and advise on adding to it.

### Is double glazing worth it?
It makes the biggest difference when windows are being replaced anyway, especially in cold climates. Close-fitting curtains with pelmets and secondary glazing can improve existing windows at lower cost.

### Do whirlybirds help?
They can help warm, moist air leave the roof space, but they do not replace keeping bathroom and kitchen moisture out of the roof by venting fans outside.

### What is loose-fill asbestos insulation?
A loose, fluffy asbestos product blown into some roof spaces as insulation decades ago, found in some homes in the ACT and parts of New South Wales. If you suspect it, do not enter the roof space and contact your state asbestos authority.

### Why did mould appear after I insulated?
A warmer, tighter house holds more moisture if it is not ventilated. Vent bathroom and kitchen fans outside, air the house daily and keep moisture-producing rooms ventilated.

### Where should I insulate an older house first?
Usually the ceiling: it is the easiest to reach and often gives the biggest improvement. Underfloor insulation suits raised timber floors with subfloor access; walls are best insulated during renovation or recladding.

### Is it safe to put insulation over old wiring and downlights?
Only after a licensed electrician has checked the wiring, and with the required clearances: Sustainability Victoria gives at least 200 mm above recessed halogen downlights and 50 mm around transformers. Keep foil insulation away from wiring.

### What R-value should ceiling insulation be?
It depends on your climate and local requirements. The ACT recommends at least R5 for ceilings, for example. A certified installer can check what you have and what to add.

### Can insulation cause condensation and mould?
Not by itself, but a warmer, tighter house without enough ventilation can trap moisture. Vent bathrooms, kitchens and laundries outside, air the house and keep subfloor vents clear.

### Where should a bathroom exhaust fan vent?
Outside, through a duct. A fan that vents into the roof space moves moisture into the roof, where it can condense on the roof and damage insulation and timber.

### Why do my windows drip with condensation in winter?
Warm, moist indoor air is meeting cold glass and frames, especially single-glazed or aluminium windows. Reduce moisture, ventilate, keep rooms evenly heated and consider better glazing where it is severe.

### Should I block old wall vents to stop draughts?
Ask first. Some older homes rely on wall vents for ventilation, and rooms with open-flued gas heaters need replacement air. Seal draughts elsewhere before closing vents.

## Method
We treat heat, air and moisture as one system: where to insulate first and how to do it safely, how to find and seal draughts, and how to ventilate so condensation does not follow, with a fictional example.

## Limitations
R-value requirements and installer licensing vary by climate zone and state. Electrical checks and clearances must follow the wiring rules and a licensed electrician.
