guides.question: How do I check a home’s outside walls, windows, render and cladding?
guides.title: Outside walls: windows, render, cladding and lintels
guides.summary: How to read a home’s outside walls: windows and doors, render, cladding, sealants, paint, flashings and weep holes, the steel in the brickwork, combustible cladding in apartment buildings, and what to sort out before repainting.
guides.answer: The outside walls keep weather out through a combination of materials and details, and they usually fail at the details: window sills and flashings, sealant joints, render that has cracked or come loose, paint that has stopped protecting timber, and steel lintels or wall ties rusting inside brickwork. Walk each side of the house looking for peeling paint, cracks above windows, stains, soft timber and gaps around frames.
guides.methodology: We walk the outside of the house from the signs owners notice, through windows, render, cladding, sealants and paint, to the hidden steel in brickwork, with a fictional example.
guides.limitations: Concealed lintels, ties and cladding junctions need exposure or specialist inspection to confirm. Lead and asbestos need testing.
guides.researchNote: Cladding and masonry principles follow YourHome; lead and asbestos screening follow the national Lead Alert guide and asbestos agency; wall-tie durability and corrosion draw on AS 2699.1 and Australian corrosion research.

cluster.label: Read the building
cluster.blurb: Use age and construction as a starting hypothesis, then test it against evidence and physical inspection.

sections.heading: Opening
sections.markdown:
### Walls fail at their details
- **Openings:** Sills, flashings, frames and the sealant around them
- **Surfaces:** Render, cladding and paint that shed the weather
- **Hidden steel:** Lintels and wall ties that can rust inside brickwork

_Fresh paint tells you about the paint, not the wall._

Treat paint applied before 1970 as possibly containing lead and fibre-cement made before 1990 as possibly containing asbestos until tested. A horizontal crack with displaced bricks above a window, or regular horizontal cracks in older cavity brick, can mean rusting steel and needs assessment.

sections.heading: What you'll notice
sections.markdown:
Walk each side of the house, ideally after rain, and compare the weather side with the sheltered side. These are the signs that matter.

**Signs by sense**

| Sense | Sign | Where to read next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| See | Peeling, blistering or chalky paint, worst on the weather side | [Paint and coatings](#paint) |
| Feel | Soft or spongy timber at window sills, sashes or door frames | [Windows and doors](#windows) |
| See | A horizontal crack above a window or door, with bricks pushed out of line | [The steel in the brickwork](#steel) |
| See | Regular horizontal cracks along mortar joints in older brick walls | [Wall ties](#steel) |
| See | Cracked, bulging or hollow-sounding render | [Render](#render) |
| See | Hard, cracked or missing sealant around windows and in joints | [Sealants and joints](#sealants) |
| See | Stains below windows inside, or water marks down walls outside | [Windows and doors](#windows) |
| Feel | Draughts or rattling around window sashes | [Draughts](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/insulation-ventilation-and-condensation#draughts) |

sections.heading: Windows and doors
sections.markdown:
Windows and doors are the most common way water gets into a wall. The frame, the sill below it, the flashing above it and the seal around it all have to work together.

**Window types and their weak points**

| Type | Where you find it | What to check |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Timber sashes and casements | Older homes, and many renovations | Rot at sills, bottom rails and joints; failed putty or glazing beads; paint condition; sash cords and balances |
| Aluminium | Very common from the 1970s onward | Worn rollers and catches, perished seals, condensation on cold frames, corrosion near the coast |
| uPVC and thermally broken frames | Newer homes and upgrades | Seals, drainage holes kept clear, hardware |
| Door thresholds and frames | All homes | Rot at the base of frames, water entering at sills, gaps under doors |

Look under each window inside for staining or swollen linings, and outside for a sill that falls away from the wall, a drip groove underneath, and a head flashing or weather bar above. Condensation on aluminium frames is common in winter; see [condensation](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/insulation-ventilation-and-condensation#condensation).

sections.heading: Render
sections.markdown:
Render is a coating over brick, block or a board, and it behaves differently depending on what it covers. Cement render on brick can crack with movement and hide earlier cracking. Acrylic texture coatings on lightweight boards rely on sound joints behind them. On older soft brick, hard cement render can trap moisture and push damp higher, as the [heritage guide to salt damp](https://www.environment.nsw.gov.au/sites/default/files/salt-attack-and-rising-damp-guide.pdf) explains.

**Render problems**

| Sign | What it can mean | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fine crazing | Shrinkage of the render surface | Usually cosmetic; recoat |
| Cracks that follow a pattern, such as stepped or from window corners | Movement in the wall behind | Read with the [cracks guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/cracks-structural-or-cosmetic) |
| Hollow or drummy sound when tapped, or bulging | Render coming away from the wall | Remove and repair loose areas before they fall |
| Damp or salts at the base of a rendered old wall | Render bridging or trapping moisture | See [salt damp](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/damp-and-moisture-in-your-home#salt-damp) |

sections.heading: Cladding: fibre-cement, foam and others
sections.markdown: Fibre-cement sheets and planks are durable when their joints, edges and penetrations are sealed and painted. Fibre-cement made before 1990 may contain asbestos; the [national asbestos agency](https://www.asbestossafety.gov.au/about-asbestos/finding-asbestos/home) advises testing before drilling, cutting or sanding. Expanded polystyrene (foam) cladding with a render finish is vulnerable to impact damage and to water getting in at penetrations, joints and the base. [YourHome](https://www.yourhome.gov.au/materials/cladding-systems) explains how cladding systems manage water behind the finish. For timber boards, see [weatherboard homes](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/weatherboard-homes); for brick, see [brick veneer vs double brick](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/brick-veneer-vs-double-brick).

sections.heading: Sealants and joints
sections.markdown: Sealants close the gaps that materials cannot: around window and door frames, at control and articulation joints in brickwork, and at junctions between different materials. They harden, crack and pull away with sun and movement, and when they fail, water reaches the wall behind. Renew sealant that is hard, cracked, shrunken or missing, with a product suited to the joint. Never fill an articulation joint with mortar; see the [cracks guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/cracks-structural-or-cosmetic#patterns).

sections.heading: Paint and coatings
sections.markdown:
**Common paint failures**

| Failure | Usual cause | What to do |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Peeling or flaking | Moisture behind the paint, or poor preparation | Find and fix the moisture before repainting |
| Blistering | Moisture or heat under the coating | Check for leaks or damp behind; repaint once dry |
| Chalking | Age and sun breaking down the paint | Clean and recoat; normal ageing |
| Cracking in a crazed pattern | Old, brittle, many-layered paint | Often means a strip back; test for lead first |
| Mould or algae staining | Shade and lasting moisture | Clean, improve drainage and airflow, and recoat |

Paint applied before 1970 may contain lead. The national [Lead Alert guide](https://www.agriculture.gov.au/sites/default/files/documents/lead-paint-fifth-edition.pdf) explains how to test and how to work safely; dry sanding, heat-gun stripping and pressure-cleaning old lead paint spread lead dust. Test before any preparation.

sections.heading: Flashings, damp-proof courses and weep holes
sections.markdown:
Walls are built to let some water in and then lead it out again. Flashings above windows and doors, damp-proof courses near the base of masonry walls, and weep holes in the bottom course of brickwork all do that job. They only work if they stay clear and in place.

**The hidden water path in a wall**

| Part | What it does | What goes wrong |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Head flashing over windows and doors | Turns water in the cavity out over the opening | Missing or too short, so water runs into the frame and the room |
| Damp-proof course | A barrier near the base of masonry walls that stops ground moisture rising | Bridged by soil, paving, render or garden beds built up against the wall |
| Weep holes | Gaps in the bottom course of brickwork that let cavity water out | Covered by soil or paving, or filled with mortar or sealant |
| Sill flashings and trays | Catch water at the base of window openings | Missing or damaged, so water stains the wall below the window |

Keep soil, mulch and paving below the damp-proof course and weep holes. Covering them traps moisture in the wall and can hide termite entry. The [damp guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/damp-and-moisture-in-your-home) and [termites guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/termites-in-australian-homes) explain why.

sections.heading: The steel in the brickwork: lintels and wall ties
sections.markdown:
**Lintels** are the steel angles or beams that carry brickwork over windows and doors. When they rust, the steel expands and lifts the bricks above, causing a horizontal crack along the bottom of the brickwork over the opening, sometimes with the bricks pushed out of line and rust staining. Early repair, by cleaning and treating or replacing the lintel, is far cheaper than rebuilding the brickwork above it.

**Wall ties** are the small metal ties that join the outer leaf of brick to the frame or inner leaf. They are graded for corrosion resistance under AS 2699.1, from R1 to R4, with R4 for severe exposures such as the coast. Research on Australian walls notes that corrosion is often worst where the tie sits in the mortar, so tie failure is easy to miss until it is advanced ([MDPI study](https://www.mdpi.com/2624-5558/2/4/35/htm)). Signs include regular horizontal cracks along mortar joints, bulging or leaning brickwork and cracks at corners. sections.heading: A walk around the outside
sections.markdown:
**What to look at on each side of the house**

| Where | What to look for |
| --- | --- |
| Top of the walls and eaves | Water stains, peeling eaves linings, gaps where the roof meets the wall |
| Around every window and door | Head flashings, sill condition, sealant, stains below, soft timber |
| Brickwork faces | Cracks, especially above openings, displaced bricks, mortar loss, efflorescence |
| Render and cladding | Cracks, drummy or bulging areas, open joints, damaged edges |

guides.contentMarkdown:
# Outside walls: windows, render, cladding and lintels

The outside walls keep weather out through a combination of materials and details, and they usually fail at the details: window sills and flashings, sealant joints, render that has cracked or come loose, paint that has stopped protecting timber, and steel lintels or wall ties rusting inside brickwork. Walk each side of the house looking for peeling paint, cracks above windows, stains, soft timber and gaps around frames.

## Research note
Cladding and masonry principles follow YourHome; lead and asbestos screening follow the national Lead Alert guide and asbestos agency; wall-tie durability and corrosion draw on AS 2699.1 and Australian corrosion research.

## Opening
### Walls fail at their details
- **Openings:** Sills, flashings, frames and the sealant around them
- **Surfaces:** Render, cladding and paint that shed the weather
- **Hidden steel:** Lintels and wall ties that can rust inside brickwork

_Fresh paint tells you about the paint, not the wall._

Treat paint applied before 1970 as possibly containing lead and fibre-cement made before 1990 as possibly containing asbestos until tested. A horizontal crack with displaced bricks above a window, or regular horizontal cracks in older cavity brick, can mean rusting steel and needs assessment.

## What you'll notice
Walk each side of the house, ideally after rain, and compare the weather side with the sheltered side. These are the signs that matter.

**Signs by sense**

| Sense | Sign | Where to read next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| See | Peeling, blistering or chalky paint, worst on the weather side | [Paint and coatings](#paint) |
| Feel | Soft or spongy timber at window sills, sashes or door frames | [Windows and doors](#windows) |
| See | A horizontal crack above a window or door, with bricks pushed out of line | [The steel in the brickwork](#steel) |
| See | Regular horizontal cracks along mortar joints in older brick walls | [Wall ties](#steel) |
| See | Cracked, bulging or hollow-sounding render | [Render](#render) |
| See | Hard, cracked or missing sealant around windows and in joints | [Sealants and joints](#sealants) |
| See | Stains below windows inside, or water marks down walls outside | [Windows and doors](#windows) |
| Feel | Draughts or rattling around window sashes | [Draughts](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/insulation-ventilation-and-condensation#draughts) |

## Windows and doors
Windows and doors are the most common way water gets into a wall. The frame, the sill below it, the flashing above it and the seal around it all have to work together.

**Window types and their weak points**

| Type | Where you find it | What to check |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Timber sashes and casements | Older homes, and many renovations | Rot at sills, bottom rails and joints; failed putty or glazing beads; paint condition; sash cords and balances |
| Aluminium | Very common from the 1970s onward | Worn rollers and catches, perished seals, condensation on cold frames, corrosion near the coast |
| uPVC and thermally broken frames | Newer homes and upgrades | Seals, drainage holes kept clear, hardware |
| Door thresholds and frames | All homes | Rot at the base of frames, water entering at sills, gaps under doors |

Look under each window inside for staining or swollen linings, and outside for a sill that falls away from the wall, a drip groove underneath, and a head flashing or weather bar above. Condensation on aluminium frames is common in winter; see [condensation](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/insulation-ventilation-and-condensation#condensation).

## Render
Render is a coating over brick, block or a board, and it behaves differently depending on what it covers. Cement render on brick can crack with movement and hide earlier cracking. Acrylic texture coatings on lightweight boards rely on sound joints behind them. On older soft brick, hard cement render can trap moisture and push damp higher, as the [heritage guide to salt damp](https://www.environment.nsw.gov.au/sites/default/files/salt-attack-and-rising-damp-guide.pdf) explains.

**Render problems**

| Sign | What it can mean | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fine crazing | Shrinkage of the render surface | Usually cosmetic; recoat |
| Cracks that follow a pattern, such as stepped or from window corners | Movement in the wall behind | Read with the [cracks guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/cracks-structural-or-cosmetic) |
| Hollow or drummy sound when tapped, or bulging | Render coming away from the wall | Remove and repair loose areas before they fall |
| Damp or salts at the base of a rendered old wall | Render bridging or trapping moisture | See [salt damp](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/damp-and-moisture-in-your-home#salt-damp) |

## Cladding: fibre-cement, foam and others
Fibre-cement sheets and planks are durable when their joints, edges and penetrations are sealed and painted. Fibre-cement made before 1990 may contain asbestos; the [national asbestos agency](https://www.asbestossafety.gov.au/about-asbestos/finding-asbestos/home) advises testing before drilling, cutting or sanding. Expanded polystyrene (foam) cladding with a render finish is vulnerable to impact damage and to water getting in at penetrations, joints and the base. [YourHome](https://www.yourhome.gov.au/materials/cladding-systems) explains how cladding systems manage water behind the finish. For timber boards, see [weatherboard homes](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/weatherboard-homes); for brick, see [brick veneer vs double brick](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/brick-veneer-vs-double-brick).

## Sealants and joints
Sealants close the gaps that materials cannot: around window and door frames, at control and articulation joints in brickwork, and at junctions between different materials. They harden, crack and pull away with sun and movement, and when they fail, water reaches the wall behind. Renew sealant that is hard, cracked, shrunken or missing, with a product suited to the joint. Never fill an articulation joint with mortar; see the [cracks guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/cracks-structural-or-cosmetic#patterns).

## Paint and coatings
**Common paint failures**

| Failure | Usual cause | What to do |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Peeling or flaking | Moisture behind the paint, or poor preparation | Find and fix the moisture before repainting |
| Blistering | Moisture or heat under the coating | Check for leaks or damp behind; repaint once dry |
| Chalking | Age and sun breaking down the paint | Clean and recoat; normal ageing |
| Cracking in a crazed pattern | Old, brittle, many-layered paint | Often means a strip back; test for lead first |
| Mould or algae staining | Shade and lasting moisture | Clean, improve drainage and airflow, and recoat |

Paint applied before 1970 may contain lead. The national [Lead Alert guide](https://www.agriculture.gov.au/sites/default/files/documents/lead-paint-fifth-edition.pdf) explains how to test and how to work safely; dry sanding, heat-gun stripping and pressure-cleaning old lead paint spread lead dust. Test before any preparation.

## Flashings, damp-proof courses and weep holes
Walls are built to let some water in and then lead it out again. Flashings above windows and doors, damp-proof courses near the base of masonry walls, and weep holes in the bottom course of brickwork all do that job. They only work if they stay clear and in place.

**The hidden water path in a wall**

| Part | What it does | What goes wrong |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Head flashing over windows and doors | Turns water in the cavity out over the opening | Missing or too short, so water runs into the frame and the room |
| Damp-proof course | A barrier near the base of masonry walls that stops ground moisture rising | Bridged by soil, paving, render or garden beds built up against the wall |
| Weep holes | Gaps in the bottom course of brickwork that let cavity water out | Covered by soil or paving, or filled with mortar or sealant |
| Sill flashings and trays | Catch water at the base of window openings | Missing or damaged, so water stains the wall below the window |

Keep soil, mulch and paving below the damp-proof course and weep holes. Covering them traps moisture in the wall and can hide termite entry. The [damp guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/damp-and-moisture-in-your-home) and [termites guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/termites-in-australian-homes) explain why.

## The steel in the brickwork: lintels and wall ties
**Lintels** are the steel angles or beams that carry brickwork over windows and doors. When they rust, the steel expands and lifts the bricks above, causing a horizontal crack along the bottom of the brickwork over the opening, sometimes with the bricks pushed out of line and rust staining. Early repair, by cleaning and treating or replacing the lintel, is far cheaper than rebuilding the brickwork above it.

**Wall ties** are the small metal ties that join the outer leaf of brick to the frame or inner leaf. They are graded for corrosion resistance under AS 2699.1, from R1 to R4, with R4 for severe exposures such as the coast. Research on Australian walls notes that corrosion is often worst where the tie sits in the mortar, so tie failure is easy to miss until it is advanced ([MDPI study](https://www.mdpi.com/2624-5558/2/4/35/htm)). Signs include regular horizontal cracks along mortar joints, bulging or leaning brickwork and cracks at corners. The [Australasian Corrosion Association](https://www.corrosion.com.au/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/Sample-2-ACA2023-20189-Research-paper-example-1.pdf) notes that walls with corroded or missing ties performed badly in the 1989 Newcastle earthquake.

Wall-tie and lintel problems need a builder or engineer experienced in masonry repair. Older homes, coastal homes and walls with past damp are the most at risk.

## Combustible cladding on apartment buildings
In apartment and other multi-storey buildings, some aluminium composite panels and expanded polystyrene cladding have been found to be combustible. Several states have run audit and rectification programs, and owners corporations may have obligations and costs as a result. If you own or are buying into an apartment building, ask the owners corporation whether the building has been assessed, what was found and whether any rectification or special levies are planned. The [strata risks guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/strata-risks-for-owners) covers how to read those records. For houses in bushfire-prone areas, cladding choices are also governed by the site's bushfire attack level; the [extreme weather guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/preparing-your-home-for-extreme-weather) explains BAL ratings.

## A walk around the outside
**What to look at on each side of the house**

| Where | What to look for |
| --- | --- |
| Top of the walls and eaves | Water stains, peeling eaves linings, gaps where the roof meets the wall |
| Around every window and door | Head flashings, sill condition, sealant, stains below, soft timber |
| Brickwork faces | Cracks, especially above openings, displaced bricks, mortar loss, efflorescence |
| Render and cladding | Cracks, drummy or bulging areas, open joints, damaged edges |
| Base of the walls | Weep holes clear, damp-proof course not bridged, ground falling away |

## Common misreads
**Things often said about outside walls**

| What people say | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |

| "Render protects the brick" | On old soft brick, hard render can trap moisture and make damp worse. |

| "Sealant lasts as long as the building" | Sealants harden and crack with sun and movement; they need periodic renewal. |
| "Sanding old paint is just preparation" | If the paint predates 1970 it may contain lead; test first. |

## Worked example: a crack above the front window
**Illustrative reasoning example, not an inspected property.** A 1960s brick-veneer house near the coast has a horizontal crack running along the bottom of the brickwork above the front window, with a brown stain and two bricks slightly proud of the wall. The window frame inside is fine.

## Frequently asked questions

## Method

## Limitations
Concealed lintels, ties and cladding junctions need exposure or specialist inspection to confirm. Lead and asbestos need testing.

guides.question: What should I check inside a house: ceilings, walls, floors and doors?
guides.title: Inside the house: ceilings, walls, floors and doors
guides.summary: How to read the ceilings, walls, floors, tiles, doors and stairs inside a home, which signs need prompt action, a room-by-room walk, how to spot past repairs and what to ask about them, and what to know about lead paint before sanding.
guides.answer: Inside, most problems are either cosmetic wear or a sign of something happening elsewhere: movement in the structure, moisture, or loads in the roof space. Ceilings need the most attention: a loud cracking sound, sagging sheets or cornices, and a line of small circles or blisters (nail pops) can be warning signs of collapse and need prompt repair.
guides.methodology: We walk the interior by element, start from what owners notice, separate cosmetic wear from signs of movement, moisture or overload, and flag the ceiling signs that need prompt action, with a fictional example.
guides.limitations: Interior signs often point to causes elsewhere in the building; confirmation may need subfloor, roof-space or specialist inspection.
guides.researchNote: Ceiling warning signs follow [Western Australia's building regulator](https://www.wa.gov.au/government/announcements/be-aware-of-the-signs-of-stressed-ceiling). Floor, wall, tile and door readings are general indicators, linked to the structural, damp, termite and asbestos guides for confirmation.

cluster.label: Read the building
cluster.blurb: Use age and construction as a starting hypothesis, then test it against evidence and physical inspection.

sections.heading: Opening
sections.markdown:
### Wear, or a sign of something elsewhere
- **Ceilings:** Cracking sounds, sagging and nail pops need prompt action
- **Floors:** Bounce and slope point to the subfloor; cupping to moisture
- **Doors:** Seasonal sticking or year-round movement

_Most interior signs are clues about the structure, the roof or the moisture._

Squeaky or bouncy timber floors point to fixings or the subfloor; cupped boards point to moisture below. Hollow or cracked tiles suggest movement or failed adhesive, and doors that stick can be seasonal swelling or structural movement. Older vinyl flooring and wall sheeting may contain asbestos.

sections.heading: What you'll notice
sections.markdown:
Walk each room and use all your senses. Some signs below are urgent; the ceiling signs in particular should not be left.

**Signs by sense**

| Sense | Sign | Where to read next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Hear | A loud cracking sound from the ceiling | Urgent; see [ceilings](#ceilings) |
| See | A ceiling or cornice that sags, drops or bulges | Urgent; see [ceilings](#ceilings) |
| See | A line of small circles or blisters (nail pops) across a ceiling | [Ceilings](#ceilings) |
| See | Cracks in plaster walls, especially from door and window corners | [Walls](#walls) |
| Hear | Squeaks or creaks as you walk | [Floors](#floors) |
| Feel | Bouncy, springy or sloping floors | [Subfloors](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/subfloors-stumps-and-restumping) |
| See | Timber boards that are cupped (edges higher than the centre) or have widening gaps | [Floors](#floors) |
| Hear | Hollow sounds when tapping floor or wall tiles | [Tiles](#tiles) |
| Feel | Doors that stick, swing open or will not latch | [Doors](#doors) |

sections.heading: Ceilings: the signs that need prompt action
sections.markdown:
Ceiling collapses are rare, but they happen, often with warning signs that owners did not recognise. Western Australia's building regulator reports about 10 ceiling collapses each year there, and lists the warning signs: **a loud cracking sound, sagging or dropping of the sheets or cornice, and visible cracking or a line of small circles or blisters (nail pops)**, which can mean the sheeting is pulling away from the framing above ([WA Building and Energy](https://www.wa.gov.au/government/announcements/be-aware-of-the-signs-of-stressed-ceiling)).

If you see these signs, keep people out from under the area and have a ceiling fixer or builder brace and inspect it. Common causes include failed adhesive or fixings, loads stored or installed in the roof space, people walking on ceiling joists, and moisture from leaks or exhaust fans venting into the roof. [The regulator's guide](https://www.wa.gov.au/system/files/2025-11/2510337_spontaneous_ceiling_collapse.pdf) advises against storing items in the roof space and recommends that exhaust fans discharge outside.

**Ceiling types and what to watch**

| Type | Where you find it | What to watch |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Lath and plaster | Many pre-war homes | Plaster can lose its grip on the timber laths and sag or drop in sections; cracks and bulges matter |
| Fibrous plaster sheets | Many homes from the early twentieth century to the post-war decades | Sagging where fixings have weakened; ornate cornices and roses can be heavy |
| Plasterboard | Most homes from the post-war decades onward | Nail pops, joint cracks, sagging between joists, water damage |

Hairline cracks along the cornice that open and close with the seasons are common and usually minor; see the [cracks guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/cracks-structural-or-cosmetic#patterns). Water stains on a ceiling point upward to the roof or a bathroom; see [roofs](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/roofs-tiles-metal-and-leaks) and [leaking showers](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/bathroom-waterproofing-and-leaking-showers).

sections.heading: Walls
sections.markdown: Internal walls are usually plaster on masonry in older homes and plasterboard on a frame in newer ones. Cracks from the corners of doors and windows often reflect movement in the structure or footings, and are worth reading as a pattern in the [cracks guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/cracks-structural-or-cosmetic). Nail pops and joint cracks in plasterboard are common and usually cosmetic. Plaster that sounds hollow or crumbles, or stains low on walls, points to damp; see [damp and moisture](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/damp-and-moisture-in-your-home). Older wall sheeting, especially in wet areas, may contain asbestos; see [asbestos in the home](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/asbestos-in-the-home).

sections.heading: Floors
sections.markdown:
**Timber floor signs and what they usually mean**

| Sign | Usual cause | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Squeaks and creaks | Boards moving against fixings or each other | Re-fix the boards; usually minor |
| Bounce or springiness | Decayed, undersized or poorly supported joists or bearers | Check the [subfloor](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/subfloors-stumps-and-restumping) |
| Sloping or uneven floor | Settled or failed stumps, or footing movement | [Subfloors and restumping](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/subfloors-stumps-and-restumping) |
| Cupping (edges higher than centre) | Moisture from below, such as a damp subfloor or a leak | Find the moisture before sanding or replacing |
| Gaps that widen in winter | Seasonal shrinkage, often worse with heating | Usually normal; avoid filling gaps rigidly |
| Soft or crumbling boards | Decay or termite damage | [Termites](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/termites-in-australian-homes) and a timber pest inspection |

Under carpet or floating floors, the structural floor is hidden; lift a corner where it is easy, or check the subfloor. Older vinyl tiles and the backing of sheet vinyl may contain asbestos, so test before lifting old floor coverings; see [asbestos in the home](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/asbestos-in-the-home).

### Tiles

A hollow (drummy) sound means the tile has lost its bond; a few at edges is common, but widespread hollow tiles, cracked tiles or tiles that lift suggest movement in the floor below, failed adhesive or water underneath. sections.heading: Doors
sections.markdown: A door that sticks only in wet or humid weather is often seasonal swelling, and may need little more than adjustment. A door that sticks or swings in all seasons, has an uneven gap at the top, or sits in a frame that is visibly out of square suggests movement in the wall, floor or footings. sections.heading: A room-by-room walk
sections.markdown:
**What to check in each room**

| Room | What to look for |
| --- | --- |
| Entry and hallways | Floor level and bounce, cracks from door corners, doors that stick or swing |
| Living areas | Ceiling sags or nail pops, cornice cracks, floor slope, signs of past patching |
| Kitchen | Swollen cabinet bases and kickboards, damp under the sink, loose or drummy floor tiles |
| Bathroom and laundry | Swollen skirting and door frames, drummy tiles, mould, damage in rooms that share a wall; see the [waterproofing guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/bathroom-waterproofing-and-leaking-showers) |
| Bedrooms | Mould behind wardrobes and on external walls, condensation on windows, cracks |

sections.heading: Signs of past repairs, and what to ask
sections.markdown:
Past repairs are normal in any house, but they are worth reading. Fresh paint over one patch of ceiling, a section of cornice that does not match the rest, plaster that sounds different when tapped, patched floorboards or a few new tiles in an old floor all tell a story. That story might be an old leak that was fixed properly, or a recurring problem that has been covered up.

**Repair clues and the question to ask**

| What you see | Question to ask |
| --- | --- |
| Fresh paint on one area of ceiling | Was there a leak above, what caused it and was the cause fixed? |
| Mismatched cornice or new plaster in one room | Was a wall removed or a crack repaired, and is there a permit or invoice? |
| Patched or replaced floorboards | Was there decay, termites or a plumbing leak below? |
| A few new tiles among old ones | Were tiles drummy or cracked, and did the cause get fixed? |
| Filled cracks that have reopened | Is the movement ongoing, and has anyone assessed it? |

Ask for invoices, reports and dates, and keep what you are given in your [home record](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/keeping-a-record-of-your-home). A repair with a clear cause and paperwork is reassuring; a cosmetic patch with no explanation is a question for the inspector.

sections.heading: Lead paint inside older homes
sections.markdown: Paint applied before 1970 may contain lead, and older homes often have it under newer layers on walls, ceilings, doors, skirting and window frames. Intact paint is low risk, but sanding, scraping or heat-stripping it creates lead dust that is especially harmful to children and pregnant women. Test before any preparation, and use a painter who works lead-safe if lead is present. The [outside walls guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/outside-walls-windows-render-and-cladding) links to the national lead paint guide.

sections.heading: Kitchens and cupboards
sections.markdown: Kitchens hide slow leaks. Swollen or peeling cabinet bases, a soft floor in front of the sink or dishwasher, a musty smell inside cupboards and staining on the kickboards all point to water. Check flexible hoses and connections under the sink, the dishwasher and fridge connections, and the seal between the benchtop and the splashback. sections.heading: Common misreads
sections.markdown:
**Things often said about interiors**

| What people say | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| "A sagging ceiling is just cosmetic" | Sagging sheets or cornices, cracking sounds and lines of nail pops can precede a collapse. Act promptly. |

faqs.question: What should I check inside a house before buying?
faqs.answer: Ceilings for sagging and nail pops, walls for cracks from door and window corners, floors for slope and bounce, tiles for hollow sounds, doors for sticking, and wet areas and cupboards for signs of leaks. Look behind furniture and inside wardrobes where you can.

faqs.question: Is fresh paint on a ceiling a red flag?

faqs.question: Why are my kitchen cabinets swelling at the base?
faqs.answer: Usually water from a leak under the sink, the dishwasher or the fridge connection, or from mopping. Check the connections and do a water meter test for hidden leaks.

faqs.question: Are hollow-sounding floor tiles a problem?
faqs.answer: A few hollow tiles at edges are common. Widespread hollow, cracked or lifting tiles suggest movement in the floor or a failed bed, and are worth having checked.

faqs.question: What are the warning signs that a ceiling may collapse?

faqs.question: Are cornice cracks serious?

faqs.question: What does cupping in timber floorboards mean?
faqs.answer: Board edges sitting higher than their centres usually means moisture is reaching the boards from below. The cause is often under the floor, such as poor subfloor ventilation, drainage or a plumbing leak, so check there before sanding or replacing boards. The subfloors guide explains what to look for.

faqs.question: Why is my timber floor bouncy?
faqs.answer: Usually because joists or bearers beneath are decayed, undersized or poorly supported. Have the subfloor inspected.

faqs.question: What does a hollow sound from floor tiles mean?
faqs.answer: The tiles have lost their bond. A few at the edges is common; widespread hollow, cracked or lifting tiles suggest movement, failed adhesive or water below, and in a bathroom can signal a leaking shower.

The cause is often under the floor, such as poor subfloor ventilation, drainage or a plumbing leak, so check there before sanding or replacing boards. The subfloors guide explains what to look for.

### Why is my timber floor bouncy?
Usually because joists or bearers beneath are decayed, undersized or poorly supported. Have the subfloor inspected.

### What does a hollow sound from floor tiles mean?
The tiles have lost their bond. A few at the edges is common; widespread hollow, cracked or lifting tiles suggest movement, failed adhesive or water below, and in a bathroom can signal a leaking shower.

### Why does my door stick?
If only in wet weather, usually seasonal swelling. If it sticks all year, swings open or sits in a frame out of square, look for movement in the walls, floor or footings.

### Can I store things in the roof space?
It is best not to. Ceilings are not designed to carry stored loads, and regulators warn that roof-space storage can stress the ceiling below.

## Method
We walk the interior by element, start from what owners notice, separate cosmetic wear from signs of movement, moisture or overload, and flag the ceiling signs that need prompt action, with a fictional example.

## Limitations
Interior signs often point to causes elsewhere in the building; confirmation may need subfloor, roof-space or specialist inspection.
